member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Angle
member.summary:
Represents an angle as a single value that can be read as either radians or degrees.
The value is stored in radians because every angular API built on this type works in radians: GeoVector2.GetAngleTo and GeoRectangle2.AngleRad in the plane, GeoVector3.GetAngleTo and GeoTransform3.RotationX in space, and Tolerance.EqualAngleRad in both. Degrees are a view over that value, converted on read.
There is deliberately no public constructor taking a bare double. The reason this type exists is that a number on its own does not say which unit it is in, so the unit has to be named at the point of creation: use or .

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeItem.Rectangle
member.summary: Gets or sets the rectangle of the object the label belongs to, to stand along its long side; null, and so the is used, unless set.

remarks.para: A rectangle takes the place of the leader: the candidate positions spread out from its centre, in rows on either side of its long side, each sliding along it. The gaps , and are measured from the long edges, not from a line through the middle: a rectangle 2 000 long and 300 across, a label 100 high and the default gap of 50 put the first row 250 above the middle line, 100 above the edge. The top and the bottom are the two long edges, the top the one that faces up in the drawing, as for a leader; a rectangle whose long side is vertical has its top on the left. keeps the label to one of them.

The long side is the width, or the height where that is greater; of a square, the width. The rectangle may be turned by any angle. A rectangle with no long side, within the point tolerance of the options, cannot be arranged along, and the label is left where it is. With both a rectangle and a set, the rectangle is used and the leader is ignored.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeItem.Offset
member.summary:
Sets the least gap between the edge of the label and the leader on both sides of it at once: and both take the value. It only sets, and holds nothing of its own, so it cannot be read; the sides are what placement reads.
The gaps belong to the label rather than to because labels differ: a large text may have to stand further off than a small one.
member.remarks: Setting it overwrites both sides, whatever they held. To give a side a gap of its own as well, set that side after it: new ArrangeItem { Offset = 50.0, OffsetTop = 20.0 } stands 20 off above and 50 below, where new ArrangeItem { OffsetTop = 20.0, Offset = 50.0 } stands 50 off on both sides.
member.exception: The value is NaN or infinite; neither side is changed.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeItem.OffsetTop
member.summary: Gets or sets the least gap between the edge of the label and the leader on the side of the leader that faces up in the drawing, towards greater Y; 50 unless set, here or through . The first row of candidates on that side lies half the height of the label plus this from the leader.
member.remarks: Which side faces up does not depend on which way the leader runs: one drawn from right to left has the same top as one drawn from left to right. A vertical leader, to within the angle of the options' , has its top on the left, towards smaller X, where the text of a vertical dimension stands.

member.summary: Labels smaller than this size will be considered invalid/erroneous and ignored.

Measured along its leader and across it from its corners, as they round where the scene lies, it may come to a hair less, and counts as large enough to within the point tolerance of : a label 20 by 10 turned along its leader, at the default 10, is arranged wherever it lies.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeOptions.MaximumCandidates

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeOptions.PlaceMostConstrainedFirst
member.summary: Sorts placement order so that the most constrained label (fewest options) is placed first. Recommended as the greedy algorithm has no backtracking mechanism. Set to false to sort purely by default geometric order.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeOptions.FreedomSampleSize
member.summary: Number of candidates evaluated when measuring label freedom degree, serving the option.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeOptions.LookAheadCandidates
member.summary: Number of empty positions evaluated before selection. Among these candidates, the position with the maximum clearance wins. Set to 1 to select the first found empty position immediately.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeOptions.PlaceFromInsideOut
member.summary: Sorts labels from the inside out (from area centroid to boundary). Helps labels in crowded center regions get priority placement.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeOptions.Tolerance
member.summary: Tolerance used for geometric calculations and intersection checks: as it stands when the options are made, unless set.
member.remarks:
A place that comes within the point tolerance of a region, a line or another label collides with it, though their boxes do not overlap: at a tolerance of a thousandth, a label whose place ends half a thousandth below a line, or below another label, is not put there, and two labels that touch collide wherever the scene lies.
How far a label stands from the centre of them all, or how far along, is counted in whole steps of the point tolerance, and labels on the same step are placed in the order they were given; a label as large as is arranged however its corners round. So a scene moved elsewhere is arranged as it was, moved, but where something falls within rounding of an edge drawn exactly: two lengths within rounding of half a step can round to different steps, and a block within rounding of the edge of a label's reach is weighed or not as its coordinates round. A label 20 by 10 on a leader from (0, 0) to (100, 0), 5 off it, with a block line from (185, -5) to (185, 5), goes to (-3.25, 10) at the origin and to (0, 10) at 2 of 20 000 places a thousand to ten million off it.
Of the free places a label is weighed at, the most open wins, and clearances up to the point tolerance count as nought, so two places 0.0004 and 0.0007 off what they keep clear of are as open at a tolerance of a thousandth, and the one tried first wins. Clearances beyond it that differ by no more than a thousandth of it are as open too: places 0.5 and 0.50000001 clear at a thousandth. A run reads this tolerance throughout, never as it stands at the time.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Arranging.Arranger
member.summary: Places labels so that they overlap neither one another nor what they have to keep clear of.

remarks.para: Every label is tried at the same candidate positions around its leader, those lists, and the labels are placed greedily, one after another and never taken up again: by default those with the fewest free places first, and of two with as few the one nearer the middle of them all, each at the most open of its first few free places, and each kept clear of by every label after it.

A run goes over the labels twice. The first pass places every label under every constraint. The labels it leaves overlapping something are tried once more with the block lines lifted, keeping clear of the labels the first pass placed. Whether each label is placed is then judged on the final layout as a whole.
The items are only read, and a result comes back for each, in the order the items were given.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Arranging.Arranger.Judge(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeItem},GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector2[],GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeOptions)
member.summary:
Judges, on the final layout, whether each label overlaps nothing.
A pass only knows the layout at the moment it places a label, so what it knows means "this spot was clear when my turn came". A label placed later, when stuck, may fall back onto one placed earlier, which would still believe itself clear. What the caller needs to know is whether the final layout has overlaps, so that is judged here, after every label has settled.
member.returns: For each item, whether it is placed; false for a null entry.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Arranging.Obstacle.CollectStatic(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GeometryHelper.Arranging.ArrangeItem})
member.summary:
Collects and deduplicates static obstacles from the given list of labels.
Duplicate obstacles are deduplicated to retain only a single instance. A common library usage pattern is to assign the same set of blocked regions to every label — e.g., each label avoids all other path segments — causing the list to grow quadratically with the number of labels, even though the number of distinct geometries remains small. Deduplication here benefits both passes and the final judgement alike.
member.param: The labels; a null entry is passed over.
member.returns: A list of deduplicated obstacles.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Arranging.ObstacleSpatialIndex
member.summary: The obstacles a run keeps clear of, held so that those whose boxes overlap a region are found without going over every one: a tree of boxes, each branch the box around those below it, taken in one obstacle at a time.

remarks.para: What a query finds is what going over every obstacle in the order it was added, and keeping each whose box the region overlaps, , finds: the same obstacles, in that order. Each is tested with that very call, and the tree only passes over branches none of whose obstacles could pass it. A branch box is made from the boxes below it by , which takes each side as it is, so it holds them exactly, and a region overlapping a box overlaps any box holding it: each of the four comparisons of the overlap only grows easier to meet. That holds for a region turned inside out by a negative margin as well.

An obstacle whose box has a side that is not a number overlaps nothing, as every comparison with it fails, and is kept out of the tree. The others go in where they enlarge the boxes on the way least, and the tree is kept balanced as it grows, the two children of a branch never more than one level apart in height, so that its depth grows with the logarithm of the count whatever the sizes, regions as large as the sheet beside labels 20 wide, and whatever the order the obstacles come in: 10 000 boxes added one after another along a line, the worst order for a tree left unbalanced, stand 15 levels deep, and 10 000 lines from a millionth to ten times the sheet long, 17.
Which obstacles come back never follows the shape of the tree: each is numbered in the order it was added, and those found are put back in that order.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Clash.Clash3
member.summary: Checking many parts against each other at once: which run into each other, which touch, and which come nearer than a clearance.

remarks.para: The check asks, of every pair, the questions a clash report is made of, cheapest first. Every part is prepared once — its openings cut, its surface indexed — and the boxes are swept along one axis so that only pairs whose boxes come within the clearance of each other are looked at, which in a model is a small share of all the pairs. Those are checked in parallel: the surfaces through their indexes, then, for a pair that touches, the volume the two share, one body per region, and where there is none, the patches where they lie against each other.

Openings are honoured throughout: a bolt through its hole is no clash. The results come back in the order of the pairs' indexes, whatever order the threads finished in. A pair whose check throws is reported as , with the error, and logged, so that one part the library cannot read does not cost the report for the rest of the model.

Reinforcement can be checked without building its bodies: a is a centre line and a radius, and a bar runs into a part where the part comes nearer its centre line than the radius. The two ways stand side by side; see .

remarks.para: A bar runs into a part where its centre line runs inside the part, or comes nearer the part's surface than the radius; it touches where it comes exactly the radius away, and comes too near where it comes within the clearance of that. Openings are honoured, as for bodies: a bar through a hole it clears is no clash.

What a clash between bodies measures as a volume, a bar measures as a depth and a length: how far the part reaches into the bar () and how much of the centre line runs inside it (), lying along a face within the tolerance of it counting as inside, and so does every other stretch within the tolerance of the surface, but the short one beside a crossing of a face at a slant steeper than about 6 degrees. No body is built, so is empty and nought, and does not apply; does. The gap of a bar too near a part runs from the bar's surface.
The ends are read rounded (see ), so right at an end a part up to a radius beyond it is found to clash.

member.remarks: Sorted by their low coordinate along that axis, a box can only meet the boxes still open when it starts — those whose high coordinate has not been passed — so each is compared with a handful rather than with every other. member.summary: Checks one pair, the same whichever of the two is listed first.
member.remarks: The boolean, the contact and the walk of the two indexes each work from one body towards the other, and the last digits of what they give follow which body that was, and so do the loops of the faces of the overlaps and the patches of contact. So does the depth, which is the smallest side of the least box fitted round the corners of the region the two share: cut from one body by the other it lists other corners than cut the other way, and where several boxes tie for the least volume, as a skewed block of three pairs of parallel faces gives one for each pair, which of them is taken, and so which side is the smallest, follows the rounding of their volumes. Of 359 random pairs, 11 to 23 had depths over a millionth apart that way. (A depth 20.126 one way and 24.003 the other was a different fault, in the hull the box is fitted to, fixed in .) So the pair is always measured with the body that sorts first as the first, and a result that names a side, the patches of contact and the gap, is turned back to the side it was asked for.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Clash.Clash3.Compare(GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoPreparedSolid3,GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoPreparedSolid3)
member.summary: Puts two bodies in an order that depends on what they are and nothing else: their boxes, then their faces.
member.remarks: The numbers are compared as the bits they are, not within a tolerance. The order is only there to pick one of the two to measure from, and a tolerance would make the pick depend on which of two near-equal bodies was listed first, which is what it is there to prevent. Two bodies of one box and one set of faces tie, and either is then measured from. What preparing a body within another tolerance can change is whether it is judged convex and how its surface is meshed; a body and its copy share all of their volume, so the pair is a hard clash settled by the boolean of the two materials; convexity is read by the convex shortcut only when both are convex, and by the parting test for each body in turn, so neither depends on which is first. A body notched 0.005 across its top, prepared within 1E-3 and within 1E-2, is the same either way round.

member.summary: A round bar to check for clashes by its centre line and its radius, without building its body.

remarks.para: Checked as a body, a bar is the body builds: a polygon swept along the centre line, a few hundred faces for a bar with two bends, lying a chord tolerance inside the round bar it stands for, and a boolean for every part it runs into. Checked by its centre line, a bar runs into a part where the part comes nearer the centre line than the radius: found exactly on the straight runs and within the chord tolerance on the bends, and measured by how deep the part reaches into the bar () and how much of the centre line runs inside it () instead of by a volume, with nothing built.

The ends are read rounded. A ball rolled along the centre line reaches a radius past each end, where a real bar ends flat, so right at an end a part up to a radius beyond it is found to clash: the check errs on the side of reporting.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Clash.ClashResult.Depth
member.summary: Gets how deep the two run into each other, for a clash; nought otherwise.

remarks.para: For two bodies it is the least thickness of the region they share, the smallest side of the least box round it (), and of the deepest region where they share more than one: a bar grazing a flange by half a millimetre is half a millimetre deep however long the graze, and a bar through a plate as deep as the thinner of the two. Of boxes as small standing on faces of the hull of a region, the thinnest is read: a block 18 by 24 by 40 meeting a prism on its corner's triangle is 14.4 deep. For a region of no simple shape it is an estimate, a close one.

For a bar checked by its centre line () it is how far the part reaches into the bar, across it. Where the centre line stays outside the part it is the radius less the centre line's nearest approach, exactly. Where the centre line runs inside, it is the radius and as far again as the centre line runs beneath the part's surface, at most the diameter, measured at points an eighth of a radius apart and so to within a sixteenth of the radius (on a stretch inside over 512 radii long, the points are spread wider). A plate thinner than the bar that the bar passes through is the radius and half the plate deep, where two bodies read the least thickness of what they share, the plate's own: however thin, the plate cuts the bar through.
A clash reported as touching for being shallower than or smaller than keeps the depth it was found with.

So does one coming off a face, or crossing one at a slant shallower than about 6 degrees, for as long as it stays within the tolerance of the face, each stretch within it counted however often it leaves the tolerance and comes back: 125 for a bar from 0.0007 over the top of a box at 250 before its edge to 0.0015 over it 1 000 along. member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc2
member.summary:
What can be asked of an arc: where a point falls on it, how far a shape is from it, and where it meets a segment, a circle or another arc.
An arc is part of a circle, so every answer here is the circle's answer kept only where the arc actually reaches. A crossing beyond the ends of the arc belongs to the circle, not to the arc, and is left out; a point off the ends is measured to whichever end is nearer.
What an arc and a ray in the plane ask each other.
member.remarks: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so against an arc it is cut: into the segment from its origin out past the farthest the arc's circle reaches along it, the centre brought onto the ray and the radius added, by a margin of a millimetre or a hundred point tolerances, whichever is more. Every point of the arc lies behind that end, so the segment meets the arc where the ray does and is asked as any segment is. Against an arc of radius 50 round the origin, the ray from (-100, 0) along X is asked as the segment from there to (51, 0).

member.summary: Gets the point of an arc closest to a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.
member.param: The point; it does not have to lie on the arc.
member.returns: The point of the arc closest to the given point, which is one of its ends when the point falls beyond them.

The arc of radius 50 from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, 50) is 49.9991 from (0, -0.0009), at a tolerance of a thousandth. The projection keeps that snap.

member.summary: Gets the distance between an arc and a segment, within a tolerance.
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.
member.remarks: The nearest pair is either at an end of one of them, or where the segment runs straight at the centre of the arc. Both are checked, so the answer is exact rather than sampled. A segment ending 0.0005 above the top of the arc of radius 50 about the origin is 0.0005 from it, whatever the tolerance; the tolerance only reads a segment no longer than itself as its start point, and an arc bowing less than its own rounding as its chord. The place facing the centre counts however near the centre the segment passes: at a hundredth, the half circle of radius 0.004 below the origin is 0.004 from the segment along y = -0.008, not the 0.008 of its ends.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc2.TryIntersectWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Finds where an arc meets a segment, within a tolerance.
member.param: The crossings, empty when there are none.
member.returns: true if they meet at least once; otherwise, false.
member.remarks:
The circle carrying the arc may be met where the arc itself does not reach, and those crossings are left out. A segment that meets the arc nowhere so still touches it where it comes within the point tolerance of it, exactly where says they collide: once, at the foot of the perpendicular from the centre when its line runs inside the rim within the tolerance of it, the foot is on the segment and the arc holds it, else at the point of the segment nearest the arc. At a tolerance of 0.001, a segment ending 0.0002 from the end of an arc, its line 0.0002 inside the rim, touches the arc at that end of the segment; and the arc of radius 50 about (0, 50.0002) starting 0.0045 radians past its bottom, at (0.2249992, 0.0007062), touches the segment along the x axis below that start, though its circle passes the segment where the arc does not reach.
A segment or an arc with a coordinate or an angle that is not a finite number meets nothing, and the answer is false: the arc from (200, 0) to (NaN, 0) threw "A radius has to be a number".

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3
member.summary: Where an arc in space crosses the surface of a box or a body, and whether it touches one.

remarks.para: The surface of a box or a body is flat faces, so this is the union of what the arc does against each of them, with the shared edges counted once. Nothing new is worked out here.

A pierced body needs the same care its signed distance needs. Its boundary is its own faces and the walls of every opening, openings of openings included, so the walk gathers candidates from all of them and then keeps only the ones the body itself calls — which throws out a point on an outer face where an opening has taken the material away.

Touching is not the same as crossing here, because a body has an inside. An arc wholly within the material crosses no face and touches all the same, so where it starts is asked as well. An arc wholly within an opening is not in the material, and that same question rules it out.

member.summary: Where a circle in space crosses a plane, a segment or a ray, and whether it touches one.
member.remarks: A circle is an arc that sweeps a whole turn, which takes as equal start and end angles, so every pair here hands the work to the arc rather than working it out a second time. Nothing is lost: a whole turn reaches every point of its circle, so the sweep test the arc applies never rejects anything.
member.summary: Where an arc in space crosses a plane, a segment or a ray, and whether it touches one.

remarks.para: None of this is sampled. An arc in space lies in a plane, and every flat-faced shape in the library is made of planes, so every crossing has a closed form and there are never more than two of them per plane. Two readings do all the work.
Coplanar. Where the other shape shares the arc's plane, both go down into that plane through and the whole of answers, which is code already worn in.

Not coplanar. Two distinct planes meet in a line, and every point the arc shares with anything lying in the other plane must be on that line. A line meets a circle in at most two points, so the candidates are found by solving one quadratic and are then handed to whatever test the other shape brings. No iteration, and no tolerance bargain.

Distance is the one thing not offered. The distance from an arc in space to anything but a point has no closed form — a segment wants a quartic — and ToPolyline3(chordTolerance) remains the way to ask for it, erring on the safe side because a sampled chain lies inside the arcs it stands for.

member.summary: Where two curves in space cross each other, and whether they touch.

remarks.para: Both cases come down to a line, which is why they share .
Not coplanar. The two planes meet in a line and anything common to both curves is on it.

Coplanar. Two circles in one plane meet on their radical line, which is square to the line joining their centres and at (d² + r₁² - r₂²) / 2d along it. Every point of one circle on that line is on the other as well, so the candidates come out of the same quadratic as everywhere else and no projection into the plane is needed.

Two arcs of one circle are the case that is not about points at all. Concentric circles of equal radius lie on each other and share a whole stretch, so there is nothing to name as a crossing; whether they touch is settled by asking whether either holds an end of the other, which is where an overlap begins and ends. reaches the same answer the same way in the plane.

member.summary: Where an arc in space crosses a flat region, and whether it touches one.

remarks.para: A flat region has a plane and a boundary, and which of the two the answer comes from depends on how the arc lies.

Not coplanar. The arc meets the region's plane in at most two points, and each of those counts only if the region holds it. That is a crossing of the region's material, and it is the case a bar leaving a plate is.

Coplanar. The arc runs in the plane of the region, so it crosses nothing by piercing it and the answer is where it cuts the boundary — the outline, and for a face the rim of every hole. An arc lying wholly within the material crosses nothing and still touches, which is the one place the two questions part, as it is for a plane.

member.summary: Cutting an arc in space in two.
member.remarks: An arc in the plane could be cut at a parameter or at a point and an arc in space could not, though a whole chain of them could be. Nothing new is worked out: the centre, the radius and the plane all stay, only the sweep is shared out between the two pieces, so the pieces put back end to end draw exactly what went in.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.IsCoplanar(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether a plane is the very plane the arc lies in.
member.remarks: Being parallel is not enough: two parallel planes a metre apart share nothing. The arc's centre has to lie in the other plane as well, and that is what separates the one case where the whole arc is in the plane from the case where it merely runs alongside.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.TryBulgeThrough(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,System.Double@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3@)
member.summary: Gets the bulge and the normal of the arc from a start through a point to an end, read from its chord.
member.param: From the start to the end.
From the start to a point of the arc between its ends.
The bulge, positive: the arc runs counter-clockwise round the normal.
The unit normal of its plane.
member.returns: false when the three points lie on one line to the last digit, so no arc runs through them.
member.remarks: Nothing is measured from the centre: the sag is worked out across the chord, so an arc 100 long bowing a trillionth, of radius 2.5E13, comes out as exactly as a half circle. The point need not be the arc's middle: an arc stretched unevenly is answered with the arc through where its ends and its middle land.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.LiesIn(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether an arc between two points lies in a plane: whether no point of it stands further off the plane than the planar tolerance.
member.param: Its bulge; nought for a straight piece.
The unit normal of the plane it bulges in.
The tolerance; its planar threshold decides.
member.remarks: Its normal against the plane's says nothing on its own: a half circle 1 000 across turned 0.99 degrees out of the plane stands 8.64 off it, and an arc 100 long bowing a ten-millionth turned 30 degrees stands 0.0000025 off. See .

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.StandOff(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3)
member.summary: Gets how far an arc between two points may stand off a plane: no less than any point of it does.
member.param: Its bulge; nought for a straight piece.
The unit normal of the plane it bulges in.
member.returns: The greatest distance from the plane of a corner of the box the arc lies in, never below the arc's own.
member.remarks: It is read from the chord rather than the centre, so an arc 100 long bowing a trillionth, of radius 2.5E13, is read as exactly as a half circle, where its centre is known only to about 0.005. An arc of up to a half turn lies in the box between its chord and the line beside it through its middle, its sag of half the chord times the bulge away on the side it bows to; a longer one runs on past the ends of its chord, by up to its radius from the chord's middle either way. The distance from a plane changes evenly across the box, so its greatest is at a corner: an arc whose ends stand 0.0004 above the plane and which bows down across it to 0.0004 below stands 0.0004 off, not the 0.0008 of its ends and its dip added up.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.StandOff(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3)
member.summary: Gets how far an arc in space may stand off a plane: no less than any point of it does.
member.returns: The distance.
member.remarks: Up to a half turn it is read from the chord, as . Past a half turn the chord may be lost to rounding, its two ends one point to the last digit an arc a hair short of a whole turn, while the centre is well known: the distance is read round the circle, at the arc's ends and wherever between them the rim stands furthest up or down.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.PointsOnLine(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the points of the arc that lie on an endless line, which is at most two.
member.param: The direction of the line; it need not be a unit vector.
member.returns: The points shared by the arc and the line, in order along the line.
member.remarks: The line is read as endless, so a caller holding a segment or a ray has to say afterwards which of the answers its own shape reaches. Solving |origin + t*direction - centre|² = radius² finds every point of the arc's circle on the line; then keeps the ones the arc actually sweeps, which is also what rules out a line that lies in a parallel plane rather than the arc's own.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.PointsOnPlane(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the points of the arc on the line where its own plane meets another plane.
member.remarks: The workhorse of every not-coplanar pair. Where the two planes are parallel and apart there is no line and nothing to find; where they are the same plane the caller has to handle that itself, because what to do then depends on the shape, not on the arc. The line is found from the arc's own centre rather than from the planes' distances to the world origin: two circles 30 000 out along each axis, in planes a thousandth of a degree apart, lost both their crossings to the rounding of that distance.

member.remarks: Two faces of a body share an edge, so an arc crossing that edge is found twice. The answer has to name the place once.

member.summary: Adds a point to a list unless a point already there stands in the same place, and where the one there is the point of a touch and this one a crossing, puts the crossing in its place.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets every point where an arc crosses a segment, within a tolerance.
member.returns: At most two points, and only ones the segment itself reaches: the arithmetic reads the segment as the endless line carrying it and then keeps what lies between its ends. Where the two only touch, as reads a touch, without a crossing, the point of the arc nearest the segment: the segment from (0, 50.0006, 1) to (0, 50.0006, -1), through the plane of the arc of radius 50 about the origin 0.0006 beside its rim, touches it at (0, 50, 0). A point of the circle on the segment's line, held by the arc and by the segment each within the point tolerance, is given only where the segment, at its point nearest it, comes within the point tolerance of the arc, each point on its own: the segment from (0, 0, 0.0008) to (49.9992, 0, 0.0008) ends 0.00113 from that arc and is given nothing, where it was given (50, 0, 0.0008) and collided with nothing, and the one from (-60, 0, 0.0006) to (49.9994, 0, 0.0006), ending 0.000849 from it, touches it at both rims. A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly cross the arc: it is given its start where that lies within the point tolerance of the arc, and nothing where it does not. A longer one crosses where it does however short: at a millionth, the segment from (0, 9.9999995, 0) to (0, 10.0000015, 0) meets the arc of radius 10 about the origin at (0, 10, 0), as it does a hundred times larger, where, shorter than the vector tolerance of 1E-5 read as a length, it was given its start.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether an arc touches a segment, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Neither has an inside, so they touch where the exact gap between them is no more than the point tolerance, in space and in whatever plane they lie: the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (50, 0, 0) a quarter turn counter-clockwise touches the segment from (50.0005, 0, 0) to (80, 0, 0), 0.0005 off its start, and not the one from (50.0015, 0, 0), and the one from (20, 40, 0.0003) to (40, 40, 0.0003), hovering 0.0003 over the arc where it crosses (30, 40), touches it. A segment no longer than the tolerance is read as its start unless it truly meets the arc.

member.returns: The points the two share, the same to the last digit whichever is asked first, in order along a line: in one plane the line square to the one between the centres, otherwise the line the two planes share. remarks.para: Two arcs in one plane are crossed from the smaller circle, so a nearly flat arc keeps its crossings whichever is asked first: the edge 100 long of bulge 1E-7 from (0, 0, 0) to (100, 0, 0), an arc of radius 2.5E8, crosses the arc of radius 40 about (50, 30, 0) sweeping 1.6 radians at (23.54249, 0, 0) either way round.

Each arc is read against the other, and a place both readings name is given once, as the first names it: the first reading is that of the arc lying within the planar tolerance of the other's plane, or, where both or neither do, of the one that comes first by centre, radius, normal and angles. Where the two pass within the point tolerance of each other and no reading names a place there, as reads a touch, the middle of the shortest line between them is the place: the arc of radius 100 about the origin in the plan and an arc of radius 50 leaning 0.01 radians, the end of its diameter along X 0.0005 above (0, 100, 0) and running square to the first there, touch at (0, 100, 0.00025). Read from the arc asked first alone, 37 of 4 000 pairs tilted 1E-7 to 1E-3 radians off each other gave a different number of places the one way round and the other, and 356 collided and were given none.

Two circles whose centres stand further apart than the point tolerance are crossed however near the centres are: at a millionth, the arcs of radius 10 about the origin and of radius 9.999999 about (0.000002, 0, 0) cross at (5.0000007, ±8.6602536, 0), as they do a hundred times larger, where the line they share, as long as the centres are apart and so shorter than the vector tolerance of 1E-5 read as a length, was taken for no line at all and one of the crossings was lost. The line is laid in the plane of the circles: two of radius 39.7 in a plane leaning every way, about centres 1.4E-7 apart, cross twice on both at a ten-millionth, where the line, carried 14 along the difference of the centres, leant out of the plane by its rounding and the crossings lay up to 1.4E-7 off both.

member.summary: Cuts an arc at a normalized parameter, within a tolerance.

The tolerance: a cut within it of either end leaves the arc whole.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Arc3.TrySplitAt(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts an arc at the point of it nearest a point, within a tolerance.
member.param: Where to cut it; a point off the arc cuts at the point of the arc nearest it.
The pieces in order along the arc, or the arc whole when the method returns false.
member.returns: true when the arc was cut in two; otherwise, false.
member.remarks:
A point off the arc is answered by the place of the arc nearest it, the same way the plane answers, and a point off the plane by what stands under it: only the direction from the centre decides.
A point on the arc, within the tolerance of it, cuts it where its distance to the arc is measured to, found at no tolerance, so a point on a small arc near its centre is not carried to the start, which left the arc whole: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the half circle of radius 0.001 about the origin in the plan, from (0.001, 0, 0) through (0, 0.001, 0) to (-0.001, 0, 0), is cut by (0, 0.0007, 0) at (0, 0.001, 0). A point off the arc whose foot falls within the tolerance of the centre is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and leaves the arc whole, as it did: the half circle of radius 50 from (50, 0, 0) through (0, 50, 0) to (-50, 0, 0) is not cut by (0.0005, 0.0003, 0), 50 from it, whose direction from the centre is no surer than the tolerance.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcChain2
member.summary:
The walking a chain that may curve needs, shared by every operation over one.
Everything here measures along the arcs rather than across them, so a chain of arcs answers the same questions a straight one does and answers them exactly. Only the region operations, which go through Clipper, need the chain flattened first.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcChain2.Encloses(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Determines whether a loop that may curve encloses a point, not counting its boundary.
member.remarks:
Walking the arcs rather than the chords adds the piece each arc cuts off its chord where the arc bulges outward, and takes it away where the arc bulges inward. So the answer is the straight loop through the vertices, turned inside out once for every such piece the point lies in. It is exact: no arc is approximated anywhere in it.
No tolerance is read here: a point within the tolerance of the true boundary is on it, and is settled before this is asked. A chord is not the boundary, so the straight loop and each piece read the side of a chord by one exact rule, , and agree on every point near it. A point exactly on a chord counts as lying a hair towards +X of it, or a hair towards +Y of a chord that runs along X.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcChain3
member.summary: Where one chain in space crosses another, and whether two chains touch.

remarks.para: What makes it worth offering is that the work per pair is decided before any arithmetic is done: each edge carries a box round itself, and a pair whose boxes do not overlap is dropped without being solved. Bars in a model are mostly far apart, so the pairs that survive are the few that could possibly meet. The boxes of the second chain are worked out once and kept, rather than once per edge of the first.

The answer itself is the union of what the edge pairs answer, with each place named once, which is the same reading every other chain question takes. Two edges lying along each other meet along a length and name no place, so CollidesWith is what says they touch — the reading two arcs of one circle get.

member.summary: One chain in space against another: the six pairs the walk over edge pairs answers.
Where a curved chain or loop in space crosses another shape, and whether it touches one.
member.remarks: A chain or loop touches another shape where any one of its edges does, so it touches where the exact gap between them in space is no more than the point tolerance. A loop is its outline and a circle its rim, so a loop round a square 20 by 20 in its plane, 5 off its sides, touches nothing.
member.summary: Where a curved chain or loop in space crosses a segment or a ray.
member.remarks: These two probes were missing from the set, not refused: a bar could be asked about a plane, an arc, a triangle, a polygon, a face, either box and a body, and not about a segment. The reason was one step back — a offers a direction only where a segment and a bend answer with the same shape of call, and a segment's crossing with another segment was offered as one point rather than as a list. With that written out as a list, these follow.
member.summary: Walking a run of edges in space that may curve.
member.remarks: The twin of , and deliberately much smaller. Everything here works on the curve itself — its length, a point along it, the point of it nearest another point — and every one of those is exact, because answers a point in closed form. What is missing is everything that measures a run against another shape, which in space has no closed form once the two are not in one plane.
member.summary: Cutting a curved chain or loop by a box, or by several cutters at once.

remarks.para: A chain could be cut by one body and a could be cut by a box or by a whole array of them, which is what a bar is really asked: not "does this one opening cut you" but "what is left of you once every opening on the drawing has had its say".

Nothing new is worked out. Every cutter is asked where it crosses the chain, all the places are cut at once, and each piece is then filed by where its middle falls — never by an end, because every end is on a surface by construction and a surface belongs to neither side. A piece is inside when it is inside any cutter, so overlapping cutters behave as the one region they cover.
A null cutter inside an array is passed over rather than throwing, as the straight version does: an array gathered from a model has gaps in it, and the caller is asking what cuts, not what exists.

member.summary: Cutting a curved chain in space, and keeping the bends.

remarks.para: This is the question a bar is asked most often and the one it could not answer: a bar stopped at a pour break, or trimmed to the face of a member. can be cut twelve ways; a curved chain could not be cut at all, and turning it into a polyline first to cut it there throws away the thing that makes it a bar.

So the pieces come back as chains of arcs. Cutting an arc gives two arcs of the same radius, which already does, so the pieces put back end to end draw exactly what went in and each piece's length is still a length a bar schedule can use.

A cut landing on a corner of the chain, within the point tolerance of it, breaks it between the two edges rather than inside either, which is why the walk asks about the end of each edge separately: splitting at a parameter of nought or one is refused, and rightly, since it would leave a piece with nothing in it, and so is splitting within the tolerance of an end, which would leave a piece shorter than the tolerance.

member.summary: Where a curved chain in space crosses another shape, and whether it touches one.

remarks.para: A chain is a run of edges and an edge is a straight leg or a bend, so every answer here is the union of what its edges answer, with the shared corners counted once. Nothing new is worked out: the arithmetic is 's, reached through , which reads each edge as whichever of the two it is.
This is the shape a reinforcing bar is, so these are the questions a bar is asked: where it crosses a pour break, whether it hits an embed, where it leaves the concrete.

member.remarks: A segment passing a chain beside the corner where an arc meets a straight leg was given a place on each of them, 0.001 apart at a tolerance of a thousandth, both within it of the corner: one meeting named twice. Places further from the corner are kept however close the two legs run: a segment crossing both legs of a hairpin 0.0009 across, at 50 from its tip, crosses them 0.043 apart, and is given both.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcChain3.Sorted(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3[],System.Func{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,System.Boolean},GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3[]@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3[]@)
member.summary: Files each piece by where its middle falls, joining neighbours that landed on the same side.
member.remarks: The joining is the point. Several cutters name several surfaces, and two of them can sit inside the one region they cover between them — the face where two overlapping openings meet is a surface, and the chain is cut there, but it never leaves the material. Handing those back separately would report three pieces of bar inside one opening. So a run of neighbours on the same side becomes one piece, and what the method returns is whether there was more than one run, which is the same rule Splition3 keeps for a straight chain.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcFillet2
member.summary:
Rounding the corner between two pieces of a chain when either of them curves.
A circle of radius r touching two curves has its centre exactly r from both, which is to say on each of those curves moved sideways by r. So the centre is where the two moved curves cross, and finding it needs nothing but the intersections the library already works out: a line moved sideways is a line, and an arc moved sideways is a circle about the same point.
The arc has to run the way the pieces run and turn the way the corner turns, so its centre lies on the inside of the turn from both of them: each piece is moved towards that side only, never away from it. A circle moved off the other side touches the pieces too, but the arc on it runs back against them and leaves a cusp; at a corner turning 144.5° and a radius of 0.002, the nearest such circle touched the first piece 0.00064 past the corner. Of the crossings left, the one taken has both touching points on the pieces as they stand, neither of them past the corner, so that rounding shortens the pieces rather than stretching them, and of those the one nearest the corner.
A corner that does not turn, by no more than , has no inside and nothing to round. That is the joint where a straight piece runs on into an arc it is tangent to, as along a bent bar, and it is left as it is rather than given an arc of no sweep.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcFillet2.Meet(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2},GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Adds where two circles cross.
member.remarks: Two circles that only touch, outside or inside each other, give no centre, as a line touching a circle gives none: the one point they share lies on the line through their centres, so the arc about it touches the two curved pieces at the ends of one diameter and sweeps half a turn, which never takes. Where they touch is read to the rounding of the numbers they come from, , not to nought: a shade of overlap the rounding leaves gives two centres a root of it apart, their arcs a hair short of half a turn, and these were taken or not as the rounding fell. Two arcs of radii 10 and 7 about centres 12 apart, crossing at (8.125, 5.83), filleted at 2.5, the radius of the circle filling the lens between them from (5, 0) to (10, 0), were rounded by a half circle at that size and left square at a thousandth of it and at a thousand times it.

member.remarks:
A line that only touches the circle, or misses it, gives no centre. The one it would give is the point of the line nearest the circle's centre, square to the line from it, so the arc about it touches the line and the curved piece on that one square: it sweeps half a turn, which never takes. Such a centre was let in where the difference of the squared radius and the squared distance, an area, was within the tolerance, a length, and its arc was then taken or not as the rounding of its sweep fell: the cap of the circle of radius 12 above a chord 4 from its centre, turned by half a radian and moved to (30, 40), filleted where the chord runs into the arc by 4.000025 within 1E-4, a quarter of the tolerance more than the largest circle in it, was left square, and the same cap 1 000 times smaller, within 1E-7, was rounded by a half circle.
Where the line touches is read to the rounding of the numbers, , as for two circles: a line worked out to touch the circle, and passing into it by a shade of rounding, gave two centres a root of that shade apart, and a half circle at one size and none at another. The same cap filleted at 4, the radius of the largest circle in it, was left square at its size and at a thousandth of it, and rounded by a half circle at a thousand times it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcLanding
member.summary: Whether an arc moved under a transformation lands within a tolerance of where the transformation puts its points everywhere along it, not only where it is asked.

remarks.para: A point of the arc moved, read from the moved start across the arc, is p cos φ + q sin φ - w: the two axes of its plane the radius long, carried by the transformation, the angle round the old centre, and where the start was. Against the circle the moved arc lies on, of radius r, the centre c across from the moved start, the square of the point's distance from the centre less the square of the radius is g = |a|² - 2 a·c, a sum of cosines and sines of the angle and of twice it, and the point stands g / (√(r² + g) + r) off the circle, which grows with g: the worst of a stretch is at the greatest or the least g. Its second derivative is no more than the bend, the sizes of its two halves, one and four times over, so between two points asked a share w of the sweep apart g strays from the line between them by no more than the bend times the square of the angle over eight. A stretch that cannot reach the tolerance so is settled; one that can is halved and its middle asked, until it is settled or the middle lands off. The height off the moved plane, in space, is a sum of a cosine and a sine, and is bounded alike.
Asked at sixteen points only, a stretched arc of radius 12.7 scaled by 87 landed 0.0010043 off between two of them at a tolerance of 0.001, and was moved.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcOffset2
member.summary: Offsetting a loop that crosses itself, the way the straight offsets read one: even-odd.

remarks.para: The offset of one loop is built piece by piece and joined at the loop's vertices, so it can tell nothing of two edges that cross each other away from a vertex, and a loop that crosses itself cannot be offset to one side: half of it runs the other way round. The straight offsets read such a loop even-odd, a point being inside when it lies inside an odd number of the simple loops the crossings cut it into, and offset that region. So is this done, with the arcs kept: the loop is cut at its crossings into the pieces between them, each piece is turned to run with the region on its left (counter-clockwise round the outside of it, clockwise round a hole), the pieces are joined again at the crossings as the corners of the region are, all of them are moved to the right of the way they run together, pruned against the whole shape and against the region, and put back into the loops they make.
A loop that does not cross itself is not touched by any of this: it is offset as it always was.

member.summary:
Offsetting a chain or a loop that may curve, keeping its arcs as arcs.
Clipper, which resolves the straight offsets, knows only straight edges, so it is no use here. Nothing is needed from it: offsetting one piece is exact and easy — a segment moves sideways and an arc keeps its centre and changes its radius — and what is left is joining the pieces up again and throwing away the parts that fold over. Those two are what this file is. An arc whose radius runs out is carried through its centre and folds over all along, and the corners either side are joined about its own two ends.
The test that decides what folds over is the one fact an offset cannot break: every point of a valid offset stands exactly the offset distance away from the shape it came from. Each piece is cut where it comes to that distance from another part of the shape, and the stretches standing nearer have been folded over and go; the rest of the piece stays.
What the pruning of a curved offset reads off the shape it came from.

member.param: The edges of the loop, each starting where the one before ended, the last coming back to the first.
The tolerance, which says how near a crossing may lie to an end of an edge and still be at it.
The simple loops the crossings cut it into, which say what lies in the region: inside an odd number of them.
The loops that bound the region, each running with it on its left.
How many places two edges were found to cross each other at, whether or not the loop could be cut there.

true to join the chains at a crossing of two lobes round the quarters of the region, so that each tip of the region there is a corner of its own: the corners a region grown with miters or chamfers fills. false to join them round the quarters of the space that is not the region.
member.returns: true when two edges cross each other, other than at a vertex, and the loop was cut.
member.remarks:
A crossing is a place two edges cross each other, away from the ends of both: edges that meet at a vertex, or touch with an end, do not cross. A loop that only touches itself is not cut, and is offset as it always was. Two arcs that leave a vertex one over the other and cross again beside it, as the neighbours of a gear's inner vertex do, make a lens that the loop runs round the other way: that lens is a loop of its own.
The loops the crossings cut it into can cross each other at a crossing, where the region lies in two opposite quarters and the space that is not the region in the other two, so which side of a piece the region is on is read for each piece, off the loops it is not part of. At a crossing each piece arriving is then joined to the piece leaving next round from it, counter-clockwise: the pair that bound a quarter of the space that is not the region, as the corner of a polygon is. The corner of the offset there is the corner of the region, a quarter of space narrower than the offset being filled up to where its sides meet.
A region grown with miters or chamfers is joined the other way, each piece arriving to the piece leaving next round clockwise, round a quarter of the region: each tip of the region at the crossing is then a corner that opens, and its miter runs the two pieces on past the crossing round their own circles, or its chamfer cuts it square, as at any corner. Joined round the space between, the tip was no corner, and where the quarter across the crossing was too small to hold the join, it was left out: a loop of ten corners crossing itself at nine places, grown by 0.3 with miters, lost 1.89 near (0, -4.4). Only a crossing of two lobes is so joined, its two quarters of the region in two lobes once the region is cut at every crossing; one whose quarters are one lobe running round a hole is joined round the space between, as the straight path reads it. So is a place where more than two pieces cross, crossings within the tolerance of each other made one: there the quarters are not the region's own, and joined round them, a loop at a tolerance of 0.01 whose edge crosses a spike's two sides 0.0085 apart, grown by 0.3, kept 1.0 that is not the offset. So is a crossing a corner of the loop lies within the tolerance of, or a piece through it ends at a corner within it, a vertex the loop runs straight on through being no corner, and one beside a lobe that is a sliver within the tolerance.

The other loops are read at the middle of the chain's longest piece, where they do not touch it. Loops cut off a crossing cross each other at others, so one loop's chains may lie on both sides of another, and this is told chain by chain and not loop by loop. Where the loops are many only those whose boxes hold the point are read, found in a tree of the boxes: the 320 358 chains of a plus of 80 000 teeth to each arm were each read against all its 160 002 loops, and cutting it took over four minutes on .NET 10, where it takes about a second.

member.remarks: The arc's own offset is folded over all along, so what is left of the offset there is where the joins about its two ends meet: the corner the arc collapses to. The rectangle 100 by 30 with its right side bowed 6 in, a radius of 21.75, grown by 40: the joins of 40 about (100, 0) and (100, 30) cross at (100 + sqrt 1375, 15) = (137.081, 15), and the offset runs round the one into the other there. Cut here, the crossing is found even where it lies within the tolerance of the spent arc's ends, which the pruning takes for the pieces' own ends and leaves uncut.

member.summary: Deals with one corner of the offset: trims the two pieces back to where they cross, or puts a join in between them when they no longer reach each other.
member.returns: The piece that follows the corner, cut back when the corner closed up.
member.remarks: Only a corner that turns towards the side the offset goes closes up, and only there are the pieces cut back to where they cross: a crossing at a corner that opens lies further along them, where one folds over the other, and is the pruning's to deal with. A closing corner whose pieces do not reach each other is tied by a chord and never filled, and the pruning throws the chord away with the parts of the pieces the shape comes nearer to. The chain 10 along x and then round an arc of bulge 0.5 that leaves turning 168 degrees back to the left, offset by 1 to the left: the moved segment and the moved arc never meet, and what stands 1 from the chain is the segment as far as x = 7.271 and the arc from (7.484, -1) on.

member.remarks: A corner turning right back, within the point tolerance over its edges, turns both ways at once, and is read by how the two edges bend away from the line they leave it along: towards the side the offset goes, the corner opens round the tip of the cusp; away from it, or for two straight edges, it closes, and where its pieces cross, they are cut back to the crossing. The chain along x to (100, 0), round the half circle of radius 50 back over itself to (100, 100) and along x again, offset by 10 into the U: the moved line y = 10 and the moved circle of radius 60 meet at (55.28, 10), where the corner closes. The rectangle 20 by 10 whose left side is a half circle bowed in to (5, 5), grown by 2: the half circle leaves both its ends back along the sides there, bending away from them, and the offset goes round each end on a half turn of radius 2.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcOffset2.RoundJoin(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,System.Double)
member.summary: Bridges an opened corner with an arc of the offset distance about the corner it came from.
member.remarks: Where the two ends lie on one line out from the corner, the arc about it runs from a point back to the same point, a whole turn or none, while the pieces stop apart. That is no turn to round, and the two are joined straight instead, held to the distance like the rest. Both moved pieces end the distance from the corner they share, so this happens only past an edge that was dropped, such as an arc whose radius ran out: the U from (10, 0) to the origin, round the half circle of radius 2 about (0, 2) and back to (10, 4), offset 2.5 to its inside, ends the two straights at (0, 2.5) and (0, 1.5), both straight above the origin.

member.summary: Bridges an opened corner by running both pieces on to where they would meet, or, when that point is further away than the miter limit allows or there is none, cuts the corner off square at the limit.
member.remarks: The pieces are run on along the curves behind them, so an arc reaches further round its own circle rather than being cut straight across: that is what AutoCAD's OFFSET does at a corner. A miter can run away at a sharp corner, and the limit is where it is given up on: the corner is squared off there, as says and the straight offsets do. Where there is no sharp corner and no square to cut, because the curves never meet and there is no limit, or an arc's circle never reaches the cut at the limit, the corner is rounded off on the circle of the distance about it, which stands exactly the distance from it, as it is beside an arc whose radius ran out. The chain 100 along x and round an arc of bulge -0.9 to (140, 60), offset by 20 to its right, would be squared off 200 from the corner (100, 0), which the arc's moved circle, of radius 16.256, never reaches: it is rounded off by the circle of 20 about the corner instead.

member.summary: Bridges an opened corner by cutting it off square: both pieces are run on to the line square to the corner's bisector a given reach from the corner, and joined along it.
member.param: The run so far, ending with the piece before the corner.
The edge of the shape arriving at the corner.
The edge of the shape leaving it.
Where the piece before the corner ends.
Where the piece after it starts.
The vertex the corner was moved from.
How far out from the corner the cut lies.
true to run an arc on round its own circle, as a miter does; false to run every piece on along the line it leaves its end by, the tangent of the round join there.
The joins whose inside the pruning leaves out, which this one is added to.
Set to the piece after the corner, run back to the cut.
member.returns: false, leaving the run as it was, where a piece cannot be run on to the cut: running it on takes it away from the cut, or it is an arc whose circle does not reach the cut short of a whole turn.

remarks.para: A chamfer is the cut at the offset distance, touching the circle a round join would draw where it crosses the bisector, between the lines that touch that circle where the two pieces end: the round join's corner drawn as three straight sides, as the straight offsets cut it. Next to a segment the line is the segment run on; next to an arc it is a short straight piece leaving the arc's end along its tangent. The square of side 10 grown by 2 with chamfers is cut at the corner (10, 0) from (8 + 2 sqrt 2, -2) to (12, 2 - 2 sqrt 2), 2 from the corner at its middle, and encloses 193.255.

A miter past its limit is the miter cut off at the limit times the distance, as the straight offsets cut it: the pieces are run on as the miter runs them, an arc round its own circle, until they reach the cut. The triangle with a tip of 10 degrees at the origin, grown by 1, would miter 11.47 from the tip, past the default limit of 10, and is squared off 10 from it, from (-9.973, -0.743) to (-9.951, -1). Pieces that cross short of the cut, as two arcs curling towards each other can, meet where they cross.

member.summary: Gets the part of an edge from a point on it to its end.
Throws away the parts of the offset that folded over, and puts what is left back into runs.
member.remarks: Every point of a valid offset stands exactly the offset distance from the shape it came from. A piece is cut wherever it crosses another piece, and wherever it comes to that distance from another part of the shape: where it crosses the curve that part moves to on either side, or the circle of the distance about one of the shape's vertices. Each stretch between the cuts then stands the distance away or nearer, and the nearer ones go. One more thing marks a fold where a piece crosses a join, which may stand further than the distance: the part of a piece leaving a crossing to the side of the other piece that faces the shape is inside the offset, and goes too. The hairpin 1 wide, 10 along x, 1 down and 9 back, offset by -0.6 into its inside, keeps the first leg moved to y = -0.6 as far as x = 0.553, where it comes within 0.6 of the chain's end, and nothing else.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcOffset2.DropCovered(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Collections.Generic.KeyValuePair{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge2,System.Boolean}}[],GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Drops each kept part that runs along another kept part, within the tolerance from end to end: of two that run along each other end to end, the later.
member.remarks: Two pieces can stand the distance away along the same stretch: two edges on one line, either side of a notch, each moved and run on to its miter, or the teeth of a comb whose feet line up. The offset passes there once. Kept twice, the stretch leaves the run it belongs to ending where the next one does not begin, and a loop round it never closes. Which of the two goes does not depend on which came first: the shorter goes, and the longer carries the run on. Grown by 20 with chamfers at a tolerance of 0.1, a notch whose two outer sides lie all but on one line is crossed by the straight piece leaving one side's moved arc and by the other side's moved arc, 0.04 apart; when the shorter was kept for coming first, the loop broke open at it from four of its eight starting corners. Parts running the other way along each other are a spike, and stay.

The piece that runs through it.

The loop of 30.86 left of a region of 33.2 with a thin lens in it that touches the corner of a triangle, shrunk by 0.05, is two runs ending 0.0043 from each other's starts at both ends, and a loop of 186.18 is two runs 0.0076 apart through two stretches of 0.0038 each: both were lost.

remarks.para: Where three pieces cross within a few hundredths of a millimetre, the last of the run can be a spur: a stretch the pruning kept that runs on past the place the loop closed, and ends where nothing joins it. The loop is whole without the spur, and with it is lost. A run can as well pass through one place twice: two holes that meet at a point, grown by 0.3, are one run that closes on itself at that point and goes on to close on itself again. What is left of the run once the first loop is split off is a run in its own right, and is closed in turn.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcOffset2.Shape
member.summary: The shape being offset, read for what the pruning asks of it: how near it comes to a point, and where a piece comes to the offset distance from one of its parts.

remarks.para: A point stands nearer than the distance wherever any part of the shape does, an edge or one of its ends, and nothing else is asked. The part of the shape nearest a point is the inside of an edge, the foot of the perpendicular, or a vertex, and then the point lies in the wedge between the two edges' normals there: so a circle about a vertex bounds the offset only in that wedge.

In the wedge of a corner tied by a straight chord, where nothing else could join it, what the offset leaves out is the triangle between the corner and the chord, not the circle: the chord cuts inside the circle, and a piece passing between the two still bounds the offset there. In the wedge of a corner joined by a miter or cut off square, it leaves out the whole of the join, which reaches beyond the circle: from the corner out to the pieces' ends, along them as run on, and across the cut.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ArcOffset2.BoxOrder
member.summary: Boxes in order along the axis a point lies within fewest of them on, so that those that can hold a point are found without trying every one: the boxes starting at or before the point along that axis, back to where none of the ones before reaches it.
member.remarks:
The axis is read off the boxes, as a sweep's is: on a shape long in x every box spans little of x, and a point lies within few of them along it. Ties are broken by the order the boxes came in, so the order never depends on the sort.
No axis serves a shape long in both, as a plus of two combs is, whose long edges along the arms reach every box along either axis: each piece of the plus of 8 000 teeth to each arm, grown at a thousandth, was read against the boxes of the pieces along the axis, 992 million of them for the 189 152 pairs read for crossings. Where more than 64 boxes reach a box or a point along the axis, those that overlap or hold it are found in a tree of the boxes, and given in the order a reading along the axis gives them; boxes of no number or that run out to infinity are read along the axis only, as they always were.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Boolean2
member.summary:
The boolean operations over the loops that may curve.
These flatten first, and say so by what they give back: Clipper resolves every region operation in this library and knows only straight edges, so there is no form of a boolean that keeps arcs. The straight result is the honest one — an answer of the curved type would be a promise that the arcs had survived, and they have not.
is the exception, and the reason is worth knowing: offsetting is done piece by piece, so an arc can be offset exactly and stay an arc. A boolean cannot be done piece by piece.

Provides static methods that combine regions in the plane: union, intersection, difference and exclusive or, as AutoCAD's UNION, INTERSECT and SUBTRACT do for regions.
A polygon is read as the region it encloses under the even-odd rule, as reads it, and a face as its boundary less its holes. The result is always a set of faces: combining regions can leave several pieces, and pieces with holes, which a polygon alone cannot carry. The faces come back largest first, every boundary counter-clockwise and every hole clockwise, so that signed areas add up. An empty result is an empty array.
The work is done by Clipper2, on integer coordinates in a frame placed at the first shape, so the answer does not depend on rounding luck and loses no precision far from the origin. Points closer than the point tolerance are merged, and pieces thinner than it are dropped as the seams two outlines leave where they almost meet.
