member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision2.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether an arc touches another arc, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Neither has an inside, so they collide where they cross or come within the point tolerance of each other. At a tolerance of a thousandth, an arc ending half a thousandth above the top of the circle of radius 50 about the origin collides with its upper half, and one ending two thousandths above does not. They collide exactly where is at most the point tolerance, also for arcs of a radius smaller than it: two arcs of radius 0.0004 about the origin, one of them 1E-7 outside the other, collide where their spans overlap. Two arcs of one circle cross nowhere, but an overlap of them always begins and ends at an end of one, which the nearest pair weighs.

member.remarks: A circle is read as a filled disc, so an arc lying wholly within one collides with it, and so does one coming within the point tolerance of its rim from outside.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3
member.summary: Whether a triangle touches a body, and whether a flat region or a plane touches a box.

remarks.para: A region reaches a body's material when an edge of the region crosses the surface, an edge of the body crosses the region, or the region lies inside, which one of its corners then says. The body is read by its material, every opening cut in, so a triangle wholly inside an opening touches nothing.

A box is read through its body: each answer about a box is the answer about , or about ToObb().ToSolid() for an axis-aligned one, as has always read it. A box flat on some axis, or no thicker than the point tolerance on two, has no body and is read as the shape it has become: flat on one axis its rectangle, on two its segment, on all three its point. A box 100 by 100 by 0 is the square it spans, missed by a triangle lying 20 over it and touched by one standing across it.

member.summary:
Provides static methods for deciding whether two 3D shapes overlap.
CollidesWith answers yes or no and says nothing about where. Shapes that merely touch count as colliding, and so do shapes within the point tolerance of each other: for points and straight shapes in space the answer is exactly whether Distance3 reports no more than the point tolerance for the same pair. A triangle with no area, by , is the segment it has collapsed to and touches what comes within the tolerance of it, as its distance says: the triangle 0.003 by 0.003 is a triangle at the default tolerance, and the sliver 100 long and 1E-8 high touches a segment through its middle. Two bodies and a plane are not read so (see Distance3). Where the shapes meet is Intersection3, and how far apart they are when they do not is Distance3.
Whether an open shape reaches a flat one, whether a ray reaches a box, and whether an axis-aligned box reaches a body.

remarks.para: A segment, a ray and a flat region have no thickness between them, so there is nothing for them to overlap in: they touch where the gap between them is no longer than the point tolerance, as measures it. The gap is exact, nothing widening either shape: a segment in the plane of the square 100 by 100 starting 0.0005 off its side is 0.0005 from it, from either end, and touches it at a tolerance of a thousandth; one starting 0.0012 off its corner, 0.00085 off in each direction, is 0.0012 from it and touches nothing; one hovering 0.0003 over it is 0.0003 from it, and one 0.0009 up and 0.0009 out from its side, 0.00127 away, touches nothing. A segment lying in the plane of a region and crossing it is nought from it and touches it, and so does one lying wholly inside it.

A ray against a box is the one that needs a second question. A box is bounded, so a ray that starts inside it always leaves and does cross the surface — but a ray starting on the inside is the case a crossing count is least sure of, so where it starts is asked first, as it is for a ray against a solid.

member.summary: Whether a straight chain in space touches another shape.

remarks.para: A could say how far off nine kinds of shape were and whether it touched three. Everything the distance needed was there; what was missing was the shorter question. A chain is a run of segments, so every answer here is the union of what its segments answer, and a already answers all of it — nothing new is worked out.
Two segments share a vertex, so a crossing at a vertex is found twice and named once. This is the walk keeps for a chain that curves; the two differ only in what a piece is.

member.summary: Whether a ray reaches a body.
Whether two flat regions in space touch, whether a plane touches a region, a ray or a body, whether two rays touch, and whether a region touches a body or a box.

remarks.para: Two regions. A triangle, a polygon and a face are read filled, a face by its material. Two of them touch exactly where an edge of either reaches the other region, which is the segment against a region asked once for each edge, a region lying inside the other included. A square 20 by 20 standing upright in the middle of a hole 40 by 40 in a plate 100 by 100 touches nothing.

Within the tolerance. Two regions touch wherever the gap between them is no longer than the point tolerance, the gap measures, exact and in space, whether they lie level, tilted or in planes that are not one: a plate one side 0.0002 and the other 0.0011 over a square in the floor is 0.0002 from it and touches it, as it does lying level 0.0009 over it, and a square lying beside it 0.0012 off its side does not touch it. Nothing is laid out flat for the purpose: a region off another's plane by less than the planar tolerance is as far from it in space as it is.

A plane. A bounded shape touches a plane when the heights of its corners above it change sign or reach nought within the point tolerance, as a straight chain is measured against a plane. A body touches it when one of its faces does, read over the material, so a body in two pieces either side of the plane does not.

member.summary: Whether two straight pieces in space touch.
member.remarks: A collision between two open shapes is the crossing test with the place thrown away, except in the one case where there is no place to throw away: two pieces lying along each other touch along a length and name no point. So this is not GetIntersections(...).Length > 0 — it is the shortest line between the two having no length, which answers that case as well, and is the same reading two arcs of one circle already get.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether a triangle touches the material of a solid, within a tolerance.
member.param: The solid, read by its material.
member.returns: true when the triangle comes within the point tolerance of the surface, crossing it included, or lies in the material; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: A triangle wholly inside the body crosses no face and touches it all the same, so where its first corner is is asked once nothing crosses. A box 100 by 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin is touched by a triangle lying across it at half its height and by one wholly inside it, and not by one standing 10 clear of its top. A triangle with no area is the segment it has collapsed to, and touches as its distance says. Whether a point is in the body is asked to within rounding, a billionth of a millimetre (1E-9, not nought), so that rounding in a body turned about in space cannot lose a crossing: a point within 1E-9 outside the body reads as in it, and a point 5E-10 outside a box is nought away from it. Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size.
member.exception: Thrown when the solid is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether two oriented boxes overlap, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance; boxes closer than this count as touching.
member.returns: true if the boxes overlap or touch; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: This is the separating axis theorem. Two convex shapes miss each other exactly when some direction exists along which their shadows do not overlap, and for a pair of boxes it is enough to try fifteen directions: the three axes of each box, and the nine cross products pairing one axis from each. The first six catch a face separating them and the last nine catch an edge, the case where two boxes pass by each other at an angle with no face facing the gap. Along every one of them the boxes may stand the point tolerance apart and no more, so two boxes whose nearest edges cross at a sine of a tenth, 0.005 apart, do not touch, and 0.0009 apart they do.

member.summary: Checks whether a line segment reaches into an oriented box, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The box is read as its body, as reads it, and they touch where that distance is no longer than the point tolerance: the box 100 by 100 by 50 with its top in the floor is touched by a segment in the floor starting 0.0005 off its side, and not by one starting 0.0012 off its corner, 0.00085 off in each direction.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3)
member.summary: Checks whether two triangles overlap, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether two triangles overlap, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Two triangles that are not coplanar can only meet along a line, so it is enough to ask whether any edge of one pierces the other. Coplanar triangles meet across an area instead and that test finds nothing, so they are handled separately by looking for a vertex of one inside the other or for a pair of edges crossing. They count as coplanar when their normals are parallel and either lies wholly within the planar tolerance of the other's plane, as two flat regions do, so the answer is the same whichever is asked first. Two that do neither touch where they come within the point tolerance of each other, the gap their distance measures.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.ComeWithin(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether two triangles that neither cross nor overlap in one plane still come within the point tolerance of each other, the gap their distance measures.
member.remarks: Two flat regions touch wherever their gap is no longer than the point tolerance (), and a triangle is answered the same way: a pair 0.0006 apart, turned a hundred-thousandth of a radian against each other so that neither lies in the other's plane, touches, as two boxes 0.0009 apart do. Apart, the nearest pair lies on two edges or on a corner of one and the other triangle, as measures them; each against the other's plane and the boxes of the two are asked first, so that a pair plainly apart pays nothing more.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.IsClearOf(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether a triangle lies wholly to one side of another's plane, clear of it by more than twice the larger of the point and planar tolerances.
member.param: The triangle whose plane is the dividing one; it must not be degenerate.
member.remarks: Such a pair cannot meet, and three distances to a plane say so for the price of a cross product, where the full test asks six edges whether they cross a face. The margin is what makes it safe. Every way the full test finds contact — an edge of one reaching the other's plane with the segment stretched by the point tolerance at each end, a point placed on the other triangle within the point or the planar tolerance, the two lying in one plane within the planar tolerance — puts some point of within the larger of the two tolerances of this plane, and all of it lies farther away than that.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether two solids overlap, within a tolerance.
member.returns: true if the solids share any space; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: Two closed bodies overlap in one of exactly two ways: their surfaces cross, or one sits wholly inside the other with no surface contact at all. The first is found by testing the surface triangles against each other, the second by testing a single vertex of each body against the other, which settles it because a body that is inside without touching is entirely inside. Bounding boxes are checked first, since that rejects most pairs before any triangle is touched.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.SurfacesTouch(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3[],GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3[],GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether any triangle of one mesh touches any triangle of another.
member.remarks: Comparing every pair costs time in the product of the two counts, which is fine for a handful of triangles and hopeless for a real model. Above a threshold the meshes are indexed first and walked as a pair of trees instead, so a pair of boxes that miss each other discards everything beneath them at once. The threshold exists because building the index is itself work: below it, the plain scan wins.

member.summary: Checks whether a line segment reaches into a solid, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A segment lying wholly inside the body touches it without crossing its surface, so where its ends lie is asked as well as where it crosses. They touch where is no longer than the point tolerance, the openings the segment can reach cut in: a segment in the plane of the top of the box 100 by 100 by 50, starting 0.0005 off its side, touches it, and one starting 0.0012 off its corner, 0.00085 off in each direction, does not. Whether a point is in the body is asked to within rounding, a billionth of a millimetre (1E-9, not nought), so that rounding in a body turned about in space cannot lose a crossing: a point within 1E-9 outside the body reads as in it, and a point 5E-10 outside a box is nought away from it. Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size. The boxes are asked first as far apart as that too, which reaches every point tolerance below that billionth, or below 1E-15 of the largest coordinate further out than a million: at a tolerance of nought, and of 1E-12, 1E-10 or 3E-10, the segment standing up from 5E-10 over the top of the box 100 by 80 by 50 touches it, as it is nought from it, and so does the one from 1E-7 over the top of that box a thousand million out at nought, where the boxes were asked at the tolerance given and they touched nothing.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether a ray starts inside a solid or runs into it, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A ray leaving from inside the body never crosses its surface on the way out of nothing, so where it starts is asked before any face is tried. They touch where is no longer than the point tolerance: a ray in the plane of the top of the box 100 by 100 by 50, starting 0.0005 off its side and pointing away, touches it. Whether a point is in the body is asked to within rounding, a billionth of a millimetre (1E-9, not nought), so that rounding in a body turned about in space cannot lose a crossing: a point within 1E-9 outside the body reads as in it, and a point 5E-10 outside a box is nought away from it. Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.RayTouches(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether a ray comes within the point tolerance of the surface of a body or starts in it, as reads it, to a billionth or, further out than a million, to 1E-15 of the largest coordinate: the one test the body is asked about a ray by, by CollidesWith and by the list of where they meet alike.
member.param: The body, its openings already cut in where the ray can reach them.
member.remarks: A face further from the ray than the reach of the tolerance cannot come within it and is passed over unweighed. The origin is asked of the body whatever its box: one further outside it than the body holds a point is settled by the box alone. It was not asked further than a millionth outside, which 2E9 out is less than the body holds: the ray from 1.4E-6 over the top of a box there, pointing away, was nought from it and did not collide.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Collision3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether a body touches a plane, within a tolerance.
member.param: The solid, read by its material.
member.returns: true when the heights of the corners of one of its faces above the plane change sign or one of them is nought within the point tolerance; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: Every face is flat and its outline runs unbroken round it, so a plane meets the face exactly when the corners of the outline are not all on one side of it, and a plane meeting the body meets a face, since the body is bounded and the plane is not. Asked over all the corners at once, the test would find a body in two pieces either side of the plane touching it; asked face by face, it does not. The openings the plane passes through are cut in first, so a plane through an opening alone touches nothing. A box 100 by 100 by 100 standing on the floor is touched by the plane z = 50 and by the plane z = 100 through its top, and missed by the plane z = 101.
member.exception: Thrown when the solid is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Containment2.Locate(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Says where a point lies against a loop that may curve, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The answer is exact, with no arc cut into pieces anywhere in it: it is the straight loop through the vertices, turned inside out once for every piece an arc cuts off its own chord that the point happens to lie in. Only the true boundary, arcs and all, is read with the tolerance: a point within it of the boundary is on the side, and every other point is in or out exactly, however near a chord it lies. The square from the origin to (100, 100) with its top bowed 20 inwards (bulge -0.4) has the point (50, 99.95), 0.05 under the chord, outside at a tolerance of 0.1: it is 19.95 above the arc. A point exactly on a chord that is not the boundary is read as lying a hair towards +X of it, or towards +Y of a chord running along X.
member.exception: Thrown when the loop is null.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Containment3
member.summary:
Provides static methods for deciding where a point sits relative to a 3D shape.
IsPointOn asks about the boundary of a shape, Contains asks whether the shape holds the point at all, and Locate returns which of the two — or neither — applies. Only shapes that enclose something offer Contains; a curve has no interior, so asking it to contain a point would only restate IsPointOn.

member.summary: Checks whether a point lies on a line segment, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Containment3.IsPointOn(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether a point lies on a line segment, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The segment is bounded, so a point on its infinite carrier but past an endpoint is not on it. A degenerate segment is a single point, and the test reduces to comparing against that point.

member.summary: Checks whether a point lies on a ray, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A ray starts at its origin, so a point on its carrier line but behind the origin is not on it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Containment3.Locate(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Locates a point relative to a triangle, within a tolerance.
member.returns: when the point lies on the triangle away from its edges, when it lies on an edge, and otherwise.
member.remarks: A triangle is a planar region, so a point counts as inside only when it lies on the carrier plane as well as within the edges: a point hovering above the middle of a triangle is outside it. A triangle with no area, by , has no interior: it is the segment it has collapsed to, and a point within the point tolerance of one of its sides is on it, the rest outside. The centroid of the triangle 0.003 by 0.003 is on it at the default tolerance, 0.001 from two of its sides, where it was outside, and so is the middle of the sliver 100 long and 1E-8 high. The area is read at the tolerance given: at 1E-5 the triangle 100 long and 0.0005 high holds (50, 0.0002, 0) inside it, though it has no area at the default.

member.returns: when the point lies on the polygon away from its edges, when it lies on an edge, and otherwise.
member.remarks: A polygon is a planar region, so a point counts as inside only when it lies on the carrier plane as well as within the boundary: a point hovering above the middle of a polygon is outside it. Within the plane the test is the even-odd rule, counting how many edges a ray from the point crosses, which is why a self-crossing polygon reports its doubly-enclosed lobes as outside.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Containment3.IsInsideLoop(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3},GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Counts edge crossings of a closed loop to decide whether a coplanar point is enclosed.
member.remarks: The loop is flattened onto the two in-plane axes and read with the even-odd rule. Working in the plane rather than in space is what makes this a 2D problem with a known answer; the caller is responsible for having checked that the point lies on the plane, and for the on-edge band, which this method does not handle and would otherwise decide arbitrarily.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Containment3.Locate(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Locates a point relative to a solid, within a tolerance.
member.param: The solid; its boundary is assumed closed.
member.returns: when the point lies where the material ends — on a face of the solid outside every opening, or on the wall of an opening where that wall runs through the body — when it lies in the material, and otherwise, openings included.
member.remarks:
Interior points are found by counting how many faces a ray from the point crosses: an odd count means it started inside. The answer is only as good as the boundary — an open shell has no inside and the count means nothing — which is what is for.
An opening is asked first, because it takes away everything strictly inside it, the body's own skin included. A plate's top face is a whole square even where a bolt hole passes through it, so a point in the middle of the hole at the level of that face is on a face and in empty space at once, and empty space is the answer. The wall of an opening drawn overshooting a face, as a through-hole usually is, is boundary only where it runs through the body.
However small the tolerance, a face holds a crossing to the rounding of the body's coordinates, 1E-15 of the largest, on its plane and past its rim, and below that rounding a crossing within twice it of a rim sends the ray off in another direction; whether a face lies ahead of the point or behind it is read by the tolerance given. At a tolerance of nought a point on the axis of a cylinder is inside it, though the first ray cast runs through the seam of two of its sides, and so are the 1 000 points tried inside a cylinder 40 across and 50 tall and a cone, their axes leaning in space, where the rounding refused the crossing of nearly every face and read most of them outside. The planes of fan triangles far out can be rounded by more, and a point on the axis of a cylinder of 1 080 sides 1E7 out may still be read outside.
A body far out, reaching more than 2^20 and more than 1 024 times the size of its box from the origin, is asked near the origin, in the frame its booleans are worked out in, the point moved in with it coordinate by coordinate; so are its distance, its signed distance, its nearest point and its shortest line to a point, and where a ray, a segment or a line meets it, collides with it or stands from it, what has a place moved back out. Where it stood, its openings were cut and its faces read within a trillionth of the coordinates: of 636 points half a thousandth in and out from a plate 200 by 100 by 3 a thousand million out, with two openings up from its floor whose ceilings stood 0.0009 apart, 12 had another nearest point than at the origin. Below a trillionth of the coordinates a 256th of the reach out the body is asked where it stands, as before.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Containment3.IsInsideByRayCast(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Decides whether a point sits inside a closed boundary by counting ray crossings.
member.remarks:
A ray that grazes an edge, or passes exactly through a vertex, is counted once by one face and twice or not at all by its neighbour, and the parity comes out wrong. Rather than trying to resolve those cases the ray is simply thrown again in another direction, since the chance of several unrelated directions all landing on an edge is negligible. The directions are fixed rather than random so that the same question always gets the same answer.
Every direction comes back ambiguous where the body is thinner than twice the band and the point stands near one of its sides: every ray crosses a face within the band of a rim, the side itself if it reaches it. A point of a cell of a plate 0.035 thick, 0.013 in from its side, was called outside so. There the faces are summed by the turns they make about the point, which no edge makes ambiguous; see . A boundary that turns no whole number of times, as one open somewhere can, is not read, and claims no point.
The point stands further than the point tolerance from every face, as settled before it asked.

The triangles in a face do not come within the point tolerance of the point.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ConvexHull2
member.summary: The smallest convex polygon holding a set of points in the plane.
member.remarks: Andrew's monotone chain: the points sorted along X, the lower and upper chains walked once each, a corner dropped whenever the chain would turn the wrong way or run straight on, judged exactly, so that no corner of the hull is ever lost to the tolerance. The tolerance then takes out the corners that do not matter: a corner within it of the segment between its neighbours, and one within it of the corner before. No point stands more than the tolerance outside the hull that is left, however many corners go. A set thinner than the tolerance may still get a hull, because the tolerance is spent corner by corner and may run out before the corners are gone; a set that lies within the tolerance of a segment, all of it, may have none. Points that differ in X by a trillionth and in Y by 15 still make their corner: a hull of (0, 0), (1E-12, -15.8), (2E-12, -6.25) and (20, 0) is a triangle of 158 square units.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ConvexHull3
member.summary: The smallest convex body holding a set of points in space.

remarks.para: Built incrementally: a tetrahedron on four points far apart, then each further point in turn. A point within the point tolerance of the hull so far, or inside it, changes nothing. One outside it sees some faces; those go, and the rim they leave — the horizon — is joined to the point with a fan of new faces. The triangles are merged where they lie in one plane, so a box comes back with six faces.

Which faces a point sees is read in floating point there, and a point is taken only where it stands further than the tolerance off a face's plane. That build stops at the first rim that is not one loop, or as soon as it stands more triangles than a closed surface on the points taken can have; and where the hull it gives does not close, folds back over itself, or leaves a point further than the tolerance outside its triangles, the hull is built again with an exact test of sides, from the widest tetrahedron the points give, each point left out only where it is within the tolerance of the triangles themselves. A hull that closes and holds every point is kept as it was built, to the bit. The faces of a plate a few thousandths thick meet at its rim so nearly flat that a point 10 off the rim stands within a thousandth of every plane: of 300 sets of 40 points on plates 0.002 thick, every hull was open or wound against itself, 185 left a point out, by up to 24, and none does now; and 200 points in a plate 100 by 100 and 0.002 thick ran the faster build out of memory, as 10 000 in a cube and 3 000 on a sphere did, and take from under a millisecond to an eighth of a second now. Merging the triangles within the tolerance can stand a face as far again from a point: 5 of 1 000 plates 100 by 100 and from 0.002 to 1 thick left a point up to 1.08E-3 outside the merged hull. Where a point stands further than the tolerance outside it, the triangles are merged again within a tenth of the planar tolerance, then a hundredth, and kept as they are where that does not hold it either, so every point is within the tolerance of the hull given; a merged hull that holds every point is kept as it was, to the bit.

A point is read only against the faces that can stand below it, found by the way they face, so the work no longer grows with the square of the points where they all lie on the hull: 10 000 points in a cube take 50 milliseconds as they did, and 12 000 on a sphere 0.18 seconds where they took 2.4. It is still not meant for a laser scan.

remarks.para: A triangle is put in only for a point further than the tolerance off the plane of a face it sees, so the faces beside the ones it replaces can be left standing a little above its own, and the hull folds in there; and where it reads which faces a point sees wrong in the last bit, it can come out folded over itself, closed edge for edge. A fold of a thousandth in the rim of a plate 0.005 thick left a point below every plane 0.0042 outside, and the rim of one 0.01 thick, convex at every edge, wound twice round a point 0.0016 inside it, which the hull then held outside.

A hull with no corner above the plane of any triangle by more than rounding is convex: it holds what stands below all its planes, and is nearest a point outside on a triangle the point stands above. A point left out below every plane of the hull it was asked of is within what that hull's corners span, and so within this one, and is not asked again. A hull that folds by more, as 4 in 30 hulls of 200 points on a sphere and two in three of points on a lattice with copies do while holding every point, is taken only where no triangle is laid back over its neighbour and each point is held: one within the tolerance of a plane by being within it of a triangle, and one further inside all of them by the surface winding round it once, counted by the solid angles its triangles fill seen from the point.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.ConvexHull3.FacesByNormal
member.summary: The faces of a hull being built, filed by the way they face, so that those a point may stand above are found without reading the others.

remarks.para: Every point was read against every face built so far, standing or gone: 12 000 points on a sphere, each outside the hull of those before it, were read against tens of thousands of faces each, and took 2.4 seconds. The normals are filed on the faces of a cube, each cut into cells, and a cell's normals lie within a cone round its middle. How far a point can stand above the plane of a face is then bounded for the whole cell: no further than it reaches along the nearest normal in the cone, measured from a point inside the hull, less the least distance from there to a plane of the cell. Only the cells where a point can stand as high as asked, rounding allowed for, are read, each face as before, and the faces it sees put oldest first, as every face was read; so the same faces are found, and the hull is the same to the bit. Until the faces outnumber the cells sixteen times over every face is read, which is faster for so few.

Where a point's side of a face is read exactly, the normal worked out in floating point is off the exact one by an angle its rounding bounds; the cone is widened by that angle, and the distance to the plane taken less by as much, and a face so thin that its normal is not known to half a radian is read every time.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Corner2
member.summary:
Reshapes the corners of a chain or a polygon, as AutoCAD's CHAMFER does.
A chamfer replaces a corner with one straight cut across it, measured back along each of the two edges that meet there. What comes back is the kind of shape that went in, because cutting a corner square adds no curvature: a polygon gives a polygon, a chain gives a chain.
is the other end of the same family: it builds a corner where two loose segments would meet, rather than cutting one that already exists.
Rounding the corners of a chain of straight pieces in the plane.

remarks.para: Chamfering a or a was offered and rounding them was not, though a straight chain is exactly what a fillet is usually asked of and space had it all along through . The plane was behind space here, the reverse of everywhere else.

A rounded corner is an arc, so a straight chain cannot hold the answer and the return type is the curved one — for a chain, for a loop — which is the same shape of answer space gives. Nothing new is worked out here: the chain is read as a curved one with every bulge at nought, and the rounding that already exists does the rest.

It is read corner for corner, a leg shorter than the global tolerance and all, so the index of a corner is the index of the vertex: at a millionth, the chain (0, 0), (10, 0), (10.0004, 0.0004), (10.0004, 10), (0, 10) rounded by 1 at its vertex 3 turns at (10.0004, 10), where the leg 0.00057 long was dropped first and vertex 3 was the chain's end.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Corner2.Build(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2},System.Boolean,System.Double,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.String)
member.summary: Cuts every corner that has room for it and returns the vertices of the result, or null when no corner could be cut and the caller should hand back what it was given.
member.remarks:
Every cut is measured on the shape as it came in, never on a shape half cut already: measuring as it goes would make the answer depend on which vertex the walk happened to start at.
An edge can only give away as much as it is long, and two neighbouring corners both eat into the edge between them. Where they ask for more than it has, the corner asking for more on that edge is dropped, and dropping it may free enough for others, so the check runs again until every edge is within its length. Each pass drops at least one corner, so it ends.

member.summary: Rounds every corner of a chain that has room for it with an arc of a given radius, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance: a corner straighter than is left alone, as where a straight edge runs on into an arc it is tangent to.
member.returns: The filleted chain.
member.remarks:
Each arc lies on the inside of its corner and runs the way the chain runs, and it touches both edges on the edges themselves, never past the corner; a corner no circle of the radius fits that way is left alone. The chain (0, 0), (10, 0), (3, 5) filleted at 0.002 is cut back 0.0062 along both edges and turns through an arc of 144.5°, as much as the corner turns.
Where the corners at an edge take all of it, give or take the tolerance, nothing of the edge is left and the arcs either side meet at one point, midway along it; past the tolerance the corner taking more gives way. The chain's own end points never move. Three sides of the square of side 10 filleted at 5.02 at a tolerance of 0.1 run from (0, 0) to (4.98, 0), turn a quarter to (10, 5), another to (4.98, 10), and end at (0, 10).

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Corner3
member.summary: Rounding the corners of a chain in space.

remarks.para: This is what a reinforcing bar is made of: straight runs with a tangent arc at every bend, one bending radius, and the bends free to lie in whatever planes they like. A corner between two straight runs is flat whether or not the chain around it is, so each is rounded in its own plane, by the same arithmetic uses, and the answer is lifted back. Nothing is approximated.

The rule for two corners wanting the same edge is the one the plane already uses, and it carries over untouched because it is about lengths along edges and not about dimensions: an edge can give away no more than it is long, counting both ends, and where it cannot the corner taking more of it gives way.

Only a corner between two straight pieces is rounded. A leg that already curves lies in a plane of its own, which need not be the plane of the corner, so there is no one plane to do the arithmetic in; such a corner is left alone rather than answered approximately.

member.summary: Cutting the corners of a chain in space, and rounding the corners of a loop.

remarks.para: Rounding was offered in space and cutting was not, the opposite way round from the plane. A chamfer needs no plane at all: it moves back along one leg and forward along the other, so the two points it leaves are on the legs themselves and the answer is exact wherever the chain goes. That is why this sits beside rather than inside the per-corner frame the fillet needs.

The rules are the plane's, rule for rule: a corner that does not turn has nothing to cut off, a corner is left alone when a leg is shorter than the distance asked of it, and an edge can give away no more than it is long counting both of its ends — where it cannot, the corner taking more of it gives way, and on a tie the earlier one, so the answer does not depend on where the walk began.

Only a corner between two straight legs is cut, the same rule the fillet keeps. A leg that curves leaves at a tangent, so cutting the corner off it would move the cut onto the arc and change its radius.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.CurveMeet2
member.summary:
Where the endless curves behind two edges cross: the whole line a segment lies on, and the whole circle an arc was cut from.
The public intersections stop at the ends of the pieces they are asked about, which is what a caller almost always wants. Two things here want the opposite: rounding a corner, where the centre of the fillet lies on the curves moved sideways whether or not the pieces reach that far, and mitering one, where the pieces are run on until they meet. Both are about the curves rather than the pieces.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance2
member.summary: Measuring a straight shape against one that curves.
member.remarks: The curved shapes could already be measured against the straight ones; these are the pairs that had no mirror image to fall back on, so that a polygon can be asked about an arc, and a rectangle about a chain, in the same breath as everything else. A rectangle is read as its own polygon, and an arc is measured as an arc rather than cut into pieces first.
member.summary: Provides static calculation methods for geometric distances, squared distances, and closest point projections.
Measuring a ray in the plane against another shape.
member.remarks: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so against a shape with an end to it, it is cut: into the segment from its origin out past the farthest the shape reaches along it, by a margin of a millimetre or a hundred point tolerances, whichever is more. Every point of the shape lies behind that end, so nothing past it is nearer the shape than the end itself, and the segment is measured as any segment is. Against the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin, the ray from (-50, 150) along X is measured as the segment from there to (101, 150), 50 from the square. Against a point or another ray nothing is cut: every candidate is one the ray really holds, an origin brought onto the other or the place where the two cross. Every answer against a cut is the cut segment's, with the tolerance passed through.
member.summary: How far a point stands from a closed shape, and on which side.

remarks.para: reads a closed shape as a filled region, so a point anywhere inside one is nought away and how far in it sits cannot be recovered from the answer. SignedDistanceTo keeps that depth: the magnitude is the distance to the **boundary**, whichever side of it the point is on, and the sign says which side.

The rule is tied to and is the whole of the definition: negative where Locate answers , nought where it answers , and positive where it answers . So Math.Abs(shape.SignedDistanceTo(point)) is the distance out to the outline, and shape.SignedDistanceTo(point) < 0.0 says the same as Contains does, bar the boundary.

Within the tolerance band around the boundary the sign is not worth reading, because the answer there is nought either way and which side of nought it falls on turns on rounding. That is what a tolerance means everywhere else in this library too.
The library already carried this idea for a flat surface, in , and names it the same way it names beside .

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3
member.summary:
Provides static methods for distance calculations in 3D space.
Every distance here is the shortest gap between the two shapes, and is zero when they touch or overlap. A bounded shape is measured as the set of points it actually occupies: a segment ends at its endpoints, a triangle includes its interior, and a plane is infinite in every direction.
Measuring a chain in space against the shapes around it.

remarks.para: A chain could be measured to a point and to nothing else, which left the way out of a curved chain leading nowhere: hands back a straight chain following the arcs as closely as asked, and there was then nothing to ask it. These are the pairs that close that gap, and every one of them is exact for the straight chain it is given.

So the way to measure a bent bar against anything is to say how closely it should be followed and then ask the ordinary question: bar.ToPolyline3(0.1).DistanceTo(slab). The accuracy sits in the call where it can be seen, which is the same bargain offers.

member.summary: Measuring a ray against a face or a body.
member.remarks: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so it cannot be cut into a segment and measured that way without choosing how far to cut. Every candidate here is one the ray really holds: an end of the other shape brought onto the ray, the origin of the ray brought onto the other shape, or the place where the two run past each other.
member.summary: Measuring two flat regions in space against each other, a region or a ray against a plane, a segment, a chain or a ray against a face, a ray against a polygon, a ray or a chain, a body against a face, and a box against those.

remarks.para: Two shapes that truly meet are nought apart, a rim counting as meeting, and otherwise the distance is the gap, measured exactly: the least of every edge of the first against the second and every edge of the second against the first, a ray standing in for an edge. Nothing widens a shape by the point tolerance, so two regions in one plane 0.0005 apart are 0.0005 apart, and a region hovering 0.0003 over another is 0.0003 from it; they collide exactly where that gap is within the point tolerance.

A plane is measured by the heights of the corners, as a chain is (): nought where it touches, otherwise the height of the nearest corner. A body is read solid through, as it is against a polygon. A box is read through its body: each answer about a box is the answer about , or about ToObb().ToSolid() for an axis-aligned one, so an empty axis-aligned box is refused, as refuses it. A box flat on some axis, or no thicker than the point tolerance on two, has no body and is read as the shape it has become: flat on one axis its rectangle, on two its segment, on all three its point. A box 100 by 100 by 0 is 20 from a triangle lying 20 over it.

member.summary: How far a point stands from a body, and whether it is inside it.

remarks.para: The same idea as in the plane: reads a body as solid through, so a point anywhere inside is nought away, and SignedDistanceTo keeps the depth instead. The magnitude is the distance to the surface, whichever side of it the point is on, and the sign says which side.
The rule is tied to : negative where it answers , nought where it answers , positive where it answers .

Only the shapes that enclose a volume are offered. A , a and a are flat regions standing in space and enclose nothing, so a point is inside one only when it is also on its plane: a sign for them would be negative on a set of no thickness at all and would read as though it meant more. already answers the question that does make sense for something flat, which is which side of it a point is on.

member.remarks: The triangle counts as a filled surface, so a point sitting directly above its interior is measured to the surface rather than out to the nearest edge, and a point on the surface is at distance zero. The gap is measured from the triangle's own corners and plane, so a point on a sliver 0.0001 wide and 100 long reads nought, where the closest point found by projection could be 0.0005 away. Where the triangle is so nearly on one line that the rounding of its normal could lean the foot further at the reach of the point than the triangle is high, the gap is measured to its sides, which no point of it is further from than that height: from the triangle (35, 54, -67), (88, 96, -11), (88, 96.0000000000001, -11) the point 5E-14 from its second corner is 5E-14 away, where it was measured 2.12 away. Such a triangle is no higher than about 3E-8 of its length, for a point no further from it than that length.

member.remarks: Nought only where the two truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly and the same whichever is asked first: two segments meeting end to end, one tilted by 8E-6 radian, are as far apart one way as the other. A segment no longer than the tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly meet the other. The segment from the origin to (60, 0, 0) and the one from (60.0004, 0, 0) to (100, 0, 0) are 0.0004 apart.

member.remarks: Nought for a point in the material or on its surface, otherwise the gap to the nearest face, openings cut in, measured exactly: a point 0.0005 outside the box 100 by 100 by 50, in the plane of its top, is 0.0005 from it. member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between two triangles, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Two triangles that touch or cross are at distance zero. Otherwise the closest pair of points lies either on a pair of edges or on a vertex of one and the face of the other — there is nowhere else it can be once the two no longer meet — so the gap is the least of those. It is measured exactly, nothing widening either triangle: two triangles in one plane 0.0005 apart are 0.0005 apart, and a triangle hovering 0.0003 over another is 0.0003 from it. A sliver is measured where it is: the foot of a point on a triangle is taken along its own normal, and the side tests that decide a crossing decide it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceToWithinBand(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between two triangles as the surfaces of two bodies meet: nought wherever says they touch, which includes a pair within the point tolerance, and otherwise the gap.
member.remarks: The distance between two bodies is the least of the distances of their triangles, and a pair of bodies within the point tolerance of each other touch, so the search for the nearest triangles takes this reading.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.Nearest(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the gap between two triangles that do not cross: the least of every edge of one against every edge of the other and every corner of one against the other.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between a line segment and a triangle, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Nought only where the segment truly meets the triangle: crosses it, ends on it, lies across it in its plane. Otherwise the gap, measured exactly and nothing widening the triangle: the segment from (-10, 10, 0.0004) to (110, 10, 0.0004), level over the triangle with corners (0, 0, 0), (100, 0, 0) and (0, 100, 0), is 0.0004 from it. A segment no longer than the point tolerance that does not pass through the triangle is read as its start.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3)

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between a line segment and a polygon, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The polygon counts as a filled surface, so a segment ending directly above its interior is measured straight down rather than out to the nearest edge. This is nought only where the segment truly meets the polygon, crossing it, ending on it or lying across it in its plane, and otherwise the gap, measured exactly and nothing widening the polygon: the segment from (100.0005, 50, 0) to (150, 50, 0) is 0.0005 from the square 100 by 100 in the floor with a corner at the origin, whichever way round it is asked, and one 0.0003 above it is 0.0003 from it. A segment no longer than the point tolerance that does not pass through the polygon is read as its start.
member.exception: Thrown when the polygon is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between a line segment and a solid. A segment reaching into the body is at distance zero.
member.remarks: Whether a point is in the body is asked to within rounding, a billionth of a millimetre (1E-9, not nought), so that rounding in a body turned about in space cannot lose a crossing: a point within 1E-9 outside the body reads as in it, and a point 5E-10 outside a box is nought away from it. Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size.

member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between a solid and a triangle, within a tolerance.
member.returns: Zero where the triangle reaches into the body, otherwise the gap between the two surfaces.
member.remarks: A triangle lying wholly inside the body meets none of its faces, so it is caught by asking where its corners are before any face is measured. One that passes through is caught by the faces it cuts, which are at no distance from it. Whether a point is in the body is asked to within rounding, a billionth of a millimetre (1E-9, not nought), so that rounding in a body turned about in space cannot lose a crossing: a point within 1E-9 outside the body reads as in it, and a point 5E-10 outside a box is nought away from it. Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size.

Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between a solid and a plane, within a tolerance.
member.returns: Zero where the body reaches the plane or crosses it, otherwise the gap.
member.remarks: A plane is flat and endless, so nothing needs measuring but the corners of the body: the nearest point of a solid to a plane is always one of them. The body reaches the plane where one of its faces does, the corners of that face changing side or one of them lying on it within the point tolerance, as reads it; asked over all the corners at once, a body in two pieces either side would read as crossing. The boxes 40 by 40 from z = 10 to 20 and from z = -20 to -10, read as one body, are 10 from the plane z = 0, and so is the box from z = -20 to 20 with an opening from z = -10 to 10 cut right across it.

member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between a solid and an oriented box, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A box is a solid of six faces, so the two are measured against each other as two solids are. A box flat on some axis, or no thicker than the point tolerance on two, bounds no body and is read as its rectangle, its segment or its point: a box 100 by 100 by 0 lying on the floor is 20 from a cube 40 on a side standing 20 over it.

member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between a solid and an axis-aligned box, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The answer of for ToObb(): a box flat on some axis, or no thicker than the point tolerance on two, is read as its rectangle, its segment or its point, and the box from the origin to (100, 100, 0) is 20 from a cube 40 on a side standing 20 over it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between two solids, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Bodies that touch or overlap are at distance zero, which includes one sitting wholly inside the other without their surfaces meeting. Otherwise both surfaces are indexed and walked as a pair of trees, so a pair of boxes farther apart than the closest triangles found so far discards everything beneath it. Two bodies within the point tolerance of each other are nought apart by this search, as they collide: unlike a point or a straight shape against a body, which is the exact gap, a body against a body still reads the band, so two solid boxes 0.0004 apart are nought apart.

member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between two oriented boxes.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Distance3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between two oriented boxes, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Boxes that overlap or touch are at distance zero, which the separating axis test settles outright. Apart, they are measured as the bodies they are. Oriented boxes within the point tolerance of each other are nought apart, as for two solids: the exact gap is not read between bodies. A box flat on some axis, or no thicker than the point tolerance on two, bounds no body and is read as its rectangle, its segment or its point, measured exactly against the other box: a box 100 by 100 by 0 lying on the floor is 10 from the same box lifted by 10, and 20 from a cube 40 on a side standing 20 over it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2
member.summary: Whether an ellipse touches another shape, and whether it holds one whole.
member.remarks: The rule is the circle's: two shapes collide when they come within the point tolerance of each other, the rims meeting or one lying inside the other. The ellipse and every closed shape are regions; a segment, a polyline, an arc and a curved chain are curves, which collide only by reaching the region.
member.summary:
What can be asked of an ellipse: how long its rim is, where a point falls on it, whether a point lies inside it, how it moves, and how it is cut into straight pieces.
An ellipse is a region, as a circle is: it has an area, and a point inside it is in it. Its rim is walked by the eccentric angle t, the point Center + a cos t MajorAxis + b sin t MinorAxis, counter-clockwise from the end of the major axis. That is not the direction seen from the centre: on an ellipse 300 by 100, t = 45° is the point (212.1, 70.7), which lies 18.4° from the axis seen from the centre.
Every answer is exact or worked out to rounding, none of them sampled: the length of the rim by the arithmetic-geometric mean, a length part of the way round by Carlson's elliptic integrals, and the point of the rim nearest a point by Eberly's method. An ellipse whose radii are equal is a circle, and answers as one.
How far an ellipse is from another shape.

remarks.para: The ellipse is a filled region here, as a circle is: a shape that reaches into it, crosses its rim or lies inside it is nought away. A polygon, a rectangle, a triangle, a circle, another ellipse and a curved loop are regions too, so one holding the ellipse is nought away as well; a segment, a polyline, an arc and a curved chain are curves.

Whether the two reach each other is decided exactly, in the ellipse's own frame, with no slack: a distance is nought only where they truly meet, a point of one lying inside the other or on its rim, or the rims crossing, and otherwise the gap, measured exactly. A polyline, a chain or a polygon 0.0005 outside the ellipse 300 by 100 is 0.0005 from it whatever the tolerance, and so is the material of a face. Two ellipses, or a thin ellipse and an arc of radius 0.5 to 2.5, placed less than about 1E-6 from touching can be misread, as the guide says. The distance between two that do not meet is worked out to rounding: from a segment, where its ends or the rim point whose tangent runs along it are nearest; from a circle or an arc, along the normals of the rim through its centre; from another ellipse, by Brent's method on the distance from the rim of the one to the other, started from 36 points round it: 32 spread evenly half a step off the axes and the four ends of the axes.

member.summary: Where the rim of an ellipse crosses another shape.

remarks.para: A segment is read in the ellipse's own frame, scaled so that the ellipse is the unit circle: there the segment is still straight, and where it crosses the rim is a quadratic, solved exactly. Whether it only grazes the rim is judged as a distance: the rim point whose tangent runs along the segment is within the point tolerance of it, as a circle judges a segment by how near its centre's foot comes to the circumference.

A circle, an arc or another ellipse is read along the rim: its equation at the point of the rim at angle t is a function of t made of two harmonics, a polynomial of degree four in z = e^{it}. Its turning points come from the roots of that polynomial, and between two of them it runs one way, so each crossing is found inside a bracket and to the last digit. A rim that comes within the point tolerance without crossing touches it, and gives one point, midway between the two curves; two crossings no further apart than twice the point tolerance, their half chord within it, are one point at the middle of the chord, as two circles' are.

The order is the circle's. Crossings of a circle, an arc or another ellipse come in the order of the eccentric angle of this ellipse, from the end of its major axis round counter-clockwise, ties broken on X and then Y. Those of a segment run along the segment; those of a polyline, a polygon, a rectangle, a triangle or a curved chain or loop come edge by edge in the shape's own order, each edge's in its own order; those of a face come from the outline, then from each hole.

member.summary: The numbers behind an ellipse, each read on the ellipse scaled so that its major radius is one and its minor radius is the ratio of the two, which keeps every one of them between nought and one whatever the drawing measures.
The shortest segment joining the rim of an ellipse to another shape, and which edge of a shape lies nearest it.
member.remarks: The segment runs from boundary to boundary, as a circle's does: it starts on the rim and ends on the other shape's edge or curve, so a shape lying wholly inside the ellipse still gets the gap out to the rim, where reads the region and answers nought. Where the two cross, the segment has no length and sits at the first crossing, in the order the circle's would come: along a segment, edge by edge round a polygon, by the eccentric angle round a circle, an arc or another ellipse.
member.summary: What an ellipse asks of a ray in the plane.
member.remarks: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so against an ellipse it is cut: into the segment from its origin out past the farthest the ellipse could reach along it, the centre brought onto the ray and the major radius added, by a margin of a millimetre or a hundred point tolerances, whichever is more. Every point of the ellipse lies behind that end, so the segment meets the ellipse where the ray does and is asked as any segment is. Against the ellipse round the origin with radii 50 and 30, the ray from (-100, 0) along X is asked as the segment from there to (51, 0). The ray asks nothing of the ellipse: the ellipse is asked from the ellipse.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.GetClosestPointOnBoundary(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Gets the point of the rim of an ellipse nearest a point, including for points inside it.
member.returns: The nearest point of the rim.

remarks.para: Worked out by Eberly's robust method: the point is reflected into the first quadrant of the ellipse's own frame, the one root of the equation of the nearest point found there by halving a bracket, and the answer reflected back. It is right at the centre, on both axes, inside and outside, and for an ellipse a thousand times longer than it is wide.

Where two points of the rim are equally near, one is picked. The centre of an ellipse 300 by 100 is 100 from the two ends of the minor axis, and the one at t = 90° is given. A point on the major axis inside, nearer the centre than the centre of curvature of the end of the axis, is nearest two points mirrored across the axis, and the one on the positive side of the minor axis is given. The centre of a circle is as near every point of the rim, and the end of the minor axis at t = 90° is given there too, so that the answer does not jump between radii equal and radii a hair apart; gives the point at angle nought instead.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2)
member.summary: Applies a transformation to an ellipse. Every transformation that does not flatten the plane gives an ellipse: a move, a turn, a mirror, a scaling even or uneven, and a shear.
member.returns: The transformed ellipse.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.
Thrown when the transformation flattens the plane onto a line or a point: when the area it scales by is no more than 1E-12 of the square of its size.

remarks.para: The radii and the major axis come from the singular values of the transformation applied to the two semi-axes: a circle of radius 100 scaled by 3 along X and 1 along Y is the ellipse 300 by 100 along X. The zero of the eccentric angle goes to the end of the new major axis nearer where the old one went, so it is generally not the image of the old zero. When the two new radii agree to 1E-12 the result is a circle, and its major axis is where the old one went, so a turn carries the zero of the angle round with it.

A transformation that turns the plane over, a mirror or a negative scaling, reverses the way the eccentric angle runs round the rim as seen in the old frame: the new ellipse still runs counter-clockwise, so the points the old one reached at increasing angles are reached by the new one at decreasing angles.

Whether the two radii agree to 1E-12, the major axis then along the first semi-axis.
member.remarks: Inlined, so that taking it out of costs that no time: called, it made a million transformations 45 ms to 53 ms on .NET 10.

member.summary: Approximates the rim of an ellipse as a polygon that strays no further from it than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between an edge and the rim, in drawing units. Zero picks of the minor radius, which is the circle's share when the radii are equal.
member.returns: A polygon inscribed in the ellipse, counter-clockwise from the end of the major axis, its first point not repeated; symmetric about both axes, with a corner at each end of each.
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is negative or not a number, or needs more than 1 048 576 corners.
member.remarks: The corners are spaced by the bend of the rim, close where it turns sharply at the ends of the major axis and far apart along the flat sides: an ellipse 1 000 by 1 at the automatic tolerance of 0.002 takes 84 edges, where an even step in the angle would need about 1 571. A circle takes as many as gives, or up to three more to make a multiple of four; the same bend decides the count however fine the tolerance, up to 1 048 576 corners in all, and a tolerance that needs more is refused.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.ByChord(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,System.Double,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Gets the corners of the rim spaced by its bend so that no chord strays further than a tolerance.
member.remarks: A chord over the eccentric angles t to t + h strays furthest from the rim at the middle angle, the point where the rim runs parallel to it, by exactly 2 sin²(h/4) ab / (a² sin² m + b² cos² m)^½ at the middle angle m. The first quarter is walked out from the end of the major axis, each step the longest that keeps that within the tolerance, and mirrored into the other three. The rim bends less and less along the first quarter, so a step worked out at its start is safe and is lengthened while it stays so.

The edge's own end points are weighed beside the arc's, so an edge ending on the rim is nought away.

member.returns: Nought when the two overlap; otherwise how far the circle's centre is from the rim, less its radius. The circle of radius 50 about (0, 300) is 150 from the ellipse 300 by 100 centred on the origin.

member.summary: Gets the distance from an ellipse to an arc, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance; not read, since a distance is measured rather than judged.
member.returns: Nought only where the arc truly meets the region, crossing the rim or lying inside; otherwise the shortest gap, measured exactly. The left half of the circle of radius 0.0008 about (60.0013, 0) is 0.0005 from the ellipse 60 by 25 about the origin at a tolerance of 0.001, where its ends alone were weighed and 0.0013 was read.
member.remarks: The nearest pair is at an end of the arc, or on a normal of the rim that runs through the arc's centre, since there the gap runs square to both. Whether any of the arc lies inside is read exactly, from the turning points of the ellipse's equation along the arc.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2)

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the distance between two ellipses.
member.param: The tolerance; not read, as two circles read none.
member.returns: Nought when the two overlap, one inside the other included; otherwise the shortest gap between the rims. The ellipse 300 by 100 centred on the origin and the one 100 by 50 about (0, 250) along Y are 50 apart.
member.remarks: Whether they overlap is read exactly, from the turning points of the equation of the one along the rim of the other. The gap is the least distance from a point of the first rim to the second, found by Brent's method from each least of 36 starting points round the first, each side of it on its own: 32 spread evenly half a step off the axes, so that none of them is an end of one, and the four ends of the axes, where a thin ellipse turns fastest. Checked against a dense independent search on 80 000 pairs apart, 20 000 from each of four seeds, as thin as a thousand to one: the worst relative error was 3E-13.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Reaches(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2)
member.summary: Says whether a segment reaches into the region at all: its point nearest the centre, in the frame where the ellipse is the unit circle, lies inside.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Reaches(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2)
member.summary: Says whether an arc reaches into the region at all: an end lies inside, or the arc crosses the rim.
member.remarks: An arc with both ends outside reaches in only by crossing the rim, where the circle carrying it does. Those are the changes of sign of the circle's equation along the rim, |P(t) - c|² - r², which is read in drawing units however the two compare in size; each is kept when the arc sweeps over it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Reaches(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2)
member.summary: Says whether two ellipses overlap at all: either centre lies inside the other, or the rim of one reaches into the other.
member.remarks: The rim read is the one that keeps the reading well scaled: the equation of an ellipse grows as the square of distances over its radii, so the larger one's equation is read along the smaller one's rim, and a hair-thin ellipse a millionth of a unit from a large one is not taken for one touching it by rounding.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Nearest(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@)
member.summary: Gets the shortest pair joining the rim to a segment that does not cross it.
member.remarks: The pair is at an end of the segment, or at the rim point whose tangent runs along the segment and its foot on it, where the gap runs square to both. Inside the ellipse the gap to the rim bends down along any segment, so there the nearest is always an end. The start is weighed first and ties keep the first.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.NearestToCircle(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@)
member.summary: Gets the shortest pair joining the rim to the circumference of a circle that does not cross it.
member.remarks: The nearest point of a circle to a point of the rim lies straight out from its centre, |P - c| - r away, so the pair is on a normal of the rim through the centre: at the rim point nearest the centre, or at another foot of a normal from it, the furthest among them when the ellipse lies inside the circle.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Outward(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Gets the point of a circle straight out from its centre towards a point, or the end of its radius along X when the point is the centre.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.NearestToArc(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@)
member.summary: Gets the shortest pair joining the rim to an arc that does not cross it.
member.remarks: The pair is at an end of the arc, or on a normal of the rim through the arc's centre, on either side of the centre; each candidate is clamped onto the arc, with no tolerance, and joined to the rim point nearest it, so every pair weighed is one the two shapes really hold. A tolerance would snap a candidate within it of the arc's centre to the arc's start: an arc of radius 0.0008 would be weighed at its two ends only.

member.summary: Gets the least distance between two rims that do not cross, and the eccentric angle on the first where it is.
member.remarks: The distance from the first rim to the second is read at 32 angles half a step off the axes and at the four ends of the axes, where a thin ellipse turns within a sliver of angle; each that is no further than its two neighbours starts Brent's method between them, and the least of what those find is the answer.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Meet(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Wave,GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Other,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets where the rim crosses or touches the curve whose equation along it is a wave.
member.remarks: Between two turning points the wave runs one way, so a change of sign there is one crossing, found to the last digit. A turning point with no crossing on either side is where the curve comes nearest without crossing; within the point tolerance it touches, at the point of the rim nearest the curve.

member.summary: Adds every touch of the rim and another ellipse: each least of the true gap between the two rims that comes within the point tolerance, away from the crossings.

remarks.para: The other's equation turns where the rim runs along a copy of it scaled about its centre, not along the curve a fixed distance off it, and for a thin ellipse the two lie far apart: a needle 1 by 0.003 resting 0.0005 above a rim has its equation turn where the gap is 0.16. So the gap itself is searched, and only where it can come within the tolerance. A point on the copy scaled by q lies at least |q - 1| times the other's minor radius from its rim, so the gap can be that small only where the equation, q² - 1, keeps within a band about nought; the stretches of the rim inside the band are found exactly, from the turning points and the band's edges.

A stretch holding one crossing and too short for the rims to turn parallel in it holds no touch, and is passed over: that is every stretch round a clean crossing. The others are walked with steps no longer than the gap less the tolerance, which no part of the rim nearer the other than the tolerance can hide between, and never shorter than half the tolerance; where the gap stays within the tolerance and hardly changes, the rims running along each other, the step doubles, up to 32 times the tolerance. Within twice the tolerance of a crossing the walk jumps over it, since anything found there is that crossing. Each least of the walk below one and a half times the tolerance is brought down by Brent's method between its neighbours, and kept when it is a least of the gap inside them, within the tolerance and not within twice it of a crossing. The point is midway between the rim and the other, so the same touch comes back whichever ellipse asks.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Clean(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2,System.Double[],GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2[],System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Says whether a stretch holds one crossing and is too short for the rims to turn parallel within it, so that it can hold no touch: at a touch the two tangents run along each other, at the crossing they meet at an angle, and along a length L of the rim neither turns by more than its greatest bend, a / b², times L.
