member.summary: Gets the perimeter of the ellipse with a major radius of one, by the arithmetic-geometric mean of Gauss and Kummer.
member.param: The minor radius over the major one, above nought and no more than one.
member.remarks: The mean of one and the ratio converges quadratically, so a ratio of a thousandth takes six rounds. Each round halves the gap between the two and adds twice the weight of the last round's square of that gap.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.UnitArc(System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Gets the length along the rim of the ellipse with a major radius of one, from the end of its major axis to an eccentric angle within the first quarter.
member.param: The minor radius over the major one.
The eccentric angle, from nought to a quarter turn.
member.remarks: The rim runs at a speed of the root of sin² + ratio² cos², which is the ratio times the root of 1 - m sin² with m = 1 - 1/ratio², so the length is the ratio times the incomplete integral E(angle | m) of the second kind. Written with Carlson's R_F and R_D and their arguments scaled by ratio², both terms are positive and none of them is large, however thin the ellipse.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.UnitAngleAtArc(System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Gets the eccentric angle within the first quarter at which reaches a length, by Newton's method kept inside a bracket that halves whenever a step would leave it.
member.param: The minor radius over the major one.
The length along the rim from the end of the major axis, no more than a quarter of the perimeter.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Carlson(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Gets Carlson's symmetric integrals R_F(x, y, z) and R_D(x, y, z) together, by the duplication they share.
member.remarks: Each round moves the three arguments a quarter of the way towards each other and leaves both integrals as they were; once the arguments agree to a few thousandths, a short series in their spread gives each to the last digit. The rounds stop when both series are that close, the tighter one being R_D's.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.UnitClosest(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Gets the point of the rim of the ellipse with a major radius of one nearest a point in its first quadrant, by Eberly's robust method ("Distance from a Point to an Ellipse, an Ellipsoid, or a Hyperellipsoid").
member.param: The minor radius over the major one.
How far the point lies along the major axis, nought or more.
How far the point lies along the minor axis, nought or more.
The cosine of the eccentric angle of the nearest point.
The sine of the eccentric angle of the nearest point.

remarks.para: The nearest point is (along / (1 + s ratio²), across / (1 + s)) for the one root s of the equation saying it lies on the rim. The root is found by halving a bracket, which cannot fail where Newton's method can; it is written in the denominator 1 + s rather than in s, so that a point a hair off the major axis, whose denominator is tiny, still finds its root to the last digit. Where the bracket spans more than a factor of two it is halved at its geometric middle, so a root a long way out takes a few rounds more rather than a thousand.

A point on the major axis, inside, nearer the centre than the centre of curvature of the end of the axis, is nearest two points mirrored across it; the one on the positive side is taken. The centre is nearest the two ends of the minor axis, and the positive one is taken; a circle has every point of its rim as near, and the same point is taken, the end of the minor axis, where Eberly's method left alone would give the end of the major.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Wave
member.summary: A function of the eccentric angle made of a constant and the first two harmonics: c0 + c1 cos t + s1 sin t + c2 cos 2t + s2 sin 2t.
member.remarks: The square of the distance from a point of the rim to a fixed point, and the equation of a circle or of another ellipse read along the rim, are all of this form. Written in z = e^{it} and multiplied by z², it is a polynomial of degree four, so it turns at most four times round the rim and crosses nought at most four times.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Turns(GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Wave,System.Double[])
member.summary: Gets the angles at which a function of two harmonics turns, its maxima and minima, sorted from nought up to a full turn.
member.returns: How many angles were found: none for a function that does not change at all, else two to four.
member.remarks: The slope is a function of the same form; its roots are the arguments of the roots of a polynomial of degree four in z = e^{it}, found together by the Aberth–Ehrlich iteration, which converges for every root at once from any start and needs no bracket. A root of the slope is a root of that polynomial on the unit circle, so each argument is a candidate; Newton's method on the slope itself then polishes it to the last digit. A slope whose second harmonic is rounding next to the rest is read as a polynomial of degree two, which it then is.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse2.Aberth(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double[],System.Double[])
member.summary: Finds the four roots of the monic polynomial z⁴ + c3 z³ + c2 z² + c1 z + c0 together.
member.remarks: Each round moves every estimate by Newton's step corrected for the pull of the others, which keeps two estimates from settling on the same root; the starts are spread round the unit circle, where the roots of these polynomials lie in pairs z and 1/z̄. A double root is reached more slowly, to half the digits, which is all a turning point needs: it only brackets the crossings either side of it, each of which is then found to the last digit.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse3
member.summary: Whether the rim of an ellipse in space touches another shape.

remarks.para: As the circle in space is asked: touching is crossing, read from the rim, except where the other shape holds the whole rim without crossing it. A plane the ellipse lies in, a flat region of its plane that holds it wholly, and a body or a box it lies inside all touch it and cross it nowhere; so do a curve lying on the rim along its length. Those are told by where the rim starts, the end of its major axis, as the circle tells them by where it starts.
The disc is not read. A segment through the middle of the ellipse that never reaches the rim touches nothing here, as it touches nothing of a circle; is the one that reads the ellipse as filled.

member.summary:
What can be asked of an ellipse in space: how long its rim is, where a point falls on it, whether a point lies on its disc, how it moves, how it looks seen square onto a plane, and how it is cut into straight pieces.
An ellipse in space is a flat region, as a circle in space is. Everything within its plane is 's arithmetic, read in the ellipse's own frame: the centre, the major axis, the minor axis and the normal. A point is read as how far it lies along the major axis, along the minor, and above the plane; the answers in the plane are put back the same way. So every answer is exact or worked out to rounding, none of them sampled, and an ellipse whose radii are equal answers as a does.
Where the rim of an ellipse in space crosses another shape.

remarks.para: These are the circle in space's questions, asked of the rim as asks them of a circle: the rim is what counts, not the disc, so a segment through the middle of the ellipse that never reaches the rim crosses nothing. None of it is sampled. Two readings do all the work, as for the circle.

In the plane. Where the other shape shares the ellipse's plane, it is laid out in the ellipse's own frame and answers: a segment edge by edge, a circle, an arc or another ellipse as a curve. Whether the two share a plane is the circle's test: the rim stands off the other plane by no more than the planar tolerance, and the centre lies on it. A curve laid out keeps its radii, and may lean off the plane, so a crossing read there is kept only where it lies within the point tolerance of both rims in space, a touch only where the rims come within it of each other in space, and the rim is then searched in space for where the two pass within it of each other, as it is for curves not in one plane.

Not in the plane. Two planes meet in a line, and every point the rim shares with anything lying in the other plane is on that line, where the rim is crossed in closed form; the points the other shape holds are kept. A segment or a ray not lying in the plane meets it at one point, kept when it is on the rim. Two ellipses are read from the one that comes first in a fixed order, whichever is asked first, and the rim touches another ellipse's, a circle or an arc besides where they pass within the point tolerance of each other off that line.

The order is the circle's: along the line the two planes share, along a segment or a ray, edge by edge for a flat shape, face by face for a body, and in the plane along the line square to the one through the two centres, as two circles' crossings lie along their radical line; two ellipses in the plane are put in that order from the one they are read from, and the other way round where the other is asked first. A place two faces or two edges share is named once.

member.summary: Determines whether the rim of an ellipse in space touches an arc, within a tolerance.
member.returns: true if the arc crosses or touches the rim, or lies along it; otherwise, false. A quarter of the circle of radius 100 about the origin lies along the ellipse 100 by 99.9995 about the same centre, within the point tolerance of a thousandth, crosses it nowhere, and touches it.
member.remarks: An arc lying on the rim crosses it nowhere and touches it all along, so where the ellipse is the arc's circle, within the tolerance, the two touch when either holds an end of the other, as two arcs of one circle do, or where the arc comes within the point tolerance of the rim anywhere else: an ellipse 100.0009 by 99.9995 leaning 8E-6 radians off the plane of the circle of radius 100 about its centre touches the arc running the long way round that circle from 0.3 radians past the end of its major axis to 0.3 short of it, whose ends lie 0.0011 off the rim and which comes within 0.00042 of it between. Asked so, a near copy whose ends stand off is searched along its rim, about half a millisecond, where the ends alone take a few microseconds.

member.summary: Determines whether the rim of an ellipse in space touches a circle, within a tolerance.
member.returns: true if the rims cross or touch, or draw the same curve; otherwise, false. The circle of radius 50 lying in the plan about the origin is inside the ellipse 300 by 100 about it and touches nothing: the rims are what count, not the discs.
member.remarks: Drawing the same curve, the two touch where either holds where the other starts, or where the rims come within the point tolerance of each other anywhere else: an ellipse 100.0009 by 99.9995 about the centre of the circle of radius 100, its major axis towards where the circle starts and leaning 8E-6 radians, stands 0.0012 off the circle at either start, comes within 0.00042 of it elsewhere, and touches it. Where neither start lies on the other, the rim is searched, which takes up to about a millisecond and a half, where the starts alone take a few microseconds.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse3.Passes(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse3,GeometryHelper.Core.NearPass3.Target,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether the rim passes within the point tolerance of a curve drawing the same one anywhere, searched along the rim ().
member.remarks: Two curves drawing the same one cross nowhere, and touch where either holds where the other starts; but a copy leaning off the plane by up to the planar tolerance may stand further than the point tolerance off the other there and come within it elsewhere: an ellipse 100.0009 by 99.9995 about the centre of a circle of radius 100, its major axis towards where the circle starts and leaning 8E-6 radians, stands 0.0012 off the circle at either start and comes within 0.00042 of it elsewhere, and was taken to touch nothing. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Ellipse3.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3)
member.summary: Applies a transformation to an ellipse in space. Every transformation that does not flatten the ellipse's plane gives an ellipse: a move, a turn, a mirror, a scaling even or uneven, and a shear.
member.returns: The transformed ellipse.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.
Thrown when the transformation cannot be undone, as throws for a circle's plane: judged by , within the default tolerance. One that can be undone, however hard it squashes, gives a thin ellipse.

remarks.para: The images of the two semi-axes span the new plane, and the radii and the major axis come from their singular values in it, as finds them: a circle of radius 100 in the plan scaled by 3 along X is the ellipse 300 by 100 along X. The zero of the eccentric angle goes to the end of the new major axis nearer where the old one went; when the two new radii agree to 1E-12 the result is a circle, and its major axis is where the old one went.

The normal goes where sends a plane's, and so where a circle's goes: a mirror in the plan turns an ellipse lying in it over, its normal down. Under any mirror the eccentric angle then reaches the images of the old rim's points in the opposite order: the old point at 30° goes to the new point at -30°.

One leaning more than that is given, however thin.
member.remarks: A circle of radius 300 tilted 60° from the plan is, in the plan, an ellipse 300 by 150, its major axis along the line the tilt turns about. The projection is a transformation of the ellipse's plane, so the arithmetic is that of : a circle parallel to the plane stays a circle, its angle starting where the circle's does.

Near the end of the major axis the stretch reaches back over the place named, and the run of that place, the stretch about its angle the one read holds, read at points as reads them, is left out of it: begun inside that run, the search read it and a touch beyond it as one run across the rise between, and took the touch for the place named. A rim 36.66 by 30.95 passing an ellipse 21.88 by 0.908, b² / a 3.77 tolerances at a tolerance of 0.01, within 0.0020 at two places 0.056 apart either side of its end, the gap rising 4 % above the tolerance between, was given one place.

A place found there is one already named where it stands within the tolerance of one, or where either curve runs within the tolerance of the other all the way between the two, each read at points as reads them: the end of a rim 100 000 by 1 lies within the tolerance of a copy 0.001 larger all round it, while from the larger the gap rises a hair above it round the end, and each end is one place. Where the other is nowhere so narrow, or nothing was named, it is not searched, and the answer is the rim's alone, as before.

Only the two sides of the ellipse not read are parted so. Two touches the reading of a narrow ellipse itself makes one stay one: read first, a needle 0.754 by 0.108 passing a rim 31 536 by 14 839 at two places 0.0357 apart, the gap rising 15 % above the tolerance between at a tolerance of 0.01, is given one place, its crossing of the rim's plane, which stands within the tolerance of both.

member.summary: Gets the points of the rim on the line where its plane meets another plane, in order along the line.

remarks.para: The workhorse of every pair not in one plane, as it is for the circle. The line is found from the ellipse's centre and read in the ellipse's own frame as the line u n_u + v n_v = p, n its unit normal there. With h = √(a² n_u² + b² n_v²), how far the rim reaches along n, the line cuts a chord whose half is (a b / h²) √(h² - p²) in drawing units; for a circle, √(r² - p²).

A line grazing the rim is judged as the circle judges one, by four times the square of that half chord, D = 4 (a b)² (h² - p²) / h⁴, negative for a line passing outside: below minus the square of the point tolerance it misses; within that square either way it touches, at the middle of the chord; above it, it cuts at two points. For a circle D is the circle's own discriminant and the bounds are the circle's. Judged instead by how deep the chord cuts, as a segment lying in the plane is, a chord 1.66 long cutting 0.0008 into an ellipse of radius 431 was one point at its middle, 0.8 from either true crossing, and a circle standing on one of them was found to cross the ellipse nowhere. Judged in the frame scaled to the unit circle, the bound is stretched by a / b.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Face2
member.summary: What a face meets, and how far off it is.

remarks.para: A face is an outline with holes in it, so none of this is the polygon answer: the boundary of a face is its outline together with the rim of every hole, and the material is what lies inside the outline and outside all of them.

Crossings are the union over that boundary, and the shortest joining segment is the shortest over it, which is why a probe standing on the material still gets a segment with a length: it is the reach to the nearest edge of the material, the same reading gives.

Touching is the one that needs care. A probe collides with the face when it collides with the outline and no hole has swallowed it whole. A probe that crosses no rim of a hole is either wholly inside that hole, or wholly outside it, or holds the hole within itself, and those are told apart by asking where one point of the probe falls and, for a probe that has an inside, whether the rim falls within it.

The distance reads the face by its material: nought where the probe meets it, and otherwise the gap between the boundaries, measured exactly, which is then the gap to the material. A probe wholly inside a hole is as far away as the rim of that hole, and a probe holding the whole face collides with it. Two faces are asked the same way, each one's material against the other's.

member.summary: What a face meets of a ray in the plane, and how far off it is.
member.remarks: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so against a face it is cut: into the segment from its origin out past the farthest a corner of the outline reaches along it, by a margin of a millimetre or a hundred point tolerances, whichever is more. Every point of the face lies behind that end, so the segment meets the face where the ray does and is asked as any segment is. Against the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin and a hole 40 by 40 in its middle, the ray from (-50, 50) along X is asked as the segment from there to (101, 50).

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3
member.summary: The exact gap between an arc in space and a point, a segment, a flat region, the surface of a body or another arc.

remarks.para: Nothing here is widened by a tolerance, and a crossing is not looked for by sampling. An arc is the circle it lies on less the stretch it does not sweep, and the nearest pair of an arc and anything else is one of a short list, every entry of which is a real distance from a real point of the arc, so the least of them is the gap: an end of the arc against the other shape; an end, a corner or an edge of the other shape against the arc; and the places where the distance along the arc turns, which for a straight line, a plane or a segment are the roots of a trigonometric polynomial of the second degree in the angle. That polynomial is a quartic in the tangent of half the angle measured from the middle of the arc's sweep, where no root of the arc's is near infinity, whose real roots are found between the roots of its derivatives, so none is lost to a coarse step.

Two arcs are the one case with no closed form. The distance from a point of one to the other arc is exact, and it changes by no more than the length moved, so the arc is halved until each stretch of it is proved further than the distance asked, or a point within it is found: a proof, not a sample. Circles on one axis in parallel planes stand the same distance apart at every angle, so their ends decide them. Arcs nearly so are compared with the copy of one that stands exactly on the axis of the other, which the ends decide and which is never further from it than the tilt times the radius and the offset of the centres; that proves the pair clear when the copy is clear by more. What neither settles within its budget, a pair of partial arcs nearly on one axis whose distance stays near-constant just beyond the one asked, is searched and not proved: the walk of the arcs, every low point polished, decides it.
A shape's own sides are exact. A segment a caller gave that is no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start, unless it truly meets the arc, as the straight shapes read it.

member.summary: The exact gap between straight shapes in space and flat regions: nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the length of the shortest segment between them, however small.

remarks.para: A flat region here is a triangle, a polygon or a face, read filled. Two shapes meet where an edge of one passes through the other, where one holds a corner of the other, or where they lie along each other; apart, the nearest pair always has an end of a segment on one side, so the gap is the least of four things: a segment through the region, the height of an end over it where its foot lands on it, the distance of an end to its rim where it does not, and the distance of the segment to each rim edge. Nothing here widens a shape by a tolerance: a segment starting 0.0005 off the square 100 by 100 in its plane is 0.0005 from it, and one hovering 0.0003 over it is 0.0003 from it, from either side and in whatever plane they lie. Whether the two collide is then the question whether this gap is within the point tolerance.

Shapes in one plane are laid out in it to ask where a foot lands and where a segment crosses the plane, through the containment of the plane with no slack, a rim counting as inside; the height over the plane stays in the gap, so a shape off the plane by less than the planar tolerance is as far in space as it is.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Curve.CoaxialCopy(GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Curve,GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Curve@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Makes the copy of another arc that stands on this arc's axis, turned to lie in a plane parallel to this arc's, when the two stand nearly so, and gets how far any point of the other is from its place on the copy.
member.remarks: The copy is the other arc turned about its centre until its normal is this arc's (or its opposite), then moved across to the axis, so each of its points stands from the point of the other no further than the chord of the turn at its radius, 2 r sin(a / 2), and the move. The copy is on one axis with this arc in parallel planes, whose distance the ends decide. It is made only when the shift is a quarter of the radii or less, where the bound is worth having.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Curve.Reaches(GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Curve,System.Double,System.Double@)
member.summary: Decides whether this arc comes within a distance of another arc: clear when every stretch of it is proved further than that, within when a point of it is found no further, unknown when the proof outruns its budget.
member.param: When clear, the least of the bounds that proved the stretches clear, above the distance asked; when within, a distance no more than the one asked.
member.remarks: The distance from a point of this arc to the other changes by no more than the length moved, so a stretch of width w whose ends stand f1 and f2 from the other arc is no nearer than (f1 + f2 - radius w) / 2. A stretch not proved clear is halved until the radius times its width is a millionth of the distance asked, and the least over what is left is found by golden section. So the answer is a proof where it comes. The one pair of arcs it cannot settle in the budget is two partial arcs whose distance stays near-constant just beyond the one asked, which takes a stretch as small as a hundred-thousandth of the circle; the copy on the axis () is tried first, and only if that does not prove it clear is the pair searched by the walk of the arcs, not proved.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Curve.LipschitzTo(GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Curve)
member.summary: Gets how fast the distance from a point of this arc to a whole circle can change per radian: no more than the radius, and far less where the circles lie nearly on one axis.
member.remarks: The distance to a circle has a gradient of unit length, along (h n + (q - r) e) / d for the height h over the circle's plane, the distance q from its axis, the unit direction e out from the axis and the distance d. The point moves along the tangent t of this circle, so the rate is the radius times (h (n.t) + (q - r) (e.t)) / d, which is no more than the radius times the root of (n.t) squared and (e.t) squared. Here n.t is no more than the sine of the angle between the planes, and e.t is the distance between the centres, less the height times n.t, over q, which is at least the radius times the cosine of that angle, less the distance between the centres.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Stationary(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Int32@)
member.summary: Finds the angles between two limits where c1 cos t + s1 sin t + s2 sin 2t + c2 cos 2t is nought, and the places beside them where it nearly is.
member.remarks: With z = tan(t / 2) the polynomial becomes a quartic: (c2 - c1) z^4 + (2 s1 - 4 s2) z^3 - 6 c2 z^2 + (2 s1 + 4 s2) z + (c1 + c2). Its real roots are found between the roots of its derivative, which are found between the roots of the derivative of that, so none is missed and a pair standing close together is told apart. The turning points of the quartic come with them: where a pair of roots has just left the real line, its real part is such a point, and the distance there is a real distance all the same. The angle half a turn round, where z is infinite, is asked too. Every angle is kept as it came and as Newton's steps on the polynomial in t itself polish it, since both are real distances; and a root the polynomial barely leaves the nought at, a double or a triple one, comes back as a seed for the caller to minimise the distance itself round.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.SegmentToSegment(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Gets the distance between two segments, each the segment it is however short, the same whichever is asked first and whichever way round either is given.

remarks.para: The segments are put in a fixed order before anything is worked out, each with its smaller end first and the pair by the coordinates of those ends, so the answer is the same to the last bit whichever way it is asked, and two ways of rounding the same pair cannot differ.

Two segments that cross, or whose lines come nearest inside both, are as far apart as the lines are, worked out from the point where they come nearest and corrected twice by the residual, which keeps a pair tilted a few millionths of a radian exact where the plain formula loses ten digits. Otherwise the nearest pair has an end of one segment in it, and the answer is the least of the four ends against the other segments.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Beyond(System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Determines whether a lower bound on a gap stands clear of the least gap found, so that the candidate it bounds can be passed over.
member.remarks: A candidate is passed over only when its bound clears the least by a billionth of a millimetre and a trillionth of the gap, more than rounding can make up. Two candidates of one gap round differently in the last digits, so one that merely ties is weighed all the same, and the answer is the least of every candidate whichever order they are weighed in. The same rule serves a distance and a collision, which stops at the first candidate within the distance it is asked about, so that the two weigh the same candidates and cannot disagree about a pair standing that distance apart. A bound that is not a number is never beyond it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Holds(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Determines whether a solid holds a point, on its surface included, to within rounding: the point is held where the material is and a hair outside is outside.
member.remarks: The point is located under a tolerance of a billionth of a millimetre, not of nought: a face holds a crossing of a ray only within the planar tolerance of its plane, and a crossing that rounding leaves a trillionth off the plane, as it does in a body turned about in space, would be refused by one of nought and the count of the crossings would come out wrong. Further out than a million the rounding of the coordinates is more than a billionth, and the tolerance is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point instead: a U turned about in space 5E7 out left the crossings of a ray 1.9E-9 off the planes of its faces, refused them, and held a point 0.052 outside it. The tolerance of the vectors stays a billionth, since a direction has no size.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Gap3.Fine(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Gets how far outside a body a point is held in it by : a billionth of a millimetre, which no model comes near and rounding stays well inside, or, where the body or the point stands further out than a million, 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the two, a few times the most the rounding needs there. Of some 160 000 points located in and beside bodies up to 1E9 out, 1E-16 of it got 300 wrong and 3E-16 none.
member.remarks: A coordinate that is infinite or not a number has no rounding to scale by, and the point is held to a billionth, as it always was.

member.remarks: A box is convex, so a segment clear of it has its nearest pair at an end of the segment, or between its inside and an edge of the box: against a face the distance changes linearly along the segment and is least at an end, or stays the same along it, and then an edge of the face is as near. This is the answer of the body of the box () without cutting the body into triangles.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2
member.summary: Where a straight shape meets one that curves.
member.remarks: The curved shapes could already be asked about the straight ones; these are the pairs that had no mirror image to fall back on, so that a polygon can be asked about a bare arc, and a rectangle about a chain, in the same breath as everything else. A rectangle is read as its own polygon, and an arc is met as an arc rather than cut into pieces first.
member.summary: Provides static calculation methods for geometric intersections and finding exact intersection points.
Where a ray in the plane crosses another shape.

remarks.para: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so against a shape with an end to it, it is cut: into the segment from its origin out past the farthest the shape reaches along it, by a margin of a millimetre or a hundred point tolerances, whichever is more. Every crossing lies before that end, and the end itself is never one, so the segment crosses where the ray does and is asked as any segment is, its crossings ordered and de-duplicated as a segment's are. Against the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin, the ray from (-50, 50) along X is asked as the segment from there to (101, 50), and crosses at (0, 50) and (100, 50).

The parallel test of a segment measures the drift over the longer of the two, and for the cut that is as far as the other shape reaches: the ray is drawn as far as the shape makes it. Against another ray nothing is cut, and parallel is read by angle alone.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2.TryIntersectWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Enums.LineExtension,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Tries to calculate the intersection point between two line segments, reading either or both as the infinite line carrying it, within tolerance.
member.param: Which of the two may be reached past its endpoints.
The resulting intersection point if successful.
member.returns: true if the lines meet within the reach allowed; otherwise, false.
member.remarks:
This is AutoCAD's IntersectWith with its Intersect option: finds where two axes would cross however short they are drawn, where the first would reach the second if it were extended. Parallel lines are refused whatever the extension, as they are without one: they either never meet or share a whole stretch, and neither is a single point. The point returned lies on every segment that was not extended.
A segment that is not extended is reached up to the point tolerance past its ends, and the point is clamped onto it, so that splitting, trimming and extending find the crossing on both. This places points; it is not a test of contact. The segment ending at (10, 0) and the one leaving (10.00135, 0.00078) at 60 degrees meet here at (10, 0) at a tolerance of a thousandth, though they are 0.00156 apart and do not collide.
A segment no longer than the point tolerance has no direction to be reached along, and meets the other, with neither extended, only where it truly crosses it: at a thousandth, the one from (5, 0.0004) to (5, -0.0005) meets the segment from the origin to (10, 0) at (5, 0), and the one from (5, 0.0008) to (5, 0.0002) meets it nowhere.
A segment with a coordinate that is not a finite number meets nothing, and the answer is false: the segment from (NaN, 0) to (0, 100) and the one from the origin to (0, 100), which share an end, were given a point of NaN.
member.exception: Thrown when the extension is not a defined value.

true when the second segment is one you give.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2.IsParallelOver(System.Double,System.Boolean,System.Boolean,System.Double,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether two members are parallel as far as finding the one point where they cross goes.
member.param: The sine of the angle between the two.
Whether the first is read as its infinite line.
Whether the second is read as its infinite line.
The length of the first as drawn.
The length of the second as drawn.
member.returns: true when there is no single crossing to give.
member.remarks: Two members are parallel when they draw apart by less than the point tolerance along the longer of the members drawn: to within the tolerance they are then one line or two lines side by side, and neither gives one point. The angle alone decided before, against a whole degree, however long the members — two ten-metre members crossing at 0.9 degrees, 157 apart at their ends, crossed nowhere while CollidesWith said true and DistanceTo nought. Only two infinite lines have no length to measure over, and those still go by the angle.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2.TryIntersectWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Tries to calculate the intersection points between a circle and a line segment within tolerance.
member.remarks:
A line passing outside the circle within the point tolerance of its rim touches it once, at the foot of the perpendicular from the centre. A line passing inside it crosses it twice, each crossing kept where it lies on the segment; two crossings no further apart than twice the point tolerance are one, at the foot. The segment 50 long from (0, 49.9995) along (1, 0.001), against the circle of radius 50 about the origin at a tolerance of 0.001, leaves the circle once, at (0.1791, 49.99968). A segment whose line runs inside the rim within the tolerance of it, but which crosses the rim nowhere along its length, touches it once where it comes within the tolerance: at the foot when the foot is on it. At a tolerance of 0.1 the segment from (-0.2, 49.97) to (0.2, 49.97) touches the circle of radius 50 at (0, 49.97).
Any other segment touches the circle exactly where it comes within the point tolerance of its rim, as the shortest line to the rim measures it, however far its line runs on before it would cross: once, at its point nearest the centre where it lies outside, else at its end nearer the rim. At a tolerance of 0.001, the segment from (0.05, 50.0005) to (10, 50.0005), whose line passes nearest the circle of radius 50 0.05 behind its start, touches it at its start, 0.000525 off; the one from (0, 49.95) to (2.225, 49.95) at its end, 0.00047 inside; and the one from (0.0009, 0.0019) to (1, 0.0019), whose line passes 0.0009 above the circle of radius 0.001 about the origin just behind its start, does not touch it, the start being 0.0011 off. A crossing up to the tolerance past an end, taken at that end, within twice the tolerance of the other crossing is the same touch, and counts once: the segment from (-1, 0) to (0.0004, 0) meets the circle of radius 0.0012 about the origin at (-0.0012, 0) only. A segment no longer than the tolerance is read as its start.
A segment or a circle with a coordinate that is not a finite number meets nothing, and the answer is false.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2.TryIntersectWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Tries to calculate the intersection points between a circle and a line segment within tolerance, with or without the touches of a segment that comes within the tolerance of the rim away from where its line crosses it.
member.param: The points, empty when there are none.

true for ; false for the crossings an offset cuts its pieces at, read as they were before: a segment that crosses nowhere touches only where its line runs within the tolerance inside the rim, a foot up to the tolerance past an end is taken at that end however far it is from the rim, and a crossing taken at an end is kept beside the other.

member.summary: Tries to calculate the intersection points between two circles within tolerance.

remarks.para: The crossings are worked out from the smaller circle, so they are the same two points whichever circle is asked first, and stay accurate when the other is huge. The circle of radius 2.5E8 that carries an edge 100 long of bulge 1E-7, from (0, 0) to (100, 0), meets the circle of radius 40 about (50, 30) at (23.54249, 0) and (76.45751, 0) either way round; worked from the larger circle, they came out 0.076 off.

Two circles that stay within the point tolerance of each other all the way round, their centres and their radii no more than the tolerance apart put together, are one circle and cross nowhere; so are two whose centres are closer than the tolerance where the rounding of the numbers leaves no line to cross on (see ). Otherwise the circles cross where they do, however close their centres: the circle of radius 1000 about the origin and the circle of radius 1000.0005 about (0.0006, 0) cross at (-833.33324, 552.77094) and (-833.33324, -552.77094).

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2.AboutOneCentre(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Whether two circles whose centres stand no further apart than the point tolerance are one circle, or about one centre: whether they stay within the point tolerance of each other all the way round, or the rounding of the numbers they are made of leaves the line they cross on nowhere in particular.
member.param: How far apart the centres are, no more than the point tolerance.
The largest coordinate of the centres, or radius, whichever is larger.
The radius of the first circle.
The radius of the second circle.

remarks.para: Two circles are never further apart than the distance between their centres and the difference of their radii put together; where that is no more than the point tolerance they are one circle, which meets along its length rather than at points. Two arcs of the circle of radius 750 about (1234.5678, 2345.6789) whose ends are rounded to six places have centres 1.6E-6 apart, and they cross nowhere, where they were cut at (1650.09, 2970.05). The circles of radius 1000 and 1000.00002 with their centres a ten-thousandth apart are within 1.2E-4 of each other all round and are one at a tolerance of a thousandth.

Further apart than that, two circles cross on their radical line, the difference of their squared radii over twice the distance between their centres from the centre. A rounding of the numbers, the largest of them times the rounding of a double, moves that line by about as much times the sum of the radii over that distance; where that is more than the point tolerance the line cannot be placed, and the centres are one. The circles of radius 1000 and 1000.0005 with their centres 6E-4 apart, as much as 1.1E-3 apart in places, place it to 7.4E-7 and cross. It is the rule of the line without ends (see ), whose crossing is no crossing where a double cannot place it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2.IsSimple(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2)
member.summary: Checks whether a polygon is simple, using default tolerance: no edge crosses or touches another except where neighbours share their vertex.
member.returns: true if the polygon is simple; otherwise, false.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection2.IsSimple(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether a polygon is simple, within tolerance: no edge crosses or touches another except where neighbours share their vertex.
member.param: The tolerance: edges closer than the point tolerance count as touching.
member.returns: true if the polygon is simple; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: does not check this when it is built, because the check costs more than building it. A polygon that is not simple is still read consistently, under the even-odd rule, but its area no longer means what it says. A vertex touching another edge counts as not simple, and so does an edge folding back over its neighbour. Two edges that are not neighbours touch where they come within the point tolerance of each other, measured with no slack past their ends: the loop with corners (10, 0) and (10.0009, 0.0009), 0.00127 apart, is simple at a tolerance of a thousandth and not at two. Edges are swept in order along X, so the cost grows with the number of edges whose extents overlap rather than with the square of the edge count.
member.exception: Thrown when the polygon is null.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3
member.summary: Where a flat region crosses the surface of a body or a box, and where a plane crosses a box.

remarks.para: A region and a body meet where an edge of the region crosses the surface, or where an edge of the body crosses the region; a region lying wholly inside crosses nothing. So the crossings are both of those, the region's edges first, then the body's face by face, each place named once. The body is read by its material, every opening cut in, so the walls of an opening are surface and a region inside an opening crosses nothing. A box 100 by 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin and the square 200 by 200 lying across it at half its height cross where the four upright edges of the box pass through the square, at (0, 0, 50), (100, 0, 50), (100, 100, 50) and (0, 100, 50).

A box is read through its body: each crossing with a box is the crossing with , or with ToObb().ToSolid() for an axis-aligned one, so it is exactly the answer the body would give. A box flat on some axis, or no thicker than the point tolerance on two, has no body and is read as the shape it has become, as CollidesWith and DistanceTo read it: flat on one axis it is its rectangle, crossed as a polygon is; on two its segment, and on all three its centre, crossed where the segment meets the other shape, one place at most. The plane x = 30 crosses the box 100 by 100 by 0 about (50, 50, 0) at (30, 100, 0) and (30, 0, 0), the ends of the segment they share, on its edges, and the box 100 by 0.000002 by 0.000002 about (50, 0, 0) at (30, 0, 0); both were crossed nowhere.

member.summary:
Provides static methods for finding where 3D shapes meet.
Each TryIntersectWith overload returns a single result and reports false when there is not exactly one. Two shapes that overlap along a whole line or a whole area — a segment lying in a plane, two coincident planes, two collinear segments — have no single crossing to name, so they come back false rather than picking an arbitrary point out of the overlap. Ask Distance3 or Collision3 when the question is whether they touch at all.
Where a straight chain in space crosses another shape.

remarks.para: A could say how far off nine kinds of shape were and whether it touched three. Everything the distance needed was there; what was missing was the shorter question. A chain is a run of segments, so every answer here is the union of what its segments answer, and a already answers all of it — nothing new is worked out.
Two segments share a vertex, so a crossing at a vertex is found twice and named once. This is the walk keeps for a chain that curves; the two differ only in what a piece is.

member.summary: Where a ray runs into a body.
Where two flat regions in space cross, where a plane crosses one, and where a ray crosses a ray, a plane or a region, read as a list.

remarks.para: Two regions in planes that are not one. A triangle, a polygon and a face are read filled, a face by its material. Two of them can only share points on the line their planes share, and each stretch of that line they share ends on the boundary of one of them, so the ends are where an edge of either crosses the other region. That is the segment against a region the library already answers, asked once for each edge, the first region's edges first, ring by ring for a face, and a point found twice is named once. A square 100 by 100 lying in the floor with a corner at the origin, and one standing upright across it along y = 50 from z = -50 to 50, cross at (100, 50, 0) and (0, 50, 0). An edge the segment test refuses, as it refuses one climbing no more than the planar tolerance, is read by the signs of its ends' heights instead, so a square tilted a tenth of a degree with each side cut into 80 pieces crosses where the uncut square does.

Two regions in one plane. Where the normals are parallel within the angle tolerance and either region lies wholly in the plane of the other within the planar tolerance, every edge runs in the other's plane and no segment crosses anything. The two are then laid out in that plane with , in the frame of the first unless only the first lies in the second's plane, and the plane half answers: the crossings of the outlines, lifted back in its order. Two squares 100 by 100 in the floor, the second moved 50 along X and 50 along Y, cross at (100, 50, 0) and (50, 100, 0).
A triangle with no area, by , has no plane to lay a pair out in: it is the segment it has collapsed to, and is crossed where its sides are, as the segment against a triangle reads it.

member.summary: Where two straight pieces in space cross, read as a list.

remarks.para: Two straight pieces meet at one point, so the answer was offered as one point: gives a nullable point and nothing gave a list. That is the better shape when a segment is what is in hand, and the wrong one when it is not: a is a segment or a bend and can only offer a direction where both answer with the same shape of call, so a segment could be asked about every flat and solid shape in the library and not about another segment. The plane has the same exception written out for the same reason.

So this is the one-point answer as a list of length one. Nothing new is worked out, and the reading for pieces lying along each other is the one two arcs of one circle already get: they meet along a length rather than at a place, so no place is named and CollidesWith is what says they touch.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the points where a triangle and the surface of a solid cross, within a tolerance.
member.param: The solid, read by its material.
member.returns: Where an edge of the triangle crosses the surface, in order along each edge, then where an edge of the body crosses the triangle, face by face, each place named once. A triangle lying wholly inside the material crosses nothing and gives none, which reports instead.
member.remarks: A box 100 by 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin and the triangle with corners (-50, -50, 50), (300, -50, 50) and (-50, 300, 50) lying across it at half its height cross at (0, 0, 50), (100, 0, 50), (100, 100, 50) and (0, 100, 50), where the upright edges of the box pass through it. A side shorter than the global tolerance is measured along as it is at a finer one: at a billionth, the triangle (5, 5, 0.0004), (5, 5, -0.0005), (45, 5, 10) crosses the top of the box 10 by 10 by 10 standing under the floor first at (5, 5, 0), where its side 0.0009 long passes through; it was given that side's start, (5, 5, 0.0004).
member.exception: Thrown when the solid is null.

member.summary: Tries to find the point where two line segments meet, within a tolerance.
member.param: The crossing point when the method returns true.
member.returns: true if the segments meet at a single point; otherwise, false.
member.remarks:
Two segments in space usually pass each other without meeting, so this asks for the closest approach and accepts it only when the gap is within tolerance. Parallel segments are refused even when they overlap, matching the 2D behaviour: a shared stretch is not a point.
A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly cross the other: at a thousandth, the segment from (5, 0, 0.0004) to (5, 0, -0.0005) meets the one from the origin to (10, 0, 0) at (5, 0, 0), where it crosses it; the one from (5, 0, 0.0008) to (5, 0, 0.0002) meets it at its start, which lies within the tolerance of it; and the one from (5, 0, 0.0015) to (5, 0, 0.0006) meets it nowhere, its start 0.0015 off, where its end was read within the tolerance of it. One shorter than the vector tolerance crosses where it truly does too: the segment from (5, 0, 0.000004) to (5, 0, -0.000004) meets it at (5, 0, 0), where it was given its start, too short for the vector tolerance to read a direction in.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.TryIntersectWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Tries to find the point where a line segment crosses a triangle, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
The crossing is found against the triangle's carrier plane and then tested for containment, so the edges of the triangle are decided by the same tolerance-aware test that Containment3.Contains uses. A segment lying in the plane of the triangle is refused for the same reason it is refused against a bare plane. Whether the triangle has an area is read by : the triangle 0.003 by 0.003 at the origin has, and the segment from (0.001, 0.001, -1) to (0.001, 0.001, 1) crosses it at (0.001, 0.001, 0). One with none is the segment it has collapsed to within the point tolerance, and is crossed where its sides are, the longest first: the segment from (50, 0, -1) to (50, 0, 1) crosses the sliver 100 long and 1E-8 high at (50, 0, 0). Both crossed nothing while twice the area was read against the vector tolerance. However small the tolerance, the triangle holds the crossing to the rounding of the coordinates, 1E-15 of the largest of its own and the segment's, on its plane and past its rim, as it holds a ray's, and a segment reaching from further off than the triangle is large is read from a diagonal short of it, along its line; whether the crossing lies between the ends is read by the tolerance given. Below that rounding, and only there, a segment with an end within it of the triangle, the other end off its plane, crosses it at that end where it touches it as reads it, and nowhere else. At a tolerance of nought the segment from 30 under the middle of a triangle turned about in space to 30 over it crosses it there, where the rounding refused 920 of 1 000 such triangles, and the one from 10 off the side of a box turned about in space to a point on it crosses its triangle where it touches it, and only there, where the two read alike 488 times in 1 000.
A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly cross the triangle: it meets it at its start where that lies within the point tolerance of the triangle, and nowhere where it does not, as reads one against a plane.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Finds where a line segment enters and leaves an oriented box, within a tolerance.
member.returns: The crossing points in order along the segment: none when it misses the box, one when it starts or ends inside, two when it passes through, and one, the point of it nearest the box, when it touches the box within the point tolerance on its own without crossing a face. None for a segment lying wholly inside the box, or lying along it within the tolerance, which collide with it and cross nothing.
member.remarks: This is the slab method. Taking the segment into the local frame of the box turns it into three pairs of parallel planes, and the part of the segment inside the box is the overlap of the three intervals those pairs cut out of it. The overlap is empty exactly when some axis separates them, which is the same reasoning the separating axis test in Collision3 rests on. A segment that barely moves across a pair of faces is held within them when it runs no further outside than the point tolerance, and is then given its crossings only where it comes within the point tolerance of the box, as reads it: past an edge of the box 10 by 10 by 10 a segment along X standing 0.000714 off both faces is 0.00101 from the box, and crosses nothing, where it was given two points. The other way round, the slabs of the axes it moves along are read exactly, so a segment that comes within the tolerance of an edge or a face without reaching the box touches it and crosses no face: it is given the point of it nearest the box, as the other shapes give a touch. The segment from (5, 10.1, 9.9007) to (5, 9.9007, 10.1) passes 0.0005 off the edge of that box and is given (5, 10.00035, 10.00035), where it was given nothing and collided. The touch is given only where the segment touches the box at one place: one lying along the box within the tolerance, within the planar tolerance of the plane of the face it stands over or the line of the edge it runs with all along, such as one 0.0005 over the top face and level with it, is given none, as the body of the box gives none and an arc in the same place none, a curve lying on a surface crossing it nowhere. The point is the same whichever way round the segment is given. A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly cross a face: it is given its start where that lies within the point tolerance of a face, inside the box or out, and nothing where it does not.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Finds every point where a line segment crosses the surface of a solid, within a tolerance.
member.returns: The crossing points, in order along the segment.
member.remarks: The walls of the openings count as surface, since they too separate material from void. Two crossings closer together than the tolerance are reported once, so a segment grazing an edge does not come back as having entered and left. However small the tolerance, a face holds a crossing to the rounding of the coordinates, 1E-15 of the largest of the body's and the segment's, on its plane and past its rim, as it holds a ray's; below that rounding, and only there, the two crossings of a seam within eight times it of each other are one, a segment reaching from further off than the body is large is read from a diagonal short of it, along its line, and an end within the rounding of a face meets the surface there where the segment touches the face, or the body, as reads it, and only there. At a tolerance of nought the segment 400 long through a cylinder of radius 20 turned about in space is given its two crossings, where the rounding refused the crossing of nearly every face and it was given one or none; the one along the seam of two of its sides, through its axis, from a hundred million out to a hundred million out beyond, is given the two, where it was given none; and the one from 10 off the side of a box turned about in space to a point on it is given that point, where 831 of 1 000 were given nothing though they touched the box. A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly cross the surface: it is given its start where that lies within the point tolerance of the surface, in the material or out, and nothing where it does not. A longer one is measured along itself as it is whatever the global tolerance: at a billionth, the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, -0.0005), shorter than the global thousandth, crosses the top of the box 10 by 10 by 10 standing under the floor at (5, 5, 0), where it was given its start.

member.summary: Checks whether a polygon is simple, within a tolerance: no edge crosses or touches another except where neighbours share their vertex.
member.param: The tolerance: edges closer than the point tolerance count as touching.
member.returns: true if the polygon is simple; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: checks that it is flat but not that it is simple, because the check costs more than building it. A vertex touching another edge counts as not simple, and so does an edge folding back over its neighbour. Edges are swept in order along X, so the cost grows with the number of edges whose extents overlap rather than with the square of the edge count. Where they overlap much along X, the sweep runs along whichever of X, Y and Z leaves the fewest pairs instead, with the same answer: a comb of 1 000 teeth 10 000 long laid along X, 4 000 edges, checked as it is and with a corner pushed in to touch the next tooth, took 35 ms swept along its teeth and takes 2.8 ms swept across them.
member.exception: Thrown when the polygon is null.

member.summary: How many pairs for each edge looks at sweeping along X before it chooses the axis to sweep along. Choosing costs three sorts and three binary searches for each edge, as much as the sweep itself where the edges overlap little along X, so it is paid for only where they overlap much; every axis gives the same answer.

member.remarks: The sweep along X compared the boxes of two edges, and measured the distance between them, with the edge it came to second first, and the shortest line between parallel edges is not the same in the last bit taken the other way round. member.param: The centre of the shape lying in the first plane.
The unit normal of the first plane.
How far the shape reaches across its plane, its diameter.
The point of the line nearest the centre, as an offset from it, lying in the first plane.
The unit direction of the line.

How far rounding may have moved the line across itself, a bound: a few parts in 1E16 of what each coordinate puts into the centre's height above the other plane, and of the offset, each over the sine of the angle between the planes. A plane whose stored point lies far off along the line adds nothing, since its coordinates there put nothing into the height.
member.returns: false when the two planes are parallel as far as the shape reaches, as for the circle.
member.remarks: finds the line from the planes' distances to the world origin, which planes a thousandth of a degree apart and 52 000 from the origin turn into an error of a millimetre. Here the only distance is the centre's from the other plane, measured from that plane's own point, and the rounding left is that distance's, divided by the sine of the angle between the planes.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.HeightAbove(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Gets the height of a point above a plane, worked out to the last digit of the height rather than of the coordinates it is found from.
member.remarks: The height is (P - O)·n, O the plane's stored point. Read plainly, each difference and each product is rounded to a part in 1E16 of its own size, so a plane whose point is stored 1E5 away gives a height off by 1E-11 however small the height is, and a line found from it, between planes 1E-5 apart, by 1E-6: two crossings 0.06 apart were found 0.009 out. Here each difference is split into its rounded value and the part rounding lost, each product likewise (Dekker's split, as no fused multiply-add is to be had), and the parts summed with what their sums lose kept, so that only the rounding of the height itself is left.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the points where a ray passes through the surface of a solid, within a tolerance.
member.returns: The crossings in the order the ray meets them, with repeats left out.
member.remarks:
The surface is walked as triangles, so a crossing that falls on the seam between two of them arrives twice and is reported once, the two within the point tolerance of each other. However small the tolerance, a triangle holds a crossing to the rounding of the coordinates, 1E-15 of the largest of the body's and the ray's origin, on its plane and past its rim; below that rounding, and only there, the two crossings of a seam within eight times it of each other are one, and a ray from further off than the body is large is read from a diagonal short of it, along its line, so that the rounding stays the body's. At a tolerance of nought the ray along the seam of two sides of a cylinder of radius 20, through its axis, is given its two crossings from 60 out and from a hundred million out, where it was given one or none. A ray starting inside the body has an odd number of crossings, and one starting outside an even number, give or take a face it merely grazes. The list is held to , which reads the ray by the point tolerance and the body to a billionth (further out than a million, to 1E-15 of the largest coordinate): a ray starting within the planar tolerance of a face meets it at its origin only where the origin stands within the point tolerance of the surface, whatever it meets further on, and one that collides and crosses no face is given its point nearest the surface, where that stands within the point tolerance of it, to the rounding of numbers the size of the body's, or the body holds the origin. With a point tolerance of a hundredth and a planar one of five hundredths, the ray from 0.04 over the top of the box 100 by 100 by 50, rising a hundredth for each unit along it, is given nothing, where it was given its origin and collided with nothing; the one from 0.04 off the inner wall of a U, across its gap, is given the walls of the far prong only, and the one from 0.04 under the top of the box only where it leaves, where each was given its origin besides; at a tolerance of nought the ray from the middle of a box 100 by 80 by 50 turned about in space is given where it leaves, where the rounding refused the crossing of every face and it collided and was given nothing.
A body far out is asked near the origin, as says, and the crossings moved back out, coordinate by coordinate. Where it stood, of 2 080 rays half a hundredth in and out from an L 100 by 80 by 50 a hundred million out, with a pocket up from its floor and a hole down through its other leg, at a hundredth, 9 were given other crossings than at the origin, and of 2 016 a thousand million out, 19; 1 and none are, a ray along the world's Y axis.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.NearBox(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether a ray comes within the reach of the point tolerance, and as far again as the body holds a point outside it (a billionth, or further out than a million 1E-15 of the largest coordinate), of the box of a body, as far as the farthest corner of the box: further, it neither touches the body nor starts in it.
member.remarks: A fixed billionth gave nothing 5E7 out at a tolerance of nought for the ray from 2.2E-8 over the top of a box, pointing away, which the body holds and so collides with.

member.summary: Gets where a ray crosses a triangle, as a list, within a tolerance.
member.returns: One point or nothing, and gives the same point, true exactly where this gives one. The ray is read as the line without ends along it, by how far that line climbs across the triangle, and is given what the line meets at its origin or ahead of it: the crossing, the point of a touch nearest the triangle, or none where the line lies level over the material within the planar tolerance of the triangle's plane. Where the line meets the triangle only behind the origin, or lies level over it only behind a ray running away from it, a ray whose origin touches it is given its origin. A point is given exactly where says the two touch, but where the ray holds more than the point tolerance of a part of its line lying level over the triangle.
member.remarks: A ray from (20, 20, 10) pointing straight down crosses the triangle with corners (0, 0, 0), (100, 0, 0) and (0, 100, 0) at (20, 20, 0). The ray from (50, -0.0006, 0.0003) along (1, -0.01, 0), 0.00067 from the triangle and running away from it, touches it at its origin, where it collided and was given nothing.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets where two rays cross, as a list, within a tolerance.
member.returns: The one place they cross, or nothing: two rays that miss each other name no place, and nor do two lying along one line, which meet along a length, as two segments lying along each other name none.
member.remarks: This is the reading two segments get (): the rays cross where the shortest line between them is no longer than the point tolerance, and the place named is the middle of that line. A ray runs on without end, so it draws away from another at any angle but none, and only rays parallel within rounding are read as lying along each other. A ray from the origin along X and one from (50, -50, 0) along Y cross at (50, 0, 0); one from (0, -1, 0) half a degree off X crosses the first at (114.59, 0, 0); one from (50, 10, 0) along Y misses it and names nothing.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.TryGetBridge(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3@)
member.summary: Gets the shortest line between two rays that are not parallel within rounding, from the first to the second.
member.returns: false when the two are parallel within rounding, where every facing pair is as close as any other.
member.remarks: The square of the gap is a convex function of the two distances along the rays, so the nearest pair is that of the two endless lines, the one works out with both extended, wherever both rays reach it; and otherwise it lies where one of the two distances is nought: one origin and the point of the other ray nearest it, the nearer of the two, the first ray's origin on a tie.

member.summary: Determines whether two shapes stand so far apart that they cannot meet: their boxes clear of each other by more than twice the point and planar tolerances together, or either shape wholly to one side of the other's plane, clear of it by more than twice the larger of the two.
member.remarks: The second is for any outline, and both are safe for the same reason: every way the full test finds contact puts a point of one within the point tolerance of the other along its plane and within the planar tolerance across it. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.Flat.InOnePlane(GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.Flat,GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.Flat,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3@)
member.summary: Determines whether two shapes lie in one plane, and if so the frame to lay both out in.
member.remarks: The normals have to be parallel within the angle tolerance and either shape has to lie wholly in the other's plane within the planar tolerance. A small plate lying on a large one tilted a ten-millionth of a radian off it lies in the large one's plane, though the large one's far edge stands two thousandths off the small one's: every edge of the small plate runs in the large one's plane and no segment test sees the two touch, so either way round has to be enough. The frame is the first shape's where the second lies in its plane, and otherwise the second's, so that the shape the other lies on is laid out exactly.

member.summary: Reads an edge the segment test has refused against a plane by the signs of its two ends' heights, so that a side cut into pieces too short or too level for that test to take meets the plane where the uncut side does.
member.param: Where the edge passes through, or the one end lying on the plane.
member.returns: true when the ends stand strictly either side, or one of them, and only one, lies on the plane; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: The segment test refuses an edge that climbs no more than the planar tolerance from end to end. A square 40 by 40 tilted a tenth of a degree, each side cut into 80 pieces, has no piece the test takes, though the uncut square crosses a plate under it at two points: read by its signs, the one piece that passes through meets the plate where the uncut side does. No tolerance widens the plane here: a piece merely ending near it is not taken, since the pieces either side of a crossing all end near it and would each name a place of their own. An edge lying in the plane is left to the edges at its ends, as the segment test leaves it. Two regions within the tolerance of each other without crossing are found touching by their distance instead ().

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Intersection3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets where a segment crosses a ray, within a tolerance.
member.returns: The one place they cross, or nothing.
member.remarks:
Two lines in space usually miss each other altogether, so the question is answered by the shortest line between the two: they cross where that line has no length, and the reach of each piece is already built into it. A segment lying along the ray meets it along a length and names no place.
A ray is a value type and cannot be refused for being absent, so a ray with no direction is read as its own origin and nothing more: the question becomes whether the segment holds that point.
A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly cross the ray: at a thousandth, the segment from (5, 0, 0.0004) to (5, 0, -0.0005) crosses the ray from the origin along X at (5, 0, 0), the one from (5, 0, 0.0008) to (5, 0, 0.0002) meets it at its start, and the one from (5, 0, 0.0015) to (5, 0, 0.0006) meets it nowhere, where it was given (5, 0, 0). A longer one is measured along itself as it is whatever the global tolerance: at a billionth, the segment from (5, 0, 0.0004) to (5, 0, -0.0005), shorter than the global thousandth, crosses the ray at (5, 0, 0), where it was given nothing.

Where the ray's own reading, by its crossing of the plane and the part of it over the region, gives a point within the point tolerance of the line's, that point is given, so a ray the two read alike, as one crossing the plane at a slant, is given what it always was. Where the line meets the region only behind the origin, or lies level over it only behind the origin, the ray running away from it, and the origin itself touches the region, the ray is given its origin, the one place of that meeting it holds. The list is held to CollidesWith (): a ray that touches the region and holds no more than the point tolerance of a part of its line lying level over it is given its own point, and a point given that the test does not say touches is not.
member.remarks: A ray from 0.0005 over a square 100 by 100 in the floor, falling 1E-5 for each unit along it, climbs 0.001 across the square, more than the planar tolerance of a thousandth, and is given its crossing 50 along, as its line is; one from 0.0002 over it falling 4E-6 climbs 0.0004, lies level over the square as its line does, and is given nothing. One rising a hundredth from 0.0005 under the square crosses the floor 0.05 behind its origin, and is given its origin; so is one 0.0003 over the floor and 0.0006 beside the rim of a triangle running away from it, whose line lies level over the triangle behind it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Lengthen2
member.summary:
Provides static methods that change how long a line segment is while keeping it on the line that carries it: lengthening or shortening it by a distance, extending an end out to a boundary, trimming an end back to one, and trimming or extending two segments until they meet in a corner.
The operations follow AutoCAD's LENGTHEN, EXTEND and TRIM commands, and FILLET with a radius of zero. A segment has no picked point to say which end is meant, so every method that moves one end takes a ; the other end never moves, and the direction of the segment never reverses.
TryExtendTo only ever lengthens: the end moves outward to the nearest place where the line meets the boundary. TryTrimTo only ever shortens: the end moves back to the nearest place, still within the segment, where the boundary crosses it. An end that already lies on the boundary, within tolerance, satisfies both and is left there, so either call can be repeated without moving the end again, and TryExtendTo(...) || TryTrimTo(...) fits an end to a boundary whichever side of it the end starts on.
A boundary is met where the infinite line carrying the segment crosses it. A boundary segment, polyline or polygon edge running parallel to the line is not a crossing, since it is either missed or shared along a whole stretch. A point is met where the line passes closest to it, at the foot of the perpendicular, so a point to one side of the line still pulls the end level with it.
Extending and trimming the curved shapes in the plane: an arc, and a chain whose end leg may be one.

remarks.para: Only a segment could be extended or trimmed, which left the one case a reinforcing schedule asks about every day — lengthening a bar's end leg for anchorage — with no answer but rebuilding the chain by hand.

An arc is extended along itself: the radius and the centre stay, the sweep grows, and the distance asked for is arc length and not chord. That is exact, and it is the only reading that leaves the curve where it was. A whole turn is the limit, so an extension that would pass it is refused rather than wrapped.

A chain is extended by its end leg, along that leg: a straight leg carries on straight, a curved one carries on round, keeping its radius. Every other leg is untouched, so the bends and their radii survive. A chain is extended outwards only; shortening one belongs to the cutting family, which keeps the bends, and TryTrimTo below is that cut with the end named rather than the piece.

member.param: The first segment ending at the corner, or unchanged when the method returns false.
The second segment ending at the corner, or unchanged when the method returns false.
member.returns: true if the two lines cross; false if they are parallel, one is too short to have a direction, or either has a coordinate that is not a finite number.
member.remarks: The corner is where the lines carrying the two segments cross. Each segment keeps its end farther from the corner and has its nearer end moved onto it: extended if the corner lies beyond, trimmed if the segments cross each other, so that the longer part of each is what remains. AutoCAD asks the user to pick the part to keep; keeping the longer one is what that pick would be in the usual case. When the corner lies exactly half way along a segment its end point moves.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Lengthen2.TryFilletCorner(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Rounds the corner between two segments with an arc of a given radius, within a tolerance.
member.param: The radius of the arc; it must be positive.
The arc tangent to both segments, running from the first to the second, or an arc of no meaning when the method returns false.
The first segment ending where the arc begins.
The second segment beginning where the arc ends.
member.returns: true if the corner had room for an arc of that radius; otherwise, false.
member.remarks:
This is AutoCAD's FILLET with two objects picked. The corner is where the lines carrying the two segments cross, and the arc touches each of them at radius / tan(half the corner) from it. Each segment keeps its part on the far side of the corner, as does, and gives up the part the arc replaces.
The corner needs room for the arc: the touching points must lie within the segments once they are trimmed or extended to it. Where they do not, or the segments are parallel, or one of them is too short to have a direction, the answer is false rather than an arc that overshoots.
member.exception: Thrown when the radius is not a positive number.
