member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Lengthen3
member.summary:
Provides static methods that change how long a line segment is while keeping it on the line that carries it: lengthening or shortening it by a distance, extending an end out to a boundary, trimming an end back to one, and trimming or extending two segments until they meet in a corner.
This is the 3D counterpart of Lengthen2 and follows the same rules. Every method that moves one end takes a ; the other end never moves, and the segment never reverses. TryExtendTo only ever lengthens, TryTrimTo only ever shortens, and an end already on the boundary satisfies both, so TryExtendTo(...) || TryTrimTo(...) fits an end to a boundary from either side the way Tekla Structures fits a part end to a plane.
A boundary is met where the infinite line carrying the segment reaches it. A plane is met where the line pierces it. A polygon, face or solid is met where the line pierces its surface; a line lying in the plane of a polygon or face meets it at its edges instead, and one running parallel beside it never does. Another segment is met only where the line passes within the point tolerance of it: two lines in space usually pass each other, and then there is no crossing to extend to. A point is met at the foot of the perpendicular from it.
Extending and trimming the curved shapes in space: an arc, and a chain whose end leg may be one.

remarks.para: Only a segment could be extended or trimmed, which left the one case a reinforcing schedule asks about every day — lengthening a bar's end leg for anchorage — with no answer but rebuilding the chain by hand.

An arc is extended along itself: the radius and the centre stay, the sweep grows, and the distance asked for is arc length and not chord. That is exact, and it is the only reading that leaves the curve where it was. A whole turn is the limit, so an extension that would pass it is refused rather than wrapped.

A chain is extended by its end leg, along that leg: a straight leg carries on straight, a curved one carries on round, keeping its radius. Every other leg is untouched, so the bends and their radii survive. A chain is extended outwards only; shortening one belongs to the cutting family, which keeps the bends, and TryTrimTo below is that cut with the end named rather than the piece.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Loops3
member.summary: Turns loops of corners, as a modeller gives the faces of a body, into faces: one face where the loops lie flat, triangles on their own corners where they do not.
member.remarks: A face in this library is flat, and a polygon refuses corners out of flat. The faces of a closed body can still come that way: Tekla Structures left the top face beside a notch in a beam 0.04 mm out at one corner, and refused, that face was a hole in the body, which then gave no section and the wrong volume. Split into triangles on the corners it came with, each exactly flat, the face keeps every edge it shares with its neighbours, so the body is as closed as it was given, and no corner moves. Moving the corners onto one plane would not do: a corner is shared with the faces round it, and they would come out of flat instead.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Material3
member.summary: The material of a body, for the questions that read its faces as where the material ends.

remarks.para: A body keeps its openings as whole bodies subtracted from it, so its faces run straight across every hole. Every question that reads the faces — or the mesh made from them — as the boundary of the solid goes through here first, and gets a body without openings whose faces are where the material ends.

How many openings are cut in depends on the question. Whether a probe touches the body, or where it crosses it, only needs the openings the probe can reach: an opening out of its reach takes away nothing the probe could meet, so a bolt checked against a plate with twenty holes costs one cut, not twenty. How far apart the two are needs them all, because the place of the body nearest the probe can lie inside an opening the probe never comes near, and the true answer is then on that opening's rim. A caller asking many such questions of one body cuts it once with and asks the result.
A body whose openings take all of its material is answered by its faces, the only thing it still describes — the same as does.

member.remarks: Cut at a tolerance of nought, the openings of a plate turned about in space came out as a shell left open, and a point 0.0005 under the plate read 3.0005 from it. Of 50 000 points and rays drawn beside prisms turned about in space, most of them with openings, 0 to 4E9 out, 1 226 points were measured more than a millionth off their distance and 531 rays read as colliding where they missed, or missing where they collided; 3 points and no ray are now. A ray's collision disagreed with its distance 141 times and does 10, on plates a million and more out, the ray starting within three times the fine tolerance outside, where the cut material holds the origin and the body does not. Above the rounding nothing changes, bit for bit.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Measure3
member.summary: The volume, mass, centroid and surface area of a body, by the method asked, and every method side by side.

remarks.para: A body is measured over its faces. The divergence theorem makes its volume, centroid and moments sums over the triangles of its surface, each taken as a tetrahedron to the middle of the body's box, so that a part far from the origin loses nothing to the size of its coordinates. Over flat faces the sums are exact, and every gives the same answer but for the rounding. A face a hair out of flat, as the planar tolerance lets one be, is no one surface, and there the methods part; says by how much, and how far the faces close.

The volume, the mass, the centroid and the surface area are the material's: every opening is cut in first, so a bolt hole comes out of the weight, moves the centroid, and its walls add to the surface. A body its openings take whole holds nothing. The material is the one measures, cut once for a tolerance and kept by the body, so measuring it every way costs one cut. An opening that cannot be cut in is left in the material, the log warns of it, and says so.
A density is the mass of a unit of volume in the model's units: for a model in millimetres weighed in kilograms, kilograms per cubic millimetre, which for steel is 7.85E-6.

member.returns: One segment per unbroken stretch, in order along the subject.

member.remarks:
Pieces arrive here already sorted onto one side of the cutter, so two that touch were parted by a cut that turned out to separate nothing — the far side of it landed on this side too. Handing back both would report a seam the caller has no way to account for.
Joining start to end looks careless, since it discards whatever lay between them, but every piece here was cut from a single straight subject and the discarded point was on the line joining the two ends. The polyline form cannot take this shortcut and has to decide, which is what is for.

member.remarks:
Unlike the segments arrive in no particular order and pointing in no particular direction, so a run is grown outwards from a seed segment in both directions at once, turning round whatever it picks up when that is what makes it fit.
Which segment a run takes up where three or more meet at a point is settled by input order, there being no geometric reason at a fork to prefer one branch over another. The answer is the same every time for a given input, but reordering the input can move a branch from one run to another.
Segments are found through a grid keyed on their endpoints rather than by trying every pair, so the cost follows the number of segments instead of its square. The grid cannot be a plain lookup on the point, since two ends near enough to count as touching need not be identical and would hash apart; cells one tolerance wide put any two such points in the same cell or in adjoining ones, so the cell only narrows the field and the tolerance comparison still decides.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Merge2.JoinBackup(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Joins line segments into polylines by comparing every pair of runs, the way went about it before it was given a grid to search.
member.returns: An array of joined polylines.
member.exception: Thrown when is null.
member.remarks:
Kept as the plain reading of what joining means, to hold against. It tries every pair of runs and starts the sweep again after each merge, which is short enough to check by eye, at a cost that grows with the square of the number of segments: around four thousand of them it takes half a second where takes a few milliseconds. So it is for reading and for testing against, not for drawings.
The joining is as it was. The two guards around it are not: a null argument used to come back as a NullReferenceException, and a segment of zero length used to survive to the end and yield a polyline with two identical vertices, which the public GeoPolyline2 constructor refuses. Putting those back alongside a working would only be putting back two faults.
Both hand the finished run to , which is itself unchanged from the original. What differs between the two is how runs are found, and that is the part worth holding one against the other.

The tolerance deciding whether two endpoints are the same point.

member.remarks: Each piece is used exactly once. Starting from an unused piece, the walk extends forwards from its end and then backwards from its start, reversing pieces as needed, until nothing more attaches; then the next unused piece starts a new chain. Where three or more pieces meet at a point the walk takes the first one it finds, since there is no ground for preferring another, so a branching set comes back as several chains rather than one.

member.remarks: A chain that has come back to where it started is finished, and growing it further is not merely unnecessary but wrong. Several pieces can meet at one point — two outlines touching at a corner, a vertex where four edges arrive — and carrying on there welds the next loop onto this one. The result is a single figure-of-eight whose two lobes run opposite ways, so its area is their difference rather than their sum, and a surface merged from it reports a size it does not have.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Merge3.CoplanarFaces(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3})
member.summary: Merges the faces of a set that share a plane and touch, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Merge3.CoplanarFaces(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Merges the faces of a set that share a plane and touch, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance deciding which faces share a plane and which edges meet.
member.returns: The faces with each touching coplanar group replaced by the single face covering it.
member.remarks:
Cutting a body leaves its surface more finely divided than it needs to be: a face split in two by a plane comes back as two faces even on the half where the cut did not really separate anything. Repeated cutting compounds that, and the face count grows without the shape changing. This puts the surface back into as few faces as describe it.
Faces are grouped by the oriented plane they lie on, so a face and one facing the other way are never merged: they are different surfaces that happen to be flat in the same place. Within a group, the edges shared by two faces cancel out and what is left is the outline of the union, which may be several separate outlines and may have one inside another — merging a ring of faces leaves a hole in the middle, and that hole is kept as a hole.
Faces in the same plane that do not touch are left as separate faces, since nothing joins them.
Two faces count as touching only where they share a whole edge. A face whose edge runs the length of two edges of its neighbours meets them at a T-junction, and nothing cancels there, so that particular join does not happen and the faces come back separate. The rest of the group still merges normally, and the total area is unchanged either way: merging under-joins rather than guessing at an outline. Surfaces that come out of cutting are free of T-junctions, since a cut divides both sides of every edge it crosses.
Vertices left in the middle of a straight run are kept rather than tidied away. They carry no shape, but removing them would leave the merged face meeting its neighbours at a T-junction wherever one of them still has the vertex, and a surface with a T-junction no longer reports itself closed.
An edge within the tolerance of two others is taken for the edge it shares with the nearer, the one that leaves the least area between them. The two long sides of a face thinner than the tolerance are within it of each other, and the edge of the face beside that one side shares is nearer. A beam 2 000 by 200 by 300, turned and cut by a plane meeting its floor within the tolerance, left on each side a sliver 2 000 long and up to 0.001 high below the plane, a square millimetre. Its sides cancelled each other, the beam's sides merged 0.72 and 0.49 square millimetres short, and the beam less a bent bar ending the tolerance over its floor came out 32.9 cubic millimetres short; the sliver's top cancels the pieces above it now, and the side merges whole.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Merge3.MergeGroup(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3},GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Merges the faces of one coplanar group into as few faces as cover them.
member.remarks: The union of a set of coplanar faces is bounded by exactly those edges that belong to one face only: an edge two of them share is interior to the union, and it appears twice among the collected edges running in opposite directions, so cancelling opposed pairs leaves precisely the outline. Where an edge is within the tolerance of two that run the other way, the pair nearest each other cancels first. If what is left does not close into loops the group was not a well formed surface, and the faces are handed back untouched rather than replaced by a guess. So are faces that each lie in the plane within the tolerance but whose outline does not: a face turned a hair against the others leaves a hole standing further than the tolerance off the plane of the loop round it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.NearPass3
member.summary: Where a rim in space, an ellipse's, a circle's or an arc's, passes within the point tolerance of another curve without crossing it where the line two planes share says.

remarks.para: The crossings of two curves not in one plane are read where the one's rim pierces the other's plane, kept where the other curve is within the tolerance. Two rims passing 0.0005 apart, the gap square to the other's plane, have none, since the first rim reaches that plane a long way off: of 2 514 pairs of ellipses of 4 000 drawn to pass within 0.0012 of each other, not in one plane, 1 517 came within 0.00098 and touched neither way round, and of 2 000 ellipses and circles so drawn 1 056.

A point of the rim within the tolerance of the other curve is within it of the other's plane, and the height of the rim above that plane is a constant and one harmonic of its angle, so the angles where the two can meet are one or two stretches, found in closed form, and cut to what an arc sweeps. A stretch is passed over when the gap at its middle, or a bound under it, is more than the rim can close over half of it, its major radius times its half angle. Otherwise the runs of it within the tolerance of the other curve are found by branch and bound on the gap (), and each run is one place: where the gap along it is least, brought down by Brent's method, the middle of the shortest line between the two there, unless a place already named lies on the run, stands within the tolerance of it, or both pass within it of the point halfway between the two. Read only every 32nd of a turn, a rim 139 by 121 passing 0.0005 from one 139 by 32 was missed between two readings.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.NearPass3.Search
member.summary: The search along a rim for the stretches within the tolerance of another curve, by branch and bound on the gap.

remarks.para: Three bounds the gap cannot be under on a piece of angle, the greatest of them taken. The gap changes no faster than the point of the rim moves, at most the root of a² sin² t + b² cos² t over the piece, so a piece of width w whose ends stand f1 and f2 from the other is no nearer than (f1 + f2 - speed w) / 2. The gap is never less than the rim's height above the other's plane, a constant and one harmonic of the angle, least over the piece. And the gap is never less than the distance from the rim's foot on that plane to the ellipse or circle the other lies on, whose root is the root of the height squared and that distance squared: where the foot lies wholly outside that ellipse over the piece, or wholly inside, as the ellipse's equation read along the foot, a constant and two harmonics whose turning points are found once, tells. The foot runs from its chord no further than an eighth of its greatest bend times the width squared. Outside, the distance to the filled ellipse is convex, so along the chord it lies above the tangent planes at the ends; inside, the distance to the rim is concave, and lies above the lesser end. Rims running along each other just outside the tolerance, which the first bound alone proves clear only in pieces a millionth of the rim's speed wide, are proved so in far fewer.

The stretch is read every 64th of a turn first, then the piece with the least bound is halved first. A piece proved further than the tolerance is passed over. A piece with an end within the tolerance is halved only to a 64th of a turn: there the two run along each other, and a run of such pieces is one place, unless halved further it holds two runs the gap rises above the tolerance between (). Any other piece is halved until the rim runs no more than twice the tolerance along it, and is then kept: at 64 tolerances, a rim crossing a needle 0.03 across held both its sides in one piece, and the touch was missed. So nothing is passed over that is not proved clear. Halving stops after 384 readings in a call, and what is left is kept too. Of 400 pairs drawn to graze each other, thin or huge, none reaches that; of 400 copies, or rims running along each other within a few tolerances for a long way, up to 234 do. Along pieces kept and not within the tolerance, each reading no higher than its neighbours is brought down by Brent's method between them, so a touch there is found where the gap between two readings has one least: that, and nothing else, is not proved. Walked instead in steps of the gap less the tolerance and stopped after 20 000 readings, the search dropped the touches of rims running along each other just outside the tolerance, as two ellipses 3 000 by 1 000, the one 0.0012 above the other and leaning, 0.0001 apart at the end of the minor axis, named a place where it stopped, and took up to 10 milliseconds.

member.summary: Gets the runs a group of pieces within the tolerance somewhere holds: the run read from the whole group, the least reading and the group's ends, where the group, halved further, holds one run within the tolerance; otherwise a run for each stretch of readings within it, from the reading before to the reading after, and for each reading above it no higher than its neighbours between them.
member.remarks: Pieces with an end within the tolerance are kept by at a 64th of a turn, so two touches closer than that along the rim fall into one group: a circle of radius 247 passing within 0.018 and 0.017 of a rim 5 995 by 2 863 at two places 11.4 apart, the gap rising to 0.069 between, at a tolerance of 0.05, was given one. Here the pieces are halved again, those with an end within the tolerance first, until the rim runs no more than twice the tolerance along each, a piece with no end within it is proved clear, or one with both ends within it is proved within it throughout (). Halving stops after another 384 readings in a call, and what is left is kept. A piece proved clear, or a reading above the tolerance, between two readings within it parts two runs, unless the other curve runs within the tolerance of the rim all the way between them (); a group that holds one run is read as it was, and nothing is passed over that was not before.

member.summary: Turns the readings of a whole turn, the last the first again, to start and end at the highest, so that a run over the ends is read as one: read from the start of the turn, one rim of 314 by 4.5 and another a hair larger, running along each other within the tolerance across it, gave a place at either end of the run. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.NearPass3.Search.Most(GeometryHelper.Core.NearPass3.Search.Piece,System.Double)
member.summary: Gets a bound the gap cannot be over on a piece: from the gap at its ends and the rim's speed; or from the gap D between the rim and a point carried evenly along the other between its points nearest the ends, where those lie on it.
member.remarks: D strays from its chord by no more than an eighth of the width squared times the greatest D'', and the chord is no longer than the greater gap at the ends. Both are ellipses read by angle, whose second derivatives are their points less their centres: with the other's angle k times the rim's, D'' is no more than a + k² A, the major radii a of the rim and A of the other, which bounds a small rim passing a large one; and D'' = -D + (k² - 1)(Q - C) + (C' - C), C the other's centre and C' the rim's, which, solved for the greatest D, bounds two rims running along each other, bending alike. The rim's speed alone proves a rim of radius 500 running 0.0005 from a copy of itself within a tolerance of 0.001 only in pieces a thousandth long, the last in pieces a radian long.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Offset2
member.summary: Offsetting the chains and loops that may curve.

Provides static methods that offset shapes: move a curve sideways to a parallel copy, or grow and shrink a region by a distance, as AutoCAD's OFFSET does.
A curve has no inside, so its offset goes to a side of its direction of travel: a positive distance moves it to the left, a negative one to the right, which for a segment drawn from left to right is up and down. The left is the side points to.
A region grows by a positive distance and shrinks by a negative one, whichever way round its vertices run. The result is the exact offset region for the corners asked for (), not the edges moved one by one: where a shrinking region pinches off it comes back in several pieces, where it shrinks past its own width it comes back empty, and where a growing region closes a gap around empty space that space comes back as a hole. Round corners are drawn as short straight segments, since the plane library has no arc type.
The work is done near the origin, so a drawing placed hundreds of kilometres out loses no precision, and a distance within the point tolerance returns the shape unchanged.

member.remarks: Nothing is flattened: an arc of radius R comes back an arc of radius R plus or minus the distance, about the same centre, and a corner that opens up is filled the way says. This is the one region operation that does not go through Clipper, which is why it can keep the arcs at all.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Offset2.Offset(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2,System.Double,GeometryHelper.OffsetOptions,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Offsets a loop that may curve, with options, within a tolerance.
member.param: How far to move the boundary: outward when positive, inward when negative.
How to fill a corner that opens up, and how far a miter may run.
member.returns: The offset loops, which may be none when the loop is eaten away, or more than one when it is pinched in two. Outer loops run the way the loop ran; where a growing loop closes a gap around empty space, that space comes back as a hole wound the other way, so that signed areas add up, as the straight offsets give it, whether the hole is a lens of two arcs or one of two a pinch leaves: the square of side 100 with a lens cut into it, tips (-20, 0) and a mouth 1 wide, sides of bulge -0.5, grown by 3, keeps the lens of radius 22.002 as a hole of 327.842.
member.remarks:
An arc whose radius runs out has no offset left, and the loop goes round its two ends instead, on the circle of the distance about each, whatever the join: that is what stands the distance from the shape there. The rectangle 100 by 30 with its right side bowed 6 in, a radius of 21.75, grown by 40 with round joins: the circles of 40 about (100, 0) and (100, 30) meet at (137.081, 15), and the loop encloses 18 397.80, the same whichever corner it starts from and whichever way it runs. A loop whose pieces meet out of the order they were cut in is put together where they meet, and a lens left between two arcs comes back as a loop of three corners.
A corner that opens is filled as the straight offsets fill it. A chamfer is cut square to the corner's bisector at the distance, touching the arc a round join would draw: the square of side 10 grown by 2 is cut at its corner (10, 0) from (8 + 2 sqrt 2, -2) to (12, 2 - 2 sqrt 2), and encloses 193.255. A miter that would reach further than times the distance is squared off there, its pieces run on as the miter runs them: the triangle with a tip of 10 degrees, grown by 1, is squared off 10 from the tip, from (-9.973, -0.743) to (-9.951, -1). Two straight edges a fraction of a degree off straight are mitered like any others. Where there is neither a miter nor a square to cut, because an arc and the piece next to it never meet and the miter has no limit, or an arc's circle never reaches the cut, the corner is rounded off at the distance.
A loop that crosses itself is read as the straight offsets read one, even-odd: a point is inside when it lies inside an odd number of the simple loops its crossings cut it into, and that region is what is offset, its arcs kept. The loop from (-7.818, 3.764) round an arc to the origin, round another to (-8.573, 2.412) and straight back crosses itself at (-1.980, 0.198), where its two arcs meet again beside their corner, and runs round a lens there the other way: grown by 0.1 with round joins it is one loop of 5.9555 and grown by 0.5 one of 14.5114 (the straight path, on the loop cut within 1E-5, 5.9555 and 14.5114); it was none. A gear of 642 teeth, whose arcs at each inner vertex cross again 0.0079 away and make a slit there, grown by 0.5 is one loop of 31 667.81, and shrunk by 0.5 one of 28 106.67, each slit holding its disc of 0.5 out of it. The loops come back wound as the signed area of the loop says it runs, outer ones that way and holes the other. Grown with miters or chamfers, each tip of the region where two lobes of it cross is a corner of its own and is mitered or cut as any corner is: the bow tie from (-10, 2) to (1, -0.2), (1, 0.2) and (-10, -2), its back an arc of bulge -0.25, grown by 1, keeps the miter of its long lobe out to (5.099, 0), past the small lobe, and encloses 54.460; the miter was cut off at x = 2, 52.539. A loop of four corners whose first and last edges cross 1.3 degrees apart, grown by 3 with chamfers, encloses 212.058, where it lost 0.83 beside the crossing. Where the two quarters of the region at a crossing are one lobe running round a hole, as the straight path reads them, they are no tips: the square 10 by 10 whose bottom edge curls up into a loop from (6, 2) to (4, 2), grown by 3, is 253.263. A loop that does not cross itself is offset as it always was. A vertex that lies on another edge is a crossing when the edge before it comes from one side of that edge and the edge after it leaves to the other: the loop from the origin to (10, 0), up to (10, 10) by an arc of bulge 0.2, back to (5, 0) and on to (3, -6) by an arc of bulge -0.2 crosses itself at (5, 0), and grown by 0.5 with round joins is one loop of 74.484 (the straight path 74.483), shrunk by 0.5 two of 21.342 and 10.017. A vertex that touches an edge with both its own edges on one side of it, or a hair off it, does not cross it. A spike the loop runs out to and straight back from, between two straight edges whose far ends lie within the point tolerance of each other, is dropped first, as the straight offsets drop it, the two ends of its foot one corner: the square 10 by 10 with a needle 0.0005 wide at its foot and 6 tall on its top, grown by 0.3 at a tolerance of 0.001, is the square grown, 112.283 with round joins, as the straight path gives it; it kept a strip 0.6 wide about the needle, 115.845. A region shrunk with miter corners can lose a small island that a miter wedge covers: the offset arcs run on round their own circles and are cut square at the miter limit times the distance, and what lies inside that wedge is not left. A loop of five vertices shrunk by 1 with the default limit of 10 has two loops where round corners give three, the third of 0.203 wholly in a wedge; with a limit of 2 it stays.
At a tolerance coarse beside the loop, two moved pieces can cross within the tolerance of where one of them ends and are not cut there. Where that leaves the offset open, the loop is offset again within a hundredth of the tolerance, and where a run is still open within a ten-thousandth: at each step cut at its crossings wherever it crosses itself there, and as a simple loop only where it crosses itself nowhere there. An answer is taken where it leaves fewer runs open and no fewer loops, with any loop of it finer than the tolerance, as the answer within the finer step has it. At a tolerance of 0.1 the loop of twelve straight corners in a box 7.9 by 5.1, grown by 4 with round joins, is one loop of 150.317, as the straight path gives it (150.320); it was none.
Crossings of a loop that crosses itself lying within the tolerance of each other, or linked through others that are, are one place, as long as each lies within the tolerance of the place, where the edges through it are cut: a row of forty crossings 0.09 apart is twenty places of two. A loop with two places too near along an edge to cut it at both is cut within a hundredth of the tolerance, or failing that a ten-thousandth, and offset within that: a loop of fifteen corners 1.2 across, grown by 1 at a tolerance of 0.1, is cut within 1E-5 and is one loop of 7.858. A loop that cannot be cut at any of the three is offset as a simple loop, as it always was. The loop whose three crossings lie 0.070, 0.084 and 0.101 apart, grown by 0.3 at a tolerance of 0.1, is an outline of 181.68 and three holes, as within 1E-3; it was none. A loop that crosses itself at more than 2 000 places within the tolerance is read within the tolerance only, cut where it can be and otherwise offset as a simple loop, since where its crossings bunch the work of a loop cut at them grows faster than their square: 60 diameters of a circle, 6 903 crossings, cut within 1E-5 took 21 s. The star {71/35} of radius 10, 2 414 crossings, grown by 0.3 at a tolerance of 0.1 is so the one loop of 302.631 round it.
Grown or shrunk with miters or chamfers, a loop is cut again within a hundredth of the tolerance, and then a ten-thousandth, where the tolerance does not tell a crossing from what lies beside it: within it two crossings made one place turn the blunt end of the sliver between them into a point, and a corner of the loop beside a crossing turns the tip there by its own turn, and a miter runs the error on. A step the loop cannot be cut at is passed over; one is taken where it is coarse at fewer places than the step before, until none is left, and the loop is offset within the last taken. A step coarse at as many places, as where three edges cross at one point, ends it, so a loop is cut at most twice more. A loop of the answer that is a point within the tolerance asked for is left out. The bow tie above with a corner on its first edge 0.005 past the crossing, where it turns by 1 degree, grown by 1 at a tolerance of 0.01, keeps the miter of its long lobe and encloses 54.419; the miter was left out, 52.501. A loop of four corners whose spike 2.4 degrees wide is crossed by an edge where it is 0.0057 wide, grown by 3 with miters at 0.01, is 386.351, as within 1E-4; it was 387.385.
A loop is put together edge for edge, its corners counted within the tolerance asked, not the global one: at a millionth, the rectangle 100 by 50 grown by 0.0004 with round joins keeps its four arcs, 0.00057 across, and encloses 5 000.12, where they were dropped within the global tolerance of a thousandth.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Offset2.Offset(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2,System.Double,GeometryHelper.OffsetOptions,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Offsets a chain that may curve, with options, within a tolerance.
member.param: How far to move it, to the left of the way it runs when positive.
How to fill a corner that opens up, and how far a miter may run.
The tolerance, which also says where two pieces of the offset meet.
member.returns: The offset chains, which may be none when nothing survives.
member.remarks:
The pieces are joined within the tolerance given, and the chains are put together within it too, not within the global one: the chain from the origin to (-5, 0) and round an arc of bulge -0.5 to (-7, 5), offset by 0.3 with an unlimited miter at a tolerance of 0.1, is one chain from (0, -0.3) to (-7.256, 5.156). A curve that cannot stand the distance away anywhere gives nothing: the U from (10, 0) to the origin, round the half circle of radius 2 about (0, 2) and back to (10, 4), offset by -2.5 to its inside, which is 4 wide. A piece is cut where another part of the chain comes nearer than the distance, and what still stands the distance away stays: the hairpin 1 wide, 10 along x, 1 down and 9 back, offset by -0.6 into its inside, keeps the start of its first leg, from (0, -0.6) to (0.553, -0.6), short of the circle of 0.6 about the chain's end. An arc whose radius runs out has no offset left, and the chain goes round its two ends instead, on the circle of the distance about each, whatever the join: the chain 10 along x, a half turn of radius 5 below the axis to (20, 0) and 10 more, offset by 10 upwards, runs along y = 10 to (10, 10), round the circle of 10 about (10, 0) to (15, 8.660), round the circle about (20, 0) to (20, 10) and on to (30, 10), 30.472 long.
A corner that opens is filled as the straight offsets fill it: a chamfer square to the corner's bisector at the distance, and a miter past squared off at the limit. The chain (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 10) offset by -2 with a chamfer runs along y = -2 to (8 + 2 sqrt 2, -2), across to (12, 2 - 2 sqrt 2) and on to (12, 10). Where there is neither a miter nor a square to cut, the corner is rounded off at the distance.
What a miter fills is read within the tolerance given, however small the miter: a chain of nine corners some 0.005 across, grown by 0.00137 with miters at a billionth, is one chain, as the same chain a million times larger is within a thousandth, where a miter smaller than the global tolerance went unread and a stray piece 0.00004 long inside it was kept.

A shrinking polygon that pinches off gives one per piece, largest first, and one that shrinks away gives none. A growing polygon that closes a gap around empty space also gives that space: each outer loop is followed by the holes inside it, and a hole is wound the other way round, so its signed area counts against the total. Outer loops run the same way round as the polygon. Use on a face to get the holes attached to their boundary.
member.remarks: A polygon whose edges cross is read under the even-odd rule first, as reads it, and a spike doubling back on itself is dropped, since it encloses nothing.

member.summary: Gets the curve parallel to a polyline at a distance to its left, as the options say, within tolerance. A negative distance goes to the right.
member.param: How far to move it, to the left of its direction when positive.
The shape of the corners on the outside of its turns.
member.returns: The pieces of the parallel curve, in order along the polyline and running the same way. Usually one. Where the polyline turns tighter than the distance, the parallel curve would loop back over itself; those loops are cut away, as AutoCAD does, and a curve cut clean through comes back in several pieces. Each piece takes its place by the middle of its longest edge, so a piece that runs on across a pinch, or one left closed, comes where most of it lies.
member.remarks: The parallel curve is the edge of the band the polyline sweeps sideways, minus the polyline itself and the band's two ends. Its corners are joined on the outside of each turn, so it keeps the distance from every segment on the side it was offset to. At a turn on the inside sharper than a right angle, the stretch of each moved segment that runs on past the other leg is cut away with the loop: the chain (10, 10), (0, 0), (10, 0) offset by 1 is the one piece from (10.707, 9.293) through (2.414, 1) to (10, 1). Where the edge of the band lies along another part of the polyline, within the tolerance, it is the polyline itself and goes: the step (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 1), (-5, 1) offset by 1 is the one piece from (0, 0) to (-5, 0).
member.exception: Thrown when the polyline or the options are null.
Thrown when the distance is not a finite number.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Offset3
member.summary: Offsetting a curved chain in space within its own plane.

remarks.para: A could be offset within a plane and a could not, though the plane library offsets a curved chain and a closed curved loop in space already offsets itself. A bar set out at one cover and wanted at another had to be straightened first, which throws the bends away.

A chain holding an arc has a plane of its own, taken from the arc rather than from the vertices — three vertices are always flat, so the vertices cannot be trusted to give it. The chain is laid out in that plane, the plane library answers, and the answer is lifted back: exact, with the arcs still arcs and their radii moved by the distance. A chain holding no arc is handed to the straight version, so the two cannot disagree, and a chain running straight along one line still has a plane picked for it by the normal, as the straight version does.

member.summary:
Provides static methods that offset shapes in space: move a curve sideways to a parallel copy, or grow and shrink a flat region within its own plane.
A line in space has a whole circle of directions square to it, so "sideways" has to be pinned down. Each method takes what does that: a plane to offset within (as AutoCAD's GetOffsetCurvesGivenPlaneNormal does), a direction to offset towards, or an up direction that fixes a left and an up for the segment, as Tekla Structures positions a part relative to its reference line. Within a plane the conventions of Offset2 hold: seen from the side the plane normal points to, a positive distance moves a curve to the left of its direction of travel.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Parallel3
member.summary:
Provides static methods for checking parallelism, perpendicularity and coplanarity between 3D entities.
Every method takes degenerate input to mean "no answer" and returns false for it. A zero-length vector has no direction, so it is neither parallel nor perpendicular to anything, and saying so keeps a caller from reading a confident true out of geometry that carries no information.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Parametrization2
member.summary:
Provides static methods for locating positions along a curve, either by a normalized parameter or by an arc length measured from the start of the curve.
The parameter is normalized: 0 is the start of the curve and 1 is its end, whatever the curve actually measures. The distance is a true arc length from the start, running from 0 to the total length. The two are proportional, so distance = parameter * length.
Each curve starts where its own geometry says it does: a line at its StartPoint, a polyline or polygon at its first vertex, a rectangle at its LowerLeft corner, and a circle at angle zero, that is the point directly right of its centre. All of them run in the direction their vertices are ordered, and a circle runs counter-clockwise.
Values outside the natural range follow the shape of the curve. A closed curve — a polygon, a rectangle, a circle — wraps around, so a parameter of 1.25 is the same position as 0.25. A polyline clamps, because it is an open chain with no natural extension. A line segment extrapolates along the infinite line that carries it, which is the behaviour GeoLine2.GetPointAtParameter has always had.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Parametrization3
member.summary:
Provides static methods for locating positions along a 3D curve, either by a normalized parameter or by an arc length measured from the start of the curve.
The parameter is normalized: 0 is the start of the curve and 1 is its end, whatever the curve actually measures. The distance is a true arc length from the start, running from 0 to the total length. The two are proportional, so distance = parameter * length.
Values outside the natural range follow the shape of the curve. A line segment extrapolates along the infinite line that carries it, and so does a ray, which likewise has a well defined carrier. A polyline clamps, because it is an open chain of segments with no single direction to extend along. A closed curve — a polygon, a circle — wraps, so a parameter of 1.25 is the same position as 0.25.

member.summary: Gets the arc length from the start of a polyline to the point on it closest to the supplied point, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance; every leg is measured as it is, so it changes nothing here.
member.returns: How far along the polyline its point nearest lies.

remarks.para: A polyline can pass near the same point more than once, so the closest edge is found first and the arc length is measured to that. Walking the chain and stopping at the first edge within tolerance would give a different answer depending on which end the chain was built from.

A leg is the leg it is however short, as reads it: at a hundredth, the polyline (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0.006, 0), (0, 0.006, 0) puts (10.03, 0.003, 0) 10.003 along, 0.003 along its leg 0.006 long, where it put it 10 along, at the start of that leg.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.PlanarMap
member.summary: Carries geometry that curves between the plane and space.

remarks.para: The rest of carries points, segments, polylines, polygons and faces. Arcs were missing, and that left the round trip half open: a curved edge of a plate could be brought into the plane to be worked on, but the answer could only be put back by flattening it and losing the curves.

A bulge in the plane is read counter-clockwise about the Z axis, so lifting one keeps the bulge as it is and hands the frame's Z axis to the edge as the plane it bulges in. Bringing one back is the same step in reverse, with one thing to watch: an arc whose normal runs against the frame is the same arc seen from behind, so its bulge changes sign on the way down. An arc lies in the plane when no point of it stands further off it than the planar tolerance, however its own plane is turned; one that stands off it does not, and the Try forms say so rather than flattening it.

member.summary:
Carries flat geometry between the plane and space: a shape lying in a plane in space is laid out in two dimensions, worked on there, and put back.
Everything goes through a , the frame the flattening is measured in. Hold on to it: the same frame has to be used to put the answer back, or it lands somewhere else. A frame built from a shape by turns with the shape, so the local coordinates of a plate are the same whichever way the plate is oriented in the model.
Flattening drops the local Z, so a point off the plane is a question rather than an answer. The Try forms refuse one farther from the plane than ; the plain forms project it onto the plane and say so in their name.
Carries splines between the plane and space.
member.remarks: A spline is carried by carrying its control points, which is exact: the laying of the plane into space and the projection of space onto the plane are both affine, and an affine map takes a NURBS to the NURBS of the carried control points with the same weights and knots. A spline lying in the plane of the frame comes back from the plane as it went in, to rounding.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.PlanarMap.ToArc3(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2)
member.summary: Lifts an arc out of a frame into the plane of that frame in space.
member.param: The frame the arc is laid out in.
member.returns: The same arc, standing in the plane of the frame.
member.remarks: The arc is built on its circle lifted into the frame, so a whole turn lifts as well as a part of one, and an arc a hundredth long bowing a thousandth of its chord off it as exactly as a half circle. It runs counter-clockwise round its normal, which is the frame's Z axis or its reverse.

member.remarks: An arc that does not lie in the plane of the frame comes back as the arc through the projections of its ends and its middle, which is a different arc. refuses that case instead of answering it.

member.summary: Lays an arc out in a frame when it lies in the plane of that frame, within a tolerance.
member.param: The arc in the plane, when it lies in one.

member.remarks: The arc lies in the plane when no point of it stands further off it than the planar tolerance, which a circle of the right tilt sitting above the frame does not. Its centre may lie far off the plane: an arc 100 long bowing a ten-thousandth has its centre 250 000 away, and turned a tenth of a degree out it still lies within a ten-thousandth of the frame.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection2
member.summary: The shortest segment joining a chain or loop that may curve to something else.

remarks.para: Both ends of the segment sit on a boundary, so a shape lying wholly inside a closed one still reports the gap out to its outline rather than nothing at all. takes the opposite view and reads a closed shape as a filled region, so the two deliberately disagree for that pair; everywhere else the segment is exactly as long as the distance, except for a point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc, which is carried to the arc's start. A point beside a straight side is joined to the side as it is however short.

Against anything but a point, every side is joined as it is however short, as the distance measures it: at a hundredth, the loop (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is joined to the segment from (10.03, 0.003) to (10.05, 0.003) by the line from (10, 0.003), 0.03 long, where read as its start its side 0.006 long gave one from a corner 0.0301496 long. Where the two come within the tolerance without meeting, the segment may still be one of no length, a touch.
Arcs are measured as arcs, not cut into pieces first, so the answer is exact. Where the two boundaries cross, the segment has no length and sits at the crossing.

member.summary:
Provides static calculation methods for geometric projections of points and vectors onto lines, circles, rectangles, polygons, and polylines.
Projecting onto a closed shape lands on its boundary: the circumference of a circle, or one of the edges of a rectangle, polygon, or polyline. That holds even when the point is already inside, which is carried out to the nearest edge rather than returned unchanged. The geometry types expose the same operation as GetClosestPointOnBoundary.
does not follow this rule at all: it treats a closed shape as a filled region, so the distance to a point inside it is zero.
GetShortestLineTo extends the same idea to a pair of shapes and hands back the shortest segment bridging their two boundaries, with its start point on the first shape and its end point on the second. Overlapping shapes give a zero length segment sitting on a point where the two outlines cross. Where a whole stretch of pairs is equally close, as happens when two edges run alongside each other, the segment is anchored at the middle of that stretch rather than at either end of it.
Against anything but a point, every side of a rectangle, a polygon or a polyline is joined as it is however short, as the distance measures it: at a hundredth, the polygon (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is joined to the segment from (10.03, 0.003) to (10.05, 0.003) by the line from (10, 0.003), 0.03 long, where read as its start its side 0.006 long gave one from a corner 0.0301496 long. A point is joined to such a side as it is too, and so is its closest point found. Where two shapes come within the tolerance without meeting, the segment may be one of no length, a touch, and only there: two sides whose lines cross within the tolerance past the ends of both can be twice as far apart, and are joined by the gap. Two squares 100 by 100 whose corners are 0.00085 apart in x and in y are joined at a thousandth by the line between the corners, 0.0012 long. A segment you give no longer than the tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly meet the other shape, and is joined from there, as a point is.
The tolerance is used for the projections themselves and for the endpoint slack when deciding whether two edges meet. It is deliberately not used as a cutoff for the edge scans: those stop early only on an exact zero, so widening the tolerance cannot make a search settle for a nearer edge it has not looked at yet.
The shortest segment joining a straight shape to one that curves.
member.remarks: The same segment as the one the curved shape would hand back, turned round so that it leaves the shape it was asked of. A rectangle is read as its own polygon; an arc is joined as an arc.
member.summary: The shortest segment joining a ray in the plane to another shape.

remarks.para: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so against a shape with an end to it, it is cut: into the segment from its origin out past the farthest the shape reaches along it, by a margin of a millimetre or a hundred point tolerances, whichever is more. Every point of the shape lies behind that end, so a shortest segment the cut gets rightly is the ray's own, and the cut is asked as any segment is. Against the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin, the ray from (-50, 150) along X is asked as the segment from there to (101, 150), and gets a segment 50 long down onto the top edge.

Both ends sit on a boundary, as for every pair here, and the segment leaves the first shape named. Against a point or another ray nothing is cut: every candidate is one the ray really holds, an origin brought onto the other or the place where the two cross.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection2.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining a curved loop to a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.
A straight edge is joined as the edge it is however short, as the distance measures it: at a hundredth, the loop (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the line runs from (10, 0.003), 0.03 long, where its edge 0.006 long, no longer than the tolerance, gave one from (10, 0), 0.0301496 long.
member.returns: A segment from the point gives to , measured on the arcs. Like every shortest line in this class it runs from boundary to boundary, so a point inside is carried out to the nearest edge and the segment is as long as the depth to it, where reads the loop as filled and answers nought. Outside, by more than the tolerance, it is as long as , which takes a point within the tolerance outside as in, but near the centre of an arc, as the remarks say; on the boundary it has no length. Where two edges are equally near, the first of them round the loop is taken.
member.exception: Thrown when the loop is null.

At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.
A straight edge is joined as the edge it is however short, as the distance measures it: at a hundredth, the loop (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the line runs from (10, 0.003), 0.03 long, where its edge 0.006 long, no longer than the tolerance, gave one from (10, 0), 0.0301496 long.
member.returns: A segment from the point gives to , measured on the arcs, so it is exactly as long as but near the centre of an arc, as the remarks say. Where two edges are equally near, the first of them along the chain is taken.
member.exception: Thrown when the chain is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection2.TryGetCrossingPoint(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.Boolean,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2@)
member.summary: Reports whether two segments cross, and where.
member.remarks:
This deliberately does not call , which treats any pair meeting at less than the angular tolerance as parallel and reports no intersection. That is the right call when the intersection point itself is wanted, because a near-parallel crossing pins it down very poorly. Here only the distance matters and it is exactly zero, so applying the angular gate would make a crossing pair report the gap between their endpoints instead - an error that grows with segment length.
With a crossing of the two lines up to the point tolerance past the end of either counts, as it does for that method, and the point is clamped onto the first: the shortest line reads two segments meeting so as touching. Past the ends of both it counts only where the two come within the tolerance. Without it the crossing has to lie on both, which is how the distance and the collision read them: the segment ending at (10, 0) and the one leaving (10.00135, 0.00078) at 60 degrees, whose lines cross at (10.0009, 0), cross nowhere, and are 0.00156 apart, too far for a touch either way.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection2.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Finds the shortest line segment connecting a point on the boundary of to within tolerance.
member.returns: A from the point gives to . Like every shortest line in this class it runs from boundary to boundary, so a point inside is carried out to the nearest edge and the segment is as long as the depth to it, where reads the polygon as filled and answers nought. Outside, by more than the tolerance, it is as long as , which takes a point within the tolerance outside as in; on the boundary it has no length. Where two edges are equally near, the first of them round the polygon is taken. Inside the square 100 by 100 on the origin, the point (50, 30) gets the segment from (50, 0), 30 long. Beside a side no longer than the tolerance it runs from the side as it is: at a hundredth, the polygon (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the segment runs from (10, 0.003), 0.03 long, where it ran from the side's start (10, 0), 0.0301496 long.
member.exception: Thrown when the polygon is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection2.ProjectToPolylineArc(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the point of a chain that may curve nearest a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The answer lies on the arcs themselves, not on the chords that stand in for them elsewhere. A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991. A straight edge offers its nearest point as the edge it is however short, as the distance measures it: at a hundredth, the loop (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the closest point is (10, 0.003), 0.03 away, where its edge 0.006 long, no longer than the tolerance, offered its start (10, 0), 0.0301496 away.
member.exception: Thrown when the chain is null.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection3
member.summary: The shortest segment joining a segment or a straight chain to a plane, a polygon, a triangle or another chain.

remarks.para: These are the pairs could measure and could not draw. Each is built from the joining lines already here: segment to segment, segment to triangle, and point to shape. The segment leaves the shape named first and lands on the other, both ends lie on their shapes, and it is as long as the distance. A segment to a polygon and the chain to a segment or to another chain are where those distances are now read from.

A polygon is read as a filled surface, as its distance reads it, so a chain passing through one meets it in a segment of no length at the crossing, and a chain ending above it is joined straight down. A chain that comes at a polygon or a triangle end-on and stops within the point tolerance of it is read as crossing it, as the segment to a triangle always has: the segment of no length then sits at that end, up to the tolerance off the surface, while reads the gap, which is exact: the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, 9) over the square 100 by 100 in the floor is joined by a segment of no length at (5, 5, 0.0004), and is 0.0004 from it by its distance. One lying level within the tolerance is joined by its true gap, which is its distance too.

A plane is endless, so a shape that crosses or touches it is joined by a segment of no length at the first point of contact in the shape's own order: along a segment from its start, and edge by edge along a chain. A shape clear of the plane is joined from its nearest point, which is a vertex, and where several are equally near as the arithmetic reads them, from the first of them. A shape lying parallel to a plane that is not level has heights that differ in their last digits, so it may be joined from any of its nearest vertices; the length is the same. The segment is never snapped: a chain standing 0.0004 above the plane is joined by a segment 0.0004 long, though its distance, read within the point tolerance, is nought.
Where two candidates are equally short, the one met first stands: the edges of a chain in order, and for two chains, each edge of the first against every edge of the second in turn.

member.summary:
Provides static methods for geometric projections in 3D space.
Every ProjectTo... method answers the same question: which point of the target shape is closest to the supplied point. For a bounded shape the answer is clamped to the shape, so projecting onto a segment never returns a point past its endpoints, and projecting onto a triangle never returns a point outside its edges.
The point of a face nearest another point.
member.remarks: A face is a flat region with holes in it, so the nearest point of one is not simply the foot of the perpendicular: a point over a hole is over nothing, and the nearest material is the rim of that hole. The reading matches , which answers with a point of the region where there is region under the foot and a point of the outline where there is not.
member.summary: The shortest segment joining a shape in space to a point.

remarks.para: Each segment leaves the point of the shape that the matching ProjectTo... gives and ends on the point, and measures the distance from that same nearest point, so the segment is exactly as long as the distance.

A flat region is read as its distance reads it: a triangle, a polygon, a face and a disc are filled, so a point above one goes straight down to it where its foot lands on the material, and a point lying on it gets a segment of no length. Only a solid differs, since its segment runs to the surface even from inside; see .

member.summary: The shortest segment joining two flat regions in space, a region or a ray to a plane, a segment, a chain or a ray to a face, a ray to a polygon, a ray or a chain, and a body to a face.

remarks.para: These are the pairs neither side could measure. Each is the least of the joining lines already here: every edge of the first shape against the second, then every edge of the second against the first, a ray standing in for an edge. Two flat regions that do not meet always have their nearest pair on an edge of one of them, so nothing else need be weighed. The segment leaves the shape named first and lands on the other, and both ends lie on their shapes.

A face is its material, the outline less its holes. A segment crossing the material meets it in a segment of no length; one passing through a hole is joined to the nearest rim, or straight down from an end that stands over the material.

Where the two meet, the segment has no length and sits at the first point of contact walking the edges in that order: for two regions in planes that are not one, the first of the crossings names. As for the segment and the chain against a polygon, an edge coming at a region end-on and stopping within the point tolerance of it is read as crossing it, so the segment of no length sits at that end, though the distance there is the true gap; a region lying level within the tolerance is joined by its true gap, which is its distance too. The segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, 9) over the square 100 by 100 in the floor is joined by a segment of no length at (5, 5, 0.0004), and is 0.0004 from it by its distance.

A plane is read by the heights of the corners, as a chain is: a shape that crosses or touches it is joined by a segment of no length at the first point of contact walking its edges in order, and a shape clear of it from its nearest corner, the first of those equally near. No tolerance widens the plane here, so a shape a hair off it is joined by a segment that short.
Where two candidates are equally short, the one met first stands. A length that is not a number is kept, so a shape with a corner that is not a number is not a number away.

member.summary: The shortest segment joining a solid, a triangle or a segment in space to another of them.

remarks.para: The library could already say how far apart two of these stood; this says between which two points. The segment is exactly as long as that distance, and each of its ends lies on the surface it came from, so it can be drawn as it is.

Both ends sit on a surface. A body lying wholly inside another therefore reports the gap out to the skin of the other, where reads a solid as a filled region and answers nothing at all. The two disagree there on purpose, the same way they do in the plane.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection3.ProjectToTriangle(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Projects a point onto a triangle, clamped to its edges.
member.returns: The point of the triangle closest to the supplied point.
member.remarks: This is the Voronoi region method: the space around a triangle divides into seven regions — one per vertex, one per edge, and the interior — and each is recognised by the signs of a handful of dot products before any division happens. Solving the barycentric system directly instead would divide by a determinant that vanishes for a degenerate triangle, which is exactly the input the fallback at the end of this method handles. On a long thin triangle the products the regions are told apart by cancel, and the point found is checked against the gap measures: one further off it than the triangle is high, or a billionth of the triangle's reach where it is higher, is replaced by the point that gap is measured to. From a point 0.00004 from the triangle (-2385.64, -1816.731, -2875.223), (1513.515, -1634.873, 3521.065), (3037.692, -1563.784, 6021.375), 9 000 long and 0.0024 high, the point found was 2.08 away; it is 0.00004 away now. A triangle at least a hundredth as high as it is long, or as the point is far from its first corner where that is further, is answered as before, bit for bit, and so is every point the regions found right.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection3.ProjectToSolid(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Projects a point onto the surface of a solid, within a tolerance.

remarks.para: The answer is always on the boundary, interior points included, because a solid is described only by its faces and there is nothing else to land on.

The boundary is where the material ends, openings included. A body keeps an opening as a whole body subtracted from it, so its faces run straight across every hole, and the nearest point of a face can sit in the middle of one. The nearest point of the material is then on the rim, which is a point of neither the faces nor the opening alone — it only exists once the opening is cut in. So the openings within reach are cut in and the answer is taken from what is left; see for which are within reach.

A body with openings asked at a point tolerance below the rounding of the coordinates, a quadrillionth of the largest of them, nought among them, has its openings cut and its faces read within that rounding: at nought, a point in the middle of a hole 20 by 20 through a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space was projected 1.5 from it, onto a face across the hole; it is projected onto the hole's wall, 10 off.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Projection3.ProjectToMaterial(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Projects a point onto the surface of a body with openings, cutting in only the openings that can change the answer.

remarks.para: Cutting every opening in for every point would make a plate with twenty bolt holes cost twenty cuts per question. An opening farther from the point than the answer found without it cannot change that answer: the material within that distance of the point is the same whether it is cut in or not, and the answer is the nearest boundary within it. So the openings are taken on in rings — those within the distance found so far — until none is left within it.
A body whose openings take all of its material has no boundary to land on; the faces are answered then, as the only thing the body still describes.

A point tolerance below the rounding of the coordinates is raised to it, for the openings as for the faces they leave: at nought, a point in the middle of a hole 20 by 20 through a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space was projected onto a face across the hole, 1.5 off, and a thousand and more out onto the rim of the hole's wall, 10.11 off, the wall's face read at nought; it is projected onto the wall, 10 off.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Ray2
member.summary: How a ray in the plane is cut into a segment to be asked of a shape with an end to it, and where a point falls on it.

remarks.para: Every point of the shape projects to at most t, so every point of the ray past R is further from every point of the shape than the end of the cut is. Where the segment code answers rightly, the end of the cut is never a crossing, a touching point or an end of a shortest segment, and the cut answers what the ray would. Where it does not, the ray shares the fault: a segment starting just inside a circle's rim and running nearly along it misses where it leaves, and its shortest segment runs from its far end. A NaN anywhere is carried into the cut, and a ray of no direction, a default one, is cut to the single point of its origin.

member.summary: Finds where two rays cross, at any angle, placed on the first ray and never behind its origin.
member.remarks:
Two rays cross unless they are parallel by rounding, by the rule of the line without ends (see ): a sine below 1E-15, or a sine of 1E-9 or less with a crossing further along than a double can place within the point tolerance, measured by the larger of the two distances along, so that both ways round agree; a NaN has none either. A ray rebuilt through two points a hundred apart of another moved 10 to its side is a sine of some 1E-14 off it at coordinates of ten thousand, and crosses it nowhere: the crossing would lie 1E15 along. Two rays at half a degree that cross a thousand along cross there, though calls them parallel by angle: distance, collision and the shortest line ask where the rays are, not whether the crossing is well placed.
With a crossing up to the point tolerance behind either origin counts, as it does for that method, which places the point. Without it the crossing has to be at or ahead of both origins, which is how the distance, the collision and the shortest line read two rays: the ray from (0.0009, 0) along X and the one leaving 0.0009 along 120 degrees from the origin, whose carriers cross 0.0009 behind each, cross nowhere and are 0.00156 apart.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Shells3
member.summary: Separating a body into the pieces of material that do not touch.

remarks.para: A is a bag of faces, and nothing stops the faces from bounding two blocks that never meet. The booleans produce such bodies all the time — a bar through two blocks shares two separate regions with them — and so does cutting a body by a plane that passes exactly along the wall of a hole: the strip either side of the hole comes out as one body in two pieces. Anything that then decides what the body is by asking one point of it decides for every piece at once, and is wrong for all but one. That is how subtracting a box that overlapped an existing hole once threw away a whole block of material that was nowhere near the box.

Faces belong together when they share part of an edge. An edge is matched by overlap along a common line rather than by its end points, so a long edge beside two short ones — which merging coplanar faces leaves behind — still joins all three. Where exactly two faces share a stretch of edge they are one piece. Where more meet — two blocks touching along an edge, four faces round one line — the faces are taken in turn round the line, and two neighbours are joined only when the wedge between them is material, which is what keeps two blocks that share nothing but an edge apart.
A cavity is a closed shell of its own, wound inwards, and belongs to the piece around it rather than being a piece in itself. Each opening goes with every piece its box reaches.

A group of faces enclosing nothing — a lone face, or two lying back to back as a sheet of no thickness — is no piece either. It goes with the piece holding it, so that nothing the body was given is lost, and is dropped only when no piece holds it. Such a group once reached the constructor of a body and made splitting throw.

remarks.para: The sweep tries every pair its axis cannot tell apart, and where the edges of a body meet at a point it cannot tell them apart along any axis: a cone of 16 000 sides has 16 000 edges to the apex, each overlapping the others in the sweep and none of them lying along another. When the sweep would try more than pairs for each segment, the segments are matched through their end points instead. Two segments overlap only where the shorter has both its ends within the tolerance of the line of the longer, and so for each segment the points within the tolerance of its line, a few, are found in a tree, and only the segments with both their ends among them are tried against it, each with the sweep's own test of whether they could meet and its own test of overlap. The pairs tried are among those the sweep tries, every pair it joins is tried, and the lines come out the same.

member.summary: Gets the tolerance the edges of faces are matched within as and match them: the one given, raised to the rounding of the coordinates of the faces where it is below it, as a ray's crossing of a face is held (). The rounding is a quadrillionth of the largest coordinate of all the faces, the whole body's, not of each part of it.
member.remarks: An edge and its twin, run back along it by the face beside, have the same corners to the bit, but the twin's far corner, measured off the line of the edge, stands off it by the rounding of that reckoning: at a tolerance of nought a cube of 100 turned in space, and a cylinder of 24 sides standing at the origin, read open along nearly every edge. At every tolerance at or above the rounding nothing changes, bit for bit. The largest coordinate is the whole body's: a cube of 1 at the origin and a box a million out, one body, are matched within a billionth, so a gap of a hundred-billionth in the small cube reads closed with the box and open without it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Shells3.PairsUp(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Determines whether every edge of the faces longer than the point tolerance is run as many times one way as the other, each with its face on the left, its corners taken on a grid a sixty-fourth of the point tolerance across: each stretch of each is then covered an even number of times, and there is nothing for to find open. A hole is wound as the boundary is, so its edges are run the other way round.

remarks.para: Two faces a boolean cut apart carry the corner they share as each worked it out, which can differ in the last bits: a plate 3000 by 1000 by 20 with 100 holes drilled far from the origin pairs 26 622 of its 29 976 edges to the bit and all of them on the grid. Corners either side of a line of the grid do not pair, and the full reading is asked.

Why a body paired so reads closed to . Two corners in one cell of the grid stand less than its diagonal d, the step times the root of 3, apart, so an edge and the one run back along it, its twin, differ in length by less than 2d. An edge no longer than the tolerance is left out here as AddLoop leaves it out, and where an edge is within 2d of the tolerance either way the full reading is asked: so of an edge and its twin either both are left out or both are kept, and both kept are longer than the tolerance and 2d. The twin's ends then lie within d of the edge's line and overlap it by more than its length less 2d, more than the tolerance, so joins the two into one line, by the sweep or by the points. Along that line the stops of the two ends of each lie within d of each other, so a stretch whose middle one of them covers and the other does not is no longer than d and is passed over; every stretch longer than the tolerance is covered by both of each such pair or by neither, once each way, and no stretch is covered an odd number of times. Two copies of an edge either side of the tolerance, one kept and one not, are what the margin is for: paired on the grid, they read open.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Slice3
member.summary: The volume of a body's material within some bodies and outside others, worked out by slicing it level by level, with no body built.

remarks.para: A level plane cuts each body in a section, and the volume is the area of the section added up the height. Between two heights where nothing happens, no corner of a body, no edge of one body through a face of another and no three faces of three bodies meeting, every corner of the section moves along a straight line, so its area is a polynomial of the second degree in the height. Milne's rule, the sections at a quarter, a half and three quarters of the layer weighed 2/3, -1/3 and 2/3, then adds the layer up exactly: a box 30 by 20 by 10 turned about two axes comes out 6 000 to the rounding.

A section's area is swept across in x. Between two x where nothing happens, the end of a segment of a section or two segments crossing, the length of the material along a line of constant x is linear in x, so the line through the middle of the strip gives the strip exactly. Along that line the inside of each body is read by the segments it crosses, odd and even, so the way the faces are wound does not matter. A section crossed an odd number of times gives no volume: the two faces of an edge must cross a level at the same point, and a corner that sits more than about 1E-9 off the edge of its neighbour, a T-junction, leaves a gap in the section that a line through it crosses once. , which reads within a tolerance, may accept such a body all the same.

The bodies are sliced across the axis whose sections cost the least, z where two cost the same, then x, then y, the coordinates swapped whole so that the volume is the one the swapped bodies give along z, to the bit. A wall and a curved girder of a Tekla model, sliced in 0.31 to 0.36 seconds across z, take 0.03 to 0.04 across x; a slab 6 000 by 6 000 by 200 sloped 5 degrees with 200 round openings scattered over it, 29 seconds across z and 0.37 across x.

The material of a body is the body less its openings; the openings' own openings are not read. Nothing is snapped to a tolerance, so a shell 0.02 thick is counted as one. The coordinates are moved to the subject's least corner first, so that a part some hundreds of metres from the origin loses no digits. Nothing throws: inconsistent faces, or a number that is not finite, give false.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Slice3.Up(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Core.Slice3.Shape},GeometryHelper.Core.Slice3.Extent)
member.summary: The axis to slice across: the one whose sections cost the least, z, x and y in that order where two cost the same.

remarks.para: Each section costs about the faces it crosses, so an axis costs about the faces each corner level within the region crosses, added up, and a section for each level besides. The edges through faces of other bodies, which add levels too, are left out of the count; they are as many whichever way the bodies are cut.

A curved girder in a curved wall has its facets at many heights along z, and each level crosses most of the facets of both; across x, few levels cross few faces, and the pair takes a tenth of the time. A slab sloped 5 degrees with openings scattered over it crosses nearly every opening at every level along z, and only those in a strip across x: with 400 openings, 156 seconds against 1.4.
