member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Sphere3
member.summary: What a ball in space is asked: how far its centre stands from a shape, where its surface is crossed by a line or a curve, and the circle two surfaces share.

remarks.para: A ball is a point grown by its radius, so the gap between it and any shape is the gap between its centre and that shape less the radius, and nought where the shape reaches into it. The shape's own distance to a point does the measuring (a closed shape is read as filled, a curve as a curve, a disc as a disc), and the shortest segment leaves the surface of the ball for the point of the shape nearest its centre.

A line, a ray or a segment crosses the surface where the quadratic of the distance from the centre has its roots. The foot of the centre on the line is found first and the roots stand either side of it by the half chord, the square root of (r - rho)(r + rho) where rho is the distance from the centre to the line, so that a line grazing the surface loses no digits to a difference of squares. A curve in a plane is cut by the circle the plane makes with the surface, and the crossing of two curves in one plane is the library's own.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Spline3
member.summary: The queries of a spline in space against every other shape in space: how far apart they are, where they meet, and the shortest segment between them. Each shape is cut into pieces the spline can work out its meetings with, one maths for all, so that the spline and the shape agree to the bit asked from either side.

remarks.para: A flat shape, a triangle, a polygon or a face, is filled: a spline that pierces it, or lies in it, is nought from it, and the crossings are the places it pierces and where it meets the outline. A circle and an ellipse are discs for the distance, as their own distances to a point read them, and their crossings are those of the rim. A body, a box, an oriented box, a solid or a ball, is material: a spline in it is nought from it, the crossings and the shortest segment are those of its skin, and the shortest segment out of a body that holds the spline is the gap out to the skin. A curve, a chain or a loop of arcs and segments, is the path it is.

In space two curves seldom meet, so a place is where the distance of the spline from the shape is least within the point tolerance: a crossing is such a place, where the distance comes to nought, and a near miss within the tolerance is another; the distance itself is never read through the tolerance, only the places and the collision are.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition2
member.summary: Cutting a chain or a loop that may curve, along the arcs rather than across them.
Cutting an area in the plane into areas.

remarks.para: A and a could be cut in two and a and a could not, though the plane is where that is usually wanted. Everything already cut in the plane — segments, chains, loops — came back as lines; nothing came back as an area.

Nothing new is worked out here. The shape is laid flat in the world frame at z = 0, cut by the exact arithmetic already holds, and projected back. Lifting adds a nought and projecting drops it, so the round trip costs no accuracy, and the two readings cannot drift apart because there is only one of them.

The cutter is a read as the whole straight line through it, which is what a is to space: unbounded, and dividing everything into two sides. Its length is ignored — a segment crossing half the shape cuts all of it. Where a bounded cutter is meant, the cut line overload takes a chain that has to start and finish on the boundary.

member.summary:
Splits open geometry — line segments and polylines — at a position along it, or wherever a cutter meets it. A cutter may be a point, a line, a polyline or a polygon, singly or as an array, and several polygons behave as their union.
Pieces come back in order along the subject, so the first piece always holds its start point and the last piece always holds its end point. Splitting against a polygon sorts them by side instead, each side still in order. Geometry that closes back on itself is a and is a cutter here, never a subject.
A false return says nothing was cut, not that the call failed: the out parameters are left usable either way, holding the subject whole rather than nothing at all.

member.param: A segment, read as the whole straight line through it; its length is ignored.
The pieces on the left of the cutter's direction of travel.
member.returns: true when the line divided the loop, leaving something on both sides; otherwise, false, and the loop comes back whole on the side it lies on.
member.remarks:
Left and right are read from the cutter's own direction, so reversing the cutter swaps the two answers and nothing else. A concave loop can give several pieces to a side, which is why each side is an array.
The loop and the pieces are taken corner for corner at the tolerance asked, never at the global one: at a millionth, the line through (0.0005, 0) and (0, 0.0005) cuts the square 10 by 10 at the origin into its corner, a triangle of 0.000000125 square units, and the rest, where the global tolerance of a thousandth read the corner as no polygon and threw.
member.exception: Thrown when the loop is null.

member.remarks: A hole the line misses stays a hole in whichever piece keeps it; a hole the line crosses opens into the outline of both pieces, which is why a face can come back with fewer holes than it went in with. A face whose boundary or a hole encloses no area at the global tolerance, as the points (0, 0), (100, 0) and (50, 0), is not cut: false, and the face comes back whole on the left.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition2.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts a loop in two along a chain drawn across it, within a tolerance.
member.param: The chain to cut along. Both of its ends have to sit on the loop's boundary and everything between them has to stay inside, or nothing is cut.
The two pieces, or the loop alone.
member.returns: true when the chain divided the loop in two; otherwise, false.
member.remarks:
This is the bounded cutter: the chain gives the exact line of the cut, so a piece keeps the chain's own vertices rather than a straight line between its ends. A chain that leaves the loop and comes back would divide it into more than two, so it is refused rather than answered in part.
An end that meets the boundary within the tolerance of a corner is cut from the corner, so both pieces keep it and nothing of the loop is lost: at a hundredth, the square 10 by 10 cut from (0.004, 0) to (10, 5) gives the triangle of 25 square units from (0, 0) and the rest, of 75, where the rest lost a sliver of 0.02 square units at the corner.
The loop, the chain and the pieces are taken corner for corner at the tolerance asked, never at the global one: at a millionth, the square 10 by 10 with its corner (0, 0) cut off by a side 0.00057 long is cut from (0, 5) to (10, 5) into the top of 50 square units and the bottom of 50 less the 0.00000008 the cut-off corner takes, where the global tolerance of a thousandth dropped the short side and refused the cut.
member.exception: Thrown when the loop or the chain is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition2.KeepCrossings(System.Double,System.Double[],System.Func{System.Double,System.Boolean},System.Boolean[]@)
member.summary: Drops the cut positions where the subject does not actually change sides.
member.param: Reports whether the subject is inside the cutter at an arc length.
Which side each surviving piece falls on, one entry longer than the returned positions.
member.returns: The positions that are real crossings, a subset of .
member.remarks:
A region cutter can meet the subject without the subject passing through it: grazing a corner, or touching at a vertex and turning back. Those meetings are intersection points like any other, so they arrive here as cut positions, and cutting there would leave two pieces on the same side of the cutter with a seam between them for no reason.
Rather than trying to recognise each way that can happen, this samples the midpoint of every interval and keeps only the positions where the answer differs on the two sides. Tangency, corner grazing and a vertex resting on the boundary all resolve themselves, with no special case for any of them.
The classification is handed back rather than left to be recomputed on the surviving pieces. Probing a merged piece would sample its midpoint, and when a dropped position sat halfway along it — which is exactly what happens when a path touches the boundary and turns back at its own midpoint — that probe lands on the boundary and reports the whole piece as inside. The samples taken here sit strictly between crossings, so they never have that problem.

A point handed in by the caller has to be checked, because GetDistanceAtPoint answers for the nearest position on the subject whether or not the point is anywhere near it — cutting there would be cutting somewhere nobody asked for. member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3
member.summary:
Provides static methods for cutting 3D geometry into pieces.
A curve is cut at a position along it or wherever a plane crosses it, and the pieces come back in order along the subject, so the first piece always holds its start point and the last holds its end point. A region or a body is cut by a plane and the pieces come back sorted by side.
Every overload reports false when there was nothing to cut — the cutter missed, or it only grazed an endpoint — and in that case still hands back the subject as a single piece rather than a null array, so a caller can use the result either way.

member.summary: Splits a line segment at a point on it, within a tolerance.
member.returns: false when the point does not lie on the segment, or lies on one of its endpoints.

remarks.para: A point off the subject is refused rather than being projected onto it and cut at, because a caller who passed the wrong point would otherwise get a plausible answer to a question they did not ask.

The place is measured along the segment as it is however much shorter than the global tolerance, so are those a plane, a polygon or a face cut it at, and those of the cuts by an oriented or axis-aligned box and of the cuts of a polyline's legs by a plane, a box, a polygon or a face: at a billionth, the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, -0.0005) is cut at (5, 5, 0), where the place was measured at the global thousandth, at its start, and the segment came back whole.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.SplitAtDistances(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3,System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.Double},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Splits a polyline at several arc lengths at once, within a tolerance.

remarks.para: A cut position that falls within tolerance of an existing vertex snaps onto it rather than adding a vertex beside it, so no edge comes back shorter than the tolerance either.

Every piece starts where the one before it ended, on the polyline: at a hundredth, the polyline from (0, 0, 0) to (10, 0, 0) and on to (10, 10, 0) cut at 9.995 comes back as two pieces meeting at the corner, where the second started at (10, -0.005, 0), the cut carried back along the next leg off the polyline, and cut at 10.005 the second started 0.005 past the corner the first ended at. A cut on a leg no longer than the tolerance is made where the piece before it ends. The pieces keep what the tolerance asked keeps, however much shorter than the global tolerance: at a billionth, the polyline from (0, 0, 0) to (10, 0, 0) cut at 5 and 5.0005 gives a piece 0.0005 long, where it threw.

The last piece ends where the polyline does. A last leg no longer than the tolerance takes the corner before it, as a first one is taken by the start: at a hundredth, the polyline from (0, 0, 0) to (10, 0, 0) and on to (10, 0.006, 0) cut at 5 gives the pieces from (0, 0, 0) to (5, 0, 0) and from there to (10, 0.006, 0), where the second ended at the corner (10, 0, 0) and the end was lost. Cut at 9.995, the cut lands on the corner and would leave only that leg, 0.006 long, after it, so it is not made and the polyline comes back whole, where it came back as one piece ending at the corner.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.EndAt(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3},System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Ends the last piece of a polyline cut at distances where the polyline ends, its end within the tolerance of where the piece so far ends.
member.remarks: A last leg no longer than the tolerance takes the corner before it, as a first one is taken by the start, unless the point before that corner is itself within the tolerance of the end, where the polyline folds back: the leg is then kept as it is, since without the corner the piece would be shorter than the tolerance. Where only the last cut is left within the tolerance of the end, that cut is not made and the piece before it ends there.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Splits a polygon by a plane, within a tolerance.
member.param: The pieces on the side the cutter normal points towards.
The pieces on the other side.
member.returns: false when the plane does not cut the polygon into two.
member.remarks:
Every piece keeps the orientation of the subject, so each one reports the same normal the original did. A concave polygon can fall into more than two pieces — a plane through the waist of a U leaves one piece on one side and two on the other — which is why each side comes back as an array rather than a single polygon.
When the method returns false the subject is handed back whole on whichever side it lies, and the other side comes back empty.

member.param: The face to cut, holes included.
The pieces on the side the cutter normal points towards.
The pieces on the other side.
member.returns: false when the plane does not cut the face into two.
member.remarks: The holes are cut along with the boundary rather than being sorted onto one side afterwards. That matters when the plane passes through a hole: the piece on each side then has a boundary made partly of the old outer edge and partly of the old hole rim, so the topology changes and no amount of sorting whole holes would produce it. A hole the plane misses stays a hole, and is attached to whichever piece encloses it.

member.summary: Tells apart the vertices on the cutting plane that the ring really crosses at from those it only touches, and reclassifies the ones that are not crossings.
member.remarks:
A vertex sitting on the plane does not by itself mean the boundary passes through to the other side. It may only have come down to the plane and gone back the way it came — the tip of a notch resting exactly on the cut, a corner grazing it. Reading such a vertex as a crossing costs more than an extra entry in the list: the crossings are paired off in order along the cut line on the understanding that they alternate entering and leaving the material, so one touch makes the count odd and leaves the last crossing without a partner, and two of them pair a touch with a real crossing. Either way the walk that follows runs off the end of a chain, and the pieces come back overlapping — a body cut that way gains volume out of nothing while both halves still report themselves closed.
What settles it is the side the ring is on before reaching the plane against the side it is on after leaving: the same side means a touch, opposite sides mean a crossing. A run of vertices on the plane — an edge lying along the cut rather than a single corner — is judged as one unit for the same reason, since the whole run is one visit to the plane.
Where a run crosses, the stretch it lies along is boundary of the side whose material it borders, and that is what decides which end of it is the crossing: the end the other side leaves the plane from. Cutting an L along the plane of its own notch, the piece the notch edge borders runs along that edge to its far end, and the piece on the other side stops at the near end, which is where the two meet. Picking the end the other way round would leave the other half with a spur of zero width running out to a vertex that is not on it.
It is the same end for both sides, so the two pieces of a face share their crossings, pair them the same way, and meet along the same edges. Picked by the side being built instead, the piece the run borders stepped over it straight from the other end, which is the same line only while the run lies exactly in the plane. A run within the tolerance of it is not: a notch edge within a thousandth of a millimetre of the plane, at the end of a cut seventy metres long, left a sliver nine ten-thousandths across between the pieces of a slab's faces, which belonged to neither half, and the two halves were ten thousand cubic millimetres short of the slab.
member.param: The side of each ring entry; anything that is not a crossing is rewritten in place.
The side the piece being built lies on.
The ring the sides are of, walked with the material on its left.
The normal of the face the ring bounds, which fixes what its left is.
The normal of the cutting plane, pointing to the side 1 stands for.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Splits a solid by a plane, within a tolerance.
member.param: The solid to cut; its boundary must be closed and wound outwards.
The piece on the side the cutter normal points towards.
The piece on the other side.
member.returns: false when the plane misses the solid or only grazes it, or a body that closes would not come apart into two halves that close.
member.remarks:
The body may be concave and its faces may carry holes. Each face is cut on its own, and the new surface closing each half is built from the edges the cut left behind: every such edge is traversed once by the face beside it, so the same edge traversed the other way belongs to the cap. Chaining those reversed edges gives the section, which may be several loops and may have one loop inside another — cutting a hollow tube leaves a ring, not a disc — so the loops are nested into faces rather than assumed to be a single boundary.
An edge shared by two faces that both survive on the same side is traversed both ways among the collected edges and cancels out, which is what keeps interior edges from being mistaken for section boundary.
A plane that parts a body without crossing any of it — between two blocks of one body, or along the edge where two parts of it meet, as a body cut through a corner of its notch touches itself — leaves every edge on the plane run both ways within each half. Each half is closed as it is, and the body is split with nothing to cap. A plane crossing the body where it is thinner than the point tolerance leaves the two sides of the section within the tolerance of each other, and their edges cancel too; but they are two edges, not one, and the halves would be open by the sliver between them, so the body is not split.
A body that closes as reads it comes apart into two halves that close so too, or not at all. A plane a hair over the tolerance inside a face, and all but parallel to it, cuts off a slab whose every edge down its sides is about the tolerance long, and cut within the tolerance such a slab can come out open: the body is cut again within a finer tolerance, or failing that the slab is welded closed, the halves taken only where they add up to the body. A hull 20 across cut 0.0011 inside a face gives a slab of 0.022 cubic millimetres, closed.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.ClosesOrRecuts(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Takes the halves a plane cut a closed body into where both close as reads them; otherwise cuts the body again within a tenth of the tolerance and then a hundredth, and where neither gives two closed halves that add up to the body, welds what is open closed; false where none of these does.
member.param: The half above the plane; replaced by what closed.
The half below it; replaced by what closed.
member.returns: false where no two closed halves could be had of a body that closes.
member.remarks:
A plane a hair over the tolerance inside a face, and all but parallel to it, cuts off a slab little thicker than the tolerance, every edge down its sides about the tolerance long. Cut within the tolerance, some pieces of the faces meeting at a corner of the face were too thin to be faces and were left out, and the slab came out open: a hull of fourteen points 20 across, cut 0.0011 inside a face, gave one of 0.022 cubic millimetres open by an edge 0.0011 long, seven of the twelve faces the plane crossed giving it a side. Of 3 000 such hulls cut so, 79 gave a half open to Validate. Within a tenth of the tolerance every edge down the slab is ten times the tolerance long: that closed 78 of them, and a hundredth the last, the halves of 77 adding up to the body within a hundred-millionth of a cubic millimetre and of the other two within 0.00025. The cut again is tried first because it moves nothing: a weld closed only 38, and of those the halves of six held up to 0.032 less than the body and the rest up to 0.045 off it, within the bound but far from what a finer cut gives.
Two closed halves are taken where they hold the body between them within the tolerance times the area of the section, as far again as a weld moved them, and the rounding: the section is no larger than half the skin of either half, which stands over it. A body that does not close is cut as it is and its halves are not checked, halves that close as they are come back as they were, and with no tolerance the halves come back as cut. Where neither a finer cut nor a weld closes the halves, the cut is refused though the halves were given before: of 4 000 cuts near a face of boxes whose faces each carry their own copy of every corner, a hair apart, 12 are refused so, whose halves had been open to Validate and their slabs 5 to 45 % off what the plane cuts off.

member.summary: Gets the tolerance a body is cut within when an opening is cut into it: the one given, with a corner read as on the plane where it stands off it by no more than the planar tolerance and what rounding the body's coordinates can add to that.
member.remarks: A corner standing off the plane by the tolerance to the last few bits is read on one side of it by its distance and within the point tolerance of the point where its edge crosses the plane by where that point was rounded to, and the piece of a face between them is then a polygon with those two corners made one: a body 100 by 60 by 40 cut by a plane 0.0010000000000000009 inside its floor, an opening's, read every corner of the floor beyond the plane, and cut its sides into strips that lost a corner, so that the slab beneath the plane came out open, and the body with its opening cut 7.66 cubic millimetres short. A trillionth of the size of the coordinates is far beyond the rounding and far within any tolerance. Only the cutting of openings reads a corner so, the differences that take them out one at a time where it gives no material to trust, all through (see Boolean3.TakeOutOneAtATime), a union worked out once more where it came out wound against itself both other ways (see Boolean3.Union), and a union, a common part or a difference asked within a few roundings of the coordinates (see Boolean3.NearTheRounding), or below them, raised to the rounding (see Boolean3.BelowTheRounding); a section or the cells of a body asked below the rounding are cut within a trillionth of the coordinates outright (see ). The cells of a boolean cut so read a slab exactly the tolerance thick, in or beside a turned body, as on the plane at some corners and off it at others: of 2 700 unions, differences and intersections of such slabs and chips with a cube turned at random, six that were valid came out open or wound two ways.

None does now. Raised to the rounding alone, a quadrillionth, with a corner read on the plane within a trillionth, 5 of 4 000 planes still cut nothing and 2 of 1 000 bodies came out in the wrong cells: the corners of the material of a body with openings, cut at nought, stand further apart than the rounding. member.param: The body to cut it by; its boundary must be closed.
The pieces lying within the body.
member.returns: false when the chain never crosses the surface, so there was nothing to cut.
member.remarks:
A closed body has no side the way a plane does, so the pieces come back sorted into within and beyond rather than above and below. The chain is cut at every crossing of the surface, which is what makes each piece lie wholly on one side and lets a single sample decide which.
A leg is crossed as it is however short, and the place is measured along it as it is: at a hundredth, the chain from (2, 5, 0.054) down to (5, 5, 0.004), through the top of the box 10 by 10 by 10 standing under the floor to (5, 5, -0.005) and on to (8, 5, -0.055) is cut within the tolerance of (5, 5, 0), where its leg 0.009 long crossed no face and the chain came back whole. A cut within the tolerance of a corner is made at the corner, as makes it.
A piece lying on the surface counts as inside, following Containment3.Contains, which reads the boundary as part of the body. A chain running along a face is therefore reported as inside along its whole length.
The body is assumed closed, as Containment3.Locate assumes it: an open shell has no inside and the answer means nothing. That is not checked here, because checking costs a pass over every edge of the body on every call; ask once instead.

member.remarks:
The bodies act as their union: a stretch counts as inside when any one of them holds it. That is what separates this from cutting by each in turn, where the pieces of the first cut would have to be sorted again against the second and the runs joined back up by hand.
Because the union is what is being asked about, two bodies that overlap do not each claim their own piece of the answer, and two that meet face to face do not leave a cut between them: the stretch running through both comes back as one piece, since a cut that separates nothing is not a cut. An empty array is the degenerate case of the same rule — nothing holds anything, so the whole chain is outside.
Every body is assumed closed, as Containment3.Locate assumes it. That is not checked here, because checking costs a pass over every edge of every body on every call; ask once instead.

member.summary: Splits a polyline by several oriented boxes at once, within a tolerance.
member.param: The boxes to cut it by; null entries are skipped.
The pieces lying within at least one of the boxes.
The pieces lying beyond all of them.
member.returns: false when the chain crosses no box, so there was nothing to cut.
member.remarks:
The boxes act as their union, exactly as several solids do, and for the same reason: cutting by each in turn would leave the caller to sort the pieces of the first cut against the second and to join the runs back up by hand.
A box is far cheaper to cross-check than a solid, because the crossings come from the slab test rather than from walking a surface, so no mesh is built or traversed here.

member.returns: false when everything landed on one side, meaning nothing was really cut.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.CollectSurfaceCrossings(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Collects where one segment crosses the surface of a body, as arc lengths offset by how far along a longer chain the segment starts.
member.remarks:
The openings of the body are walked as well as its outer faces. An opening is a void, so its walls are as much a boundary between inside and outside as the outer surface is; missing them would leave a piece spanning both material and void, with nothing to say which it belongs to.
Faces whose bounding box cannot reach the segment are skipped before any real work is done, which is what keeps a chain against a large body from costing a full surface walk per edge.

member.summary: Splits a polyline by a plane and sorts the pieces by side, within a tolerance.
member.param: The pieces on the side the cutter normal points towards.
The pieces on the other side.
member.returns: false when the chain stays on one side, so there was nothing to cut.
member.remarks:
This is the same cut as the overload that hands back the pieces in order along the chain; what differs is how the result is presented. Use that one to divide a chain up, and this one to keep or discard a side.
A stretch lying in the cutting plane goes with , so that side reads as "not strictly below". That follows the convention the rest of the library keeps, where Contains means "not strictly outside" and a piece on a surface counts as inside it.
Neighbouring pieces that end up on the same side are joined back together, so what comes out is the longest run on each side rather than a chain chopped at positions that separate nothing.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Splits a polyline wherever it passes through a polygon, within a tolerance.
member.param: The region to cut it with.
The pieces, in order along the chain.
member.returns: false when the chain never passes through the region.
member.remarks:
A bounded region is not the plane that carries it. This cuts only where the chain actually goes through the region, so a chain that crosses the carrying plane out beyond the outline is left alone — which is what is wanted when the cutter stands for a physical plate rather than for an endless surface. Cut against instead to get the other reading.
The pieces come back in order along the chain rather than sorted, because a bounded region has no side to sort them onto: a chain can pass through it and come back without ever having been anywhere the region divides.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@)

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Splits a polygon along a chain drawn across it, within a tolerance.
member.param: The two pieces the chain divides the region into.
member.returns: false when the chain does not divide the region in two.
member.remarks:
This is cutting a plate along a line marked on it. The chain has to lie in the plane of the region, start and finish on its outline, and stay inside in between — anything else does not separate the region into two and is refused rather than answered.
Each piece is bounded by part of the original outline and by the chain, so the two pieces share the chain as their common edge and their outlines together cover the original. Both keep the orientation of the subject.
An end of the chain that meets the outline within the tolerance of a corner is cut from the corner, as a polyline cut within the tolerance of a vertex is: both pieces keep the corner, and nothing of the region is lost. At a hundredth, the square 10 by 10 cut from (0.004, 0, 0) to (10, 5, 0) comes back as the triangle of 25 square units from the corner (0, 0, 0) and the rest, of 75, where the rest ran from (0, 10, 0) straight to (0.004, 0, 0) and the sliver of 0.02 square units between was in neither piece. Of two corners within the tolerance, the nearer is taken; two ends on one corner meet the outline at one place and are refused.
A chain that wanders back out of the region and in again would cut it into more than two, which needs the crossings paired up the way a plane cut pairs them; that is not attempted here.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.PlaceOnOutline(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,System.Double@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Places an end of a cut line on a polygon's outline: on the corner within the tolerance of where it lands, or else where it lands.
member.param: How far round the outline the end lands; set to the corner's distance where it snaps.
member.returns: The corner, the nearest where two are within the tolerance and the first of the polygon's of two as near; or the place it lands.
member.remarks: A place beside a corner would leave the corner within the tolerance of the cut, which no piece can keep: the piece round it ran straight past, and the sliver between was in neither piece.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.BoundarySpan(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,System.Double,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Collects the run of a polygon outline from one arc length round to another, going forwards, from one given point to another.

A corner within the tolerance of either end is left out, as a polygon would drop the one or the other.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@)

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Splition3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Splits a polygon by a solid, within a tolerance.
member.param: The body to cut it by; its boundary must be closed.
The pieces lying within the body.
member.returns: false when the body does not divide the region.
member.remarks:
This answers which part of a plate is embedded in a body and which part stands clear of it.
The region is cut by the plane of each face of the body in turn. That works because the surface of the body never leaves those planes, so once the region has been cut by all of them no piece can straddle the boundary, and a single sample decides each piece. The pieces are then joined back up where they agree.
Cutting by every plane divides the region more finely than the body itself does, and joining the pieces afterwards recovers most but not always all of that: two pieces that ended up split by different planes can meet at a T-junction, which nothing joins. What comes back therefore covers each side exactly, but may be in more pieces than strictly necessary.
A body with many faces means many cuts, so this is meant for cutting a plate against a member, not against a whole model. Planes that miss the region cost almost nothing, since a cut that separates nothing is rejected before any work is done.

member.summary: Collects one plane per distinct flat surface of a body, its openings included.
member.remarks: Several faces of a body often share a plane, and a face and one facing the other way describe the same flat place. Cutting by each of them separately would divide the region again for no gain, so a plane already collected — in either direction — is not collected twice: one that stands within the planar tolerance of it over the body's box; see .

member.remarks: Every body is built face by face and checked by its signed volume, so it always comes back wound outwards whatever way round the profile was drawn. member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Triangle2
member.summary: What a triangle of the plane meets, how far off it is, and the rest of what the shapes of the plane ask each other.

remarks.para: A triangle is the polygon of its three corners, and every question here is asked of that polygon, so a triangle and the polygon makes of it give the same answers. The one thing a polygon cannot be is a triangle two of whose corners stand on each other, within the point tolerance: a polygon has three distinct corners at the least. Such a triangle has no width, and is asked as the segment between its two corners furthest apart, which is all of it there is. The walk along the edges is the one exception: it goes round the corners as they stand, A to B to C and back, so it reads no tolerance and a triangle of one point is walked too.
Each pair is worked out here one way only, the triangle first; the other shapes ask from their side by coming here, and turn a shortest segment round so that it leaves them.

member.summary: What a triangle of the plane asks of a ray.
member.remarks: A ray runs on for ever in one direction, so against a triangle it is cut: into the segment from its origin out past the farthest corner along it, by a margin of a millimetre or a hundred point tolerances, whichever is more. Every point of the triangle lies behind that end, so the segment meets the triangle where the ray does and is asked as any segment is. Against the triangle (0, 0), (100, 0), (0, 100), the ray from (-50, 20) along X is asked as the segment from there to (101, 20).

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Triangle2.TryAsPolygonByItsSides(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2@,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2@)
member.summary: Gets a triangle as a polygon for measuring and colliding it: its sides are its own, so a side shorter than the caller's tolerance is the side it is, not a reason to read the triangle as its longest side alone. Only corners that coincide exactly, which no polygon can hold apart, make it a segment, so the answer reads no tolerance at all, the global one included. The polygon is built as it stands, without the merging of the constructor that takes the corners alone, which reads the global tolerance.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.Weld3
member.summary: Makes the corners of a body's faces that stand within a tolerance of each other one point, and puts each corner on the edges of other faces it stands on, so the faces meet on the same edges exactly.

remarks.para: A boolean cut within a tolerance closes within that tolerance, and no closer. Two faces of what it gives meeting on an edge each have it where their own planes put it, and where a plane of one body passes within the tolerance of a face of the other, those are a few hundredths apart: a slab cut within 0.05 by the planes of a part beside it, one of which passed 0.011 off the back of a notch in the slab metres from the part, had the pieces cut along that plane meet the notch's own faces on copies of their edges 0.0113 apart, closed within 0.05 and open within 0.01, the default. Of 10 314 cuts within 0.05 of the parts of a Tekla model by the parts they meet, 14 came out that way, every one of them by copies of edges 0.010 to 0.048 apart.

The corners within the tolerance of each other are taken together as one, however they chain, and each group is moved to the corner of it that moves the volume least: a corner moved along the faces it is a corner of moves nothing, and one moved off them sweeps the triangle it makes with its neighbours on each, a neighbour the face's edge runs straight on past taken for the corner the face turns at further along. A slab's top ran out to a point 0.0095 off the corner of the wall beside it, the end of a sliver along the wall's top edge; moved to the top's point, as the corner with the most face round it, the wall's corner tilted the wall, 21.8 metres long, and the slab came out 41 925 cubic millimetres short, where the point moved to the wall's corner along the top moves nothing. A corner standing within the tolerance of another face's edge, between its ends, is put on that edge, as the corner where a long edge meets two short ones. What comes of it is kept only where it closes within the default tolerance and within its own, and holds the volume it held within the tolerance times its area: a corner moved is moved no further than the tolerance, and a face moved off flat by that much is flat within it.

A corner the face lies all round, a hole's corner or one where the face's edge turns back into a notch, or along one side, part way along a straight edge, makes no triangle of the face with its neighbours, and weighs next to nothing taken off the face's plane. Where the weld tilts faces by more than a hundredth of the tolerance and moves the volume by more than a tenth of the tolerance times their area, or where it tilts one and does not close or moves the volume too far, it is made again with such a corner, taken off the face's plane further than a hundredth of the tolerance, weighed by the whole face: once with each group taken to the corner of it that takes the most of the group, and once to the corner that moves the volume least first. Of those that close wound alike and tilt less of the faces than the first, the one moving the volume less is taken where it moves it less than the tilt, or, folding nothing, where the first weld is not taken; one tilting the same faces moves the volume otherwise, no nearer. A column 300 by 300 by 1 000 and a beam 160.1 by 160.8 whose end stood exactly 0.01 clear of the column's side, turned and joined within a hundredth, had two corners of the hole in the column's face taken 0.01 off it to the beam's, weighed by the triangles the hole's corners make, which are no part of the face: the face, 274 255 square millimetres, came out tilted, and the union held the two and 918.9 cubic millimetres where filling the gap holds 257.4. Weighed by the face, the beam's corners are taken onto the column's face along the beam's sides, and the union holds the two and 214.5. A beam 141.8 by 164.8 running exactly 0.01 into such a column had a corner of the column's face taken 0.01 off it to a sliver's corner, the one more of its group stood within the tolerance of, and the union came out 1 216.9 short of the two less their overlap; taken to the corner moving the volume least, it holds the two. A column whose faces come in strips, joined to a beam framing 0.002 into its flange, is welded as before, the ends of the beam's flanges beyond the column tilted: weighed by the faces, every corner goes where it went. Corners of a group that move the volume by nothing but rounding are told apart by the faces round them, the one tilting them least taken; see .

Only a body open within the default tolerance, or within its own where that is the finer, is welded; one closed within it is left as it is, closed as the boolean promised and as a caller asks. Welded wherever it did not close within an eighth of its tolerance, 36 of the cuts of those parts within the default came out other than they were, 17 of them further from the same cuts within a thousandth and 15 nearer, the worst 7 369 cubic millimetres further. A body open within its own tolerance is welded too, where that closes it: a slab's side bent by 3.3E-5 rad at one corner and its top at another 18.28 further along, the edges past the bend on two lines the tolerance could not take for one, and each corner put on the other's edge closed it.

Where that does not close it, the corners of the edges still left unpaired, and those only, are taken together within twice the tolerance, and then four times, as far as a sliver is closed across (see ), the rest within the tolerance as before. The faces are built again within the tolerance itself, so that one a corner moved takes off flat comes as triangles on its corners, and what comes of it is kept on the same terms, its volume held within the wider reach times its area. A slab of a Tekla model, cut one after another by the parts it meets within a thousandth, had a face stepped by 0.00107 where two faces lying back to back across the step had been taken from each other, and the faces either side of the step met on copies of an edge 0.00107 apart: open within a thousandth, and closed welded within two. Of eight such cuts of slabs of two Tekla models that came out open, six close so; the two left open share slivers two to six thousandths thick with what cuts them, which a cut within a thousandth takes for material.

member.summary: Gets a body a boolean made sealed as seals it, within the tolerance the boolean was given and no other, taken as closed only where reads it so as well (), and only where the weld moves the volume no further than moving each corner it moves by the point tolerance can: one that calls closed on two copies of an edge about the tolerance apart is welded too.
member.remarks: Moving a corner by a distance sweeps, on each face it is a corner of, no more than the distance times a third of the triangle it makes with its two neighbours: so much, at the point tolerance, for each corner moved, bounds the weld. Bounded only by the volumes the operation can give, the union of a cube of 100 and a block 40 by 30 by 50 running 0.001 into its top over an edge, the two turned, welded closed held 1 059 999.53 cubic millimetres, less than any reading of the block: 1 060 000 without the overlap, 1 060 000.6 with it.

How far the weld taken moved the volume; nought where none was.

Gets the faces of a weld that moves no corner off the plane of a face it is a corner of; null where the steps it leaves do not close.

remarks.para: A face keeps a corner where it would be moved off its plane, and takes the corner it is welded to where that lies on it; where a face moves a corner along its plane and a face beside it, sharing an edge at that corner, keeps it, the one takes both, the corner it keeps between, so the two meet on their edge as they did. What is left open between the corners kept and the corners moved to is a step a few thousandths across, closed by a face of its own; a corner is put on an edge only where it lies on the edge's line.

A column 300 by 300 joined to a beam 383 wide and 366 high whose end stood 0.008 clear of the column's face, at a tolerance of a hundredth, welded with the beam's end corners on the column's face: the parts of the end beyond the column, two strips 41.6 wide, were tilted into wedges, and the union held 999.8 cubic millimetres more than the two, where filling the gap holds 878. Kept on their plane, with a face 0.008 wide closing each side of the gap, it holds the two and the gap filled. And a box less a cube in its corner had a corner of its top 0.0099 in from the edge put on the edge of its side, which took the side 4 000 square millimetres off flat, fanned, 6.5 cubic millimetres short; the sliver between the top's corner and the side's edge is closed by a face of its own.

member.summary: Gets the edges the rings run more often one way than the other, each the way a face closing it runs it, as many times as it is left unpaired, in order.

Gets the faces closing the gap between loops of unpaired edges that face each other a few thousandths apart, corner over corner: one strip along each edge of a loop, from it to the edge over it; false where the edges left open are not such loops.
member.remarks:
A face kept on its plane where it lies against a face of the other body a gap within the tolerance away leaves both rims of the gap open, each a loop, and no step: a strip runs along an edge from one loop to the other, and is no loop of edges left open. A column 300 by 300 joined, within a hundredth, to a beam 387 wide and 118 high whose end stood 0.008 clear of the column's face was welded with the beam's end on the column's face: the parts of the end beyond the column, two strips 43.5 wide, were tilted into wedges, and the union held 41.06 cubic millimetres more than the two and the gap filled. Closed by four strips round the gap, it holds the two and the gap filled.
Only a gap is closed so: the faces running the two rims face each other across it, each toward the other rim, and what lies between them is no material of either. Rims a few thousandths apart whose faces face away from each other bound a slab both bodies hold: a beam 252 wide whose end ran exactly a hundredth into a column 300 by 300, joined to it within a hundredth, came out with such rims, the column's face and the beam's end within it, and closed by strips round them held the slab twice, 375.06 cubic millimetres over the union.

A loop folded back on itself encloses next to no area however far it runs, and is no step.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Weld3.Turns(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3},System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32}}[],System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3},System.Double)
member.summary: The corner each point turns on each ring it is a corner of, as an area vector, worked out the first time it is asked for: half the cross of the edges to the nearest corners either side that the ring does not run straight on to, a corner standing within the reach of the line from the point to the corner after it, between the two, passed over; and, where the face lies round the point rather than within that triangle, the face's normal times its area, nought otherwise (see the remarks on the class).

remarks.para: A face cut into strips keeps a corner on its edges where each strip ended, and a corner beside them makes a sliver of a triangle with its neighbours, a strip wide, however far the face reaches. Weighed by that triangle, the weld closing the step of a beam's end 0.002 into a column's flange of 300 strips took the column face's corner to the beam's, off the face's plane, where it moved the face's fan from its first corner, and the union came out 98.92 cubic millimetres short of the two where their overlap is 17.04; weighed by the corner the face turns, its edges 750 and 120 long, the beam's end is tilted instead, as with the column in one piece, the two less 18.96.
Only the points of a group are weighed, so only theirs are worked out: walking every corner of a face of 1 000 strips to the end of its edge took a quarter of a second.

member.summary: The position each point is welded to: the points within the tolerance of each other, however they chain, are one group, and each goes to the point of it that takes the most of the group within the tolerance of it and of those moves the volume least, the first met of those; the rest of the group is settled the same way among themselves.

The position each point is welded to, as the overload without marks gives it, of the points marked only where marks are given: every other point stays where it is. Asked to, each goes to the point that moves the volume least first, and of those that move it by less than the reach cubed apart to the one that takes the most of the group. Points that only rounding tells apart, given, are settled as settles them.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Weld3.MostTaken(System.Int32[],System.Double[])
member.summary: Of the points of a group, weighed as weighs them, the one that takes the most of the group, then the one that moves the volume least, then the first met.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.Weld3.MovingLeast(System.Int32[],System.Double[],System.Double)
member.summary: Of the points of a group, weighed as weighs them, the one that moves the volume least taking those within the tolerance of it, of those that move it less than the slack further than that the one that takes the most of the group, then the one that moves it least, then the first met.

The point of a group a weld takes the others to where the one chosen moves the volume no more than rounding times the area weighed, which rounding alone tells from moving nothing: of those that take as many of the group and move the volume no more than that further than it, the one that tilts the faces lying round the others least, within rounding times that area too, then of those the one that moves the volume least, then the first met. Where the one chosen moves the volume more, it is kept.
member.remarks: A cube of 100, turned, and a block 40 by 30 running exactly 0.001 into its top, joined within a thousandth, came out with two corners 0.0003 apart part way along the edges of two faces, each 10 000 square millimetres, whose triangles weigh nothing: they moved the volume by 3.3E-18 and 2.1E-17 cubic millimetres, and the first was taken. The second stands on the first one's face, and the first 0.0003 off the second one's, so that weld tilted the second one's face, and the union held 1.39 less than the two less their overlap, where the tolerance times the area where they meet is 1.2; taken to the second, it holds 0.39 less. Three corners a box 100 by 60 by 40 less a cube of 0.59 a thousandth inside its corner came out with, each moving the volume by 3.5E-4, are kept to the one moving it least: taken to the one tilting the faces least, the cut came out valid and 1.68 short, where the cube holds 0.21. Nor is a corner the face turns at taken before one part way along a straight edge: a column joined to a beam whose end runs exactly 0.001 into it then held the slab they share twice, 51.86 over.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.XLine2
member.summary: How an infinite line in the plane is cut into a segment to be asked of a shape with an end to it, and where a point, a ray or another line meets it.

remarks.para: The cut runs from the point at N - m to the point at F + m along the line, where N and F are the least and the greatest distance along it at which any point of the shape projects, and m = max(1, 100 · EqualPoint) is the margin. For a straight shape N and F are taken over its corners; for a circle, an arc or an ellipse they are the centre brought onto the line less and plus the radius, or the major radius. The origin of the line is not part of the cut: a shape a million along it is asked as the stretch round the shape.

Every point of the shape projects between N and F, so every point of the line outside the cut is further from every point of the shape than the nearer end of the cut is. This is the ray's reasoning (see ) with an end to cut at on both sides, and its faults are the ray's: where the segment code answers rightly, the ends of the cut are never a crossing, a touching point or an end of a shortest segment, and the cut answers what the line would; where it does not, the line shares the fault. A NaN anywhere is carried into the cut, and a line of no direction, a default one, is cut to the single point of its origin.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.XLine3
member.summary: How an infinite line in space is cut into a segment to be asked of a shape with an end to it, and where a point, a plane, a ray or another line meets it.

remarks.para: The cut runs from the point at N - m to the point at F + m along the line, where N and F are the least and the greatest distance along it at which any point of the shape projects, and m = max(1, 100 · EqualPoint) is the margin. For a straight shape N and F are taken over its corners, for a body over the corners of its box; for a circle or an ellipse they are the centre brought onto the line less and plus the radius, or the major radius; for an arc they are its two ends and, where the arc holds them, the points of its circle furthest ahead and furthest behind along the line. The origin of the line is not part of the cut: a shape a million along it is asked as the stretch round the shape.

Every point of the shape projects between N and F, so every point of the line outside the cut is further from every point of the shape than the nearer end of the cut is. This is the reasoning of in space, and its faults are the segment's: where the segment code answers rightly, the ends of the cut are never a crossing, a touching point or an end of a shortest segment, and the cut answers what the line would; where it does not, the line shares the fault. A NaN anywhere is carried into the cut, and a line of no direction, a default one, is cut to the single point of its origin.

A plane has no end to cut at, and two lines or a line and a ray are answered in closed form: two lines in space come nearest where their common perpendicular stands, found from the closed form with its cross products taken to a rounding of their own, and are parallel by rounding on the same rule as in the plane (see ).

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.CellContact3
member.summary:
Which cells of a grid share part of a face: cells cut apart by one plane with no joint between, whose material meets on it over some area.
Neighbours are found by where they stand, not by their indexes: a cut moved onto a corner, or one not made, leaves a cell meeting one two places on along the axis, and each slab and bar is cut to its own corners, so that a cell can meet one a place over across it. A cell's material strays from its line on each axis by no more than the snap distance and a needle's point, which the cells themselves say; only the cells that far along each line are tried.

member.remarks: Two cells a place apart across the plane as well share no more than an edge, and the rounding, or the tolerance, lets their extents overlap by as much along it: over the point tolerance squared alone, nought at nought, a quarter of the grids cut at fine tolerances from prisms with openings, turned about in space, counted such cells as neighbours. member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.CellGrid3
member.summary:
Lays the cells of a grid through a body and cuts the body into them.
Along each axis the cells are laid as its says, measured between the body's furthest corners along it, or from the placement's origin. A box whose sides the grid's axes run along is cut by arithmetic, every cell a box. Any other body is cut by planes: along X first, the rest of the body cut off cell by cell, then each slab along Y, and each bar along Z, so that every cut is made through as little of the body as can be. A cut coming within the snap distance of a corner of the piece it cuts is moved onto that corner, so that no slice thinner than that is cut off: within it of the piece's far side it is not made at all, and the slice stays with the cell beside, nor where, moved onto a corner, it would take off less than four point tolerances. A piece standing wholly on one side of a cut goes to that side, however thin. What a cell holds in several pieces is split into them.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.EarClipping
member.summary:
Breaks a flat face into triangles that each lie inside it, holes included.
This is what a fan triangulation cannot give. Fanning a polygon from one vertex covers a convex one exactly, but on a concave one some triangles reach outside the boundary and others overlap them wound the other way. For a signed sum — area, centroid, volume — that is harmless, because the overhang cancels against the overlap. For anything geometric it is not: a triangle spanning the notch of an L is material where there is none, and whatever reads the mesh as a surface believes it.
The face is mapped into the 2D frame of its own plane, the holes are bridged into the outer loop so that one simple loop describes the whole face, and that loop is reduced by clipping ears. Every vertex of the result is one of the vertices that went in — the bridging joins existing vertices rather than inventing points — so the triangles are carried back to 3D by looking the originals up rather than by mapping coordinates back, and no round-trip error is introduced.
The same works on loops of corners a little out of flat, seen from a frame of their own: the triangles are built on the corners themselves, so each is flat, and that is how keeps such a face.

member.summary: Triangulates a face into triangles that each lie within its material.
member.param: The tolerance deciding what counts as a degenerate triangle.
The triangles covering the face, wound to share its normal.
member.returns: false when the loop could not be reduced — a self-intersecting boundary, or a hole that reaches outside the face. The caller is expected to fall back rather than to treat this as an error.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.EarClipping.TryTriangulateSurface(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3[]@)
member.summary: Triangulates a face for a mesh of its surface, refusing where the triangles might not all lie within it.
member.param: The tolerance deciding what counts as a degenerate triangle, and how near two rings may come.
The triangles covering the face, wound to share its normal.
member.returns: false when the loop could not be reduced, as returns, and also when two rings of the face come within the point tolerance of each other, or a ring of itself apart from where its edges meet.
member.remarks: The clipping holds only while the loop it reduces is simple, and a loop joined from rings that touch is not. A hole whose edge lay along the boundary was bridged along that edge, the loop doubled back on itself there, and the clipping, which only ever cuts off a corner turning the right way, was left with a last triangle turning the wrong way, laid across the notch of an L. Triangular holes meeting at their corners left a triangle across one of them. The sums of the areas came out right both times, so nothing showed. A triangle wound backwards still adds up, and the face keeps its own corners, which is what and the booleans need of the clipping; a mesh standing for the surface needs every triangle within the material, so such a face is refused here instead.

Joins every hole into the outer loop, leaving one simple loop describing the whole face.
member.remarks:
Each hole is cut into the boundary along a bridge traversed once each way. That leaves a loop with zero width at the bridge, which is exactly what makes the material of the face into one connected region that ear clipping can reduce.
The holes are taken rightmost first. A bridge is drawn to the outer loop as it stands, so a hole joined earlier is already part of it and a later bridge can land on that hole instead of crossing it. Working from the right means the hole a bridge would have to cross has always been dealt with already.

A second bridge to the same vertex has to leave from the copy that opens toward its hole: from the other, it runs across the first bridge, the loop crosses itself, and no ear can be clipped from it. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.EarClipping.NearestInTheWay(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Core.EarClipping.Node},GeometryHelper.Core.EarClipping.Node,System.Int32,System.Double)

A bridge to it ran along the edge of the near hole, the loop touched itself there, and no ear could be clipped from it. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.EarClipping.TryClip(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Core.EarClipping.Node},GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.Double,System.Boolean,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3[]@)
member.summary: Reduces a simple loop to triangles by repeatedly cutting off ears.
member.remarks:
An ear is a convex corner whose triangle holds no other vertex of the loop, so cutting it off removes material that belongs to the face and leaves a smaller loop of the same shape. Only reflex vertices are worth testing against: a convex one cannot sit inside an ear without a reflex one being there too.
A vertex on the edge of an ear blocks it as surely as one inside: the cut would run through the boundary there. Testing strictly let an I lose its flanges first and then take, as an ear, a triangle across its web and the gap beside it, with a corner of the web on its edge; the loop stuck after that and the face fell back to the fan. What does not block an ear is a vertex standing on one of its own corners — the doubled ends of a hole's bridge — or no ear next to a bridge would ever be accepted.
On an edge means within of it, measured from that edge, while another ear can be found: the point tolerance, or wider when loops out of flat are clipped again because a triangle stood up. An ear passing a corner closer than the tolerance would leave a triangle thinner than it, which on loops out of flat, seen from a frame of their own, can stand up across the loop. When none can be found, within a millionth of the tolerance, the reach of rounding: a corner that close outside an ear is passed by, not cut through. Read as the point tolerance times the width of the face, as an area, and with nothing to fall back to, a corner a tenth of a millimetre outside an edge 100 mm long blocked it on a plate a metre across, and along a rib a millimetre wide between two holes every corner across the rib blocked every ear: none was clipped, and the plate fell back to the fan of its outline, laid across every hole. So it went with a corner on the line of an ear with no width, three corners a hair out of a row: read by area, it lay on all three edges of every such ear along a needle of a hole.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.FaceEars
member.summary:
Breaks a face of a mesh of the plane into triangles on its own corners, every corner of it a corner of one.
A face of a mesh is a simple polygon running counter-clockwise, and may have corners in a row where the face beside it has a corner on their side. Clipping ears from it as it stands keeps them: a corner in a row is never the tip of an ear, since it does not turn, but is taken into the ear clipped beside it, and an ear whose closing side would pass through or touch another corner is not clipped. So no triangle has no area and none leaves a corner out, and the triangles of two faces side by side meet edge to edge as the faces do. It reads no tolerance: only rounding, a trillionth of the face's size, stands between a corner and a line it is on.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.GridMesh2
member.summary:
Lays the cells of a grid over the material of a face and keeps what of each the material holds.
The grid is laid along two axes turned by an angle, its cells a width by a height and a joint apart, standing where the alignments or an origin say. Row by row, the region is first cut to a band about the row, so that each cell is cut against the little of the region near it rather than all of it; a cell no edge of the band comes near is then wholly inside or wholly outside, and its middle tells which, so that only the cells along the boundary and the holes are cut at all. Cutting goes through , which gives every corner its full precision back: the face's own corners, and the crossings of its edges with the cells' computed in double precision. A cut cell that holds a hole whole is split across, through the middle of the hole, so that no face has one.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly
member.summary:
Turns a loose set of edges and loops into faces.
Two different jobs end in the same place. Cutting a body leaves a rim of edges that has to be closed into the surface capping each half; merging the coplanar faces of a body leaves the outlines of several faces that have to be closed into one. Both need the edge pairs running the same stretch in opposite directions removed, both need the survivors chained into loops, and both need those loops nested so that one inside another becomes a hole. That shared middle lives here rather than being written twice.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly.EnumerateMaterialRings(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3)
member.summary: Walks every ring of a face in the direction the material lies to one consistent side: the outer boundary as given, each hole reversed.
member.remarks: This library stores a hole wound the same way as the boundary that carries it, which is what makes area and volume come out by plain subtraction. Walking the edge of the material is the other convention: there a hole runs the opposite way round, so that the material stays on the same hand throughout. Anything that traces the boundary — cutting it, or reading the edges the cut left behind — has to use this order, or the trace will turn the wrong way when it reaches a rim and lose the piece it was walking.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly.Bridge
member.summary: How many point tolerances apart the two ends of a gap in a rim may stand to be joined: the crossings of two copies of one edge a point tolerance apart, met at a slant of fifteen degrees.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly.TryBridgeGaps(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3},GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3}@)
member.summary: Joins the ends a rim leaves open where two faces crossed the edge they share on copies of it a hair apart: each end left with no edge after it to the start left with none before it that is nearest, and the other way round.
member.param: The tolerance deciding which ends are one point.
The edges, and an edge across each gap; null when the method returns false.
member.returns: false when no end is open, or an open end has no open start that is its nearest and it the start's, within point tolerances.
member.remarks: Two faces of a body can share an edge within the tolerance whose ends are not one point, as the booleans leave corners a few thousandths apart, and the body is closed across them. Each face crosses the plane on its own copy, and where the plane meets the edge at a slant the crossings stand further apart than the copies' ends do: copies whose top corners stood 0.0045 apart in height above a plane meeting them at 22 degrees crossed it 0.0112 apart, and the rim did not close. A short edge between the two crossings closes it, and lies within the tolerance of both copies, as the stretch of the edge between the crossings does. Putting both faces' crossings on one point instead took the two sides of a tube's wall thinner than the tolerance for one, and its section for none.

member.summary: Closes the slivers a half of a cut is left open by where its rim was bridged: each strip between two copies of an edge that stood further apart at the cut than the tolerance, closed by a face across it.
member.param: The faces of the half, its caps included.
The tolerance deciding which corners are one point.
The tolerance the closing faces are built within; see .
The faces closing the slivers, none where nothing is open; null when the method returns false.
member.returns: false when the edges left open do not chain into loops one way only, or a loop is no sliver: wider across than point tolerances, or no face.
member.remarks: Two faces sharing an edge on copies a hair apart are closed across it, the corners at each end one point within the tolerance. A cut takes each copy as it finds it, and where a face's two crossings stand within the tolerance of each other they are one corner, the one on the far copy as often as not: the crossings were left 0.0119 apart, the rim was bridged, and the strip between the copies, from the cut up to where they meet, was a sliver no face covered, 102.8 long. It is a piece of a face of the body all the same, and a face across it closes the half, where one point for both copies would take the two sides of a wall thinner than the tolerance for one. A loop of no area is an edge run beside two that make it up, which the surface closes as it is, and is passed over.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly.TryChainLoops(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3},GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3}}@)
member.summary: Chains a set of directed edges into closed loops.
member.param: The edges; each is used once and each must have a neighbour at both ends.
The normal of the plane the edges lie in, which fixes what a left turn is.
The tolerance deciding whether two endpoints are the same point.
The closed loops the edges form.
member.returns: false when any chain came back open, meaning the edges do not close.
member.remarks:
An open chain is a failure rather than a partial answer: a rim that does not close cannot be capped and a set of outlines that does not close is not a face, so guessing at either would produce geometry that looks right and is not.
More than two edges can meet at one point — two outlines touching at a corner, a vertex four edges arrive at — and there the walk has a choice to make. Taking whichever edge comes first welds the two outlines into a single figure of eight whose lobes run opposite ways, so its area is their difference rather than their sum and the surface built from it reports a size it does not have. The choice is settled by turning: of the edges leaving the vertex, the walk takes the one reached first by rotating from the direction it arrived on, counter-clockwise about the plane normal. Since every edge is directed so that the material lies to its left, that keeps the walk on the outline it is already following and leaves the other to be traced on its own.

An edge carrying straight on is therefore preferred to any turn, and a turn back the way the walk came is taken only when there is nothing else.

member.summary: Checks whether one loop lies inside another. The two must not cross.
member.remarks:
Loops that do not cross are either wholly inside or wholly outside one another, so one vertex settles it. Vertices sitting on the other loop say nothing, which is why the scan keeps looking until it finds one that does.
A hole can touch the rim of the loop round it at every corner: a hole meeting the boundary at two, cut through its third, leaves one in the piece on that side. Its sides still run through the material between, so the middle of a side settles it where no corner does. Read as outside, such a hole came back as a face of its own, and the piece covered it twice.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly.LoopsThatCanLieInside(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: For each polygon, the others that can find inside it, in the order they are given: those whose first corner lies in its box, grown by a margin.
member.remarks: A loop is inside another only where its first corner is not outside it, and a corner further from the box of a polygon's corners than the point tolerance, the planar tolerance and twice what any of them stands off the polygon's plane, with rounding over, is outside: off the plane, or on it but further than the point tolerance from every edge and beyond a line in the plane from every corner, which no edge it casts its ray across can then pass on the far side of an odd number of times. The corners are found in the boxes by a sweep along the axis that leaves the fewest in the boxes it meets. The 5 001 pieces of a comb face cut across its teeth were each tried against every other, 25 million tests, and the cut took 1.2 seconds; it takes 0.05 now, with the same faces.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly.ForPieces(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the tolerance a piece of an existing surface is built within: the one given, with an area as small as its point and planar tolerances allow.
member.remarks: A polygon refuses an area below the vector tolerance read as an area: 1e-5 by default, a triangle some five thousandths of a millimetre across, and 1e-2 up to 10.0.0, some fifteen hundredths. A plane passing a few thousandths from a corner of a body leaves a sliver that small on each face meeting at it, and the pieces of a surface rejoined can close a loop as thin. Refused, the surface has a hole there. A cut that loses one does not close and fails, leaving the body whole across the plane — two blocks sharing sixty were found to share nothing that way — and a merge that loses one leaves the body open. Such a piece has two corners further apart than the point tolerance, or they would be one, and a third further than the planar tolerance from the line through them, or it would be on it, so its area is at least half the two together; an eighth keeps every one and still refuses what rounding leaves of three points in a line.

But a polygon is measured from a corner of its own, about the normal of its own corners: from a corner a hair one way, a corner a hair the other stands off by twice the tolerance, and the normal of a piece lopsided about the face turns that a little more. Measured so, a piece of a face of a turned column was 0.0146 out of flat, it was refused, and the half it belonged to could not close. A piece can be no further out of flat than the face it is cut from.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Core.LoopAssembly.SplitAtEdgeEnds(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Splits every edge wherever another edge ends partway along it, so that two faces meeting along a stretch describe it with the same edges.
member.remarks:
Faces that share a stretch of boundary need not divide it the same way. One face may have been cut in two along the way while its neighbour was left whole, and then one long edge faces two short ones across the same line — a T-junction. Cancelling looks for a pair running the same stretch in opposite directions and finds none, so all three survive and are read as boundary.
Cutting every edge at the ends of the others first removes the mismatch: after it, an interior stretch is described identically from both sides and cancels as it should. Without it the surviving edges chain into loops that look plausible and enclose the wrong area, which is how a merged body ends up reporting a volume it does not have.

The edges are first cut at one another's ends, so that a stretch two faces divided differently still cancels. See .

member.summary: Removes pairs of edges that run the same stretch in opposite directions, as does, the pairs nearest each other first: an edge within the tolerance of two others cancels the one that leaves the least area between them.

The pieces above leave nothing between them and the triangle's top, and cancel first; the triangle's bottom is left as the rim. Where each edge has one edge to cancel, or none, the same pairs cancel as in the order the edges come.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Core.MeshBuilder2
member.summary:
Gathers the faces of a mesh of the plane as loops of points and joins them into a .
The pieces come from the meshing algorithms with the tolerance already applied to the shape they were cut from, so joining them reads no tolerance: points the same but for rounding become one vertex, the shape's own corners first, so that a face meeting one takes it exactly, and a vertex standing on the side of a face across from it, within rounding, is made one of that face's corners too, so that the faces meet edge to edge. For the kinds made of triangles a triangle so given a corner on its side is split there instead, and for the triangles are then merged across every edge whose two sides stay convex together, longest edges first, as Hertel and Mehlhorn merge them.
Nearness within the point tolerance would join more, and wrongly. Where features of the shape stand closer than the tolerance the pieces between them are slivers, and their corners stand that near the sides of faces they do not belong to: joined, a sliver collapses, and a face taking in a corner across one is pulled over its neighbour.
