member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.BooleanOutcome
member.summary: How a boolean of two solids came out: a body made, nothing left of it, or no answer at all.

remarks.para: and give false both where nothing is left and where the result could not be worked out, which only the log tells apart. A net volume worked out by taking cutters off a part one after another reads the two the opposite way: nothing left takes the part to nought, as it should be taken, and no answer is a step to work out some other way, as by slicing. The overloads giving an outcome say which it was.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.BooleanOutcome.Made
member.summary: A body was made, and is the result.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.BooleanOutcome.Empty
member.summary: Nothing is left: of a difference, the tool took the whole subject; of an intersection, the two share no volume. Either is nothing too where what it made, closed, encloses no more than a slab the tolerance thick, as reads it: a plate 10 by 10 and 0.0018 thick less a box over all but 0.0018 of its width leaves a rod 0.0018 square, 0.000 032 4 cubic millimetres enclosing nothing at a tolerance of a thousandth, and is empty. A union is never empty.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.BooleanOutcome.NotWorkedOut
member.summary: The result could not be worked out, and why is written to . No body is given, and none is to be assumed: not the subject as it was, and not nothing.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure
member.summary: Why could not close a body, or nothing where it did.
member.remarks: The reason is that of the first step that could not go on, and is a point at the trouble. Where a later step closed what an earlier one could not, the body is closed and there is no reason.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure.None
member.summary: The body was closed, or was valid already.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure.NonManifold
member.summary: An open loop runs through an edge or a corner more than two faces meet on: a fin standing off the surface, or two holes touching at a corner. Which faces close with which cannot be told, and nothing is joined across it.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure.GapTooWide
member.summary: Corners stand further apart than across a gap only a weld would close.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure.HoleTooLarge
member.summary: A hole encloses more than , or is out of flat with more corners than a fill out of flat takes, 256; or no hole may be filled: the largest hole is nought, or the strategy is .

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure.HoleOffFlat
member.summary: A hole stands further out of flat than .

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure.HoleAmbiguous
member.summary: A hole can be filled more than one way, and the strategy is : one out of flat by ways closing volumes further apart than its area times the planar tolerance, or the two flat ends of a hole through the body, whose walls are missing, by caps or by walls, neither lying on a face of the body nor crossing one. Or, whatever the strategy, a hole holds another inside it where one of the two is out of flat: triangles are found across a loop with nothing inside it only, and a face takes no hole out of flat.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.ClosingFailure.StillOpen
member.summary: The body is still not valid after every step, or could not be worked out, which is logged with what was thrown: among others, a hole every fill of which would lie back to back with a face of the body, a skin of no thickness, or cross one, or a face filling a hole before it, an edge of either passing through the inside of the other, the point then where it would; and a gap the welds would close only through a face standing in it, as a crack round a blade, at the point where the face welded would pass through.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.FillStrategy
member.summary: Which holes fills: none, those it can fill one way only, or every one it may, by the least surface across it.

remarks.para: A hole is a loop of open edges with nothing across it. A flat one takes one face, and no other; but the two flat ends of a hole through a body whose walls are missing can be capped, each by a face, or walled round between them: a plate missing the four walls of a hole through it is closed over by the caps, and round the hole by the walls, and either is valid. One out of flat can be filled by triangles on its corners in more than one way, and the ways part in the volume they close: a face of four corners with one of them lifted closes a sixth of the lift times its area more split along one diagonal than along the other.

Only a way none of whose faces lies back to back with a face of the body is a way at all: such a face is a skin of no thickness. A box 10 by 1 by 1 with its top and front left out, the two faces meeting along its length, has one loop round the two. The triangles of least area across it, 15.1, cut the box along its diagonal, but each end of that cut is a triangle lying on the end face it stands in, and is no way. Of the fourteen ways of filling the loop six lie on no face: four are the two faces again, 20 of area, and close the box whole, 10, and two cut across its corner, 20.05 of area, and close 8.3. Nor is one that turns a triangle back against the loop, folding it over the outside of a concave rim: an L-shaped top lifted a little at a corner is filled across its inside, and the ways running a diagonal outside the L do not count against it. And no hole is filled by faces crossing a face of the body, or of a hole filled before it, an edge of either through the inside of the other, though the body would read valid: caps crossing it are no way, and the face of a flat hole, or the triangles of least area across one out of flat, crossing it leave the hole open.
Every hole is held to and whatever the strategy, and triangles are found across a loop of no more than 256 corners with nothing inside it.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.FillStrategy.None
member.summary: No hole is filled: a body open by one is not closed, and the report says . Corners are still welded and put on edges.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.FillStrategy.WhenUnambiguous
member.summary: A hole is filled where it can be filled one way only, as far as the volume goes: a flat one by one face; the two ends of a hole through the body only where the caps or the walls are the one way lying on no face of the body and crossing none; and one out of flat by the triangles of least area across it only where the ways of filling it lying on no face of the body close one volume within its area times the planar tolerance, the uncertainty a face called flat carries already. Otherwise the report says , as it does of the long box above, its ways closing 10 and 8.3. The default.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.FillStrategy.MinArea
member.summary: Every hole that may be filled is, the way adding the least area of those lying on no face of the body: the two ends of a hole through the body by the caps or the walls, whichever add less where both cross nothing, the caps where they add as much; and one out of flat by the triangles of least area across it, whatever the other ways would close. The long box above is filled by its two faces again, whole.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineEnd
member.summary:
Names one end of a line segment: the end an extend, trim or lengthen operation moves.
A segment runs from its start point to its end point, so the two ends are told apart by that order rather than by position. The end that is not named stays where it is.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineEnd.Start
member.summary: The start point of the segment.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineEnd.End
member.summary: The end point of the segment.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineExtension
member.summary:
Says which of two line segments an intersection may reach past, by reading it as the infinite line carrying it. This is what AutoCAD's Intersect option does for IntersectWith.
A segment that is not extended must contain the intersection itself, within tolerance. An extended one only has to point at it, however far away.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineExtension.None
member.summary: Neither segment is extended: the intersection must lie on both.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineExtension.First
member.summary: The first segment (the one the method is called on) is read as an infinite line; the second must contain the intersection.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineExtension.Second
member.summary: The second segment (the argument) is read as an infinite line; the first must contain the intersection.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineExtension.Both
member.summary: Both segments are read as infinite lines.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineSide
member.summary:
Which side of a directed segment a point lies on, seen looking along it from its start to its end.
This is the counterpart in the plane of in space. A segment is read as the infinite line carrying it, so a point beyond either end still has a side; what decides the answer is only which way the point lies off the line, never how far along it sits.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineSide.Left
member.summary: The point lies to the left of the direction of the segment: the side its normal turned a quarter turn counter-clockwise points to.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineSide.Right
member.summary: The point lies to the right of the direction of the segment.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.LineSide.On
member.summary: The point lies on the line carrying the segment, within tolerance.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.OffsetJoin
member.summary:
Says how an offset closes the gap that opens at a corner, where the two offset edges pull apart.
A gap opens on the outside of a turn: at a convex corner when a region grows, at a concave corner when it shrinks. On the inside of a turn the offset edges overlap instead and are simply cut where they meet, whatever the join. The three kinds match AutoCAD's offset gap types (OFFSETGAPTYPE 0, 1 and 2).

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.OffsetJoin.Miter
member.summary: Extends both offset edges until they meet, keeping the corner sharp. A very acute corner would send the point far out, so cuts it off square beyond a set distance. AutoCAD calls this Extend.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.OffsetJoin.Round
member.summary: Rounds the corner with an arc centred on the original vertex, of radius equal to the offset distance, drawn as straight segments within . AutoCAD calls this Fillet.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.OffsetJoin.Chamfer
member.summary: Cuts the corner with one straight segment lying at the offset distance from the original vertex, tangent to the arc a join would draw. AutoCAD calls this Chamfer.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.PlaneSide
member.summary:
Represents which side of an oriented plane a point lies on.
The sides are named after the plane normal rather than after world up, because a plane in this library carries its own orientation and may point anywhere.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.PlaneSide.Above
member.summary: The point lies on the side the plane normal points towards (positive signed distance).

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.PlaneSide.Below
member.summary: The point lies on the side opposite the plane normal (negative signed distance).

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.PlaneSide.On
member.summary: The point lies on the plane itself, within tolerance.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.PointLocation
member.summary:
Represents the spatial location of a point relative to a geometric shape or boundary.
What counts as depends on the family the shape belongs to. A volume (GeoObb3, GeoSolid3) encloses a region of space. A region (GeoPolygon2, GeoCircle2, GeoPolygon3, GeoFace3) encloses an area; in space that means a point counts as inside only when it lies on the carrier plane as well as within the boundary. A curve (GeoLine2, GeoPolyline2, GeoLine3, GeoPolyline3, GeoRay3) encloses nothing and never reports .

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.PointLocation.Inside
member.summary: The point lies strictly inside the interior of the shape.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.PointLocation.OutSide
member.summary: The point lies outside the shape.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.PointLocation.OnSide
member.summary: The point lies on the boundary (or edge / surface) of the shape within tolerance.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind
member.summary: What found wrong with the faces of a body, or worth knowing about them.
member.remarks: The first four leave a body no boolean or measure can read as the material it is meant to be, and make it not valid; the rest are noted. They come in this order in .

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.OpenEdge
member.summary: A stretch of edge an odd number of faces meet on: one, the rim of a gap, or three, a fin standing off the surface. The body is not closed.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.SameWayEdge
member.summary: A stretch of edge an even number of faces meet on, not as many running it one way as the other: a face wound the wrong way round beside its neighbours. counts the faces on an edge and not which way they run it, and calls such a body closed.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.InsideOut
member.summary: Faces enclosing less than nothing: the body is wound inwards, as sets right.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.NoVolume
member.summary: Faces enclosing no more volume than half the point tolerance times their area: a sheet, or faces lying back to back, no thicker than the tolerance, as a slab t thick encloses half its faces' area times t. A slab 100 by 100 and 0.0015 thick encloses something at a tolerance of a thousandth, and one 0.001 thick nothing; read against the whole tolerance, a slab up to twice it thick enclosed nothing. A square rod encloses a quarter of its side times its area, and so encloses nothing up to twice the tolerance across, where it was up to four times.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.NonManifoldEdge
member.summary: A stretch of edge four or more faces meet on, as many running it each way: two blocks meeting along an edge. The body is closed; noted.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.ShortEdge
member.summary: An edge of a face no longer than the point tolerance: two corners that are one point. Noted.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.SliverFace
member.summary: A face no wider on average than the point tolerance, its area no more than half the tolerance times its perimeter: within the tolerance it covers nothing. Noted.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidIssueKind.NotFlatFace
member.summary: A face with a corner further off its plane than the planar tolerance, measured as the booleans measure it, from the plane of its first corner; the booleans break such a face into triangles on its own corners before they cut it. Noted.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidRepairKind
member.summary: What changed of a body to close it, one change at a time.
member.remarks: They are made in this order, each only where the ones before did not close the body, and come in that order in : a face welded down to nothing is dropped among the welds, and a face turned again once its shell is closed is reported with the others turned. What measures is the kind's.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidRepairKind.Drop
member.summary: A face dropped: one with no area; one of two lying back to back on the same corners, a sheet inside the body that encloses nothing; or one no other face runs an edge of, lying back to back on a face of the body, a sheet of no thickness. The size is the area dropped.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidRepairKind.Flip
member.summary: A face turned over, so that the body is wound alike and outwards. The size is the area turned.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidRepairKind.Weld
member.summary: Corners standing apart across a gap made one point. The size is the furthest a corner of the group moved.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidRepairKind.SplitEdge
member.summary: A corner standing off an edge of another face, between its ends, put on that edge, which is split there: a long edge beside two short ones. Where the crack between them lies in the plane of the corner's face, the corner is moved onto the edge within that plane, and no face bends; otherwise the edge is bent through the corner where it stands. The size is how far the corner stood off the edge.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.SolidRepairKind.Fill
member.summary: A hole filled, by one face where it is flat and by triangles where it is not, or a hole through the body whose walls are missing walled round. The size is the area of the faces added across it, and the place where they would balance.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Enums.VolumeMethod
member.summary: How the volume of a body is summed over its faces: each face broken into triangles, or read flat, and every triangle taken as a tetrahedron to the middle of the body's box, as the divergence theorem has it.

remarks.para: Over flat faces every method gives the same volume, centroid and moments, but for the rounding: the divergence theorem is exact for them. They part only where a face is a hair out of flat, as the planar tolerance lets one be, and there no one surface is the face, so no one volume is the body's: a face of four corners with one of them lifted holds a third of the lift times its area more split along the diagonal through that corner, a sixth more split along the other, and a quarter more read flat. How far the methods part says how far the faces leave the volume open; sets them side by side.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.VolumeMethod.Fan
member.summary: The fan of each face's boundary from its first corner, less the fans of its holes: what sums, and the quickest. Whatever the face's shape, its fan sums to the face read flat through that corner, a third of its area vector against it, so over a face a hair out of flat the volume moves by a third of the face's area times how far its first corner stands off its middle plane. Tekla Structures reports the volume of a part read so.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.VolumeMethod.Surface
member.summary: The triangles lying in each face, on its own corners, its holes left open: the volume the faces hold as the closed surface of triangles they mesh to, which over a face a hair out of flat is bent along the diagonals the triangulation chose. What sums.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Enums.VolumeMethod.FlatFaces
member.summary: Each face read flat: laid onto the plane square to its area that runs through the middle of its corners, as Newell's method fits a plane, which is the face's own plane where it is flat. It rests on no triangulation: over a face of four corners a hair out of flat, it is the middle of the two ways of splitting it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Export.Chords
member.summary:
How the writers that have no curves cut a curve into chords, and what they refuse.
The library's cuts keep the tolerance on a large radius as they do on a small one (a circle of radius 50 000 cut within 0.01 is 4 968 corners). The counts worked out here are the library's, and a chord more where its arc cosine rounds, up to for one curve.
The points are placed by the same arithmetic as the library's ToPolyline(int), but are not handed to a or , whose constructors drop a point within the point tolerance of the one before: a circle of radius 1 cut within 1E-8 has chords of 1.3E-4, and every one of them is kept here.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Export.Chords.Most
member.summary: The most chords one curve is cut into; a tolerance that needs more is refused.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Chords.Of(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse3,System.Double)

The library's own cut now goes on by the bend of the rim past 4 096 corners with fewer of them (12 920 for radii 50 000 and 25 000 within 0.001, where the even spread is 15 708), but the writers keep the even spread so that what they write does not change.

member.summary: The chords of a spline from its start to its end: the corners cuts it at, every one kept where the chain would merge those closer than the point tolerance, and the two ends the spline's first and last control points exactly, where a rational one's are worked out a last digit off them.

member.summary: Whether an arc's circle can be placed: a radius, a sweep and a centre that are numbers. The arc of a bulge of 1E-200 has a radius of 1E202 and a centre that is not one.

member.summary: Whether the chords of the library's cut of an ellipse may be shorter than the point tolerance, so that it would drop some of them: its shortest are at the ends of the major axis, where the rim bends most, as long as the root of eight times the radius of that bend and the tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Chords.ForArc(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32)
member.summary: How many chords a circular arc is cut into so that none strays further than the tolerance: its sweep over the angle a chord may span, rounded up. The library's count is the least it gives, since it is right wherever its cap does not come first; the exact one is worked out from the arc sine, which keeps its digits at a tolerance far below the radius.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Chords.EvenSpread(System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: How many chords of an even spread in the eccentric angle keep an ellipse within a tolerance: a chord over the angle h strays from the rim by at most h² / 8 of the largest acceleration along it, which is the major radius.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Chords.Add(System.Int64@,System.Int32,System.Double)
member.summary: Adds the chords of one more curve to a chain's total, and refuses a total past .

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Export.ExactDigits
member.summary: The digits of a double worked out exactly, in whole numbers, so that every runtime gives the same text. .NET Framework 4.8 prints a double of 16 or 17 digits from 15 or 17 digits that it rounded once already (0.002986441512055773 is 0.002986441512055774 there at 16 digits, in about one double in sixteen), and a number half way between two texts goes up where .NET Core 3.0 and later send it to the even digit (6.9212722778320312 is 6.9212722778320313 at 17); its parse is not exact either. The text here is what ToString("G15"), "G16" and "G17" give under .NET Core 3.0 and later, which is right, on every runtime.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.ExactDigits.Cut(System.Double,System.UInt64@,System.UInt64@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@)
member.summary: The first 17 digits of a number, cut and not rounded, in whole-number arithmetic: the number times ten to the power of is its mantissa times five to that power, over two to the power of the difference of the exponents, so , a number of 17 digits, is that quotient and , under two to the , what is left. False where the number is subnormal, under 1E-11 or from 1E15 up in size, where the 128 bits this works in do not hold it: then works in integers of any size.

member.summary: The first 17 digits of a finite number over nought, in size, cut and not rounded: , of 17 digits, over ten to the power of is the number less what says is left, which is 0 for nothing, 1 for less than half a unit of the last digit, 2 for half, 3 for more.

member.summary: A finite number other than nought as ToString("G" + digits) prints it under .NET Core 3.0 and later, the digits correctly rounded with a number half way between two going to the even one, the zeros at the end left off, in the form with an exponent (of at least two digits) from 10^digits up and under 1E-4.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Export.Numbers
member.summary: How the library prints a double it keeps exactly, as a text that reads back to that very double, and reads a double from a text, as the double nearest it: the same on either runtime, which .NET Framework's own "R" and parser are not. No other code of the library calls double.Parse or double.TryParse.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Numbers.Exact(System.Double)
member.summary: Prints a double as the shortest of its 15, 16 and 17 digit texts that reads back to exactly that double.

remarks.para: .NET Framework's "R" is not exact: for a number in about one in 25 000 of the doubles a mesh gives, and one in 1 600 of doubles of any bits, it prints 15 or 16 digits where 16 or 17 are needed, and the number read back is another double (4.8721540113315704 prints as 4.87215401133157). Parsing the text back to see whether it fits does not help, as the Framework parser is not correctly rounded either, and its errors match those of its formatter.

So the candidates, "G15" then "G16" and at last "G17", which always fits, are judged here without a parser: a text fits when it rounds to the double, which is to say lies within half a step of it, a text exactly half a step away fitting when the double's last bit is even, as rounding ties to even. A text of at most 2^53 as digits and a power of ten within 1E22 is judged by one correctly rounded multiplication or division, which is exact and decides both ways (Clinger's fast path); any other, in integers.

The text is exact and the same on either runtime: the digits are worked out by , for the Framework's own are not always correctly rounded, so that the text it reached could differ from .NET 10's and be a digit longer, where both read back to the same double. A negative nought is -0 on both. Infinities and NaN are printed as "R" prints them.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Numbers.Fits(System.String,System.Int64)
member.summary: Whether a decimal text, of at most 17 digits, is nearer the double of the given bits than to any other, a tie going to the double with an even last bit: the number read from the text is that double. Judged in integers.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Numbers.FitsQuickly(System.String,System.Double,System.Int64)
member.summary: The same as , by Clinger's fast path where it applies: digits that are a double exactly and a power of ten that is one, so that one multiplication or division, rounded once, is the correctly rounded number and settles the matter. This needs arithmetic rounded to the 53 bits of a double, which x64 has and 32-bit x87 has under its default precision; the result is cast to a double all the same.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Numbers.Split(System.String,System.UInt64@,System.Int32@)
member.summary: The text as whole digits and a power of ten, its sign left off.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Export.Numbers.MostDigits
member.summary: The most significant digits a text is read by: past them a digit only decides which way a number half way between two doubles goes, which a digit 1 standing for all the rest that are not nought decides alike. A double's halves need at most 767 digits.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.Numbers.TryRead(System.String,System.Double@)
member.summary: Reads a finite number written in decimal, with a point and an exponent where it has them, as the double nearest it, a tie going to the double with an even last bit: the number a correctly rounding parser reads, the same on either runtime.
member.remarks: .NET Framework's parser is not correctly rounded, and lands a step away from the double now and then, so a text printed would not always read back to its double there; no runtime parser is used. A text of at most 2^53 as digits and a power of ten within 1E22 is read by one correctly rounded multiplication or division (Clinger's fast path). Any other is guessed from its first 19 digits and its exponent, a few steps off at most, and the guess moved a step at a time, judged in integers, until the text rounds to it. Of a text of more than 800 significant digits the rest count only as whether any is not nought. Spaces either side are allowed; a sign, digits with at most one point, and an exponent are read; anything else, NaN and the infinities among them, and a number too large for a double, is not a number. A text of up to 19 digits and an exponent of up to three is read from its digits and the power of ten with no array made, by , which gives the double the long way does or says it is not sure of it; the long way, , reads whatever it is not sure of.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Export.ObjWriter
member.summary: Writes geometry in space as a Wavefront OBJ file, to look at in any 3D viewer.

remarks.para: Every shape added becomes an object of its own, named as given, so a viewer lists them separately: a body as the mesh of where its material ends, a ball as the mesh of its surface, a face as its triangles, a chain as a line, a point as a dot. A polygon that turns the same way at every corner is one face, any other its triangles; a circle, an arc, an ellipse or a spline is a line of chords no further from the curve than the chord tolerance asked for, a chord shorter than the point tolerance written all the same. Coordinates are written exactly, as a text that reads back to the very double on .NET Framework and on .NET 10 alike (the digits may differ between the two, a negative nought is -0 on both), so what is looked at is what was computed, however far from the origin.

member.summary: Adds a polygon: one face of its own corners when it turns the same way at every one, as a hexagon does, and its triangles when it does not, as an L does.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.ObjWriter.Add(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.String)
member.summary: Adds a polygon as does, its triangles, where it has them, cut within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance the triangles are cut within, in place of the global one.
What the viewer calls it; a number when none is given.
member.returns: This writer, for adding the next shape.
member.remarks:
An L-shaped polygon 100 by 100 with a square of 50 taken from a corner is 4 triangles covering 7 500, wound as the polygon is. Written as one face, a viewer would fan it from its first corner over the notch. A polygon that turns the same way at every corner but goes twice round, as a pentagram does, is not one face either.
The triangles are cut within the tolerance, so a polygon that is not one face and is thinner than the tolerance comes out as an object with no face at all, by design: an L-shaped polygon with arms 0.0004 wide, built within 1E-5, is empty at the global tolerance and 4 triangles within 1E-5, where an equally thin strip, which is one face, is written at either.
member.exception: Thrown when the polygon is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.ObjWriter.Add(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3,System.Double,System.String)
member.summary: Adds a chain with bends as a line, each bend cut into chords no further than a tolerance from it.

remarks.para: The tolerance is any number above nought, infinity included, which cuts each bend into one chord; the writers and the other chord overloads here refuse infinity.

On ordinary input the points are those of : the same bends cut into the same number of chords at the same places. Four things differ from it. The end of each arc is the edge's own end point, where the library's last chord, worked out from the circle's angle, may miss it by a rounding; and an arc so shallow that its circle cannot be placed, a bulge of 1E-200 having a centre that is not a number, is read as its chord. An edge or a chord shorter than the point tolerance is kept, where ToPolyline3 drops a point within that tolerance of the one before. The count is worked out here from the arc sine, as the library works it out: a bend of radius 50 000 within 0.001 is 3 927 chords to a quarter turn, none more than 0.001 inside the bend. And at a knife-edge count the exact one may be a chord more than the library's, never one fewer. No bend is cut into more than 1 048 576 chords, the chords of all of them together likewise.

member.exception: Thrown when the chain is null.
Thrown when the chord tolerance is nought, negative or not a number, or would need more than 1 048 576 chords.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.ObjWriter.Add(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc3,System.Double,System.String)
member.summary: Adds a loop with bends as a closed line, each bend cut into chords no further than a tolerance from it.
member.remarks: The line comes back to where it started, as OBJ has no closed line: its last vertex is its first. Each bend is cut on its own radius, so a long bend of a large radius is within the tolerance too: a loop with corners of radius 50 000, within 0.001, has 3 927 chords to a quarter turn of each. The chords of all its bends together are no more than 1 048 576.
member.exception: Thrown when the loop is null.
Thrown when the chord tolerance is not a finite number above nought, or would need more than 1 048 576 chords.

The count is worked out from the arc sine: a quarter of radius 50 000 within 0.001 is 3 927 chords, none more than 0.001 inside the arc. No curve is cut into more than 1 048 576 chords.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Export.SvgWriter
member.summary: Draws shapes in the plane as an SVG picture, to look at in a browser.

remarks.para: The picture is fitted round everything added, with Y pointing up as in the drawing, and every line is drawn the same width however far the picture is zoomed. Arcs and ellipses are drawn as arcs and ellipses, not as chords, and a spline as the Bézier curves it is made of wherever SVG has them. Each shape takes a stroke colour and, where it encloses something, a fill — any colour SVG knows, such as "red" or "#3070c0". A ray is drawn on to the edge of the picture, a line without ends across it both ways, and names a shape in it.

member.remarks: The picture grows by the ellipse's bounding box, not by a square of its major radius: an ellipse of radii 30 and 10 (60 across by 20) turned 30 degrees is 52.915 wide and 34.641 high, and the picture is fitted to that.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.SvgWriter.Add(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2,System.Double,System.String)
member.summary: Adds a spline: as the Bézier curves it is made of where SVG has them, and through chords no further from it than a tolerance where it has none.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between a chord and the spline where it is drawn through chords, in drawing units; above nought.
member.returns: This writer, for adding the next shape.
member.remarks: A spline that is not rational and of degree 3 or less is drawn exactly, to the six places the picture's numbers have, cut at its knots into the Bézier pieces it is made of: a C command for each piece of a cubic, a Q for each of a quadratic and an L for each of a spline of degree 1, so that the cubic with the control points (0, 0), (100, 150), (200, 150), (300, 0) is M 0 0 C 100 150 200 150 300 0, and the tolerance is not used. SVG has no curve for a rational spline, a circle among them, nor for a degree above 3: such a spline is drawn through the corners cuts it at, every one kept, so that the circle of radius 100 within 0.01 is 256 chords. The picture grows by the box the curve fills, not by its control points, and not at all where the spline is refused.
member.exception: Thrown when the spline is null.
Thrown when the chord tolerance is not a finite number above nought, or a spline drawn through chords would need more than 1 048 576 of them.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.SvgWriter.Add(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay2,System.String)
member.summary: Adds a ray, drawn from its origin to where it leaves the picture.
member.remarks: A ray has no end, so how far it runs is settled when the picture is read: to the edge of the picture fitted round everything else. Its origin counts towards the fit and its length does not. A ray along +X from (0, 0) in a picture of a square 0 to 100 is drawn to x = 105, the edge with its margin; a ray added to nothing else is drawn in the picture a unit across centred on its origin, so that the ray along +X from (5, 5) runs to x = 5.55.
member.exception: Thrown when the ray has no direction, as a default one has.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Export.SvgWriter.Add(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoXLine2,System.String)
member.summary: Adds a line without ends, drawn across the picture from edge to edge.
member.remarks: A line has no end, so how far it runs is settled when the picture is read: both ways to the edge of the picture fitted round everything else, as a ray's one way. Its origin counts towards the fit, as a ray's does. The line along X through (0, 0) in a picture of a square 0 to 100 is drawn from x = -5 to x = 105, the edges with their margin; a line added to nothing else is drawn in the picture a unit across centred on its origin, from x = -0.55 to x = 0.55.
member.exception: Thrown when the line has no direction, as a default one has.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Export.Wkt
member.summary: Writes shapes as well-known text, which GIS tools, databases and online viewers read.
member.remarks: Every ring is written closed, its first point repeated at the end, as the format asks. A polygon's boundary goes counter-clockwise and its holes clockwise. Coordinates are written exactly, as a text that reads back to the very double on .NET Framework and on .NET 10 alike (the digits may differ between the two, a negative nought is -0 on both). A curve has no well-known text that online viewers and most tools read, so circles, arcs, ellipses, chains with arcs and splines are written through chords, no further from the curve than the chord tolerance asked for, a chord shorter than the point tolerance written all the same, and a ray or a line without ends through a length. A body or a ball is written as a POLYHEDRALSURFACE Z of triangles.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Extension.GeoPointEnumerableExtension.ToGeoLine2s(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2})
member.summary:
Builds the open chain of line segments running through the points, one segment per consecutive pair.
The chain is not closed: nothing joins the last point back to the first, so a ring has to repeat its first point at the end to come out closed. A list of n points yields n - 1 segments, and a list of fewer than two points yields none rather than failing.
Coincident neighbours are not filtered, so a repeated point produces a zero length segment. Run first when that matters.
member.param: The points to connect, in order.
member.returns: The segments joining each point to the one after it.
member.exception: Thrown when is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Extension.GeoPointEnumerableExtension.RemoveConsecutiveNearPoints(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2},GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary:
Thins a chain of points by dropping every point that lands within the tolerance of the point kept before it.
The comparison is against the last point kept, not against the original neighbour, and that is what makes the result hold its promise: no two consecutive points of the returned list are coincident within . A huddle of points collapses onto the first of them, and collapsing stops as soon as one point escapes the tolerance around that anchor, so a run is never swallowed whole however long it is.
The first point always survives; the last one is not privileged. A final point lying within the tolerance of the one kept before it is dropped like any other, which pulls the end of the chain back slightly. That matters when the points are about to become a polyline whose endpoint is meaningful.
Coincidence is measured by , so it is that decides, and the same rule the polyline constructor applies when it filters its own vertices.
member.param: The points to thin, in order.
member.returns: A new list holding the surviving points in their original order. The input is left untouched, and a list of one point or none comes back as a copy.
member.exception: Thrown when is null.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.GeometryHelperLog
member.summary:
Where the GeometryHelper libraries report what they left out or could not do.
Conversions that walk many objects skip what they cannot read rather than throw, because one bad object should not cost the rest. What was skipped, and why, is written here, so that an empty or short result can be explained: an IFC file that could not be opened, a reference model that is not IFC, a body the transformation could not rebuild.
Messages go to under the category unless is set. The Output window of Visual Studio shows them while debugging, and DebugView shows them from a plugin running inside Tekla or AutoCAD. Set to send them to a file, a status bar or another logging library instead, and to false to turn them off. has examples for the console, the status bar of Tekla Structures and a file.
Writing a message never throws: a writer that fails is ignored, so logging cannot break the work it reports on. Like , the settings are shared by the whole process.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.GeometryHelperLog.Writer
member.summary: Gets or sets what receives each message: its level, its text and the exception behind it, if any. Null, the default, writes of the message to .
member.remarks: It is called one message at a time, even when the messages come from work done on several threads at once — a clash check, the products of an IFC file — so a writer need not be safe to call from two at once. It is called on those threads, though: a writer showing messages on a form hands them over with BeginInvoke, since Invoke waits for the form's thread, which may be waiting for that very work.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoAabb3
member.summary: Whether an axis-aligned box touches another shape.

Represents an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB): the smallest box with edges along the world axes that holds a set of geometry.
This is the cheap test that comes before the expensive one. Two shapes whose bounding boxes do not overlap cannot possibly touch, and that is decided by six comparisons, so a scan over many shapes rejects nearly all of them here and only pays for real geometry on the few that survive. is the other kind of box: it carries its own orientation, describes a shape rather than a bound, and costs far more to test.
An empty box is a real value here rather than a null: it holds nothing, has no corners, and grows into a proper box as soon as a point is added to it. default(GeoAabb3) is empty, which makes it the right seed for a loop that unions boxes together.
How far an axis-aligned box is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where an axis-aligned box crosses another shape.
The point of an axis-aligned box nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
An axis-aligned box asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A box asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An axis-aligned box asked whether it touches an infinite line, how far apart they are and where they cross.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoAabb3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance from this box to a point. A point inside is at distance zero, and an empty box is infinitely far from everything.
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.
member.remarks: This is what prunes a search through a tree of boxes: a box already farther away than the best answer so far cannot hold anything nearer, so the whole branch below it can be skipped without being looked at.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoAabb3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoAabb3)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between this box and another one. Boxes that overlap are at distance zero, and an empty box is infinitely far from everything.
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.
member.remarks: The gap between two axis-aligned boxes separates on each axis independently, so the distance is the length of the vector of per-axis gaps. This is what prunes a traversal of two trees at once: a pair of boxes already farther apart than the best answer so far cannot hold a nearer pair.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2
member.summary: Whether an arc touches another shape.

Represents a circular arc in the plane: part of a circle, running from one angle to another.
An arc is a curve, so it encloses nothing and has no area. It is held as a centre, a radius, the angle it starts at and the angle it sweeps through, signed: positive sweeps counter-clockwise and negative clockwise. A sweep of a whole turn is allowed and draws the full circle; a sweep of nothing is not, because an arc that goes nowhere has no direction and no length.
How far an arc is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where an arc crosses another shape.
The point of an arc nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
An arc asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2.FromThreePoints(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Creates the arc through three points, within a tolerance.
member.param: A point the arc passes through between its ends.
member.returns: The arc from the start through the middle to the end.
member.remarks:
Which way the arc turns follows the middle point: it sweeps the way that passes through it, so swapping the start and the end reverses the arc rather than giving the other part of the circle.
The points share a line, and have no arc through them, where the middle one lies within the point tolerance of the line through the other two, or the triangle they make has twice an area of no more than the square of the point tolerance: (0, 0), (100, 0.01) and (200, 0) have the arc of radius 500 000 through them at a tolerance of a thousandth, and share a line at 0.05. Read by the area alone, (0, 7), (5000, 7 + 1.2E-10) and (10000, 7) gave an arc of radius 1E17 that missed its own start by 12.5. An arc that would miss one of its three points by more than the tolerance, its radius past the reach of the digits, is refused too.
member.exception: Thrown when the three points share a line, so no circle passes through them, or so nearly that the arc through them would miss them.
Thrown when a point is not a finite one.

member.param: Twice the area of the triangle, the length of the cross product of the chords from the start.
The length of the chord from the start to the end.
member.remarks: The middle stands twice the area over the chord off the line, a distance, which grows with the chord as the area does not: read by the area alone, the middle 1.2E-10 off the chord of 10 000 gave the arc of radius 1E17, which missed its own start by 8.8.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2.FromBulge(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,System.Double)
member.summary: Creates the arc between two points with a given bulge, the number AutoCAD stores per vertex.
member.param: The tangent of a quarter of the angle the arc sweeps: positive counter-clockwise, negative clockwise.
member.returns: The arc from the start to the end.
member.remarks: A bulge of one is a half turn, and the sign says which way it goes. A bulge of zero would be a straight segment rather than an arc, which is why it is refused here: a chain stores that as an edge with no bulge instead. The centre stands off the middle of the chord by c (1 - b²) / 4b and the radius is c (1 + b²) / 4|b|, worked out so that neither cancels: the chord of 200 000 with a bulge of 1 - 1E-8 has its centre 0.001 off the chord.
member.exception: Thrown when the bulge is zero or not a number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2)
member.summary: Applies a transformation to this arc.
member.returns: The transformed arc.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.

Thrown when the transformation would skew or stretch the arc into part of an ellipse, so that the arc through where its ends and its middle land would land further than the global point tolerance from where its points are put, or, for an arc of a whole turn, would skew or stretch it, as refuses a circle.

Thrown when a skew, a transformation would refuse for a circle, brings the two ends of an arc past a half turn within the global point tolerance of each other, so that no arc can be told through them and its middle.
member.remarks: A turn, a shift, a mirror or an even scaling moves the arc whole, by its centre and its radius, so an arc of any sweep moves; one that turns shapes round, a mirror or a negative scaling, also reverses the way the arc sweeps. One whose axes are one length and square to each other only to a share of some 1E-9, the rounding of a matrix built from axes, moves it whole where it lands within the global point tolerance so, and is read as a stretch otherwise: X stretched by a share of 4E-10 and scaled by 1 000 took the arc of radius 1E5 sweeping 6 radians to one 0.04 off, and refuses it. Any other transformation, a skew or a stretch, makes part of an ellipse of the arc, and the arc through where its two ends and its middle land, as in space (), stands for it only where it lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts the rest of it, everywhere along it, and is refused otherwise: asked at every sixteenth of its sweep only, the arc of radius 87.66 from 0.2 radians sweeping 1.51, under X stretched by 1 + 1.793E-6 and scaled by 84.1, landed 0.0010114 off between two of them, and was moved. The skew that sends Y to (0.000001, 1) moves the arc of radius 100 from 0.5 to 2 radians 0.0000069 off, and refuses it scaled by 1 000, where it would be 0.0069 off; the skew that sends X to (1, 0) and Y to (0.6, 0.8) refuses it, the arc of radius 66.09 through its moved ends and middle standing far off the ellipse it becomes. A skew that keeps both axes one length is judged as a stretch is: a turn of 0.7529 radians of a stretch of 1 + 4.29E-9 and a shear of 9.28E-5, scaled by 55.57, took the arc of radius 9 069.6 to one 9.16 off, and refuses it. A stretch of 3E-6 along X moves the arc of radius 100 from 0.5 to 2 radians at the scale it is drawn, 0.000017 off, and refuses it scaled by 1 000, where it would be 0.017 off. Each point is read from the moved start across the arc, so an arc bowing a hair off its chord is judged as surely as a half circle. An arc of a whole turn has no ends to go through: it is the whole circle, and is read as its circle is (); an arc past a half turn whose ends the transformation brings within the global point tolerance of each other is refused under a skew too. Where the ends come that close under a transformation that carries a circle, a turn whose numbers are rounded to six places, the arc is moved whole as the whole turn is: the arc of radius 100 sweeping a whole turn less 1E-9 under such a turn moves, where it threw.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2.GetClosestPointOnBoundary(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the point of this arc closest to a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.

member.remarks: A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3
member.summary: Whether an arc touches another shape.

Represents a circular arc in space: part of a circle lying in a plane, running from one angle to another.
It is the counterpart of and holds the same things, with a normal for the plane it lies in. Angles are measured counter-clockwise around that normal from the reference direction the plane supplies, as measures them: a circle in space has no natural place to start, so the zero angle sits on the first of the two axes returns.
How far an arc is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where an arc crosses another shape.
The point of an arc nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
An arc asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An arc asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An arc asked whether it touches an infinite line and where they cross.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3.FromThreePoints(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Creates the arc through three points in space, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3.FromThreePoints(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Creates the arc through three points in space, within a tolerance.
member.param: A point the arc passes through between its ends.
member.returns: The arc from the start through the middle to the end, in the plane the three points share.
member.remarks: Three points that do not share a line settle the plane as well as the arc, so nothing else has to be given. The work is done in that plane by , and the points share a line by the same rule: where the middle one lies within the point tolerance of the line through the other two, or the triangle they make has twice an area of no more than the square of the point tolerance. The points (0, 0, 0), (100, 0.01, 0) and (200, 0, 0), the middle 0.01 off the chord, have the arc of radius 500 000 through them at a tolerance of a thousandth, and share a line at 0.05. An arc that would miss one of its three points by more than the tolerance, its radius past the reach of the digits, is refused too.
member.exception: Thrown when the three points share a line, so no circle passes through them, or so nearly that the arc through them would miss them.
Thrown when a point is not a finite one.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3.FromCircle(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,System.Double)
member.summary: Creates the arc of a circle already known, running counter-clockwise round its normal from a point on it.
member.param: A unit normal; the arc runs counter-clockwise round it when the sweep is positive.
The point the arc starts at, on the circle.
member.returns: The arc, its normal turned over where the sweep is negative so that it runs counter-clockwise.
member.remarks: Nothing is solved: an arc a hundredth long that bows a thousandth of its chord off it is built as exactly as a half circle, where the three points of would lie within a point tolerance of one line. The arc comes out as the three-point build gives it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3)
member.summary: Applies a transformation to this arc.
member.returns: The transformed arc.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.

Thrown when the transformation would skew or stretch the arc into part of an ellipse, so that the arc through where its ends and its middle land would land further than the global point tolerance from where its points are put, or, for an arc of a whole turn, would skew or stretch it, as refuses a circle.

Thrown when a skew, a transformation would refuse for a circle in the arc's plane, brings the two ends of an arc past a half turn within the global point tolerance of each other, so that no arc can be told through them and its middle.
member.remarks: A turn, a shift, a mirror or an even scaling of the arc's plane moves the arc whole, by its centre and its radius, so an arc of any sweep moves: the arc of radius 100 sweeping a whole turn less 1E-9 turned 0.7 radians about any axis, which threw, its ends being too close to tell a chord between. One whose axes of the plane are one length and square to each other only to a share of some 1E-9 moves it whole where it lands within the global point tolerance so, and reads it as a stretch otherwise: X stretched by a share of 4E-10 and scaled by 1 000 took the arc of radius 1E5 sweeping 6 radians to one 0.04 off, and refuses it. Any other transformation, a skew or a stretch of its plane, makes part of an ellipse of the arc, and the arc through where its two ends and its middle land stands for it only where it lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts the rest of it, everywhere along it, not only at every sixteenth of its sweep, and is refused otherwise: a stretch of 3E-6 moves the arc of radius 100 a whole turn less 1 at the scale it is drawn, 0.00035 off, and refuses it scaled by 1 000, where it would be 0.35 off. A skew that keeps both axes of the plane one length is judged alike: the one that sends X to (1, 0, 0) and Y to (0.6, 0.8, 0) refuses the arc of radius 100 in the plan from 0.5 to 2 radians, which went to an arc of radius 177.7 far off the ellipse it becomes, and a turn of 0.7529 radians of a stretch of 1 + 4.29E-9 and a shear of 9.28E-5, scaled by 55.57, refuses the arc of radius 9 069.6, which it took to one 9.16 off. Each point is read from the moved start across the arc, so an arc bowing a hair off its chord is judged as surely as a half circle. An arc of a whole turn has no ends to go through: it is the whole circle, and is refused under a skew, since it would be an ellipse; one past a half turn whose ends the skew brings within the global point tolerance of each other is refused too. Where the ends come that close under a transformation that carries a circle, a turn whose numbers are rounded to six places or to a float, the arc is moved whole as the whole turn is.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3.LandsWithin(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3)
member.summary: Determines whether this arc, moved to another, lands within the global point tolerance of where a transformation puts its points, everywhere along it: asked at every sixteenth of its sweep, and between them by how far it can stray ().
member.remarks: Each point is read from the moved start, across the arc, and its distance from the moved circle is worked out from there as well, its height over the circle's plane and, in that plane, the difference of two squares over their sum, so that an arc bowing a hair off its chord, its radius far past the reach of its digits, is read as surely as a half circle, as in the plane ().

member.summary: Determines whether this arc, moved whole, lands within the global point tolerance of where a transformation puts its points everywhere along it, the moved arc's circle read by its own centre and radius.

member.param: The normal of the circle's plane.
The circle's centre, read from where the start lands, in the circle's plane.
The square of how far the centre stands from where the start lands, in the plane, less the square of the radius: nought for an arc through where the start lands.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3.ProjectToArc2(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3)
member.summary: Lays this arc out in the plane of a frame, dropping each point's distance from that plane.
member.param: The frame to lay it out in.
member.returns: The arc in the plane of the frame.
member.exception: Thrown when the arc stands square to the plane, where it would flatten into a segment rather than an arc.

remarks.para: An arc tilted out of the plane of the frame is, seen square onto it, an elliptical arc, which has no type here. It comes back as the circular arc through the projections of its start, its middle and its end, so those three points are right and the points between them are not: an arc of radius 300 over a quarter turn, tilted 60° about the line from its centre to its start, strays up to 10.8 from its true shadow. refuses an arc that is not in the plane, and gives the true shadow of a whole circle.

A whole turn has to be laid out from its centre rather than from three of its points, because its start and its end are in the same place and there is no third point to be found among them. Any pair of angles describes the whole of a circle, so nought to nought is as good as any. Only an arc that sweeps a whole turn is one. An arc within a degree of one is laid out from its centre too, its start and its end being too near each other to find a circle through, but from where it starts and as far as it sweeps: the arc of radius 10 from 1 radian sweeping 359.5 degrees comes down as that arc, not as the whole circle from angle nought. An arc tilted to the frame comes down as part of an ellipse, which an arc cannot be, and one within a degree of a whole turn is laid out on its own radius about its centre, so its start, middle and end stand off where they come down: some 0.056 for that arc with its normal (0.2, 0, 1), and 0.0036 with (0.05, 0, 1).

member.summary: Approximates the arc as a chain that strays no further from it than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between a piece and the arc, in drawing units. Zero picks the automatic share of the radius.
member.remarks: The promise holds however fine the tolerance and however large the radius: a quarter turn of radius 50 000 cut within 1E-4 is 12 419 pieces, not the 1 024 that 4 096 pieces a turn would allow. An arc that the tolerance would cut into more than 1 048 576 pieces is refused. Points closer together than the point tolerance are merged by the chain, so chords shorter than that are not kept, as for .

member.summary: Cuts the arc at the point of it nearest a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A point on the arc, within the tolerance of it, cuts it where its distance is measured to, found at no tolerance, so a point on a small arc near its centre cuts the arc where the arc is nearest it: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the half circle of radius 0.001 about the origin in the plan, from (0.001, 0, 0) through (0, 0.001, 0) to (-0.001, 0, 0), is cut by (0, 0.0007, 0) at (0, 0.001, 0). member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3.GetClosestPointOnBoundary(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the point of this arc closest to a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A point whose foot in the arc's plane falls within the tolerance of the centre is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the foot's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009, 0) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0, 0) through (0, -50, 0) to (50, 0, 0): the closest point is (-50, 0, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.

member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this arc to a point, using the default tolerance.
member.remarks: The segment leaves the point gives, so for a point away from the centre it is as long as : from the quarter arc of radius 50 about the origin on the XY plane, running from (50, 0, 0) round to (0, 50, 0), the point (80, 0, 40) gets the one from (50, 0, 0), 50 long. Near the centre it can be longer, as says.

member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this arc to a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
The segment leaves the point gives, so for a point away from the centre it is as long as : from the quarter arc of radius 50 about the origin on the XY plane, running from (50, 0, 0) round to (0, 50, 0), the point (80, 0, 40) gets the one from (50, 0, 0), 50 long.
A point whose foot in the arc's plane falls within the tolerance of the centre is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the foot's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009, 0) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0, 0) through (0, -50, 0) to (50, 0, 0): the closest point is (-50, 0, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.

member.summary: Approximates the circle as a polygon, cut finely enough that it strays no further from the circle than of its radius.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle2.TriangulateSurface(System.Double,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Breaks the disc into triangles fanned from its center, the rim cut so that it strays from the circle no further than a chord tolerance, within a tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between a chord and the circle, in drawing units. Zero picks the automatic share of the radius.
The tolerance deciding what counts as no area.
member.returns: The triangles, counter-clockwise; none when the disc has no area within the tolerance.
member.remarks: Fanned from the center, every triangle is the same narrow isosceles one, which clipping the rim's polygon from its own corners does not give: it fans the rim from one corner of it into slivers of every width. The rim's corners are those of , so the triangles cover the polygon it gives, which lies within the circle.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle2.ToMesh(GeometryHelper.Meshing.MeshOptions,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Breaks the disc into faces as the options say, within a tolerance: triangles, the cells of a grid, strips or convex pieces, each a simple polygon with no hole, counter-clockwise, meeting its neighbours edge to edge.
member.param: The tolerance the shape is read within: which of its rings touch, what has no area, and for a grid which cells are whole.
member.returns: The mesh; one with no faces when there is no area.

Thrown when a grid's cell is no larger than the point tolerance, or the grid would lay more cells over the shape than a mesh may have.
member.remarks: The rim is flattened first, by the options' chord tolerance, as flattens it; its triangles are fanned from the center.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle2.ToPolygonByChordTolerance(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the circle as a polygon that strays no further from it than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between an edge and the circle, in drawing units. Zero picks the automatic share of the radius.
member.returns: A polygon inscribed in the circle.
member.remarks: The promise holds however fine the tolerance and however large the radius: a circle of radius 50 000 cut within 0.01 is 4 968 corners, which 4 096 a turn would have strayed 0.0147 from. A tolerance that needs more than 1 048 576 corners is refused. Corners closer together than the point tolerance are merged by the polygon, so chords shorter than that are not kept, as for .
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is negative or not a number, or needs more than 1 048 576 corners.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle2.ToPolygonBySpacing(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the circle as a polygon whose vertices are no further apart than a spacing.
member.param: The largest distance allowed between two vertices, measured along the circumference.
member.returns: A polygon inscribed in the circle, its vertices evenly spread.
member.remarks: The circumference rarely divides by the spacing exactly, so the spacing is a limit rather than a step: the vertices are spread evenly and no two are further apart than asked, which leaves no short edge at the end.
member.exception: Thrown when the spacing is not a positive number.

member.summary: Calculates the distance from this circle to a point, negative for a point within it.

member.remarks: The face is read by its material, its outline less its holes, so this circle is nought from it where the two meet, and as far as the nearest rim where it lies wholly in a hole. member.exception: Thrown when the face is null.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3
member.summary: Whether a circle touches another shape.

Represents a circular disc in 3D space, defined by a centre, a normal and a radius.
Like a polygon, this is a planar region rather than a curve: it has an area, and a point counts as inside it only when the point lies on the carrier plane as well as within the radius.
How far a circle is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a circle crosses another shape.
The point of a circle nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A circle asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A circle asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A circle asked whether its rim touches an infinite line and where they cross.

member.summary: Gets whether this is a shape a constructor could have made: the centre is a valid point, the normal of unit length and the radius a positive number.
member.remarks: A value made by a constructor always is. A default one — an element of a new array, or what the out of a Try method holds when the method said false — may not be, and answers questions without complaint all the same. A default one has no radius and no normal.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3.ToPolygon
member.summary: Approximates the circle as a polygon, cut finely enough that it strays no further from the circle than of its radius.
member.returns: A polygon inscribed in the circle, sharing its orientation.
member.remarks: The vertices lie on the circle, so the polygon is inscribed and encloses slightly less than the circle does: about 0.26 % less at the fifty edges the automatic tolerance gives.
member.exception: Thrown when the circle has a coordinate that is not a finite number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3.ToPolygonByChordTolerance(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the circle as a polygon that strays no further from it than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between an edge and the circle, in drawing units. Zero picks the automatic share of the radius.
member.returns: A polygon inscribed in the circle, sharing its orientation.
member.remarks: The promise holds however fine the tolerance and however large the radius: a circle of radius 50 000 cut within 0.01 is 4 968 corners, which 4 096 a turn would have strayed 0.0147 from. A tolerance that needs more than 1 048 576 corners is refused. Corners closer together than the point tolerance are merged by the polygon, so chords shorter than that are not kept, as for .
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is negative or not a number, or needs more than 1 048 576 corners.
Thrown when the circle has a coordinate that is not a finite number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3.ToPolygonBySpacing(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the circle as a polygon whose vertices are no further apart than a spacing.
member.param: The largest distance allowed between two vertices, measured along the circumference.
member.returns: A polygon inscribed in the circle, its vertices evenly spread.
member.remarks: The circumference rarely divides by the spacing exactly, so the spacing is a limit rather than a step: the vertices are spread evenly and no two are further apart than asked, which leaves no short edge at the end.
member.exception: Thrown when the spacing is not a positive number.
Thrown when the circle has a coordinate that is not a finite number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3.ToMesh(GeometryHelper.Meshing.MeshOptions,GeometryHelper.Meshing.MeshPlacement3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Breaks the disc into faces as the options say, its grid standing as the placement says, within a tolerance: triangles, the cells of a grid, strips or convex pieces, each a simple polygon with no hole, counter-clockwise about the normal, meeting its neighbours edge to edge.
member.param: Which way the grid or the strips run in the plane, and where a cell starts.
The tolerance the shape is read within: which of its rings touch, what has no area, and for a grid which cells are whole.
member.returns: The mesh; one with no faces when there is no area.
member.exception: Thrown when the options or the placement are null.

Thrown when the options give an origin of the plane, a grid's cell is no larger than the point tolerance, the grid would lay more cells over the shape than a mesh may have, or the placement's direction stands square to the plane.
member.remarks: The rim is flattened by the options' chord tolerance first, and the triangles fanned from the center. The mesh's normal is the circle's.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem2
member.summary:
A local coordinate system in the plane: an origin and two orthonormal axes, the counterpart of in space.
It is the place a drawing sits rather than something done to a drawing. can say the same thing, and hands it over in that form, but a transformation may also scale, mirror or shear, and reading one backwards means inverting a matrix. A frame is rigid by construction, and reading it backwards is turning the axes round, which costs nothing and loses nothing.

member.summary: Initializes a system at an origin, with its X axis along a direction.
member.param: Which way the X axis points; its length does not matter.
member.remarks:
The Y axis follows from the X axis, a quarter turn counter-clockwise from it, so a system in the plane can never come out skewed: unlike in space, there is nothing to correct.
The axis is taken however short, only one of no length refused: (6E-7, 8E-7) points the X axis along (0.6, 0.8), where the global vector tolerance of 1E-5, read as a length, refused it as having none.
member.exception: Thrown when the axis has no length.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3
member.summary:
Represents a 3D local coordinate system: an origin and three orthonormal axes.
The axes are always orthonormal, whatever is passed in. The supplied X direction is kept, the Z axis is taken as X × Y, and the Y axis is then rebuilt as Z × X. That third step is what makes the system square: keeping the supplied Y unchanged would leave a skewed frame in which and stop being inverses of each other, and every measurement taken through it would be quietly wrong.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3)
member.summary: Initializes a new coordinate system from an origin and two directions.
member.param: The direction the local X axis should follow.
A direction on the positive Y side of the local XY plane.
member.exception: Thrown when either direction has zero length, or when the two are parallel, since parallel directions do not span a plane and leave the third axis undefined.
member.remarks:
Two directions are parallel by the angle between them, whatever their lengths: where the sine of it is within the global vector tolerance of 1E-5. Two directions 0.002 long and square to each other span a system, where the length of their cross product, 4E-6, was read against that tolerance and they were refused as parallel; two 10 long and 5E-6 of a radian apart are parallel, where their cross product of 5E-4 passed.
The X direction is taken however short, only one of no length refused: (0, 6E-7, 8E-7) points the X axis along (0, 0.6, 0.8), where the global vector tolerance of 1E-5, read as a length, refused it as having none. So a scaling however small keeps a system's axes through .

member.summary: Initializes a coordinate system whose XY plane is a given plane.
member.param: The plane; its normal becomes the local Z axis.
member.remarks: A plane fixes only one axis, so the in-plane pair comes from and is unspecified beyond being orthonormal and right-handed.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3)
member.summary: Initializes a coordinate system from axes that are already orthonormal.
member.remarks: Re-orthonormalizing a frame that is already square is not the identity in floating point: two cross products and two normalizations shift the last digits of every axis. A copy must not drift like that, so it skips the work rather than repeating it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge2
member.summary: Whether an edge touches another shape.

One piece of a chain: a straight segment, or an arc when it carries a bulge.
The bulge is the tangent of a quarter of the angle the arc sweeps, the number AutoCAD stores against each vertex of a polyline: zero is a straight segment, one is a half turn counter-clockwise, and the sign says which way it goes. Storing it rather than a centre and two angles is what makes a round trip through a drawing exact, and it is why an edge needs no more than its two ends and one number.
How far an edge is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where an edge crosses another shape.
The point of an edge nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
An edge asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge2.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether the edge touches a segment, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: An edge is a segment or an arc and nothing else, so every one of these reads it as whichever it is and asks that shape. What counts as touching is then whatever it counts as for a segment or an arc: neither has an inside, so against another open shape only a meeting counts, while a closed one swallowing the edge whole counts as well. A segment meets a segment or an arc where the two cross or come within the point tolerance, and so do two arcs.
