member.remarks: An arc sweeping a whole turn has its two ends in the same place and cannot be told from a point by its ends alone, so it is refused: a chain says a full circle with a circle, not with an edge.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge2.IsArc
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the edge is an arc rather than a straight segment.
member.remarks: An edge that bows less off its chord than the centre of its arc can be placed to is read as its chord, and is not an arc: its sag no more than 2.5 parts in 1E16 of how far the centre and the radius reach from the origin. The edge from (0, 0) to (100, 0) with a bulge of 1E-12 bows 5E-11 on a radius of 2.5E13, and its arc put its middle at (50.002, 0); it is the segment, and measures, cuts and flattens as one. A bulge of a ten-millionth over the same chord, bowing 5E-6, is an arc. Read so, its middle, its length and the area it bounds are the chord's, off the true arc's by no more than its sag, which is less than the rounding of the arc's centre; split, its pieces are straight, their bulge nought. The reading follows the reach of the edge from the origin, so moving or turning an edge near the threshold can change it.

member.summary: Determines whether the edge, carrying a bulge, bows plainly more than the centre of its arc can be placed to, settled with neither a root nor a division.
member.remarks: The chord measured along the axes, l, is no less than the chord c and no more than c times the root of 2, so the sag, c |b| / 2, is no less than 0.35 |b| l. The centre stands within the radius, c (1 + b²) / 4|b|, of the chord's middle, so the reach is no more than that middle's plus three radii, and up to a half turn no more than the middle's plus 1.5 l / |b|. Past a half turn the sag is more than half the chord, and plain.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge2.CutsOff(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Gets the circular segment of the edge: the piece between its arc and its chord.
member.returns: true when the point lies strictly inside the piece the arc cuts off its chord.
member.remarks: This is what tells an arc loop from the straight loop through its vertices: walking the arc rather than the chord adds that piece where the arc bulges out and takes it away where the arc bulges in. A straight edge cuts nothing off, so it never holds a point. The side of the chord is read exactly, by the rule the straight loop's own test reads it with (see ), so that the two agree on every point near the chord.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge2.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2)
member.summary: Gets the edge under a transformation.
member.returns: The transformed edge.
member.remarks: A bulge is the shape of the arc against its own chord, so moving, turning and scaling evenly leave it alone, and mirroring changes its sign because the arc then leans the other way. A transformation that skews the axes or scales them differently makes an arc part of an ellipse: the edge is then the edge from where its ends land through where its middle lands, as in space (), where that lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts the rest of it, as the arc is (), and is refused otherwise rather than answered with an arc visibly off the ellipse. The edge of bulge 0.5 from (0, 0) to (100, 0) under the skew that sends Y to (0.000001, 1) ends at (100, 0); under the one that sends X to (1, 0) and Y to (0.6, 0.8) it is refused, the arc through those three points standing far off the ellipse it becomes. An edge 100 long bowing by 1E-12 moves under a turn rounded to six places, where it was refused for want of digits.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.
Thrown when the transformation would skew or stretch an arc into part of an ellipse it would land visibly off.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge3
member.summary: Whether an edge touches another shape.
One piece of a chain in space: a straight segment, or an arc bulging in a plane of its own.

remarks.para: The twin of , with the one thing space needs that the plane does not. A bulge is the tangent of a quarter of the swept angle, the number AutoCAD keeps against a vertex, and in the plane it is enough on its own. In space it is not: a chord and a bulge are satisfied by an arc in any of the infinitely many planes through that chord, so the plane is carried as well, as .

A positive bulge sweeps counter-clockwise about , which is what a positive bulge means in the plane too, and that bows the curve towards the chord crossed with the normal. So a chord running along X with a normal along Z bows towards minus Y, the same way puts it.
A bulge of nought is a straight segment and the normal is then ignored, which is why is worth asking before .

member.summary: How far an edge is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where an edge crosses another shape.
The point of an edge nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
An edge asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An edge asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An edge asked whether it touches an infinite line and where they cross, as a segment or an arc by its kind.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge3.IsArc
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the edge curves.
member.remarks: An edge that bows less off its chord than the centre of its arc can be placed to is read as its chord, and does not curve: its sag no more than 2.5 parts in 1E16 of how far the centre and the radius reach from the origin, as reads one in the plane. The edge from (0, 0, 0) to (100, 0, 0) with a bulge of 1E-12 bows 5E-11 on a radius of 2.5E13; it is the segment, and measures, cuts and flattens as one. Read so, its middle and its length are the chord's, off the true arc's by no more than its sag, which is less than the rounding of the arc's centre; split, its pieces are straight, their bulge nought, and writes it as its chord, with no bulge. The reading follows the reach of the edge from the origin, so moving or turning an edge near the threshold can change it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge3.BowsPlainly
member.summary: Determines whether the edge, carrying a bulge, bows plainly more than the centre of its arc can be placed to, settled with neither a root nor a division.
member.remarks: The chord measured along the axes, l, is no less than the chord c and no more than c times the root of 3, so the sag, c |b| / 2, is no less than 0.28 |b| l. The centre stands within the radius, c (1 + b²) / 4|b|, of the chord's middle, so the reach is no more than that middle's plus three radii, and up to a half turn no more than the middle's plus 1.5 l / |b|. Past a half turn the sag is more than half the chord, and plain.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge3.ReadsAsChord
member.summary: Determines whether the edge, carrying a bulge of no more than one, bows so little that its chord is read for it: its sag no more than 2.5 parts in 1E16 of how far the centre and the radius of its arc reach from the origin.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge3.ToArc
member.summary: Gets the edge as an arc in space.
member.exception: Thrown when the edge is straight, its bulge nought, so there is no arc to give.
member.remarks: The bulge is read in the plane the normal names: the chord is laid along the X axis of a frame standing on the start point, the arc is built there exactly as it would be in the plane, and its circle is lifted back. So a curve in space and the same curve laid flat come out with the same radius and the same swept angle, and an edge 0.01 long bowing a thousandth of its chord off it is as much an arc as a half circle. The arc runs counter-clockwise round its own normal, which points against the edge's where the bulge is negative. An edge that bows so little it is read as its chord (see ) still gives the arc its bulge describes, to a caller who asks for that arc; the edge's own members, and every query, read it as the segment.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge3.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3)
member.summary: Applies a transformation to the edge.
member.returns: The edge in its new place.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.

Thrown when the transformation would skew or stretch an arc into part of an ellipse that the arc through where its ends and its middle land would stand further than the global point tolerance off, as the arc is refused ().
Thrown when the transformation has an entry that is not a finite number.
member.remarks: The normal is carried by the transformation as well, so an edge turned about any axis keeps bulging the way it did. A transformation that mirrors turns the plane over, which is why the normal is taken from where the ends and the middle of the arc land rather than rotated on its own. One that skews or stretches the arc's plane, which makes part of an ellipse of it, gives the arc through where its two ends and its middle land, where it lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts the rest of the edge, and is refused otherwise, as the arc is: the edge of bulge 0.5 from the origin to (10, 0, 0) stretched to twice along a diagonal of its plane is refused, where it was moved to an arc that stands for no part of the ellipse it becomes, and stretched by a millionth it moves, 8.3E-7 off. The middle is worked out across the chord, so an edge 0.01 long bowing a thousandth of its chord off it moves as surely as a half circle.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEdge3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the distance from the edge to a point, within a tolerance.
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.
member.remarks: The tolerance changes nothing in the distance to a bend: a point at the centre of its arc is as far from it as any other, and a point near the centre is not carried to the bend's start, as measures it. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the half circle of radius 0.001 about the origin in the plan, from (0.001, 0, 0) through (0, 0.001, 0) to (-0.001, 0, 0), is 0.0003 from (0, 0.0007, 0) as an edge, and the point is on it; the projection keeps carrying it to the start, 0.00122 away. A straight edge shorter than the tolerance is read as its start point.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse2
member.summary: Whether an ellipse touches another shape.

Represents a 2D ellipse: a centre, the direction of its major axis, and its two radii.
An ellipse is a region, as a circle is: it has an area, and a point inside it is in it. Its rim is walked by the eccentric angle t, the point Center + a cos t MajorAxis + b sin t MinorAxis, counter-clockwise from the end of the major axis. That is not the direction seen from the centre: on an ellipse 300 by 100, t = 45° is the point (212.1, 70.7), which lies 18.4° from the axis seen from the centre. An ellipse whose radii are equal is a circle and answers every question as does, but for where its angle starts, which follows its axis; the point of the rim nearest its centre, which is the end of the minor axis as for any other ellipse; and where it touches a circle or another ellipse from outside without crossing, which is midway between the two rims, where two circles of different radii touch at a point nearer the larger.
The operations live in ; the members here ask it.
How far an ellipse is from another shape, and how deep inside it a point sits.
Where the rim of an ellipse crosses another shape.
The point of the rim of an ellipse nearest a point, the shortest segment joining its rim to another shape, and which edge of a shape lies nearest it.
An ellipse asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.returns: A polygon inscribed in the ellipse.
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is negative or not a number, or needs more than 1 048 576 corners.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoEllipse3
member.summary: Whether the rim of an ellipse in space touches another shape.

Represents an elliptical disc in 3D space: a centre, the normal of its plane, the direction of its major axis, and its two radii.
Like a circle in space, this is a flat region rather than a curve: it has an area, and a point counts as inside it only when the point lies on its plane as well as within its rim. The rim is walked by the eccentric angle t, the point Center + a cos t MajorAxis + b sin t MinorAxis, counter-clockwise seen from the tip of the normal, from the end of the major axis. That is not the direction seen from the centre: on an ellipse 300 by 100, t = 45° is the point 212.1 along the major axis and 70.7 along the minor, which lies 18.4° from the axis seen from the centre.
Everything within the plane is 's arithmetic, read in the ellipse's own frame. An ellipse whose radii are equal is a circle and answers as does, but for where its angle starts, which follows its axis, and the point of the rim nearest its centre, which is the end of the minor axis as for any other ellipse. The operations live in ; the members here ask it.
How far an ellipse in space is from another shape.
Where the rim of an ellipse in space crosses another shape.
The point of an ellipse in space nearest another shape.
An ellipse asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An ellipse asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An ellipse asked whether its rim touches an infinite line and where they cross.

member.summary: Initializes an ellipse in space from its centre, the normal of its plane, the direction of its major axis and its two radii.
member.param: The normal of the carrying plane, of any length but nought; it is normalized.

The direction of the major axis, of any length but nought. An axis tilted out of the plane is laid into it: its part along the normal is taken off, and what is left is normalized, so (1, 0, 1) on a plane with the normal along Z is the axis along X.
Half the length of the major axis; a positive number, no less than the minor radius.
Half the length of the minor axis; a positive number.
member.exception: Thrown when the normal has no length or is not a finite vector; or when the axis has no length, is not a finite vector, or runs along the normal, what is left of it in the plane no more than 1E-12 of its length.
Thrown when a radius is not a positive number, or the minor radius is larger than the major one. The two are not swapped: an ellipse longer across than along is given by an axis a quarter turned.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace2
member.summary: Whether a face touches another shape.

Represents a 2D region with holes: an outer boundary polygon with polygons cut out of it.
A face is what a polygon becomes once it has to carry openings: a plate with bolt holes, a slab with a shaft through it, or the area an outward offset leaves round a courtyard it has closed off. The outer loop says where the material ends and each hole says where it is missing. It is the plane counterpart of GeoFace3.
The holes are expected to lie inside the boundary and apart from each other, but this is not checked, for the same reason does not check that it is simple. Point location reads a point inside any hole as outside the face.
How far a face is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a face crosses another shape.
The point of a face nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A face asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace2.TriangulateSurface(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Breaks the face into triangles that each lie within its material, holes left open, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance deciding what counts as no area, and how near two rings may come.
member.returns: The triangles covering the material, counter-clockwise whichever way the face runs; none when nothing is left of it.
member.remarks:
A hole is never covered over: holes that touch or overlap are taken together, and one reaching past the boundary takes away only what it covers. A hole enclosing no area takes nothing away.
The triangles keep the shape's own corners while its rings stand apart, as keeps them, a concave boundary followed rather than spanned. Rings that come within the point tolerance of each other, or cross, are read as the booleans read them and cut into strips at their corners instead: those triangles still lie within the material, but meet its edges at points of their own as well.

member.remarks: Its holes are left open: a cell of a grid holding one whole is split across, through the middle of it.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace2.Centroid
member.summary: Gets the centroid of the face: the centroid of its boundary with its holes taken out, so a plate balances at this point whatever has been cut from it.
member.remarks:
A face whose holes cancel its boundary has no centroid to give, and its boundary centroid is returned instead rather than a division by zero.
The holes are weighed however small the face: the square 0.001 by 0.001 with a hole 0.0004 by 0.0004 in its corner, of 8.4E-7 square units, balances at (0.000538, 0.000538), where an area of a millionth or less was taken for none and the boundary's centroid, (0.0005, 0.0005), given. Only a face whose area is lost in the rounding of the areas it is worked out from has none.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace2.BuildIndex
member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the boundary of this face, the rim of every hole included, for asking it many questions.

remarks.para: An index is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. Building it costs a sort of the edges, so it pays for itself over repeated queries and never on the first one; below a few dozen edges the plain walk wins outright. Every shape here is immutable, so a tree stays valid for as long as the shape exists — build it once, keep it, throw it away with the shape.
It is Build and not Get because it does work. Calling it inside a loop is slower than not having it at all, which is exactly the mistake the name is there to prevent.

member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

member.summary: Calculates the distance from this face to a point, negative for a point on the material.
member.returns: The distance out to the nearest edge, its outline or the rim of a hole, measured exactly, negative when the point lies on the material and nought when the global point tolerance calls it on an edge.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3
member.summary: Whether a face touches another shape.

Represents a flat face in 3D space: an outer boundary polygon with optional holes cut out of it.
A face is what a polygon becomes once it needs to carry openings. A plate with bolt holes, a wall with a window: the outer loop says where the material ends and each inner loop says where it is missing. Every loop shares one plane, which is checked at construction.
How far a face is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a face crosses another shape.
What a face in space can answer by working in its own plane: combining it with another flat shape lying in that same plane.
member.remarks: A shape that does not lie in this one's plane is refused rather than projected in, because projecting would report two plates a metre apart as overlapping and say nothing about it. asks the question beforehand. Everything comes back as , because joining two areas can leave a hole in the middle and only a face can hold one.
member.summary: The point of a face nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A face asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A face asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A face asked about an infinite line: whether they touch, how far apart they are, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

The tolerance deciding which corners are one, which loops enclose an area, and which lie flat.
member.returns: One face, holes and all, as the constructors would make it, when every loop lies flat on the plane of the boundary within the planar tolerance. Otherwise triangles on the corners themselves, wound as the boundary is, covering the boundary less its holes. member.remarks: This is the way to read the faces of a body a modeller gives as loops of corners. A face can come a little out of flat, as a face Tekla Structures cuts can, and a polygon refuses it; left out, it is a hole in the body. Split into triangles on the corners it came with, each exactly flat, it keeps every edge it shares with its neighbours, so the body is as closed as it was given, and no corner moves. A hole enclosing no area is left out.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3.Triangulate
member.summary: Breaks the outer boundary into triangles, ignoring the holes.
member.remarks:
The holes are left out because a fan triangulation cannot express them. What this is good for is the signed sums — area, centroid, volume — where the holes are accounted for separately by triangulating each of them and subtracting.
The triangles a fan produces do not all lie inside a concave face, so this is not a surface mesh. Use for anything that reads the triangles as material.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3.TriangulateSurface
member.summary: Breaks the face into triangles that each lie within its material, holes included, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3.TriangulateSurface(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Breaks the face into triangles that each lie within its material, holes included, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance within which rings count as meeting; a triangle is left out only when it has no width, within a millionth of its point tolerance.
member.returns: The triangles covering the face, wound to share its normal; a small one may have no normal at the global tolerance, see the remarks.
member.remarks:
This is the triangulation to use wherever the mesh stands for the surface itself — ray casting, clash detection, distance to a body. Unlike every triangle lies inside the face, a hole is left empty rather than covered over, and a concave boundary is followed rather than spanned.
The triangles are clipped from the face's own corners while its rings stand apart. A face whose rings come within the point tolerance of each other (holes sharing an edge, a hole against the boundary) or cross, or whose loop the clipping cannot reduce, is cut into strips at its corners instead, its material read as the booleans read it: holes that touch or overlap are taken together, and one reaching past the boundary takes away only what it covers. Those triangles still lie within the material and leave every hole open, but they meet the face's edges at points of their own as well as at its corners. A face with nothing left of it gives none.
The triangles cover what the face covers, to rounding, however near its corners stand to edges they are not on. The corners of its rings were once read within the tolerance before they were cut: a wall 50 by 1.50015 with corners at 1.5 up both its sides, 0.00015 under its top ones, was meshed 0.00375 short at a thousandth, and a notch 0.0002 wide was closed. They are read within rounding now; a loop thinner than the tolerance is still a seam at it, with no triangle. A face the clipping leaves a needle of, every ear of it blocked by corners within rounding of its sides, is cut into strips too, rather than the needle dropped.
Such a face used to be handed back as the fan of its boundary, laid across every hole: a slab whose pits the clipping could not get round was meshed as 5 391 m2 for its 1 836.
A clipped triangle is left out only when it has no width: its corners lie on a line within a millionth of the point tolerance. A small one is kept, so a face 0.002 by 0.002 is its two triangles at the default tolerance, where they were once dropped as too small and left a gap in the mesh of the body they closed.
Each half of a face 0.002 by 0.002 is a triangle with its and its , and reads as a face, where they threw. A triangle of the mesh thinner than the point tolerance, one 100 by 0.0008, has true, its height over its longest side being within it, and keeps its normal all the same.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3.BuildIndex
member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the surface of this face, for asking it many questions.

remarks.para: An index is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. Building it costs a sort of the triangles, so it pays for itself over repeated queries and never on the first one; below a few dozen triangles the plain walk wins outright. Every shape here is immutable, so a tree stays valid for as long as the shape exists — build it once, keep it, throw it away with the shape.
It is Build and not Get because it does work. Calling it inside a loop is slower than not having it at all, which is exactly the mistake the name is there to prevent.

The index is over triangles and the body is not. GetIntersections on the tree reports one hit per triangle, so a ray landing on the diagonal two triangles share is named twice, while the body names each place once. Ask the body where you want places; ask the tree where you want speed and can keep clear of the edges — which is what Containment3 does by throwing its ray again in another direction when a hit lands near one.

member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this face to another one, using the default tolerance.
member.remarks: The segment leaves the material of this face and lands on that of the other, of no length where the two meet; the edges of this face, outline and then holes, are walked first, and a tie goes to the first. The square 100 by 100 in the floor with a corner at the origin and a hole 40 by 40 in its middle, and the square 20 by 20 lying in the hole about (50, 50), are joined from the rim at (40, 30, 0) to (40, 40, 0), 10 long, as measures it. A shape coming end-on at the other and stopping within the point tolerance of it is read as crossing it, so the line can be of no length where the distance is the gap: the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, 9), over the square 100 by 100 in the floor, is joined by a segment of no length at (5, 5, 0.0004), and is 0.0004 from it by its distance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace2)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance from this segment to the material of a face: the same answer as .
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.
member.remarks: The face is read by its material, its outline less its holes, so this segment is nought from it where the two meet, and as far as the nearest rim where it lies wholly in a hole. The segment from (40, 50) to (60, 50) lies in the hole of the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin and a hole 40 by 40 in its middle and is 10 from its rim; the one from (10, 50) to (20, 50) lies on the material and is nought away.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3
member.summary: Whether a segment touches another shape.
Represents a 3D line segment defined by a start point and an end point.
How far a segment is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a segment crosses another shape.
The point of a segment nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A segment asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A line segment asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A line segment asked about an infinite line: whether they touch, how far apart they are, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3.GetPlaneWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3)
member.summary: Gets the infinite plane through this segment carrying a given in-plane direction.
member.param: A second direction the plane must contain.
member.returns: The plane through the start point spanned by this segment and the supplied direction.
member.exception: Thrown when the segment has no length or the two directions are parallel, since neither case pins down a plane, or when the direction is not finite. A direction along the segment, or of no length, is named inPlaneDirection: the segment from the origin to (100, 0, 0) with the direction (1, 0, 0) gives that, where the plane's own refusal named a normal the caller never gave.

member.summary: Gets every point where this segment crosses a plane.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets every point where this segment crosses a plane, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A segment meets a plane at a single point, and this is that point wrapped so that it reads like every other crossing. It is what lets a be handed on as whichever of a segment or an arc it is, since an arc can meet one twice. Where the segment only touches the plane, as reads a touch, the point is the one of it nearest the plane, as a triangle and a polygon give one: the segment from (-50, 0, 0.5) to (50, 0, 0.0005) touches the plane z = 0 at its end. A segment lying in the plane, both ends within the planar tolerance of it, meets it along its length and names no place. A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start unless it truly crosses the plane: at a thousandth, the one from (5, 5, 0.0015) to (5, 5, 0.0006) meets the floor nowhere, where it was given its end, and the one from (5, 5, 0.0008) to (5, 5, 0.0002) meets it at its start.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3)
member.summary: Gets every point where this segment crosses a triangle.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets every point where this segment crosses a triangle, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A segment meets a triangle at a single point, and this is that point wrapped so that it reads like every other crossing. It is what lets a be handed on as whichever of a segment or an arc it is, since an arc can meet one twice. The crossing is given where it stands within the point tolerance of both and the two touch, as reads it. A segment that touches the triangle within the point tolerance without crossing it is given the point of it nearest the triangle, and none where it lies level over the material, within the planar tolerance of its plane at both ends: the segment from (20, 20, 0.0005) to (20, 20, 5), ending 0.0005 over the triangle with corners (0, 0, 0), (100, 0, 0) and (0, 100, 0), is given (20, 20, 0.0005), where it collided and was given nothing. A segment lying in the plane of the triangle, both ends within the planar tolerance of it, is given none even where it crosses the outline: it meets the triangle along a stretch, which names no one place, as a segment lying in a plane names none. The segment from (-50, 20, 0) to (50, 20, 0) and the triangle with corners (0, 0, 0), (100, 0, 0) and (0, 100, 0) collide and are given no point; an arc lying in that plane is given the points where it cuts the outline. A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start unless it truly crosses: given its start where that lies within the point tolerance, as a point lying that close meets the shape, and nothing where it does not.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3)
member.summary: Gets where this segment crosses a segment, as a list.
member.remarks:
Two straight pieces meet at one place, so the list is one long or empty. It is a list because a has to be able to ask the same question of a segment and of a bend.
There is deliberately no TryIntersectWith twin taking an array here: this type already has one handing back a single point, and a second one differing only in the shape of its out would make every existing call to it ambiguous. is the single-point reading and this is the list reading of the same answer.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3
member.summary: Whether an oriented box touches another shape.

Represents an oriented bounding box (OBB): a cuboid that carries its own orientation rather than lining up with the world axes.
This is a shape, not a bound. A beam running at an angle is described tightly by an oriented box and only loosely by an axis-aligned one, which is what is for. The price is that testing two oriented boxes against each other needs the separating axis theorem rather than six comparisons, so the usual pattern is to reject with bounding boxes first and reach for this only on what survives.
How far an oriented box is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where an oriented box crosses another shape.
The point of an oriented box nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
An oriented box asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A box asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An oriented box asked whether it touches an infinite line, how far apart they are and where they cross.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3.TryExpand(System.Double,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3@)
member.summary: Grows the box by a margin on every side, or shrinks it by a negative one.
member.param: How far to move every face outwards; negative moves them inwards.
The grown box, or this one where the margin shrank it past nothing.
member.returns: true when a box came back; otherwise, false, as for a box about a centre that is not a finite point.
member.remarks:
The box keeps its axes — every face moves along its own normal, so the corners stay square and the result is exact rather than a re-fit. There is no tolerance in it, and so no overload taking one.
It draws the line exactly where its square twin draws it: a margin that takes a side to nothing gives a box with that side flat, which will say, and only a margin that would take a side past nothing is refused. Ask for the box you want and check, rather than reading false as "it got thin".

member.remarks: A box stays a box only under a transformation that keeps right angles right. A shear turns it into a parallelepiped, which this type cannot represent, and what comes back then is the box spanned by the transformed axes rather than the true sheared shape.

member.summary: Gets a small box round some points, turned to fit them.
member.param: The points, such as the corners of a part.
The tolerance deciding whether points lie in one plane.
member.returns: The box standing on the face of the points' convex hull that gives the least volume, with the rectangle of least area on that face: the smallest box of all for a block, a prism, or anything with a flat face to stand on, and close to it otherwise. Of the boxes standing on faces of the hull that are as small to rounding, the thinnest, its least side compared first, then the middle one: a prism 40 long on a right triangle with legs 18 and 24 is given the box 14.4 by 30 by 40, not the one 18 by 24 by 40. Two rectangles on one face as large are compared so too, so a body is given one box however it is turned: the tetrahedron on (0, 0, 0), (24, 0, 0), (0, 18, 0) and (0, 0, 40) is given 13.548779 by 27.340984 by 46.647615, where turned it was given 13.548779 by 30 by 42.513057. Points all in one plane give a box of no depth.
member.exception: Thrown when the points are null.
Thrown when there are no points, or a point is not a finite one.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3
member.summary: Whether a plane touches another shape.

Represents an infinite 3D plane defined by a point on the plane and a normal vector.
The plane is oriented: it distinguishes the side its normal points towards from the other side. That is what lets and answer at all, and it is why is a meaningful operation rather than a no-op.
How far a plane is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a plane crosses another shape.
The point of a plane nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A plane asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A plane asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Initializes a plane from a normal that is already normalized.
member.remarks: Normalizing a vector that is already of unit length is not the identity in floating point: the computed length comes back a bit either side of one, and dividing by it shifts the last digits. Operations that only move a plane around must not pay that, or a copy would come back unequal to its original and flipping twice would drift. This constructor is how they skip it.

member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this plane to a segment: turned round, so that it leaves this plane and lands on the segment.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this plane to a polyline: turned round, so that it leaves this plane and lands on the polyline.
member.remarks: A chain that crosses or touches this plane meets it in a segment of no length at its first point of contact; one clear of it is joined to its nearest vertex. The XY plane is joined to the chain (0, 0, 10), (50, 0, 30) from the origin to (0, 0, 10), 10 long, as measures it. The floor plane meets the triangle with corners (0, 50, -50), (100, 50, -50) and (0, 50, 50) at (50, 50, 0), and is joined to the triangle with corners (0, 50, 10), (100, 50, 10) and (0, 50, 110) from (0, 50, 0) up to (0, 50, 10), 10 long, as measures it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3.TryGetIntersectionLine(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoXLine3@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Tries to find the line where this plane meets another plane, as an infinite line, within a tolerance.
member.param: The line the two planes share, when the method returns true.
member.returns: true if the planes meet in a line; otherwise, false.
member.remarks: Parallel planes are refused whether they are apart, in which case they never meet, or coincident, in which case they meet everywhere. The floor and the wall x = 100 meet in the line along Y through (100, 0, 0), whichever way round they are asked: its origin is the point of the line nearest the world origin, and its direction the cross product of the two normals, so asked of the wall first the line runs the other way.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2.GetClosestPointOnBoundary(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the point of a arc nearest this point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3
member.summary: Whether a point touches another shape.
Represents a 3D point with double precision coordinates.
How far a point is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a point crosses another shape.
The point of a point nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A point asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A point asked how far it is from a spline, which of the spline is nearest, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A point asked how far it is from an infinite line, and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2
member.summary: Whether a polygon touches another shape.

Represents a 2D closed polygon.
A polygon is expected to be simple — no edge crossing another — but this is not checked, because checking costs more than every other thing the constructor does put together. A polygon whose edges do cross is still usable rather than undefined: containment reads it under the even-odd rule, so a region enclosed an even number of times counts as outside, and every operation built on containment follows suit. What does not survive is area. sums lobes with their own signs, so a figure-eight reports zero however large its lobes are, and reports zero with it.
How far a polygon is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a polygon crosses another shape.
The point of a polygon nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A polygon asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.remarks:
A polygon that crosses itself is covered where says it covers, under the even-odd rule.
The triangles keep the shape's own corners while its rings stand apart, as keeps them, a concave boundary followed rather than spanned. Rings that come within the point tolerance of each other, or cross, are read as the booleans read them and cut into strips at their corners instead: those triangles still lie within the material, but meet its edges at points of their own as well.

member.summary: Cuts the loop by the straight line through a segment.
member.remarks: The segment is read as the whole straight line through it, which is what a plane is to space, so its length is ignored: a segment crossing half the loop cuts all of it. Left and right are read from the segment's own direction, so reversing it swaps the two answers and nothing else.

member.summary: Cuts the loop in two along a chain drawn across it.
member.remarks: Both ends of the chain have to sit on the boundary and everything between them has to stay inside, or nothing is cut. Unlike the line, this cutter is bounded: the pieces keep the chain's own vertices.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2.Reverse
member.summary: Gets the polygon running the other way round.
member.returns: The same shape, walked in the other direction.
member.remarks:
Which way a loop runs is what tells its inside from its outside to anything that reads winding, and it is what decides which way round a pair of chamfer distances goes.
The polygon is reversed corner for corner, however short a side: at a millionth, the triangle (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 10) with every corner cut by 0.0003 reverses to its six corners, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back three.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2.BuildIndex
member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the edges of this polygon, for asking it many questions.

remarks.para: An index is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. Building it costs a sort of the edges, so it pays for itself over repeated queries and never on the first one; below a few dozen edges the plain walk wins outright. Every shape here is immutable, so a tree stays valid for as long as the shape exists — build it once, keep it, throw it away with the shape.
It is Build and not Get because it does work. Calling it inside a loop is slower than not having it at all, which is exactly the mistake the name is there to prevent.

member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

member.summary: Calculates the distance from this polygon to a point, negative for a point within it.
member.returns: The distance out to the nearest edge, measured exactly, negative when the point lies inside the polygon and nought when the global point tolerance calls it on its outline.
member.remarks: The magnitude is the distance to the outline, whichever side of it the point is on, and the sign says which side: negative inside, nought on it, positive outside. reads this polygon as filled and so answers nothing at all for a point inside, which is the one place the two part company.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace2)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance from this polygon to the material of a face: the same answer as .
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.
member.remarks: The face is read by its material, its outline less its holes, so this polygon is nought from it where the two meet, and as far as the nearest rim where it lies wholly in a hole. The square 20 by 20 about (50, 50) lies in the hole of the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin and a hole 40 by 40 in its middle and is 10 from its rim; about (130, 50) it is 20 from the outline.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3
member.summary: Whether a polygon touches another shape.

Represents a flat closed polygon in 3D space.
Coplanarity is enforced at construction. A polygon that is not flat has no normal, no area and no interior, so accepting one would leave every property on this type quietly meaningless; the constructor refuses it instead. Geometry that wanders out of a plane is a .
The polygon is expected to be simple — no edge crossing another — but this is not checked, because checking costs more than everything else the constructor does put together. A self-crossing polygon stays usable rather than undefined: containment reads it under the even-odd rule, so a region enclosed an even number of times counts as outside. What does not survive is area: the lobes of a figure-eight cancel, so it reports an area near zero however large those lobes are.
How far a polygon is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a polygon crosses another shape.
What a polygon in space can answer by working in its own plane: combining it with another flat shape lying in that same plane.
member.remarks: A shape that does not lie in this one's plane is refused rather than projected in, because projecting would report two plates a metre apart as overlapping and say nothing about it. asks the question beforehand. Everything comes back as , because joining two areas can leave a hole in the middle and only a face can hold one.
member.summary: The point of a polygon nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A polygon asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A polygon asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A polygon asked about an infinite line: whether they touch, how far apart they are, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3.#ctor(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3})
member.summary: Initializes a new polygon from a sequence of coplanar vertices.
member.param: The vertices, in order around the loop.
member.exception: Thrown when the sequence is null.
Thrown when fewer than three distinct vertices remain, when they are collinear, or when they do not lie on a common plane.
member.remarks:
Consecutive duplicates within tolerance are dropped and a repeated closing vertex is removed, so the loop closes implicitly and no zero-length edge survives. The normal and area are measured once here rather than on every read: the polygon cannot change afterwards, and the Newell sum they both come from is a full pass over the vertices.
Collinear means an area within the vector tolerance and no width: twice the area over the span, the longest side of three corners or the diagonal of the box of more, within the point tolerance. A square 0.002 by 0.002, of 4E-6 square units, is a polygon at the default tolerance, where it was refused; a triangle 0.003 long and 0.0006 high is still refused, and one 100 long and 0.0005 high, of 0.025 square units, still kept.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3.Centroid
member.summary: Gets the centroid of the polygon area.
member.remarks:
This is the centre of mass of the filled shape, not the average of the vertices. The two agree only for a shape whose vertices are spread evenly, and the average is not a useful answer for a polygon with several vertices clustered along one edge.
Each triangle of the fan is weighted by its area signed against the polygon normal, not by its plain area. For a concave polygon parts of the fan reach outside the boundary, and they are wound the other way; their negative weight is exactly what cancels them out again. Using the unsigned area would count that overhang as material and pull the answer towards it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3.GetAreaRoundingAtMost
member.summary: Gets no less than , read from the box rather than from every corner: an area larger than this is more than rounding, and the corners need not be walked to say so.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3.Triangulate
member.summary: Breaks the polygon into triangles.
member.returns: The triangles covering the polygon, sharing its orientation.
member.remarks: The polygon is fanned from its first vertex. For a convex polygon this covers it exactly. For a concave one, some triangles reach outside the boundary and others overlap them with the opposite winding, so the signed contributions still cancel to the right total: area, centroid and volume come out correct. What a fan does not give is a set of triangles each of which lies inside the polygon, so it is not the right basis for a point-in-polygon test, and Containment3 uses a winding count instead.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3)
member.summary: Applies a transformation to every vertex.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.
Thrown when the transformation flattens the polygon so that it no longer encloses an area, or has an entry that is not a finite number.
member.remarks: The polygon is transformed side for side, however short a side: at a millionth, the triangle (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0, 10) with every corner cut by 0.0003 keeps its six corners scaled by 2 or sheared, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back three. Only a corner the transformation lands on the very same point as the one before it goes. An even scaling, turned, moved or mirrored besides, carries the polygon as a move does, its area scaled: a square 100 across with a corner 0.0009 off flat scaled by 10 is kept, where it was refused as not flat, and the cut triangle shrunk by a ten-thousandth keeps its six corners, 0.0007 wide. A transformation that stretches one way more than another or shears has the polygon checked flat and enclosing an area within the global tolerance loosened as far as the transformation stretches any direction: off flat within ten times the tolerance under a stretch by 10, and wide within half of it under a scaling by 0.2, 0.25 and 0.5, which keeps a square 0.003 across as one 0.0006 by 0.00075. Neither is made finer than the global tolerance, so what was kept before is kept still. A projection that flattens the polygon to a line is still refused.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3.Reverse
member.summary: Gets the polygon running the other way round.
member.returns: The same shape, walked in the other direction.
member.remarks:
Which way a loop runs is what tells its inside from its outside to anything that reads winding, and it is what decides which way round a pair of chamfer distances goes.
The polygon is reversed corner for corner, however short a side, and however far off flat the tolerance it was built within let it lie: at a millionth, the triangle (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0, 10) with every corner cut by 0.0003 reverses to its six corners, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back three, and a square 100 across built at a hundredth with one corner 0.005 off the plane of the others reverses, where it was refused as not flat.

member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this polygon to a point, using the default tolerance.
member.remarks: The polygon is read as a filled surface, as its distance reads it, so a point above it is joined straight down and the segment is as long as : from the square 100 by 100 on the XY plane with a corner at the origin, the point (130, 50, 40) gets the one from (100, 50, 0), 50 long.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon3.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this polygon to a segment: turned round, so that it leaves this polygon and lands on the segment.
member.remarks: This polygon is read as a filled surface, as its distance reads it. The square 100 by 100 on the XY plane with a corner at the origin is joined to the segment from (20, 20, 30) to (80, 80, 60) from (20, 20, 0) straight up to its start, 30 long, as measures it. A shape coming end-on at the other and stopping within the point tolerance of it is read as crossing it, so the line can be of no length where the distance is the gap: the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, 9), over the square 100 by 100 in the floor, is joined by a segment of no length at (5, 5, 0.0004), and is 0.0004 from it by its distance.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2
member.summary: Whether a curved loop touches another shape.

A closed loop whose edges may be arcs: vertices with a bulge against each of them, the last one joining back to the first.
It is the arc-carrying counterpart of , and the same division holds as between and : this type says the shape may curve, and is the one place where curves become chords.
How far a curved loop is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a curved loop crosses another shape.
The point of a curved loop nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A curved loop asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.#ctor(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2},System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.Double})
member.summary: Initializes a loop whose edges may be arcs.
member.param: The vertices, in order; at least three distinct ones.
The bulge of the edge leaving each vertex; null or short means the rest are straight.
member.remarks: A vertex within the global point tolerance of the one kept before it is dropped, and so is the edge between the two, which has no length; the edge running on from the dropped vertex keeps its own bulge. The square (0, 0), (10, 0), (10.0004, 0), (20, 0), (20, 20), (0, 20) with bulges 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0 has five corners, and a half circle from (10, 0) to (20, 0) below its bottom. A last vertex repeating the first says nothing the loop does not already say and is dropped too, but its bulge is kept for the closing edge: the edge coming into it keeps its own bulge when it curves, and takes the repeated vertex's when it is straight. The loop (0, 0), (100, 0), (100, 100), (0, 0) with bulges 0, 0, 0, 0.25 is three corners whose closing edge, from (100, 100) back to the origin, bulges 0.25.

member.summary: Builds a loop from the start and bulge of each of its edges, in order, the last one closing it, an edge going only where it starts within a given tolerance of the start kept before it.
member.param: The tolerance whose point threshold says when an edge is too short to keep.

member.remarks:
Every bulge here is its own edge's, so an edge too short to keep goes with its bulge, the last one as well: a last edge starting within the tolerance of the first vanishes, and the edge coming into it closes the loop with its own bulge. The public constructor reads a repeated first vertex as a drawing does instead: a fillet of radius 0.0005 at the first corner of a rectangle 100 by 50 would turn the straight side before it into an arc of radius 35.
For edges already kept within a tolerance of their own, as a loop in space laying itself out in its plane: at a tolerance of nought, only an edge whose ends land on the very same point goes, so the side 0.0006 long of the loop (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.0006), (0, 10) stays, where the global tolerance of a thousandth would drop it.

member.summary: Approximates the loop as a straight polygon, cutting each arc finely enough that it strays no further than the automatic share of its radius.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.Flatten(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the loop as a straight polygon, cutting each arc so that it strays no further than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between a piece and the arc it replaces, in drawing units. Zero picks the automatic share of each radius.
member.returns: The straight polygon.
member.remarks:
The chords of an arc lie inside it, so a loop bulging outward encloses a little less once it is flattened, and one bulging inward a little more. The promise holds however fine the tolerance and however shallow the arc: the bottom of a rectangle 100 by 50 bowed 0.015 (a bulge of 0.0003, radius 83 333) cut within 1E-4 is 13 pieces and a polygon of area within 0.01 of 5 001.00000002, where one chord would leave 5 000. An arc that the tolerance would cut into more than 1 048 576 pieces is refused. The result is a polygon, which merges corners closer together than the point tolerance (1E-3 by default), so a tolerance whose chords would be shorter than that is not kept: an arc of radius 1 sweeping 1 radian within 1E-7 asks for 1 119 pieces and keeps 559, straying 3.99E-7 from the arc, where the old cut stopped at 4 096 a turn, 652 pieces, strayed 2.94E-7. Merged chords of up to twice the point tolerance can stray up to (2E-3)² / 8 r from an arc of radius r, 5E-7 on a radius of 1, further than a coarser cut that kept its corners. The writers (ObjWriter, Wkt, DxfWriter) keep every chord.
A loop so small that the merge would leave it fewer than three corners keeps every corner of its chords instead: the square 0.0005 by 0.0005 flattens to its four corners, and with its sides bowed by a bulge of 0.2 to the corners of their chords, where both were refused as having fewer than three corners.
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is negative or not a number, or needs more than 1 048 576 pieces for one arc.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2)
member.summary: Gets the loop under a transformation.
member.returns: The transformed loop.
member.remarks:
Mirroring turns every arc the other way, so the bulges change sign, and the mirrored vertices trace the opposite winding, so a loop that ran counter-clockwise comes back clockwise. A transformation that skews the axes or scales them differently makes an arc part of an ellipse, and is refused where an edge would land further than the global point tolerance off it, as reads it.
Each edge is carried on its own and the loop kept edge for edge, every arc and side however small, as keeps it; a loop scaled down keeps the sides that come out shorter than the global tolerance too.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.
Thrown when the transformation would skew or stretch an arc into part of an ellipse it would land visibly off.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.BuildIndex
member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the edges of this loop, arcs and all, for asking it many questions.

remarks.para: An index is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. Building it costs a sort of the edges, so it pays for itself over repeated queries and never on the first one; below a few dozen edges the plain walk wins outright. Every shape here is immutable, so a tree stays valid for as long as the shape exists — build it once, keep it, throw it away with the shape.
It is Build and not Get because it does work. Calling it inside a loop is slower than not having it at all, which is exactly the mistake the name is there to prevent.

member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.SignedDistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Calculates the distance from this loop to a point, negative for a point within it.
member.returns: The distance out to the nearest edge, measured exactly on the arcs, negative when the point lies inside the loop and nought when the global point tolerance calls it on its outline.
member.remarks: The magnitude is the distance to the outline, whichever side of it the point is on, and the sign says which side: negative inside, nought on it, positive outside. reads this loop as filled and so answers nothing at all for a point inside, which is the one place the two part company.

member.summary: Gets the point of the loop nearest a point.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.GetClosestPointOnBoundary(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the point of the loop nearest a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.
A straight side offers its nearest point as the side it is however short, as the distance measures it, where a segment no longer than the tolerance on its own is read as its start: at a hundredth, the loop (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the closest point is (10, 0.003), 0.03 away, where it was (10, 0), 0.0301496 away.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment leaving the outline of this loop and landing on a point.
member.remarks: It starts where lands, even for a point inside, so inside it is as long as the depth to the outline; reads the loop as filled and answers nought there. Outside, the two agree, but for a point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc, carried to the arc's start; beside a straight side they agree however short the side.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc2.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment leaving the outline of this loop and landing on a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.
A straight side is joined as the side it is however short, as the distance measures it, where a segment no longer than the tolerance on its own is read as its start: at a hundredth, the loop (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 0.006), (0, 10) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the line runs from (10, 0.003), 0.03 long, where it ran from (10, 0), 0.0301496 long.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc3
member.summary: Whether a curved loop touches another shape.
A closed loop in space whose pieces may be arcs, lying flat in a plane of its own.

remarks.para: Coplanarity is enforced at construction, exactly as enforces it. A loop that is not flat encloses nothing, has no area and no inside, so it is not this type; a bar bent out of one plane belongs in , whose ends may meet without the loop being flat.

That one rule is what makes everything else exact. Area, centroid, what is inside, offsetting and the booleans are all worked out by laying the loop out in its own plane as a , answering there, and lifting the answer back. Nothing is approximated and none of the arc machinery is written twice.
A closed stirrup with a bending radius is this type: build the loop from the points it turns at and call .

member.summary: How far a curved loop is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a curved loop crosses another shape.
What a curved loop in space can answer by working in its own plane: shaping it, cutting it, and combining it with another shape lying in that same plane.

remarks.para: A enforces coplanarity, which is what makes all of this exact rather than approximate: the loop is laid out as a in its own frame, the whole of the plane library answers, and the answer is lifted back. That is already how its area, its centroid, what is inside it, its offsets and its rounding are worked out.

A second shape has to lie in the loop's plane, and is refused when it does not. Projecting it in would be convenient and quietly wrong — two stirrups a hundred apart would report as overlapping — and sampling is neither exact nor honest. Refusing is the reading the rest of the library already takes: the loop refuses a non-planar set of vertices when it is built, PlanarMap.TryToArc2 returns false for an arc that is not in the frame, and an arc in space refuses to be measured where there is no closed form. This is the same answer to the same kind of question.

member.summary: The point of a curved loop nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.

remarks.para: Everything but the nearest point to a point is worked out in the loop's own plane: the probe is laid out there, the plane library answers, and the answer is lifted back, so it is exact.

A point needs no coplanarity and every other shape does. That is not a compromise: a point off the plane stands at the same height above every point of the boundary, so the nearest place to it is the nearest place to its shadow. Two shapes in different planes have no such shortcut, so they are refused, as they are for the booleans -- SharesPlaneWith asks beforehand.

GetClosestEdge takes a primitive probe only -- a point, a segment, an arc, a circle or an edge. The nearest edge of one many-edged shape to another is a pair of edges, which is a different question and not this one.

member.summary: A curved loop asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A curved loop asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A curved loop asked whether it touches an infinite line and where they cross.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc3.ProjectToPolygonArc2(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3)
member.summary: Lays the loop out in a given frame.
member.param: The frame; hold on to it, because putting an answer back needs the same one.
member.remarks: The loop in the plane is built as a is, so a side shorter than the global point tolerance goes, though a loop built within a finer tolerance keeps it: the loop (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0.0006, 0), (0, 10, 0), built within a billionth, has four sides and is laid out as the triangle without its side 0.0006 long. What the loop says about a point or a shape in its plane, as , , and the shortest lines to shapes in its plane do, is worked out on every side it has, and so are its area, its centroid, the check for crossings, its reverse, its fillets, chamfers and offsets.

member.summary: Determines whether no two edges of the loop cross, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: Every edge is checked as it is, however short, as the loop laid out in its plane checks it: at a millionth, the loop (10, 0, 0), (10, 10, 0), (0, 10, 0), (0.0004, 0, 0), (0, 0.0004, 0) crosses itself near (0.0004, 0.0004, 0), where it was laid out within the global tolerance of a thousandth and lost the corner the crossing comes back round by. Within a tolerance coarser than an edge, the edges either side of it meet across it, so the rectangle 100 by 50 filleted at 0.0005 at a millionth is simple within a millionth and not within a thousandth, as the same loop in the plane is; laid out within the global tolerance, it lost its arcs and read simple at any tolerance.

member.summary: Says where a point sits relative to the loop, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A point off the plane of the loop is outside it, whatever it is over: a flat loop encloses a region of its own plane and nothing above or below it.
Every side is read as it is, however short, as reads it, so the two agree on what is on the outline: at a tolerance of a ten-thousandth, the loop (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0.0006, 0), (0, 10, 0), built within a billionth, has (10.00005, 0.0003, 0) on its side 0.0006 long, and (9.9998, 0.0003, 0) inside it, 0.0002 in from that side.

member.summary: Moves the outline of the loop sideways in its own plane, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The loop is moved as it is, a side shorter than the global tolerance and all, and what comes of it is kept edge for edge, as the loop laid out in its plane keeps it: at a millionth, the square 10 by 10 with its corner (0, 0, 0) cut off by a side 0.00057 long, grown by 0.1, keeps that side, 0.0834 long now, where it was laid out within the global tolerance of a thousandth and the corner came out square.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc3.Flatten
member.summary: Gets the loop with its arcs thrown away, leaving the chords.
member.remarks: Each arc becomes the straight side between its ends, so the polygon has the loop's corners and no others, where cuts each arc into pieces; follows the arcs to an accuracy asked for. Every corner is kept, however short a side: at a millionth, the rectangle 100 by 50 standing in the plane x = 20 and filleted at 0.0005 flattens to its eight corners, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back four. The polygon is still checked flat and enclosing an area within the global tolerance, as the constructor of checks it: the half disc of radius 1 built at a millionth with its diameter bent to (1, 0.000002, 0), whose three corners enclose a sliver of 0.000002 square units, is refused as the polygon of those corners is, where it flattened to the sliver.
member.exception: Thrown when the corners do not lie flat or enclose no area within the global tolerance.

member.summary: Breaks the loop into faces as the options say, its grid standing as the placement says, within a tolerance: triangles, the cells of a grid, strips or convex pieces, each a simple polygon with no hole, counter-clockwise about the normal, meeting its neighbours edge to edge.
member.param: Which way the grid or the strips run in the plane, and where a cell starts.

member.returns: The mesh; one with no faces when there is no area.

member.summary: Cuts the loop at a point on it, within a tolerance.
member.param: The point to cut at; it has to be on the loop.
The open chains the loop came apart into.
member.returns: true when the cut was made; otherwise, false.
member.remarks:
The loop is cut where its distance to the point is measured to, so a point near the centre of a bend, which is on it, cuts the bend where it is nearest the point: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the loop (0.01, -0.01, 0), (0.001, 0, 0), (-0.001, 0, 0), (-0.01, -0.01, 0) with a bulge of 1 on its second edge about Z is opened at (0, 0.001, 0) when cut by (0, 0.0007, 0).
A point on the loop only beside a straight side no longer than the tolerance, further than the tolerance from both its corners, cuts nothing and is refused, the loop handed back opened at its start: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the loop (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0.0006, 0), (0, 10, 0), built within a ten-thousandth, holds (10.00098, 0.0003, 0), 0.00098 from it, and is not cut there.

member.summary: Gets the point of the outline nearest another point.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygonArc3.GetClosestPointOnBoundary(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the point of the outline nearest another point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A point whose foot in the plane falls within the tolerance of the centre of a bend is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and that bend offers its start, as does; the start is one candidate among the edges' points, and another edge can still be nearer. The distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the foot's offset from the centre.
A straight side offers its nearest point as the side it is however short, as the distance measures it, where an edge on its own no longer than the tolerance is read as its start: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the loop (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0.0006, 0), (0, 10, 0), built within a ten-thousandth, is 0.00098 from (10.00098, 0.0001, 0), and the closest point is (10, 0.0001, 0), 0.00098 away, where it was (10, 0, 0), 0.000985 away.

member.param: The point; it does not have to lie in the loop's plane.
member.returns: The line leaving the boundary and landing on the point.
member.remarks: A point off the plane stands at the same height above every point of the boundary, so the nearest place to it is the nearest place to its shadow. That makes this exact without any coplanarity. The line leaves the point gives, so near the centre of a bend it can be longer than , by at most twice the foot's offset from the centre, as says; beside a straight side it is as long as the distance however short the side.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline2
member.summary: Whether a polyline touches another shape.

Represents a 2D polyline: an open chain of connected line segments.
A polyline is always a path, never a region. Geometry that closes back on itself is a , which is where area, containment and winding live; converts a chain whose shape is meant to enclose something.
How far a polyline is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a polyline crosses another shape.
The point of a polyline nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A polyline asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.summary: Initializes a chain from a collection of vertices, a vertex going only where it lands within a tolerance of the one kept before it.
member.remarks: For the copies, whose vertices stand apart already, and for a chain flattened: at a tolerance of nought only a vertex on the very same point as the one before it goes, so a leg shorter than the global tolerance stays.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline2.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2[],System.Int32)
member.summary: Initializes a polyline from vertices that have already been filtered and validated.
member.param: Source array, already free of consecutive duplicates.
Number of leading entries to copy.
member.remarks:
Clone and use this instead of the public constructor. The public one re-filters vertices against Tolerance.Global, so a clone taken after that global was widened could silently come back with fewer vertices than the original, or fail validation outright. Splitting has the same need for a different reason: it receives an explicit tolerance from its caller and must not have its results re-filtered against an unrelated global one.
What this skips is the tolerance dependent work: filtering duplicates. The vertex count is still checked, because it costs nothing, reads no global state, and is what lets EdgeCount subtract one without guarding the result.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline2.ToPolygon
member.summary: Converts this polyline into a solid 2D GeoPolygon2. The chain is closed by connecting the last vertex back to the first.
member.returns: A new GeoPolygon2 instance.
member.remarks: The polygon has the chain's vertices, however short a leg; a last vertex on the first, or off it by no more than the rounding of its coordinates, 1E-12 of the largest of them and of one at the least, is the chain written closed, and goes. At a millionth, the chain round the triangle (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 10) with every corner cut by 0.0003 is the polygon of its six corners, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back three. The chain round the square 10 across from (100, 100) ending 1E-12 off its start is that square, and ending 0.0001 off, a polygon of five corners.
