member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline2.BuildIndex
member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the edges of this chain, for asking it many questions.

remarks.para: An index is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. Building it costs a sort of the edges, so it pays for itself over repeated queries and never on the first one; below a few dozen edges the plain walk wins outright. Every shape here is immutable, so a tree stays valid for as long as the shape exists — build it once, keep it, throw it away with the shape.
It is Build and not Get because it does work. Calling it inside a loop is slower than not having it at all, which is exactly the mistake the name is there to prevent.

member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3
member.summary: Whether a polyline touches another shape.

Represents an open polygonal chain of 3D points.
A polyline is always an open chain: it never joins its last vertex back to its first, and it encloses nothing. Geometry meant to enclose an area is a , and converts between them. That is why a polyline offers IsPointOn but no Contains: a curve has no interior for a point to be inside of.
The vertices need not be coplanar. A polyline may wander freely through space, which is what separates it from a polygon and is why it carries no normal and no area.
How far a polyline is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a polyline crosses another shape.
The point of a polyline nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A polyline asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A polyline asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A polyline asked about an infinite line: whether they touch, how far apart they are, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3.ToPolygon
member.summary: Gets the polygon that closes this chain, joining its last vertex back to its first.
member.exception: Thrown when the chain has fewer than three distinct vertices or is not planar, since a polygon requires both.
Thrown when the chain has a coordinate that is not a finite number.
member.remarks: The polygon has the chain's vertices, however short a leg; a last vertex on the first, or off it by no more than the rounding of its coordinates, 1E-12 of the largest of them and of one at the least, is the chain written closed, and goes. At a millionth, the chain round the triangle (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0, 10) with every corner cut by 0.0003 is the polygon of its six corners, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back three. The chain round the square 10 across from (100, 100, 0) ending 1E-12 off its start is that square, and ending 0.0001 off, a polygon of five corners. The polygon is still checked flat and enclosing an area within the global tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3)
member.summary: Applies a transformation to every vertex.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.
member.remarks: The chain is transformed leg for leg, however short a leg: at a millionth, the chain (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0, 10) with its corner cut by 0.0003 turns at both ends of the cut turned and moved, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back turning once. Only a vertex the transformation lands on the very same point as the one before it goes, so no leg is left with no length.

member.summary: Tries to get the plane every vertex lies on, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3.TryGetPlane(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Tries to get the plane every vertex lies on, within a tolerance.
member.param: The carrier plane when the method returns true.
The tolerance; the planar threshold decides how flat is flat enough.
member.returns: false when the vertices are collinear or do not share a plane.

remarks.para: Collinear vertices are refused rather than given an arbitrary plane through them: a straight chain lies on infinitely many planes and there is no ground for preferring one.

The plane is first read from the area the chain encloses when closed from its end back to its start, whose normal turns the way the chain runs. A flat chain enclosing no area, a Z or a symmetric zigzag, has its plane all the same: it is then laid through the first vertex, the vertex farthest from it and the vertex farthest from the line between those two, and its normal turns whichever way those three do. The Z through (0, 0, 2), (10, 0, 2), (0, 10, 2), (10, 10, 2) lies in z = 2.

member.remarks: The triangle is read as a filled surface, as its distance reads it, and a tie goes to the first edge of this chain. A shape coming end-on at the other and stopping within the point tolerance of it is read as crossing it, so the line can be of no length where the distance is the gap: the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, 9), over the square 100 by 100 in the floor, is joined by a segment of no length at (5, 5, 0.0004), and is 0.0004 from it by its distance.

Over the square 100 by 100 on the XY plane with a corner at the origin, the chain (50, 50, 30), (50, 50, 80), (150, 50, 80) is joined from (50, 50, 30) straight down, 30 long, as measures it. A shape coming end-on at the other and stopping within the point tolerance of it is read as crossing it, so the line can be of no length where the distance is the gap: the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, 9), over the square 100 by 100 in the floor, is joined by a segment of no length at (5, 5, 0.0004), and is 0.0004 from it by its distance.
member.exception: Thrown when the polygon is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolyline3.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this chain to a plane, using the default tolerance.
member.remarks: A chain that crosses or touches the plane meets it in a segment of no length at the first point of contact, walking its edges in order; one clear of it is joined from its nearest vertex, the first where several are as near. The chain (0, 0, 10), (50, 0, 30), (100, 0, -10) meets the XY plane at (87.5, 0, 0); the chain (0, 0, 10), (50, 0, 30) is joined from (0, 0, 10) to the origin, 10 long, as measures it. The segment is never snapped: a shape a hair off the plane is joined by a segment that short, though the distance, read within the point tolerance, is nought.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2
member.summary: Whether a curved chain touches another shape.

An open chain whose pieces may be arcs: vertices with a bulge against each of them, which is exactly how AutoCAD holds a polyline.
It is the arc-carrying counterpart of . The straight one is not going anywhere: most chains have no arcs at all, and everything the library does with regions reads straight edges, so a chain that carries arcs says so in its type. crosses from here to there, and that crossing is where exactness ends — it is the only place arcs become chords, and it asks for the tolerance that decides how close the chords come.
How far a curved chain is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a curved chain crosses another shape.
The point of a curved chain nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A curved chain asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.summary: Approximates the chain as a straight one, cutting each arc finely enough that it strays no further than the automatic share of its radius.
member.returns: The straight chain, which every operation over regions can read.
member.remarks: This is where exactness ends. A chain with no arcs comes across whole; one with arcs comes across as chords, as close as the tolerance says and no closer.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2.Flatten(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the chain as a straight one, cutting each arc so that it strays no further than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between a piece and the arc it replaces, in drawing units. Zero picks the automatic share of each radius.
member.returns: The straight chain.
member.remarks:
The promise holds however fine the tolerance and however shallow the arc: an arc of bulge 0.0003 on a chord of 100 (radius 83 333, 0.015 deep) cut within 1E-4 is 13 pieces, not the one chord. An arc that the tolerance would cut into more than 1 048 576 pieces is refused. The result is a chain, which merges corners closer together than the point tolerance (1E-3 by default), so a tolerance whose chords would be shorter than that is not kept: an arc of radius 1 sweeping 1 radian within 1E-7 asks for 1 119 pieces and keeps 559, straying 3.99E-7 from the arc, where the old cut stopped at 4 096 a turn, 652 pieces, strayed 2.94E-7. Merged chords of up to twice the point tolerance can stray up to (2E-3)² / 8 r from an arc of radius r, 5E-7 on a radius of 1, further than a coarser cut that kept its corners. The writers (ObjWriter, Wkt, DxfWriter) keep every chord.
A chain so small that the merge would leave it one corner keeps every corner of its chords instead: the chain (0, 0), (0.0005, 0), (0.0005, 0.0005) with its second leg bowed by a bulge of 0.4 flattens to the corners of the chords of that leg, where it was refused as having fewer than two corners.
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is negative or not a number, or needs more than 1 048 576 pieces for one arc.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2.BuildIndex
member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the edges of this chain, arcs and all, for asking it many questions.

remarks.para: An index is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. Building it costs a sort of the edges, so it pays for itself over repeated queries and never on the first one; below a few dozen edges the plain walk wins outright. Every shape here is immutable, so a tree stays valid for as long as the shape exists — build it once, keep it, throw it away with the shape.
It is Build and not Get because it does work. Calling it inside a loop is slower than not having it at all, which is exactly the mistake the name is there to prevent.

member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

member.summary: Gets the point of the chain nearest a point.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2.GetClosestPointOnBoundary(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the point of the chain nearest a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.
A straight edge offers its nearest point as the edge it is however short, as the distance measures it, where on its own one no longer than the tolerance is read as its start: at a hundredth, the hairpin from (0, 0) to (10, 0), on to (10, 0.006) and back to (0, 0.006) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the closest point is (10, 0.003), 0.03 away, where it was (10, 0), 0.0301496 away.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment leaving this chain and landing on a point.
member.remarks: It starts where lands, on the arcs themselves, and is exactly as long as but for a point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc, which is carried to the arc's start; beside a straight edge it is as long however short the edge.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc2.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment leaving this chain and landing on a point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A point within the tolerance of the centre of an arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and is carried to the arc's start; the distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the point's offset from the centre. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the point (0, -0.0009) and the arc of radius 50 about the origin from (-50, 0) to (50, 0) through (0, -50): the closest point is (-50, 0), 50.00000001 away, where the distance is 49.9991.
A straight edge is joined as the edge it is however short, as the distance measures it, where on its own one no longer than the tolerance is read as its start: at a hundredth, the hairpin from (0, 0) to (10, 0), on to (10, 0.006) and back to (0, 0.006) is 0.03 from (10.03, 0.003), and the line runs from (10, 0.003), 0.03 long, where it ran from (10, 0), 0.0301496 long.

remarks.para: The twin of , laid out the way a drawing holds one: vertices, with the bulge of the edge leaving each, and now the plane that bulge is read in as well. A chain like this is what a reinforcing bar is: straight runs with a tangent arc at every bend, and the bends need not all lie in one plane.

Coplanarity is not required, exactly as requires none. A chain that does happen to be flat says so through , and a closed loop of arcs that is flat belongs in instead, which enforces it and can therefore answer about area and about what is inside.

What is exact here is what can be worked out on the curve itself: its length, walking along it, the point of it nearest another point, its box, moving it, turning it round, and flattening it. Measuring it against another shape in space is not, because the distance from an arc to anything but a point has no closed form once the two are not in one plane. For that, sample it with , which puts the accuracy in the call.

member.summary: Gets the plane the whole chain lies in, when it lies in one, within a tolerance.
member.param: The plane, when there is one.
The tolerance; the planar threshold decides how flat is flat enough.
member.returns: true if one plane holds every vertex and every arc; otherwise, false.

remarks.para: The vertices alone are not enough to settle it: two straight runs and the bends between them can all share a plane while an arc bulges out of it, so every arc is asked how far it stands off the plane, and the planar tolerance decides. The angle of its own plane decides nothing: a half circle 1 000 across turned 0.99 degrees out stands 8.64 off, and a bend that barely bows lies in the plane however it is turned.

The plane is the one the vertices lie in (see ). Where the vertices all lie on one line, as the two ends of a half circle do, the first arc's own plane is taken, and holds the chain when the vertices lie in it and every other arc turns in it too.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3.Flatten
member.summary: Gets the chain with its arcs thrown away, leaving the chords.
member.remarks: This is the one operation here that loses something, and it loses it in the obvious way: each arc becomes the straight line between its ends. keeps the shape to whatever accuracy is asked for instead, as cuts each arc into pieces. Every vertex is kept, however short a leg: at a millionth, the chain (0, 0, 0), (10, 0, 0), (10, 0, 10) filleted at 0.0005 flattens turning at both ends of its arc, 0.0007 apart, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back turning once.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3.ToPolyline3(System.Double)
member.summary: Gets the chain as a straight one following its arcs to a given accuracy.
member.param: How far the straight pieces may fall inside an arc.
member.returns: A straight chain no point of which stands further than the chord tolerance from this one.
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is not a positive number, or needs more than 1 048 576 pieces for one arc.
member.remarks: This is how to measure a curved chain against anything but a point: the distance from an arc in space to a segment, to another arc or to a body has no closed form, so the library does not pretend to one. Sampling here puts the accuracy in the call, where it can be seen. The promise holds however fine the tolerance and however large the radius: a bend of radius 50 000 turning a quarter within 1E-4 is 12 419 pieces. The chain merges points closer together than the point tolerance, so chords shorter than that are not kept, as for ; the writers keep every chord.

member.remarks: This is how a reinforcing bar is built: the points it turns at, and one bending radius. Each corner is rounded in the plane of its own two legs, so the bends need not share a plane, and a corner with too little edge to give, or none to turn, is left as it was.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3.TrySplitBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3[]@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts the chain at a point on it, within a tolerance.
member.param: The point to cut at; it has to be on the chain.
The pieces, in order along the chain, when the cut was made.
member.returns: true when the chain came apart; otherwise, false, and it is handed back whole.
member.remarks:
The chain is cut where its distance to the point is measured to, so a point near the centre of a bend, which is on it, cuts the bend where it is nearest the point: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the chain (0.01, 0, 0), (0.001, 0, 0), (-0.001, 0, 0), (-0.01, 0, 0) with a bulge of 1 on its middle edge about Z comes apart at (0, 0.001, 0) when cut by (0, 0.0007, 0).
A point on the chain only beside a straight edge no longer than the tolerance, further than the tolerance from both its ends, cuts nothing and is refused, the chain handed back whole: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the hairpin built of the straight edges from (0, 0, 0) to (10, 0, 0), on to (10, 0.0006, 0) and back to (0, 0.0006, 0) holds (10.00098, 0.0003, 0), 0.00098 from it, and is not cut there.

member.summary: Gets the distance from the chain to a point.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolylineArc3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the distance from the chain to a point, within a tolerance.
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.
member.remarks: The tolerance changes nothing in the distance: a point near the centre of a bend's arc is not carried to the bend's start, as measures a bend. At a tolerance of a thousandth, the chain from (0.01, 0, 0) to (0.001, 0, 0), round the half circle of radius 0.001 about the origin through (0, 0.001, 0) to (-0.001, 0, 0), and on to (-0.01, 0, 0), is 0.0003 from (0, 0.0007, 0), and the point is on it; the projection keeps carrying it to the bend's start, 0.00122 away. A straight edge shorter than the tolerance is the edge it is, where an edge on its own is read as its start: the chain built of the straight edges from (0, 0, 0) to (10, 0, 0) and on to (10, 0.0006, 0) is 0.0009 from (10.0009, 0.0006, 0), and the point is on it, where the start of that last edge is 0.00108 away.

member.summary: Gets the point of the chain nearest another point, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
Measured on the arcs, so a point sitting over the middle of a bulge is answered with a point on the bulge and not with one on the chord across it.
A point whose foot in the plane of a bend falls within the tolerance of the centre of its arc is read as at the centre, which has no direction, and that bend offers its start, as does; the start is one candidate among the edges' points, and another edge can still be nearer. The distance to the point is the exact one, so the line can be longer than it, by at most twice the foot's offset from the centre.
A straight edge offers its nearest point as the edge it is however short, as the distance measures it, where on its own one no longer than the tolerance is read as its start: at a tolerance of a thousandth, the chain built of the straight edges from (0, 0, 0) to (10, 0, 0) and on to (10, 0.0006, 0) is 0.0009 from (10.0009, 0.0006, 0), and the closest point is (10, 0.0006, 0), 0.0009 away, where it was (10, 0, 0), 0.00108 away.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay2
member.summary: Whether a ray touches another shape.
member.remarks: A closed shape is read as filled: a ray reaching its material collides with it, and so does one starting inside it. The ray from (50, 50) along X starts inside the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin and collides with it; the ray from (-50, 150) along X passes above it and does not.
member.summary: Represents a ray in the plane: a half-line starting at an origin and running to infinity in one direction, the counterpart of in space.
member.remarks: The ray from (-50, 50) along X runs into the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin at (0, 50) and leaves it at (100, 50); turned round, it runs away from the square and meets nothing.
member.summary: How far a ray is from another shape.
member.remarks: A closed shape is read as filled, as reads it: a ray starting inside a polygon is nought from it. The ray from (-50, 150) along X passes 50 above the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin; turned round to run along -X from (150, 150), it is 50 from it too.
member.summary: Where a ray crosses another shape.
The point of a ray nearest a point, and the shortest segment joining a ray to another shape.
member.remarks: Both ends of a shortest segment sit on a boundary, and it leaves this ray. A ray runs on for ever, so one starting inside a closed shape crosses its outline on the way out, and the segment is the point where it does: the ray from (50, 50) along X inside the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin gets the segment of no length at (100, 50).
member.summary: A ray asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay2.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector2,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Initializes a ray from a direction that is already normalized.
member.remarks: Normalizing a vector that is already of unit length is not the identity in floating point: the computed length comes back a bit either side of one, and dividing by it shifts the last digits. Operations that only move a ray around must not pay that, or a copy would come back unequal to its original and reversing twice would drift. This constructor is how they skip it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3
member.summary: Whether a ray touches another shape.
Represents a 3D ray: a half-line starting at an origin and running to infinity in one direction.
How far a ray is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a ray crosses another shape.
The point of a ray nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A ray asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A ray asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A ray asked about an infinite line: whether they touch, how far apart they are, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Initializes a ray from a direction that is already normalized.
member.remarks: Normalizing a vector that is already of unit length is not the identity in floating point: the computed length comes back a bit either side of one, and dividing by it shifts the last digits. Operations that only move a ray around must not pay that, or a copy would come back unequal to its original and reversing twice would drift. This constructor is how they skip it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace3)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this ray to a face, using the default tolerance.
member.remarks: The face is read by its material: a ray running into it meets it in a segment of no length at the crossing, and one through a hole is joined to the rim. Over the square 100 by 100 in the floor with a corner at the origin and a hole 40 by 40 in its middle, the ray from (45, 50, 10) pointing straight down is joined from (45, 50, 0) to the rim at (30, 50, 0), 15 long, as measures it; from (20, 20, 10) it meets the material at (20, 20, 0). A shape coming end-on at the other and stopping within the point tolerance of it is read as crossing it, so the line can be of no length where the distance is the gap: the segment from (5, 5, 0.0004) to (5, 5, 9), over the square 100 by 100 in the floor, is joined by a segment of no length at (5, 5, 0.0004), and is 0.0004 from it by its distance.
member.exception: Thrown when the face is null.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this ray to a plane, using the default tolerance.
member.remarks: A ray running into the plane meets it in a segment of no length where it passes through, or at its origin where that lies on it; one running along it or away from it is joined from its origin. The ray from (0, 0, 10) pointing straight down meets the floor plane at the origin; pointing straight up, or along X, it is joined from (0, 0, 10) straight down, 10 long, as measures it. The segment is never snapped: a ray a hair off the plane and running along it is joined by a segment that short, though the distance, read within the tolerance, is nought.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3.GetShortestLineTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRay3)
member.summary: Gets the shortest segment joining this ray to another one, using the default tolerance.
member.remarks: The two are joined by the common perpendicular of their lines where both rays reach it, and otherwise from an origin to the nearest point of the other ray. The ray from the origin along X and the ray from (50, 30, 40) along Y are joined from (50, 0, 0) to (50, 30, 40), 50 long, as measures it; the ray from (50, -50, 0) along Y crosses the first and the segment has no length at (50, 0, 0). The segment is never snapped: rays passing a hair apart are joined by a segment that short, and are that far apart by the distance too.

member.summary: Determines whether another rectangle covers the same region, within a tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRectangle2.SignedDistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Calculates the distance from this rectangle to a point, negative for a point within it.
member.returns: The distance out to the nearest side, measured exactly, negative when the point lies inside the rectangle and nought when the global point tolerance calls it on a side.
member.remarks: The magnitude is the distance to the outline, whichever side of it the point is on, and the sign says which side: negative inside, nought on it, positive outside. reads this rectangle as filled and so answers nothing at all for a point inside, which is the one place the two part company.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRectangle2.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoFace2)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance from this rectangle to the material of a face: the same answer as .
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly.

member.summary: Finds the shortest line segment connecting a point on the boundary of this rectangle to a point on a line segment using default tolerance.
member.remarks: Both ends of the returned segment sit on a boundary, so a shape lying entirely inside another still reports the gap out to its outline rather than zero. takes the opposite view and treats a closed shape as a filled region, returning zero for that same pair.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3
member.summary: Whether a solid touches another shape.

Represents a 3D solid body as the set of faces bounding it, with optional openings carved out.
The faces are expected to be wound so their normals point out of the body, and to close it without gaps. Neither is enforced, because checking costs a full pass over every edge and most solids come from a modeller that already guarantees it; is there for the ones that do not. What the guarantees buy is and : both read the body as a filled region and neither means anything for a shell with a hole in it.
An opening is a whole solid subtracted from this one — a duct through a slab, a recess in a footing. It is not the same thing as a hole in a , which is flat and belongs to a single face.
How far a solid is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a solid crosses another shape.
The point of a solid nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A solid asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A solid asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A solid asked about an infinite line: whether they touch, how far apart they are, where the line crosses its surface and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TryClose(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3@,GeometryHelper.SolidClosingOptions,GeometryHelper.SolidClosing3@)
member.summary: Closes this body where it is open, with the least change that does it, and says what was changed; see .
member.param: The body closed: this body itself where it was valid already as the closing reads it (see the remarks); null when the method returns false.
How far apart corners may stand and still be made one, and which holes may be filled.
Each change made, in the order it was made, or why the body could not be closed and where.
member.returns: true when the body comes out valid within the options' tolerance, as the booleans read what they make: closed, wound alike and outwards, and enclosing a volume; otherwise false.
member.exception: Thrown when the options are null.

remarks.para: Each step is taken only where the ones before it did not close the body. Faces with no area, a face given twice, the two of a sheet lying back to back inside the body, and a face lying back to back on another with every edge of it open are dropped, and faces turned over so that each shell is wound alike and each closed shell inside no other outwards, a shell inside another keeping its winding against it, a block or a cavity. An open edge past a fin stops the closing. Corners standing apart across a gap are made one within the point tolerance, then twice it, four times, and so on up to , and where that closes nothing, the same again with corners standing off an edge left open put on it; no reach is taken that runs a ring out to a corner and straight back, lays a face back to back with another, or lays one through another, as across a crack round a blade standing in it. What is left open is followed round into loops, and filled where the options allow: a flat hole by one face on the body's own corners, the loops in its plane inside it the face's holes, and one a little out of flat by the triangles of least area across it on its own corners. No fill is taken that lies back to back with a face of the body or crosses one, or a fill taken before it, an edge of either through the inside of the other, and the way a shell faces is read again once it is closed. What comes of it is checked: valid within the tolerance, and the volume the welds moved no more than the reach times the area they touched.

Nothing is made up. Where closing the body is not certain, as where an open edge runs past a fin, a gap is wider than the options allow or a hole can be filled more than one way, the method returns false and the report says why and where. The body is not changed: its openings are carried over as they are, and a shell of it closed already is left as it was.

The closing reads the body as the booleans read what they make, and as
closes the cuts it would skip: within the options' tolerance as it is given, the edges paired by overlap along a line only, not as and read it, which pair two copies of an edge by their ends as well and match the edges within the rounding of the coordinates below it. So a body Validate calls valid can still be closed here, or refused: a slab 100 by 100 and 0.0012 thick whose side at one end is slid up 0.0002, valid to Validate, is refused within a thousandth, the gap too wide, and one 0.0014 thick slid by 0.0005 is welded closed, its volume moved from 14 to 11.67 cubic millimetres.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.CollidesWith(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3)
member.summary: Determines whether this solid touches or overlaps a line segment.
member.remarks: Whether a point is in the body is asked to within rounding, a billionth of a millimetre (1E-9, not nought), so that rounding in a body turned about in space cannot lose a crossing: a point within 1E-9 outside the body reads as in it, and a point 5E-10 outside a box is nought away from it. Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TurnOutwards
member.summary: Gets this solid wound outwards, its openings too: every face turned over where the whole surface faces into the body.
member.returns: This solid itself where nothing had to be turned, so that the same body back says it was the right way out.
member.remarks: Which way a closed surface is wound is the sign of the volume it encloses: positive where its faces face out of it. A modeller can hand a body over the other way round, and a mirror turns every face over. The measures read a body either way the same, but the booleans, the cuts and where two bodies lie against each other read the winding, and turn their bodies so first. The faces of a surface that does not close are turned by the same sign, which there says little. The answer is kept with the body, so asking again costs nothing.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GrossSurfaceArea
member.summary: Gets the total area of the bounding faces, the openings not cut out.
member.remarks: Each face's area as its outline gives it: the area of the material where the body has no openings, and the quick way to it that takes then. Where it has openings, the faces run straight across them and this is no area of anything; only the material is.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GrossVolume
member.summary: Gets the volume the bounding faces enclose, the openings not cut out.
member.remarks:
This is the divergence theorem: the volume of a closed body equals a sum over its surface, and for a flat-faced body that sum is one signed tetrahedron per triangle, taken back to the world origin. Where the origin sits makes no difference to the total as long as the surface closes — the parts outside the body cancel — which is why no reference point has to be chosen. The result is reported unsigned so that faces wound inwards give the same answer as faces wound outwards; a shell that does not close gives a number with no meaning either way.
Each face is taken as the fan of its boundary from its first corner, which is exact for a flat face and the quickest, and the way Tekla Structures reports a part's volume. It is the volume of the material where the body has no openings, and the quick way to it that takes then; where it has openings, it is no volume of anything, the openings not taken out.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GetSignedVolume
member.summary: Gets the signed volume enclosed by the bounding faces, the openings not cut out. It is positive when the face normals point outwards and negative when they point inwards: which way the body is wound, which sets right, and not a volume of anything with openings.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GetReferencePoint
member.summary: Gets a point on the body for the tetrahedra to be measured from.
member.remarks: The sum works out the same wherever the apex is put, because the parts of each tetrahedron reaching outside the body cancel. That is true of the arithmetic, not of the floating point: a body a kilometre from the origin measured against the origin builds tetrahedra of about 1e18 that have to cancel down to a volume of about 100, and around three per cent of the answer is lost in the cancelling. Measuring from a corner of the body instead keeps every tetrahedron the size of the body itself, and there is nothing left to cancel away.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.SumTetrahedra(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3[],GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Sums the signed volumes of the tetrahedra spanning a given apex and each triangle.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GrossCentroid
member.summary: Gets the centroid of the bounding faces, ignoring the openings: the material's where there are none, as gives it.
member.remarks: Each surface triangle is taken with the world origin as the apex of a tetrahedron, exactly as does, and the centroids of those tetrahedra are averaged by signed volume. The parts reaching outside the body carry negative volume and cancel, so the answer does not depend on where the origin is. A body with no volume has no centroid to average, and the centroid of its vertices comes back instead.

member.remarks: This is the other direction from : it turns a triangulated skin back into the flat panels it stands for, which is worth doing to a body read out of a mesh format before anything is measured against its faces one at a time. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.Triangulate(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Breaks every face into triangles, giving the surface of the solid as a triangle mesh, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance deciding what counts as a degenerate triangle.
member.remarks:
Every triangle lies within the material of the face it came from: a concave face is followed rather than spanned, and a hole cut in a face is left open.
The openings are not meshed, and so this is not the boundary of the material when there are any. They are whole bodies subtracted from this one rather than holes in its faces, so a plate with a bolt hole meshes its top face as a whole square. Anything that reads the mesh as where the material ends — clash detection, ray casting, distance — wants , which cuts the openings in first. For a body without openings the two are the same mesh.
A face thinner than the tolerance is a seam at it and has no triangles: a slab 100 by 100 and 0.0008 thick, built within 1E-5, is 12 triangles at 1E-5 but 4 at 0.001, its four sides gone, and a Debug line in says how many faces were left out whole and how much area they had; a face meshed in part is not counted. The mesh is then open edge by edge but closed within the tolerance: the top and the bottom meet along every edge where the sides were, and those 4 triangles leave 8 edges with no triangle on the other side. A mesh closed edge by edge is had at the tolerance the body was built within: the slab's 12 triangles at 1E-5.
A triangle is left out only when it has no width, its corners on a line within a millionth of the point tolerance. Each half of a small face 0.002 by 0.002 has its and its , and reads as a face, where they threw; one thinner than the point tolerance, 100 by 0.0008, has true, its height over its longest side being within it, and keeps its normal all the same.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TriangulateQuietly(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Breaks every face into triangles as does, and counts the faces it left out whole instead of saying so, for the library's own questions, which ask of a body that may be valid at a tolerance wider than one of its faces and have nothing to tell the caller.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TriangulateSurface(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Meshes the surface of the material, with every opening cut in first, within a tolerance.
member.returns: The triangles of the material's boundary: the outer faces with the parts over each opening taken away, and the walls of each opening where they run through the body. Empty when the openings take all of the material.
member.remarks:
This is the mesh to read as where the material ends, as is for a face. For a body without openings it is ; with them, it costs cutting the openings in, so a body asked many questions is better cut once with and the result kept.
The mesh can hold triangles with no normal at the global tolerance, from small faces of the body: take a triangle's normal from , not ; see for which. A face thinner than the tolerance is left out whole, and a Debug line in says so; see . The mesh is then open edge by edge but closed within the tolerance: a slab thinner than the tolerance has its top and bottom meet along every edge where its sides were.
Asked at a point tolerance below the rounding of the coordinates, a quadrillionth of the largest of them, nought among them, the openings are cut within that rounding, as cuts them: at nought, a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space, with a hole 20 by 20 through it, was meshed into triangles holding 29 999.99, its bottom lost, where it holds 58 800.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TryCutOpenings(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3@)
member.summary: Cuts every opening into this body, giving one without openings whose faces are the surface of its material.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TryCutOpenings(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts every opening into this body, giving one without openings whose faces are the surface of its material, within a tolerance.
member.param: The body with its openings cut in, or this body when it has none; null when the method returns false.
member.returns: true when some material is left; false when the openings take all of it, or when the cut cannot be worked out, or will not close, which is logged.

remarks.para: Every question this library asks of a body takes its openings into account already. Cutting them in is for a body that will be asked many questions: the queries that need it do the cutting each time, of the openings near the question, and a caller checking one plate against a hundred bolts is better off cutting the plate once and asking the result — the same bargain as . The body keeps only the cut its measures take, and the rest.

The answer is the body's material, closed as reads it where the body and its openings are: an opening drawn past a face, as a through hole usually is, takes off only what lies in the body. The openings are cut in at once; where that leaves the material open it is welded within the tolerance, or failing that the openings are taken out one at a time by a difference. They are taken out so too where a plane of an opening runs through the body and will not cut it, leaving a piece part in the opening and part out of it, which cut in at once would be kept or dropped whole. Cut in together, each opening keeps or loses a skin the tolerance thin as it would cut in alone: twelve boxes hidden 0.01 inside the faces of a plate 300 by 200 by 12, one 1.7E-7 deeper than the tolerance and another 5.7E-6 nearer the faces, cut within a hundredth, came back valid and holding 9.68 cubic millimetres more than the most its skins can leave, the plane of the deeper box's floor having cut a skin off the whole plate that the nearer kept over and under it; it loses its skins now, as it does measured by . What the differences leave is refused where it is not valid, and each reads a corner as on a plane within the planar tolerance and the rounding of the coordinates, a trillionth of their size, as cutting in at once does: a plate 300 by 200 by 12 with twelve blind holes ending the tolerance under its top, to a few bits, turned and far from the origin, came back wound two ways at its top within a thousandth, and the method returned true; it comes back valid, holding 666 657.36, eleven holes through and one under a skin 0.0010002 thick. At a tolerance at or above the rounding of the coordinates, a welded cut can hold a little more or less than measures, no more than the tolerance times the area of the openings: a plate 300 by 200 by 12 with twelve blind holes ending 0.011 under its top, turned and far from the origin, cut within a hundredth, holds 0.028 cubic millimetres more.

Where walls of two openings, or of an opening and the body, stand apart within the tolerance of one plane and further apart than a trillionth of the size of the coordinates, the openings are cut within a finer tolerance, between the gap of those walls and the most that walls meeting within the tolerance, or a face off flat, stand off one plane, where the body and its openings close within it, and what that gives is taken where it closes within the tolerance asked: the plane of an opening cuts the whole of what it reaches, and a plane of another within the tolerance of it was read as that plane, however far away: an L 100 by 80 by 50, a million out, with two blind openings 27 apart whose walls stood 0.0009 apart across it, cut within a thousandth, held 153 674.08 where it holds 153 673.56, the second opening's wall cut in the plane of the first's, and with the openings the other way round 153 673.30. Walls that meet are made one plane, as before.

Where the point tolerance is below the rounding of the coordinates, a quadrillionth of the largest of them, nought among them, the openings are cut within that rounding, as the queries read them; a planar tolerance below it with a point tolerance that is not cuts as it did. Where cutting them in together leaves the material open they are cut in one at a time, each kept only where it closes, not taken out by a difference, which within the rounding came back closed and wrong, and corners the cut leaves a rounding apart are made one where that closes the material within the tolerance given. Cut at nought, a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space, with a hole 20 by 20 through it, came back as a shell of 7 faces, its bottom lost, and was said to be cut; it comes back closed, holding 58 800. Openings that touch or overlap each other or lie flush with a face are refused more often at nought than they were cut wrong: of 120 plates with a hole flush with each face, 34 are refused. What comes back can be valid at the default tolerance and not at the rounding, for slivers a rounding thin, and at nought can still refuse it where corners stand further apart than the rounding. The measures of a body with openings, , , and , read the material this method gives: at nought that plate measures 58 800, where it measured 60 000, its hole not taken out, and TryGetVolume said that could be trusted.

A body far out, as says, is moved near the origin with its openings, by whole coordinates, cut there, and its material moved back: each corner of the body or of an opening it keeps comes back as it was given, to the bit, and only the corners the cut makes are rounded, once. Where it stood, walls of openings a fraction of the tolerance apart were cut in one plane: the L 100 by 80 by 50 that GetVolume measures a thousand million out came back holding 153 732.16 within a thousandth, 0.52 too much, the far wall of one opening cut in the plane of the other's; it holds 153 731.64 now, to 3E-5.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.IsClosed
member.summary: Checks whether the boundary closes without gaps, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.IsClosed(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether the boundary closes without gaps, within a tolerance.

remarks.para: A closed surface has every stretch of every edge shared by an even number of faces. One face on a stretch is an open rim and three are a fin standing off the surface; two close it, and so do four where two blocks meet along an edge — watertight, and measuring and holding points as they should. Hole rims count as edges like any other, since in a closed body they are shared with the surface lining the cavity behind them.

The edges are matched as matches them, so the two agree on every body but a speck: by overlap along a line within the tolerance, stretch by stretch, so that a long edge beside two short ones, which merging coplanar faces and the booleans both leave behind, is matched stretch by stretch; two copies of an edge whose ends lie within the tolerance of each other are matched however little of them lies along the other, the one no longer than the tolerance kept with the other where its own loop has an edge longer than the tolerance, and left out, as every edge that short is otherwise, where it is a speck's; and a body whose edges pair to a sixty-fourth of the tolerance is settled on a grid, in time linear in its corners. A body with no edge longer than the tolerance, a speck, is not closed here, where Validate, finding no stretch open, calls it closed and not valid, enclosing nothing.

A gap no wider than the point tolerance mostly reads closed and a wider one open: a cube of 100 whose top stands 0.0005 over the tops of its sides is closed within a thousandth, placed anywhere, and one whose top stands 0.0015 over them is open. A gap of a thousandth is so to a few bits either way, 100.001 less 100 being 0.001 000 000 000 004 8, and reads as the rounding has it. Edges matched along one line are matched one after another, so a gap wider than the tolerance is closed where other edges lie in it within the tolerance of either side: that cube with a box of 1 standing against each of its sides half way up the gap reads closed, and valid, though its top stands 0.0015 clear of its sides. So too a short copy of a side of a hole, kept with it, cuts the open side into stretches no longer than the tolerance: a speck in each side of a hole 0.0019 across keeps none of its edges and leaves the hole open, but a sliver face with an edge longer than the tolerance lying across such a side can still hide it. Below the rounding of the coordinates, a quadrillionth of the largest of the whole body's, not of each part, the edges are matched within that rounding, so that at a tolerance of nought a cube turned in space, and the union of two such boxes made within a thousandth, are closed.

The booleans, the weld, the cutting and read the bodies they work on otherwise, the ends of the edges matched first and within the tolerance given, as this did: two corners 0.0015 apart were one where a corner lay between them, and with a speck of a face at each corner of that top half way up the cube read closed, and open with the specks given last. What a boolean makes is taken as closed where the tolerance given, unraised, reads it closed along lines, so that the two differ on a body closed only to the rounding or by twin edges no longer than about the tolerance. cuts into cells only a body closed both ways.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.ClosesByCorners(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether the boundary closes, the ends of the edges matched first, each to the first corner seen within the tolerance of it, as read it before: the reading the booleans, the cutting and the contact take of the bodies they work on to choose their way, the weld to decide what it hands back, and and the material cut for the measures to decide what they trust.
member.remarks: Matched so, two corners a tolerance and a half apart are one where a corner lies between them, and the body is called closed where reads it open; and a body closed only to the rounding of its coordinates, at a tolerance below it, is open here where IsClosed calls it closed. What a boolean makes is taken as closed only where reads it so. Where an edge is not used exactly twice, the edges are matched by overlap along a line, stretch by stretch.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.BuildIndex
member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the surface of this body, for asking it many questions.

remarks.para: An index is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. Building it costs a sort of the triangles, so it pays for itself over repeated queries and never on the first one; below a few dozen triangles the plain walk wins outright. Every shape here is immutable, so a tree stays valid for as long as the shape exists — build it once, keep it, throw it away with the shape.
It is Build and not Get because it does work. Calling it inside a loop is slower than not having it at all, which is exactly the mistake the name is there to prevent.

The index is over triangles and the body is not. GetIntersections on the tree reports one hit per triangle, so a ray landing on the diagonal two triangles share is named twice, while the body names each place once. Ask the body where you want places; ask the tree where you want speed and can keep clear of the edges — which is what Containment3 does by throwing its ray again in another direction when a hit lands near one.

member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

member.summary: Builds a spatial index over the surface of this body, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance the triangulation works to.
member.returns: The hierarchy; it is a snapshot and holds no reference back to this shape.

The prepared body answers as this one does. It is Prepare and not Get because it does the work, as does: calling it in a loop is slower than not calling it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance from this solid to a point. A point inside is at distance zero.
member.returns: Nought only where they truly meet, otherwise the gap, measured exactly. Within a billionth of a millimetre of the outside of a solid it reads nought, so that rounding in a turned body cannot lose a crossing.
member.remarks: Whether a point is in the body is asked to within rounding, a billionth of a millimetre (1E-9, not nought), so that rounding in a body turned about in space cannot lose a crossing: a point within 1E-9 outside the body reads as in it, and a point 5E-10 outside a box is nought away from it. Further out than a million the billionth is 1E-15 of the largest coordinate of the body and the point, past the rounding of numbers that size.

member.summary: Calculates the distance from this solid to a point, negative for a point in the material.
member.remarks: The magnitude is the distance to the surface, whichever side of it the point is on, and the sign says which side: negative inside, nought on it, positive outside. reads this solid as filled and so answers nothing at all for a point inside, which is the one place the two part company.

member.summary: Makes the body a profile sweeps out carried along a chain, within a tolerance.
member.param: The section, drawn about the origin: its origin rides on the path, its X to the path's right and its Y up — the world's up where the path allows it.

member.remarks: The section stands square to the path at either end, and at each bend lies on the plane halving it, so the pieces meet mitred. member.exception: Thrown when the profile or the path is null.
Thrown when the path has no length or turns back on itself, or the profile or the path has a coordinate that is not a finite number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GetVolume
member.summary: Gets the volume of the material, every opening cut out, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GetVolume(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the volume of the material: the faces with every opening cut out.
member.param: The tolerance the openings are cut out within.
member.returns: The volume, positive whichever way the faces are wound; nought where the openings take all of it.

remarks.para: The openings are cut out as shapes, not taken off as numbers: the part of an opening reaching outside the body costs nothing, as a through hole drawn past the faces it runs between does, two openings overlapping are taken out once, and the material inside an opening, its own openings, stays.

A body without openings is measured by its faces at once, and nothing is cut: every part GeometryHelper.TeklaConvert reads is one, its cuts already in its faces, and a slab cut by five other parts matched Tekla's VOLUME_NET to five parts in a million million. A body with openings has them cut out once for the tolerance, and the cut kept, so its volume, area and centroid are of one material and cost one cut. An opening that cannot be cut out is left in the material and the log warns of it; says so as well. Cut in at once, the body is parted by the planes of its openings and each piece judged by one point of it; where a plane runs through a piece and will not cut it, leaving it part in an opening and part out, the openings are taken out one at a time by a difference instead. A half of a hull cut near a face within a hundredth, a box 3.5 by 3.5 by 5 standing through the cut, held 1 465.33 cubic millimetres so, the box left in, where it holds 1 434.77. An opening that will not come out so has the openings cut as cuts them before it is left in: a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space and a million out, with a notch 20 by 20 through one end and one 20 wide and 1 deep across the other, flush with three faces, measured 58 800 at the rounding of its coordinates, the second notch left in; it measures 56 800, as it holds. Where walls of two openings, or of an opening and the body, stand apart within the tolerance of one plane, the openings are cut as cuts them, within a finer tolerance: an L 100 by 80 by 50, a million out, with two blind openings 27 apart whose walls stood 0.0009 apart across it, measured 153 674.08 within a thousandth, the second opening's wall cut in the plane of the first's; it measures 153 673.56, as it holds.

Where the point tolerance is below the rounding of the coordinates, a quadrillionth of the largest of them, nought among them, the openings are cut as cuts them, within that rounding; where it refuses them, within what rounding can move a corner off a plane, a trillionth of the size of the coordinates, as cuts them; and only where that refuses them too, at the tolerance given as they were, and says the volume cannot be trusted. At nought the plate with a hole 20 by 20 through it in place of the notches measured 60 000, the hole left in, and TryGetVolume trusted it; it measures 58 800. With the notches, a thousand out, it measured nought, and that was trusted too. Such a plate at the origin, turned another way, with an opening 32.7 by 51 down from its top to 0.9 over its bottom, measured nought at nought, and the whole plate, 60 000, at 1E-15, neither trusted; it measures 56 497.83, trusted.

A body far out, reaching more than 2^20 and more than 1 024 times the size of its box from the origin, as at national-grid coordinates, has its openings cut near the origin, as a union, a common part and a difference of such bodies are worked out, and the material moved back, each corner it keeps as it was given, to the bit; the volume, the area and the centroid are of that material. Where it stood, a corner was read on a plane within a trillionth of the coordinates, and walls of openings a fraction of the tolerance apart were cut in one plane: a plate 200 by 100 by 3 a hundred million out, with two openings up from its floor whose ceilings stood 0.00015 apart, measured 0.525 too much; an L 100 by 80 by 50 a thousand million out, with an opening up from its floor and one down from its top whose far walls stood 0.0009 apart, 153 732.16 within a thousandth, and with its openings given the other way round 153 731.38, where it holds 153 731.64. Each measures what it holds now, to 1.3E-4. Below a trillionth of the coordinates a 256th of the reach out the body is cut where it stands, as before.

Each face is taken as the fan of its boundary from its first corner, which is exact for a flat face and the way Tekla Structures reports a part's volume. measures the volume other ways too, and sets the ways side by side where a face a hair out of flat makes them part.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TryGetVolume(System.Double@)
member.summary: Gets the volume of the material where it can be trusted, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.TryGetVolume(System.Double@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the volume of the material where it can be trusted: every opening cut out, and the material closed.
member.param: The volume gives; nought when the method returns false.
The tolerance the openings are cut out and the faces judged closed within.
member.returns: true when every opening was cut out and the material closes, or the openings take all of it; false when an opening could not be cut out, or the faces do not close and so enclose no volume to measure.
member.remarks:
The area and the centroid are of the same material, so the answer holds for them too. A body without openings costs one check that its faces close, and nothing is cut.
The material is judged closed with the ends of its edges matched first, each to the first corner seen within the tolerance, as the booleans judge the bodies they work on, and not as reads it, which the two can part on either way; this answer, not IsClosed, says whether the volume can be trusted. A cube of 100 whose top stands 0.0015 over its sides, a speck of a face at each corner of its top half way up given before the cube's faces, is trusted, 1 000 005, where IsClosed reads it open; the union of two turned boxes made within a thousandth is refused at a tolerance of nought, where IsClosed reads it closed to the rounding of its coordinates. A cube cracked across three faces 0.001 wide less a skewed box, at a tolerance of a thousandth, read open by IsClosed by a hair of rounding, keeps its volume, 860.046 where the cube less the box holds 860.047.
Below the rounding of the coordinates, where the openings are cut within it, a body whose own faces do not close within it is not trusted, whatever its cut gives: a cube 10 across with cracks 0.0001 wide in its faces, less a tetrahedron, cut within the rounding at a tolerance of nought, is a closed sliver of 0.000042 cubic millimetres, where the cube less the tetrahedron holds 888.41.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.ClosesWithinRounding(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Whether the faces of a body with openings close within the rounding of the coordinates, where the point tolerance is below it and the openings are cut within it; true otherwise.
member.remarks: A body that does not close within the rounding holds no closed material to trust, whatever cutting its openings in gives: a cube 10 across whose faces carry cracks 0.0001 wide, less a tetrahedron, cut within the rounding at a tolerance of nought, came out a closed sliver of 4.2E-5 cubic millimetres, where the cube less the tetrahedron holds 888.41.

member.summary: Gets the area of where the material ends: the faces with every opening cut out, the walls of the openings included.
member.param: The tolerance the openings are cut out within.
member.returns: The area; nought where the openings take all of the body.
member.remarks: Each face's area as its outline gives it, holes and all. A body without openings is measured by its faces at once: a slab cut by five other parts matched Tekla's AREA to five parts in a million million. A plate with a bolt hole loses the hole from both of its faces and gains the hole's wall. The material is the one measures, cut once.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GetMassProperties(System.Double,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the mass properties of the material at a density: volume, mass, centroid, the moments and products of inertia about the centroid, and the principal moments and axes.
member.param: The mass of a unit of volume; in kilograms per cubic millimetre, steel is 7.85E-6.
The tolerance the openings are cut in and the surface meshed to.
member.returns: The properties; openings are taken out of every one of them, and a body they take whole holds none.
member.remarks: Every integral is exact for the body's faces, taken over the surface by the divergence theorem, and the body is read as its material: a plate's bolt holes come out of its weight and move its centroid. The faces are read as the triangles lying in them, ; reads them other ways too, and sets the ways side by side.
member.exception: Thrown when the density is not a positive number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.Section(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3)
member.summary: Gets where a plane cuts the material, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.Section(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets where a plane cuts the material: the faces the cut leaves, holes and all, facing along the plane's normal.
member.returns: One face per region of the cut; empty where the plane misses the body or only grazes it.

remarks.para: The material is cut, so a hole the plane passes through is a hole in the section, and a body in two pieces gives two faces. A plane lying along a face of the body touches it without cutting it, and gives nothing there: the section is where the body has material on both sides of the plane.

Asked at a point tolerance below the rounding of the coordinates, a quadrillionth of the largest of them, nought among them, the plane cuts the material within what rounding can move a corner off a plane, a trillionth of the size of the coordinates: within the tolerance asked, the two faces beside an edge each cut their own copy of it a rounding apart, and the rim did not close. At nought a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space, at the origin or a million out, had no section, where a plane square to its face cuts 20 000 of it and one across its length 300; with a hole 20 by 20 through it, it cuts 19 600, the hole in it. It is cut so too at and above the rounding while the point tolerance is below both that trillionth and a millionth: a million out, at 2E-9, twice the rounding, or at 1E-7, the plate had no section either. At a millionth and above, the default tolerance among them, the material is cut as it was, to the bit.

A body far out, as says, is moved near the origin with the plane, by whole coordinates, cut there, and the section moved back. Where it stood, walls of openings a fraction of the tolerance apart were cut in one plane: a plate 200 by 100 by 3 a hundred million out, with two openings up from its floor whose ceilings stood 0.00015 apart, cut square to its length through the deeper opening, gave 195, the opening as shallow as the other, where the plane cuts 194.9895 of it; it gives that now, to 3E-7.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.GetMaterial(GeometryHelper.Tolerance,System.Boolean@)
member.summary: Gets the material of this body: its faces with every opening cut out, cut once for a tolerance and kept.
member.param: The tolerance the openings are cut out within.
Whether every opening was cut out; false where one could not be, and is left in, warned of.
member.returns: The body itself where it has no openings; otherwise a body without any; null where they take all of it.
member.remarks: The volume, the area, the centroid and the mass of a body with openings are all of its material, and cutting it is a boolean costing far more than any of them: the cut is kept, for the last tolerance asked, so that measuring the body every way costs one cut and the measures describe one body. The body cannot change, and so neither can its cut; two threads asking at once may both cut it, and either cut is kept.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.CutMaterial(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts every opening out of the faces: where the point tolerance is below the rounding of the coordinates, as cuts them, within that rounding, or where that refuses, within what rounding can move a corner off a plane, a trillionth of the size of the coordinates; otherwise, or where both refuse, as cuts them at the tolerance given, not to be trusted where they refused.
member.remarks: Cut at the tolerance given, the openings within the rounding came out wrong and were trusted: a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space and a thousand out, with a notch 20 by 20 through one end and one 20 wide and 1 deep across the other, measured nought at a tolerance of nought, said to be trusted so, where it holds 56 800. Where TryCutOpenings refuses them, cut as they were they can come out right, a plate a thousand out with three openings 48 758.41 at 1E-12, and are measured so, untrusted: of 5 000 bodies it refused 29 at nought, and cut as they were, 25 of those came out wrong and were trusted. Refused within the rounding, a plate with blind openings cut as they were measured nought or the whole plate, untrusted: of 4 000 prisms with up to three openings, turned about in space or not, at the origin and a thousand to a thousand million out, 22 at nought and 7 between 1E-12 and 9E-7. Cut within the trillionth, as and cut them, every one measures what it holds, and all but one star are trusted.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.CutMaterialHere(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts the material of this body where it stands, as does near the origin.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3.CutMaterialAsGiven(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts every opening out of the faces at the tolerance given: all at once, which costs least, or where that cannot be worked out, opens a body that closed or leaves a piece of it part in an opening and part out, one at a time by a difference, leaving in any one that will not come out.
member.remarks: Where an opening will not come out by a difference at the tolerance alone, or one is said to take all that is left where the cut at once left material, the openings are cut as cuts them, which reads a corner as on a plane within the rounding of the coordinates too, and only where that gives no material is the opening left in. A difference at a tolerance at or just above that rounding is read on corners the rounding puts either side of a plane: the plate with the notches a million out measured 58 800 at the rounding and twice it, the second notch left in, where TryCutOpenings gave 56 800, as it holds.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSphere3
member.summary: Whether a ball touches another shape.
member.remarks: A ball touches a shape where the exact gap between them is no more than the point tolerance, so the answer is that of DistanceTo read against it: a shape inside the ball collides with it, a shape within the tolerance of its surface collides with it, and the ball of radius 50 about the origin touches the plane 50.0005 above it and not the plane 50.002 above it. A point answers with .
member.summary:
Represents a solid ball in space, defined by its centre and its radius.
A ball is read as filled, as a solid is and as the disc of a circle is: a point inside it is nought from it, and keeps the depth of that point, negative, for the ones that ask how deep. Where only the shell matters, measures to it from either side.

remarks.para: A ball is a point grown by its radius, so its gap to any shape is the gap between its centre and that shape less the radius, and nought where the shape reaches into it: a ball of radius 50 about (0, 0, 100) is 50 from the floor and touches it when its centre is lowered to 50, and a ball of radius 10 about (200, 0, 0) is 140 from the ball of radius 50 about the origin, 200 less 50 less 10, whichever way round it is asked. Every query is answered from the centre, so it is exact to the rounding of the shape's own distance to a point.

Where its surface is crossed is a question about the surface, and answered with points: a line through the middle of the ball crosses it twice, a plane through it cuts a circle, and a line or a curve that lies wholly inside crosses it nowhere though it collides with the ball. A body is asked whether it touches the ball and how far from it; where their surfaces cross is the clash's question, asked of .

member.summary: How far a ball is from another shape, and how deep inside it a point sits.
member.remarks: The gap is the distance from the centre of the ball to the shape less the radius, and nought where the shape reaches into the ball. A closed shape is read as filled and a curve as a curve, as the shape's own distance to a point reads it: a point inside the ball, a body that holds its centre and a plane through it are all nought from it. A curved loop is the exception among the closed shapes: it is read by its outline, as its own distance to a point is, so a ball in the middle of a large curved loop is apart from it. A ball of radius 50 about (0, 0, 100) is 50 from the floor and 150 from a ball of radius 10 about (0, 0, -110).
member.summary: Where the surface of a ball is crossed by another shape.

remarks.para: It is the surface that is crossed, not the ball: a line, a ray or a segment crosses it in no point, one where it grazes it, or two, a curve in as many points as it meets it, and a flat shape where its boundary does. A line or a curve that lies wholly inside the ball collides with it and crosses it nowhere, and a curve that lies on the surface itself touches it along its length and crosses it nowhere, as two arcs of one circle cross nowhere. The points of a line, a ray or a segment run along it, those of a curve along the curve, and those of a chain or a boundary in the order of its edges, a corner on the surface once. A line that passes within the point tolerance outside the surface touches it at its foot, and one whose two crossings are no further apart than the point tolerance touches it at the one.

A plane or another ball is cut in a circle, which is not a list of points: gives it, and the one point where they only touch. Touching is read within the point tolerance, so two shells that cross within that tolerance of each other, or a plane that cuts less than that deep, touch at a point though the circle they truly share can be a few units across: sqrt(2 R tol), 4.5 for a radius R of 10 000 at the default tolerance. A body or a box is asked whether it touches the ball, and where their surfaces cross is the clash's question.

member.summary: The point of a ball nearest another shape, and the shortest segment joining the two.
member.remarks: The segment leaves the surface of the ball, on the line from its centre to the point of the shape nearest the centre, and lands on that point, so it is as long as the distance to the shape. Where the shape reaches into the ball it has no length, and lies at the point of the shape nearest the centre, the centre itself where the shape holds it.
member.summary: A ball asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSphere3.ToSolid(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the ball as a closed body of triangles, none of them further from the sphere than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between a face and the sphere, in drawing units. Zero picks 0.2 % of the radius.
member.returns: A closed body whose faces face outwards, every corner of them on the sphere.
member.exception: Thrown when the ball is not valid, as a default one is.
Thrown when the centre of the ball has a coordinate that is not a finite number.
Thrown when the tolerance is negative or not a finite number, or needs more than 1 048 576 triangles.

remarks.para: An icosahedron of twenty triangles, each cut into n by n smaller ones by lines parallel to its sides and every corner pushed out to the sphere, with the least n for which the sag of every triangle, the gap between its plane and the sphere at the nearest, is within the tolerance: a ball of radius 50 cut within 0.1 is 20 by 13 by 13, 3 380 triangles, and within 0.01 it is 20 by 39 by 39, 30 420, none of them further than that from the sphere. The corners lie on the sphere, so the body lies inside it and holds a little less than : 0.036 % less at 0.01. A tolerance that needs more than 1 048 576 triangles is refused, as for the chords of a circle: radius 50 within 0.0001 would need three million. A ball of a radius below about 0.01 has triangles thinner than the point tolerance, and its body may be one the library calls open at the default tolerance.

A ball is clashed with a body through this one: ball.ToSolid(0.01) goes where any solid goes, and its clash is as exact as the tolerance. Whether the ball touches a body, and how far apart they are, are exact without it ( and ).

member.summary: Calculates the distance from this ball to a point, negative for a point inside it.

member.summary: Gets the points where the surface of this ball crosses a segment, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSphere3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the points where the surface of this ball crosses a segment, within a tolerance.
member.returns: The crossings, none where they do not meet or where the shape lies inside the ball.
member.remarks: The segment from (0, -100, 0) to (0, 100, 0) crosses the surface of the ball of radius 50 about the origin at (0, -50, 0) and (0, 50, 0), in that order. The segment from (-10, 0, 0) to (10, 0, 0) lies wholly inside, collides with the ball and crosses it nowhere; one that ends 0.0005 short of the surface touches it, at its end. A segment no longer than the point tolerance is read as its start where it does not truly cross the surface: at a thousandth, the one from (0, 0, 50.0004) to (0, 0, 49.9995) crosses it at (0, 0, 50), the one from (0, 0, 50.0008) to (0, 0, 50.0002) meets it at its start, and the one from (0, 0, 50.0015) to (0, 0, 50.0006) meets it nowhere.
