member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2
member.summary: Whether a spline touches another shape in the plane.
member.remarks: The rule is the others': two shapes collide when they come within the point tolerance of each other, a closed shape read as filled. It is read from itself, so that a collision and a distance never disagree.
member.summary:
A curve in the plane that is not a chain of pieces but one smooth sweep: a NURBS, a B-spline whose control points may pull on it with different strengths, which is what an AutoCAD SPLINE and an IFC B-spline curve hold.
It is given by its degree, its control points, its knots and, if it is rational, its weights. The knots cut the parameter into spans, and each span is a polynomial (or a ratio of two) of the degree; the curve is clamped, so it starts at its first control point and ends at its last, and the control polygon, the chain through the control points, shows where it goes without touching it. The control points of a cubic with the corners (0, 0), (100, 150), (200, 150), (300, 0) and the knots 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1 give the Bézier curve that rises to 112.5 in the middle, at (150, 112.5), not to the 150 of the polygon. A circle is the rational quadratic of nine control points that builds, every point of it at the radius to rounding.
A spline is read over its domain, from to , the first and last knot, which are whatever the knots say: the knots are kept as they were given, so a spline read from a file goes back out as it came. Two kinds of parameter are told apart by their names, as the other curves keep them: the members named for a parameter, such as , take a share of the domain from 0 to 1, and the ones named for a knot, such as , take a value of the domain itself, which is what the knots, and a file, say. Splines made here have the domain [0, 1], where the two are the same number. Neither is a length: the members named for a distance go by length.
It is immutable: every operation gives a new spline. It is a class, as is, because it holds arrays, and what it hands out of them is read-only.
How far a spline is from a point, and whether a point lies on it, and how far it is from every other shape in the plane.

remarks.para: A shape is read as the other curves read it: a closed one, a polygon, a rectangle, a triangle, a face, a circle, an ellipse or a curved loop, is a region, and a spline inside it is nought from it; the spline itself is a curve, with no inside. The distance is nought only where the two truly meet, a crossing or a touch found to rounding, and otherwise the gap, measured exactly: it is never read through the tolerance. The pairs with a segment, a ray, a line without ends, an arc or a circle are solved as polynomials, to rounding; with an ellipse or another spline the nearest approach is found by cutting both in halves while their hulls are near enough to matter, and bringing the nearest pair to rounding by Newton's method. The parts are taken nearest bound first, and the cutting ends when the nearest bound left is no nearer than the best found less a hair, the hair being a billionth of the size of the shapes (0.001 at a size of a million) and never more than a thousandth of the distance itself, so a distance of 0.0009 at a million is never read above the point tolerance; the answer is that of a real pair of points, no nearer than the truth and within the hair of it, and to rounding wherever Newton's method settles, which is wherever the curves cross or the nearest points are not parallel.

member.summary: Where a spline crosses another shape in the plane.

remarks.para: The crossings are those of the boundary of a closed shape, in order along the spline from its start. A place is where the two meet (a crossing, or a touch found to rounding), or where the distance of the spline from the shape is least within the point tolerance, as a touch a half of a thousandth off is, or an end of the spline or of the shape comes near the other: a stationary point that is a greatest, as lies between two crossings of a line that passes a hair inside a circle, is none, and nor is a point on a slope. Places no further apart than the point tolerance, one from the next, are one place; so are near touches (not crossings) next to each other in one basin of the distance within ten times it, however many the rounding of the numbers leaves where a curve touches another. Two crossings are never one place unless they are within the point tolerance of each other, as for the exact curves: a line that cuts a circle of radius 30 a million from the origin in a chord of 0.009 meets it twice. The spline of a circle of radius 100 about the origin, from , crosses the line along X through the origin at (100, 0) and (-100, 0), in that order, and at (100, 0) again where it ends, which is the same place as its start and is not given twice, and a line tangent to a circle touches it once (a million from the origin, where the numbers are 1.2E-10 apart, up to three places within a hundredth of a millimetre). A closed spline, its first and last control points the same to the bit, has no ends: its seam is a point of it like any other, and the line tangent to the circle spline 0.003 of a radian past it, 4.5E-4 from the seam, touches it once.

A span of the spline that is an arc of a circle, as each span of and is, meets a circle, an arc or such a span of another spline as the circles meet, by the rule of : where the two arcs hold the circles' crossings or touch, and nowhere where the two circles are one circle, within the point tolerance of each other all round. That is so where the span's circle, read from its control points, is known within a hundredth of the tolerance; a flat arc, of radius 1 000 000 and chord 300, whose centre is read to no better than 2.3E-4, is met as any other span is.

Where the spline lies along the shape for a length, to rounding, no place is given along the stretch. Against an ellipse or another spline, the same is so where the two stay within the point tolerance of each other, level, for a quarter of the size of the smaller, unless the smaller is no larger than the point tolerance, which lies along nothing; see .

member.summary: The point of a spline nearest a point, where on the spline it lies, and the shortest segment joining the two; and the shortest segment from a spline to every other shape in the plane.
member.remarks: The segment runs from the nearest point of the spline to the nearest point of the boundary of the shape, so it has no length where the two meet, and where a spline lies inside a closed shape, which is nought from it, it is as long as the gap out to the outline, as it is for the other curves. The shape asked the same question gives the same segment turned round, to the bit.
member.summary: How far a spline is from another spline, whether they touch, where they cross and the shortest segment between them.

remarks.para: Two splines are asked about each other from either side with the same answer to the bit: the work is done from the one that comes first in a fixed order (degree, number of control points, then the control points, weights and knots), and the other side turns the shortest segment round and gives the same points in order along itself. The spline against itself, or against a copy, runs along it from start to end: it is nought from it, collides with it, and crosses it nowhere.

The pieces of the two splines are cut in halves while their hulls, measured by their boxes and by the shadows of their control points on the chord of each part and its square, are near enough to matter and they are not yet straight; each pair that is straight to a thousandth of its size, and whose tangents can never run the same way, or that is straight to a billionth, is measured as two segments and brought to the real curves by Newton's method. For the nearest approach the parts are taken nearest bound first, and the cutting ends when the nearest bound left is no nearer than the best found less a hair (a billionth of the size of the shapes, and never more than a thousandth of the distance); for the places two splines meet, a part is left when the hulls show no meeting in it within the point tolerance. The distance is exact to rounding where Newton's method settles, which it does wherever the curves cross or the nearest points are not parallel, and otherwise right to that hair. A crossing at any angle, however shallow, is found by the offset of the one curve from the other along its normal, which changes sign where they cross: a line 40 long that cuts a circle spline of radius 1 000 in a chord of 0.004 meets it twice, as the does. Two meetings are one place only when they are within the point tolerance of each other.

Two spans that are both arcs of circles, as the spans of and are, are met in closed form, as the two circles meet by the rule of , and measured as they are for the distance, where their circles, read from their control points, are known within a hundredth of the tolerance, and a snap for the distance; flat arcs are cut as any spans are. Two circle splines nearly about one centre were cut into millions of pairs: of radius 100 000 and 100 000.0005 with their centres 0.01 apart they took 16 s, gave no crossing and were 4.8E-5 apart; they cross at (-4 999.995, 99 874.922) and (-4 999.995, -99 874.922), as the circles do, and are nought apart, in a third of a millisecond. Two circles of radius 1 000 and 1 000.00002 with their centres 1E-4 apart are one circle at a tolerance of a thousandth, as the circles read them, and give no place, and at a tolerance of a hundred-thousandth cross at (-200, 979.8) and (-200, -979.8) at an angle of 1E-7.

Where two splines stay within the point tolerance of each other, and level (their distance changing by no more than half the tolerance) for a quarter of the size of the smaller, seen from both of them, they lie along each other, as two circles 0.0005 apart do, or a spline and a curve fitted to it: no place is given in the stretch, since the places there would be where the rounding of the numbers has them cross, the distance is the gap and no less (0.0005 for the circles), and they collide. A stretch that either leaves by more than the tolerance, as a dart of a polyline 2E-4 off a line going out a unit and back does, is cut out and the stretch cut in two there, and the crossings at the dart's edges are given. A sign change of the offset inside a stretch, by more than a hundredth of the tolerance to each side, is a crossing and is given. A touch, whose distance goes from nought to the tolerance and past it within a few units, and a crossing at any angle, are not level, and are places. A spline fitted through 37 points of a quarter circle of radius 1 000 gives its true crossings against a of that arc, which is solved exactly (72 of them, the fit being off the arc a little between its points), and is along the arc spline of it (), where only the crossings that go more than a hundredth of the tolerance to each side are given (10, in the first and last tenth of the fit). The cutting for the least distance is bounded: past 40 000 pairs of parts in one question, the curves are looked at at 128 points and the least of them brought to the real curves, and the answer is the best found. What is promised then is that it is the distance of a real pair of points, so the truth lies between it and the nearest bound left, and one Debug line gives both (); a meeting not yet found is not in the answer. Two splines a hair apart and side by side for 6 000 take 0.15 s. Short of the budget a crossing is never passed over for a nearer approach found first. The cutting for the places is bounded at two million pairs and logs one Debug line past it; nothing built in the tests reaches it, and two splines that stay within the tolerance of each other for a long stretch and are not level there, or hug each other for less than a quarter of the size at a distance that makes every part of the one a near match for hundreds of the other, could. The size is how far the control points of the smaller reach from its first, the same however the two are turned.

member.summary: Initializes a spline from its degree, control points and knots, and its weights if it is rational.
member.param: The degree, from 1 to 25: 1 for straight pieces, 2 for the conics of an arc, 3 for the cubics that draughtsmen and AutoCAD use.
The control points, at least degree + 1 and not all one point.
The knots, controlPoints + degree + 1 of them, not decreasing; the first degree + 1 equal and the last degree + 1 equal and above them, and no inner knot repeated more than degree times.

The weights, one for each control point and above nought, or null for all of them one, and no more than 1E12 to one apart (past that the length cannot be worked out right). All one is a plain B-spline, which says.
member.remarks: The numbers are copied, and kept as they are: nothing is rescaled or reordered. A spline of degree 3 with the control points (0, 0), (100, 150), (200, 150), (300, 0) takes the knots 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1; with a fifth control point it takes nine knots, such as 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 1.
member.exception: Thrown when the control points or the knots are null.
Thrown when the degree is outside 1 to 25, a weight is not a positive number, or the largest weight is more than 1E12 times the smallest.
Thrown when there are too few control points, a point or a knot is not a finite number, the knots are the wrong number or not clamped, or the control points are all one point.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.Interpolate(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2},System.Int32)
member.summary: Builds the spline that passes through a list of fit points, as AutoCAD's fit-point splines do, with the curve left to settle its own direction at each end.
member.param: The points to pass through, in order; at least degree + 1 once the ones that coincide are dropped.
The degree, from 1 to 25, and at most one less than the number of points; 3 if not given.
member.returns: The spline, not rational, over [0, 1].

remarks.para: The method is global interpolation with chord-length parameters (Piegl and Tiller, The NURBS Book, 9.2.1). Each fit point is given a parameter equal to the share of the length of the chain through the points that comes before it, so that the points are met at parameters in proportion to how far apart they are; the inner knots are the averages of degree of those parameters in a row; and the control points are what makes the curve meet every fit point, found by solving one banded system, which costs the same for each point however many there are. Four points (0, 0), (100, 50), (200, 0), (300, 50) of degree 3 give the curve through all four, met at the parameters 0, a third, two thirds and 1, the three chords being as long.
A fit point within the point tolerance of the one before it is dropped, as a polyline drops a vertex, since two points the same make parameters the same and a system that cannot be solved.

member.exception: Thrown when the points are null.
Thrown when the degree is outside 1 to 25.
Thrown when a point is not a finite point, or there are fewer than degree + 1 distinct points.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.Interpolate(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2},System.Int32,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Builds the spline that passes through a list of fit points, within a tolerance that decides which neighbouring fit points are one point.
member.param: The points to pass through, in order; at least degree + 1 once the ones that coincide are dropped.
The degree, from 1 to 25, and at most one less than the number of points.
The tolerance: a fit point within its point tolerance of the one kept before it is dropped.
member.returns: The spline, not rational, over [0, 1].
member.remarks: See . Points just above the tolerance are kept, and the chord lengths the parameters come from are then tiny beside the rest, so the curve can swing far between them: the chain (0, 0), (100, 0), (100.0011, 0.0005), (100.0022, 0), (200, 50), (300, 0) at the default tolerance of 0.001 keeps all six, its chords at the three near points 0.0012 long, and the curve through them swings 507 000 outside the box of the points; at a tolerance of 0.01 the two in the middle are dropped and it stays within about 13 of the box. Drop such points before asking, or give a tolerance that does.
member.exception: Thrown when the points are null.
Thrown when the degree is outside 1 to 25.
Thrown when a point is not a finite point, or there are fewer than degree + 1 distinct points.

The degree, from 2 to 25, and at most one more than the number of points; 3 if not given.
member.returns: The spline, not rational, over [0, 1].

remarks.para: As , with the two end conditions added to the system: the curve has two more control points. A tangent gives a direction and nothing else: the curve leaves and arrives at the speed it keeps on average, which over [0, 1] is the length of the chain through the fit points, so that three points 100 apart along X with the tangent (1, 0) at each end give the straight line through them, run at an even speed of 200, and a tangent of any other length gives the same curve.

Two fit points with two tangents of degree 3 are the Hermite cubic: the curve from (0, 0) to (100, 0) leaving upwards and arriving upwards is an S, which rises above the line, crosses its middle at (50, 0) and dips below it before it comes up to the end.

member.exception: Thrown when the points are null.

Thrown when a point or a tangent is not finite, a tangent has no length, or there are too few distinct points for the degree.

A half circle is two pieces, a whole one four, and a sweep of 100 degrees two of 50. The ends are the arc's own: the spline starts at and ends at its end point, but that an arc of a whole turn, and so the circle, ends on its start exactly, its first control point repeated.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.Length
member.summary: Gets the length of the spline, measured along it.
member.remarks: The integral of the speed, by Gauss-Legendre of ten points over each span, a span cut in halves wherever the rule over the whole and over its two halves disagree, until they agree to 1E-14 of the length of the span's control polygon, and cut at each place the speed is least, where a curve that turns back has a corner in what is integrated; a rational span whose weights are more than two to one apart is cut first. It is good to a relative 1E-12 and in practice to 1E-15: the circle of radius 100 comes out as 628.31853071796, which is 2 pi times 100. Where the speed falls to nought, at a cusp, it is good to a little less. It is worked out once.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.GetAabb
member.summary: Gets the box with sides along the axes that the spline fills exactly, from its smallest to its largest coordinates.
member.returns: The box, as an unrotated rectangle.
member.remarks: Not the box of the control points, which is larger: the cubic with the control points (0, 0), (100, 150), (200, 150), (300, 0) fills 300 by 112.5, where its control points fill 300 by 150. Each end of a span, and each place where a coordinate stops rising or falling, which is a root of a polynomial of the span found without missing any, is measured; the box is exact to rounding. A rectangle has its centre and size, so its corners can differ from the extremes by a unit in the last place.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.Split(System.Double)
member.summary: Cuts the spline in two at a normalised parameter.
member.param: The share of the domain to cut at, above 0 and below 1.
member.returns: The part before the parameter and the part after it, over the two parts of the domain.
member.remarks: Exact, as is: the share is turned into the value of the knots it comes to and the spline is cut there. A share so near an end that its knot value is the end's, to a double, is refused.
member.exception: Thrown when the parameter is not above 0 and below 1, or comes to an end of the domain.
Thrown when a part would be a spline that stands still: all its control points one point.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.SplitAtKnot(System.Double)
member.summary: Cuts the spline in two at a value of its knots.
member.param: The knot value to cut at, above and below .
member.returns: The part before the knot value, over [DomainStart, knot], and the part after it, over [knot, DomainEnd].
member.remarks: Exact: the knot at the value is raised to the degree, which cuts the control polygon without moving the curve, so the two parts are the two pieces of the spline, with the same degree and weights, and meet at the point the spline has there, which is the last control point of the first and the first of the second, to the last bit. A point of the first part at a knot value is the spline's point at it, to rounding.
member.exception: Thrown when the knot value is not above the first knot and below the last.
Thrown when a part would be a spline that stands still: all its control points one point, as a cut inside a span whose control points all coincide would leave.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.Reverse
member.summary: Gets the spline running the other way, from its end to its start.
member.returns: The spline with its control points and weights in the opposite order and its knots mirrored about the middle of the domain, so that it has the same domain: the point at a knot value is the point of the original at the knot value as far from the other end.
member.remarks: Each distinct knot is mirrored once, so knots that were equal stay equal and knots that were apart stay apart: where rounding would put two mirrored knots on one number the later is moved one unit in the last place on, and one that would land on the end of the domain one back. A mirrored knot is rounded to the last place of the domain's ends, which moves the curve by the speed times that.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.TransformBy(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2)
member.summary: Gets the spline under a transformation.
member.returns: The transformed spline: the control points carried by the transformation, the weights and knots as they were.
member.remarks: A NURBS is carried by any affine map by carrying its control points: a rotation, a scaling that differs between the axes, a shear and a mirror all give the spline that is the image of the old one, exactly, a circle among them, which an uneven scaling makes the ellipse it is. A mirror runs the spline the same way along itself. The matrix of a transformation holds nothing but the affine part, so there is nothing that cannot be carried but a transformation that squeezes the plane onto a point, which is refused.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is null.
Thrown when the transformation carries every control point to one point.
Thrown when the transformation has an entry that is not a finite number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.Flatten(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the spline as a chain of straight pieces, none of which strays further from it than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between the spline and the chain, in drawing units; above nought. There is no automatic one: a spline has no radius to take a share of.
member.returns: The chain, from the start of the spline to its end, its corners on the spline.

remarks.para: The promise holds however fine the tolerance, however sharp the bend and whatever the weights: every span is cut in halves until the piece is within the tolerance of the chord from its start to its end, which three proofs can say: every control point of a piece is within it (a piece lies in the hull of its control points); or, for a piece that is not rational, the second differences of its control points are small enough; or, for a rational quadratic, a conic, the height of its middle control point is. The circle of radius 100 within 0.01 is 256 chords, every corner on the circle, where 223 would hold, since pieces are cut in halves; the arch of (0, 0), (100, 150), (200, 150), (300, 0) within 0.01 is 128 chords.

A tolerance that would need more than 1 048 576 pieces is refused. The result is a chain, which merges corners closer together than the point tolerance (1E-3 by default), so a tolerance whose pieces would be shorter than that is not kept, as for ; the writers (ObjWriter, Wkt, DxfWriter) keep every piece.

A spline no longer than the point tolerance, all of it within the tolerance of its start, which a chain would merge into one point, is the chain of its corners as they are, the repeats of one point to the bit left out: the part 0.000245 long that at a millionth cuts off the fit through (0, 0), (30, 20), (60, -10), (100, 0) is the chord from its start to its end, where it was refused. keeps such a part, exactly, as it keeps any other.

member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is not a positive number, or needs more than 1 048 576 pieces.
Thrown when every corner the spline is cut at is the same point, to the bit: a spline that stands still, or a closed one whose chord tolerance is so large that it is cut at its ends alone.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Gets the distance from this spline to a point, using the default tolerance.
member.returns: The distance from the point to the nearest point of the curve, which is a line and not a region: a point inside a closed spline is as far from it as from the nearest of its points. Nought only where the point truly lies on it, otherwise the gap, measured exactly; exact to rounding, however the curve bends.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets the distance from this spline to a point, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance; not read, since the nearest point takes none.
member.returns: The distance from the point to the nearest point of the curve, measured exactly. The circle of radius 100 about the origin, as makes it, is 60 from (160, 0) and 100 from its own centre.
member.remarks: The nearest point is found as finds it: on each span the parameters where the curve stops coming nearer, all of them, from the roots of a polynomial in Bernstein form, and the ends; whichever span cannot be nearer than the best found, by the box of its control points, is not solved. The boxes are kept in a tree, built once, so the spans near the point are reached without looking at the rest: a query costs time in the logarithm of the number of spans and the number whose boxes are near the point, about 10 microseconds on a spiral of 100 000 spans where it was 0.5 ms before the tree, and a span solved costs about a microsecond. A spline of up to 24 spans looks at its boxes one by one, which is faster for so few.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline2.GetKnotAtPoint(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint2)
member.summary: Gets the value of the knots at the point of the spline nearest a point.
member.param: The point; it does not have to lie on the spline.
member.returns: A value of the domain, from to : the knot value, which turns back into the point. Where two points of the spline are equally near, the lower one.
member.remarks: The nearest point is a point where the spline stops coming nearer, or an end. On each span that is a root of a polynomial in Bernstein form, and all of them are found: a point inside a loop of the curve, a point on the axis of a symmetric one, the centre of an arc, a point at a cusp, all give the nearest of them, to rounding. A circle as makes it has every point equally near its centre, and answers the start.

member.param: The point; it does not have to lie on the spline.
member.returns: The share of the domain: 0 at the start and 1 at the end; gives the knot value.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3
member.summary: Whether a spline touches another shape in space.
member.remarks: The rule is the others': two shapes collide when they come within the point tolerance of each other, a flat shape and a body read as filled. It is read from itself, so that a collision and a distance never disagree.
member.summary:
A curve in space that is not a chain of pieces but one smooth sweep: a NURBS, a B-spline whose control points may pull on it with different strengths, which is what an AutoCAD SPLINE and an IFC B-spline curve hold. It is the counterpart of in space, made and read the same way.
It is given by its degree, its control points, its knots and, if it is rational, its weights. The knots cut the parameter into spans, and each span is a polynomial (or a ratio of two) of the degree; the curve is clamped, so it starts at its first control point and ends at its last. The control points of a cubic (0, 0, 0), (100, 150, 60), (200, 150, 60), (300, 0, 0) and the knots 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1 give the Bézier curve that rises to 112.5 and 45 in the middle, at (150, 112.5, 45). A circle is the rational quadratic of nine control points that builds, every point of it at the radius to rounding.
A spline is read over its domain, from to , the first and last knot, which are whatever the knots say: the knots are kept as they were given, so a spline read from a file goes back out as it came. Two kinds of parameter are told apart by their names, as the other curves keep them: the members named for a parameter, such as , take a share of the domain from 0 to 1, and the ones named for a knot, such as , take a value of the domain itself, which is what the knots, and a file, say. Splines made here have the domain [0, 1], where the two are the same number. Neither is a length: the members named for a distance go by length.
It is immutable: every operation gives a new spline. It is a class, as is, because it holds arrays, and what it hands out of them is read-only.
How far a spline is from a point, and whether a point lies on it, and how far it is from every other shape in space.

remarks.para: A shape is read as the other curves in space read it: a flat shape, a triangle, a polygon or a face, is filled, and a spline that pierces it, or lies in it, is nought from it; a circle or an ellipse is the disc it is, as its own distance to a point reads it; a box, an oriented box, a solid or a ball is material, so a spline inside it is nought from it; a plane is a surface without ends, not a half of space; and a curved chain and a curved loop are the paths they are, a loop not filled. The spline itself is a curve, with no inside. The distance is nought only where the two truly meet, a crossing or a touch found to rounding, and otherwise the gap, measured exactly: it is never read through the tolerance, and the planar tolerance is not read at all.

The pairs with a segment, a ray or a line without ends are solved as polynomials, to rounding: the part of a span's offset that stands square to the line is two signed polynomials in Bernstein form, both nought where the span meets the line, and a span in a plane through the line has its signed offset in that plane, as in the plane, so a crossing however shallow is nought; with a plane the signed offset of the span is one, and with a ball the squared distance from the centre less the squared radius; a flat shape is its plane, taken where the foot of the place stands over the shape, and its outline; a body is its faces and the test of its material. A place where the spline comes nearest a line out of such a plane is a stationary point of the squared offset, brought to its last digit by Newton's method on the distance, or where the distance has no curvature by a golden section down its slope. With an arc, a circle, an ellipse or another spline the nearest approach is found by cutting both in halves while their hulls are near enough to matter, nearest bound first, and bringing the nearest pair to rounding by Newton's method, as it is in the plane (see ); the hair that bounds the doubt is a billionth of the size of the shapes, and never more than a thousandth of the distance itself. Two splines in one plane, to a snap, are measured in that plane.

member.summary: Where a spline crosses another shape in space.

remarks.para: The crossings are those of the surface or the outline of a shape, in order along the spline from its start: a flat shape is pierced where the spline passes through it as well as crossed at its outline, a disc, a circle or an ellipse, is crossed only at its rim, a body only at its skin, and a curved loop at its outline. In space two curves seldom meet, so a place is where the distance of the spline from the shape is least within the point tolerance, as it is in the plane: a crossing is a place where that distance comes to nought, and a spline that passes a ten-thousandth of a millimetre from a line is at a place as a spline that crosses it is. A touch is told from a near miss by the tolerance alone: the line 0.0005 over the top of the ring of radius 50 touches it at (0, 50, 0) and the line 0.002 over it touches nothing. A stationary point of the distance that is a greatest is not a place, nor is a point on a slope, and one that is a least with no curvature, a spline over a line that is tangent to it and a thousandth above its plane, or the cubic y = x³ / 100 under the line along x half a thousandth above its plane, is a place all the same (the distance has risen by more than the digits can tell a thousandth, a hundredth or a tenth of the size of the spline away, inside the piece, and has fallen nowhere on the way); a least that curves up is one only where the distance falls neither way. Places no further apart than the point tolerance, one from the next, are one place, as are two near touches next to each other along the spline within ten times that with no point between them farther from the shape than at either by more than four snaps (the snap is 1E-13 of the size of the numbers); two crossings are one place only when they are within the tolerance of each other, and a least of the distance within the tolerance of a crossing is left out, so that it does not join two.

A segment, a ray or a line without ends is measured by the two signed parts of the spline's offset square to it, and a piece of the spline in a plane through the line by its signed offset in that plane, as a spline and a line of the plane are: a crossing at a millionth of a radian is a crossing, nought from the line, and the cubic y = x³ / 100 crosses the line y = 0.0001 once, at x = 0.21544, its inflection, where the offset stops and goes on, being no place. A plane is measured by the signed offset, so a dip of the spline a few snaps below it between two crossings is a greatest of the distance and no place.

Where the spline lies along the shape for a length, to rounding, no place is given along the stretch: a spline in a plane crosses the plane nowhere, and one on a ball crosses its surface nowhere. Against an arc, a circle, an ellipse or another spline, the same is so where the two stay within the point tolerance of each other, level, for a quarter of the size of the smaller, unless the smaller is no larger than the point tolerance, which lies along nothing; see . A crossing inside such a stretch is still a place: two splines in one plane, to the snap, are worked out in that plane, where the offset of the one from the other has a sign, and give the places the plane gives; an arc, a circle, an ellipse, an edge, a chain of edges, a segment, a ray or a line without ends in the plane of the spline is laid flat with it the same way, so a circle spline of radius 100 moved (0.0003, 0.0005) along its plane is one circle with its circle, as in the plane, and a segment along the first side of a polyline spline, 1.15E-6 off it, is given the one place the plane gives. A closed spline, its first and last control points the same to the bit, has no ends, as in the plane. Two curves that share no plane can still cross, as a helix crosses a straight spline along its cylinder once a turn, and inside a stretch along each other a place is a least of the distance where the two would cross if brought into one plane: a polyline spline and its copy moved 0.0005 along its plane cross at three corners, and lifted 0.0002 off the plane as well they come nearest, 0.0002 apart, at the same three.

member.summary: The point of a spline nearest a point, where on the spline it lies, and the shortest segment joining the two.
How far a spline is from another spline in space, whether they touch, where they meet and the shortest segment between them.

remarks.para: Two splines in space are asked about each other from either side with the same answer to the bit: the work is done from the one that comes first in a fixed order (degree, number of control points, then the control points, weights and knots), and the other side turns the shortest segment round and gives the same points in order along itself. The spline against itself, or against a copy, runs along it from start to end: it is nought from it, collides with it, and crosses it nowhere.

The pieces of the two splines are cut in halves while their hulls, measured by their boxes and by the shadows of their control points on the chord of each part, on the two directions square to it and on the direction square to both chords, are near enough to matter and they are not yet straight; each pair that is straight to a thousandth of its size, and whose tangents can never run the same way, or that is straight to a billionth, is measured as two segments and brought to the real curves by Newton's method. For the nearest approach the parts are taken nearest bound first, and the cutting ends when the nearest bound left is no nearer than the best found less a hair (a billionth of the size of the shapes, and never more than a thousandth of the distance); the distance is exact to rounding where Newton's method settles, which it does wherever the curves cross or the nearest points are not parallel, and otherwise right to that hair. For the places two splines meet, a part is left when the hulls show no meeting in it within the point tolerance.

Two splines that lie in one plane, every control point of both within a snap (1E-13 of the size of the numbers) of it, are worked out in that plane, as two splines of the plane are, and the points found are put back in space: the answers are the plane's, the offset of the one from the other having there the sign it has nowhere in space, and in a plane square to an axis they are the plane's to the bit. A tilted plane is laid flat by two directions of its own, so its answers are those of the plane turned, which for two curves that run a hair from each other the plane gives a place more or fewer for, as it does for the two turned in the plane.

Two curves in space that share no plane seldom meet: a place is where the distance between them is least within the point tolerance, a crossing being a place where it comes to nought. Where two splines stay within the point tolerance of each other, and level (their distance changing by no more than half the tolerance) for a quarter of the size of the smaller, seen from both of them, they lie along each other, as two circles 0.0005 apart in two planes do: the distance is the gap and no less, and a place in the stretch is a least of the distance where the two would cross if brought into one plane. Seen along the gap at the least, the first stands on one side of the second just before it and on the other just after, clear by a hundredth of the tolerance before it goes back: a polyline spline and its copy moved 0.0005 along its plane and lifted 0.0002 off it come nearest, 0.0002 apart, at the three corners where the two in the plane cross, and a copy 0.0005 across the plane with a wobble of 0.0001, lifted off it, comes nearest where the wobble brings it nearest but stays on one side, and meets nowhere, as in the plane. A spline and its own copy moved less than the tolerance out of every plane meet at each least of their distance in the stretch (a twisted cubic of 600 points and its copy moved 0.0009, at 69), since seen along the gap a curve and its copy moved along its tangent cross where the curve bends. The stretch is looked at four times as often as it is in the plane, and closer where the first spline turns, at every join of its pieces and where every join of the other is nearest it. The cutting for the least distance is bounded: past 40 000 pairs of parts in one question the curves are looked at at 128 points and the least of them brought to the real curves, and the answer is the best found, the distance of a real pair of points, with the nearest bound left in one Debug line (); the cutting for the places is bounded at two million pairs and logs one Debug line past it. Two parts that cannot meet are measured once both are no larger than the tolerance, so that two splines within the tolerance of each other round a turn tighter than a millimetre are not cut to a millionth.

A touch of two splines in space that share no plane, tangent to each other, is found to a snap or two and not to the last digit: the nearest pairs of two curves that touch lie along a valley, which Newton's method follows until a step gains less than a snap, so a spline about 1 000 across touching a parabola reads 6E-11 to 1.7E-10 from it, where the snap is 1E-10, and may read as not nought. A crossing at an angle is nought.

member.summary: Initializes a spline from its degree, control points and knots, and its weights if it is rational.
member.param: The degree, from 1 to 25: 1 for straight pieces, 2 for the conics of an arc, 3 for the cubics that draughtsmen and AutoCAD use.
The control points, at least degree + 1 and not all one point.
The knots, controlPoints + degree + 1 of them, not decreasing; the first degree + 1 equal and the last degree + 1 equal and above them, and no inner knot repeated more than degree times.

The weights, one for each control point and above nought, or null for all of them one, and no more than 1E12 to one apart (past that the length cannot be worked out right). All one is a plain B-spline, which says.
member.remarks: The numbers are copied, and kept as they are: nothing is rescaled or reordered. A spline of degree 3 with four control points takes the knots 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1; with a fifth it takes nine knots, such as 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 1.
member.exception: Thrown when the control points or the knots are null.
Thrown when the degree is outside 1 to 25, a weight is not a positive number, or the largest weight is more than 1E12 times the smallest.
Thrown when there are too few control points, a point or a knot is not a finite number, the knots are the wrong number or not clamped, or the control points are all one point.

member.param: The control points, at least degree + 1 and not all one point.
member.returns: The spline, not rational.
member.remarks: Seven control points of degree 3 have the knots 0, 0, 0, 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1, 1, 1, 1: the four spans of the curve take a quarter each of the parameter. With degree + 1 points it is the Bézier curve of the points.

Thrown when the degree is outside 1 to 25.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.Interpolate(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3},System.Int32)
member.summary: Builds the spline that passes through a list of fit points, as AutoCAD's fit-point splines do, with the curve left to settle its own direction at each end.
member.param: The points to pass through, in order; at least degree + 1 once the ones that coincide are dropped.
The degree, from 1 to 25, and at most one less than the number of points; 3 if not given.
member.returns: The spline, not rational, over [0, 1].

remarks.para: The method is global interpolation with chord-length parameters (Piegl and Tiller, The NURBS Book, 9.2.1). Each fit point is given a parameter equal to the share of the length of the chain through the points that comes before it, so that the points are met at parameters in proportion to how far apart they are; the inner knots are the averages of degree of those parameters in a row; and the control points are what makes the curve meet every fit point, found by solving one banded system, which costs the same for each point however many there are.
A fit point within the point tolerance of the one before it is dropped, as a polyline drops a vertex, since two points the same make parameters the same and a system that cannot be solved.

member.exception: Thrown when the points are null.
Thrown when the degree is outside 1 to 25.
Thrown when a point is not a finite point, or there are fewer than degree + 1 distinct points.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.Interpolate(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3},System.Int32,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Builds the spline that passes through a list of fit points, within a tolerance that decides which neighbouring fit points are one point.
member.param: The points to pass through, in order; at least degree + 1 once the ones that coincide are dropped.
The degree, from 1 to 25, and at most one less than the number of points.
The tolerance: a fit point within its point tolerance of the one kept before it is dropped.
member.returns: The spline, not rational, over [0, 1].
member.remarks: See . Points just above the tolerance are kept, and the chord lengths the parameters come from are then tiny beside the rest, so the curve can swing far between them, by hundreds of thousands where the chain turns, as it can in the plane (see ). Drop such points before asking, or give a tolerance that does.
member.exception: Thrown when the points are null.
Thrown when the degree is outside 1 to 25.
Thrown when a point is not a finite point, or there are fewer than degree + 1 distinct points.

member.summary: Builds the spline that passes through a list of fit points and leaves the first and arrives at the last in given directions.
member.param: The points to pass through, in order; at least two once the ones that coincide are dropped.
The direction at the first point; its length does not matter, and it may not be nought.
The direction at the last point; its length does not matter, and it may not be nought.
The degree, from 2 to 25, and at most one more than the number of points; 3 if not given.
member.returns: The spline, not rational, over [0, 1].
member.remarks: As , with the two end conditions added to the system: the curve has two more control points. A tangent gives a direction and nothing else: the curve leaves and arrives at the speed it keeps on average, which over [0, 1] is the length of the chain through the fit points, so that three points 100 apart along X with the tangent (1, 0, 0) at each end give the straight line through them, run at an even speed of 200, and a tangent of any other length gives the same curve.

Thrown when the degree is outside 2 to 25.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.FromArc(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoArc3)
member.summary: Builds the spline that is exactly an arc: rational quadratic pieces of a quarter turn at most, each the arc of its angle of a circle, to rounding.
member.returns: The spline, of degree 2 and rational, running the way the arc runs, over [0, 1] with each piece taking an equal share.
member.remarks: A quarter circle of radius 100 about the origin in the floor is one piece: the control points (100, 0, 0), (100, 100, 0), (0, 100, 0) with the weights 1, 0.7071, 1. A half circle is two pieces, a whole one four. The ends are the arc's own: the spline starts at and ends at its end point, but that an arc of a whole turn, and so the circle, ends on its start exactly, its first control point repeated.
member.exception: Thrown when the centre has a coordinate that is not a finite number.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.FromCircle(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3)
member.summary: Builds the spline that is exactly a circle: the rational quadratic of nine control points, four pieces of a quarter turn.
member.returns: The spline, of degree 2 and rational, from the circle's point at angle nought round counter-clockwise about its normal, closed.
member.remarks: Every point of the curve is at the radius from the centre to rounding, in the plane of the circle, and its length is 2 pi times the radius to a relative 1E-12.
member.exception: Thrown when the centre has a coordinate that is not a finite number.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.Length
member.summary: Gets the length of the spline, measured along it.
member.remarks: The integral of the speed, by Gauss-Legendre of ten points over each span, a span cut in halves wherever the rule over the whole and over its two halves disagree, until they agree to 1E-14 of the length of the span's control polygon, and cut at each place the speed is least, where a curve that turns back has a corner in what is integrated; a rational span whose weights are more than two to one apart is cut first. It is good to a relative 1E-12 and in practice to 1E-15: the circle of radius 100 comes out as 628.31853071796, which is 2 pi times 100. Where the speed falls to nought, at a cusp, it is good to a little less. It is worked out once.

member.summary: Cuts the spline in two at a normalised parameter.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.SplitAtKnot(System.Double)
member.summary: Cuts the spline in two at a value of its knots.
member.param: The knot value to cut at, above and below .
member.returns: The part before the knot value, over [DomainStart, knot], and the part after it, over [knot, DomainEnd].
member.remarks: Exact: the knot at the value is raised to the degree, which cuts the control polygon without moving the curve, so the two parts are the two pieces of the spline, with the same degree and weights, and meet at the point the spline has there, which is the last control point of the first and the first of the second, to the last bit. member.exception: Thrown when the knot value is not above the first knot and below the last.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.Reverse
member.summary: Gets the spline running the other way, from its end to its start.
member.returns: The spline with its control points and weights in the opposite order and its knots mirrored about the middle of the domain, so that it has the same domain: the point at a knot value is the point of the original at the knot value as far from the other end.
member.remarks: Each distinct knot is mirrored once, so knots that were equal stay equal and knots that were apart stay apart: where rounding would put two mirrored knots on one number the later is moved one unit in the last place on, and one that would land on the end of the domain one back. A mirrored knot is rounded to the last place of the domain's ends, which moves the curve by the speed times that.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSpline3.Flatten(System.Double)
member.summary: Approximates the spline as a chain of straight pieces, none of which strays further from it than a chord tolerance.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between the spline and the chain, in drawing units; above nought. There is no automatic one: a spline has no radius to take a share of.
member.returns: The chain, from the start of the spline to its end, its corners on the spline.

remarks.para: The promise holds however fine the tolerance, however sharp the bend and whatever the weights: every span is cut in halves until the piece is within the tolerance of the chord from its start to its end, as for : every control point of a piece within it, or the second differences of a piece that is not rational small enough, or the middle control point of a conic low enough. Pieces are cut in halves, so the circle of radius 100 within 0.01 is 256 chords where 223 would hold.

A tolerance that would need more than 1 048 576 pieces is refused. The result is a chain, which merges corners closer together than the point tolerance (1E-3 by default), so a tolerance whose pieces would be shorter than that is not kept, as for .

A spline no longer than the point tolerance, all of it within the tolerance of its start, which a chain would merge into one point, is the chain of its corners as they are, the repeats of one point to the bit left out: the part 0.000245 long that at a millionth cuts off the fit through (0, 0), (30, 20), (60, -10), (100, 0) is the chord from its start to its end, where it was refused. keeps such a part, exactly, as it keeps any other.

member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance is not a positive number, or needs more than 1 048 576 pieces.
Thrown when every corner the spline is cut at is the same point, to the bit: a spline that stands still, or a closed one whose chord tolerance is so large that it is cut at its ends alone.

member.returns: The distance from the point to the nearest point of the curve, measured exactly. The circle of radius 100 about the origin in the floor, as makes it, is 60 from (160, 0, 0), 100 from its own centre and 104.4 from (0, 0, 30), which is 100 across and 30 up from every point of the rim.
member.remarks: The nearest point is found as finds it: on each span the parameters where the curve stops coming nearer, all of them, from the roots of a polynomial in Bernstein form, and the ends; whichever span cannot be nearer than the best found, by the box of its control points, is not solved. The boxes are kept in a tree, built once, so the spans near the point are reached without looking at the rest: a query costs time in the logarithm of the number of spans and the number whose boxes are near the point, as in the plane.

member.summary: Gets the points where this spline crosses a line segment, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance: places no further than its point tolerance apart are one place.
member.returns: Every place where the two meet, once, as a point of the spline, in order along it from its start: where it crosses, where it touches without crossing, and where an end of the spline or of the shape comes within the point tolerance of the other. member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2
member.summary:
Represents a 2D transformation as a 3x3 homogeneous matrix, covering translation, rotation, scaling and mirroring.
The matrix is stored row-major and applied on the left, so a.Multiply(b) means "apply b, then a", the usual convention for column vectors. Instances are immutable: every operation returns a new transformation rather than changing this one. It is the counterpart in the plane of , and the two are built and read the same way.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2.Mirror(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine2)
member.summary: Creates a reflection across the line carrying a segment.
member.param: The segment, read as the infinite line carrying it.
member.returns: The transformation that mirrors everything across that line.
member.exception: Thrown when the segment has no length, its two ends one point.
member.remarks:
A reflection turns a shape round: a polygon that ran counter-clockwise comes back clockwise, and its signed area changes sign while its area does not.
A segment of any length carries its line: the segment from (0, 0) to (0.000007, 0.000007) mirrors (1, 0) to (0, 1), where it was read within the global vector tolerance of 1E-5 as having no direction and refused.
A line at 45 degrees swaps the two coordinates, and its matrix has whole numbers for entries: (0, 10) across the line y = x comes to (10, 0), where built from the unit direction (0.7071067811865476, 0.7071067811865476) it came to 9.999999999999998. The matrix is built from the direction divided by its greatest component, over its squared length.
member.exception: Thrown when the segment has an end that is not a finite point.

member.remarks: The determinant is judged against the size of the transformation rather than against zero: two axes of unit length turned almost onto each other give a determinant near zero, and inverting that yields numbers so large they mean nothing. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPolygon2)
member.summary: Transforms a polygon.
member.exception: Thrown when the polygon is null.
member.remarks:
A transformation that turns shapes round, a mirror or a negative scaling, reverses the winding: a polygon that ran counter-clockwise comes back clockwise.
The polygon is transformed side for side, however short a side, and however small the transformation leaves it: at a millionth, the triangle (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 10) with every corner cut by 0.0003 keeps its six corners turned, moved or mirrored, where it was put back together within the global tolerance of a thousandth and came back three, and the square 10 by 10 scaled by 1E-5 is the square 0.0001 across, where it was refused as having fewer than three corners. Only a corner the transformation lands on the very same point as the one before it goes.

member.summary: Transforms a face and its holes.
member.exception: Thrown when the face is null.
member.remarks: The boundary and each hole are transformed side for side, as transforms a polygon.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle2)
member.summary: Transforms a circle.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation would turn the circle into an ellipse.
member.remarks: A circle survives a transformation only when every direction is stretched by the same amount: when the two axes come out so nearly equally long and square to each other that the circle moved lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts each of its points, as a ball in space is read (). A turn whose numbers are rounded to six places or to a float on their own keeps the two axes alike to the last digit and moves a circle of any size; a stretch of 3E-6 along X moves the circle of radius 100 at the scale it is drawn, 0.0003 off at the most, and is refused scaled by 1 000, where it would be 0.3 off. Under a scaling that differs between the axes, or a shear, it becomes an ellipse, so the attempt is refused rather than answered with a circle of some averaged radius; transform to get the ellipse. The skew that sends X to (1, 0) and Y to (0.6, 0.8) keeps both lengths, and is refused: the circle of radius 100 would be an ellipse of radii 126.5 and 63.2.

member.summary: Determines whether the X and Y axes come out of the transformation so nearly equally long and square to each other that a circle of a radius moved by them lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts it, by : the rule by which a circle stays a circle.
member.remarks: A transformation that keeps shapes round to the rounding of a matrix built from axes, , is read by the same rule: its axes may still differ by a share of some 1E-9, which takes a circle moved to a radius of 1E8 up to 0.04 off.

member.summary: Determines whether the X and Y axes come out of the transformation of one length to the rounding of its numbers, as a turn, a skew or an even scaling leaves them, so that an arc under it is not stretched into part of an ellipse.

member.summary: Gets how far, at the most, a circle of a radius moved by two axes whose images are so long and lean on each other so much strays from where the transformation puts its points: the radius times the difference of the two lengths and the lean, the dot product over the longer of them.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2.KeepsRound(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector2,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector2)
member.summary: Determines whether the X and Y axes come out of the transformation square to each other and of one length to the rounding of a matrix built from axes, as a turn, a shift, a mirror or an even scaling leaves them: whether an arc can be moved whole, by its centre and its radius.
member.remarks: Judged as a share of the squared stretch, so alike at any size, and not against a tolerance: this asks what kind of transformation it is. A matrix rounded to six places or to a float is not one, and an arc under it goes through where its ends and its middle land.

member.summary: The share of the squared stretch by which the axes of a transformation that keeps shapes round may differ in length or lean on each other: the rounding of a matrix built from axes, as reads it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform2.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoRectangle2)
member.summary: Transforms a rectangle.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation would turn the rectangle into a parallelogram.
member.remarks: A rectangle stays a rectangle under a move, a turn, a mirror and a uniform scaling. A scaling that differs between the axes, or a shear, leaves a parallelogram instead, which this library has no type for: transform rectangle.ToPolygon() when that is what you want. The axes are read as a circle as large as the rectangle's half diagonal reads them: they have to come out so nearly equally long and square to each other that its corners land within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts them. The rectangle 100 by 50 is moved under a shear of 5E-6 at the scale it is drawn, its corners 0.00018 off, and refused scaled by 1 000, where they would be 0.18 off; a turn whose numbers are rounded to six places or to a float on their own moves it at any scale. A transformation that keeps shapes round to the rounding of a matrix built from axes is read alike: a scaling by 1 000 with X a share of 4E-10 longer moves the rectangle 200 by 100 at the scale it is drawn, and refuses the one 2E8 by 1E8, whose corners it took 44 off.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Mirror(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3)
member.summary: Creates a mirroring across a plane.
member.remarks:
Mirroring reverses handedness, so its determinant is negative and shapes come back with their winding flipped: a polygon normal points the other way afterwards.
A plane at 45 degrees swaps two coordinates, and its matrix has whole numbers for entries: (0, 10) across the plane y = x comes to (10, 0) and across y = x - 50 to (60, -50), where built from the unit normal (0.7071067811865476, -0.7071067811865476) every entry was a last digit off and the first came to 10.000000000000002. The matrix is built from the normal divided by its greatest component, over its squared length.

member.summary: Creates the transformation that takes local coordinates of a coordinate system into world coordinates.
member.remarks: is the reverse.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.ToCoordinateSystem(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3)
member.summary: Creates the transformation that takes world coordinates into the local coordinates of a coordinate system, the reverse of .

remarks.para: It does for a whole shape what does for a point: take the shape into the frame through TransformBy, work on it in local coordinates, and put the result back with . A frame given in the local coordinates of another nests by multiplying, the outer one read into first: ToCoordinateSystem(inner) * ToCoordinateSystem(outer).

A coordinate system is rigid, so nothing is inverted: its axes become the rows as they stand, and only the translation, the origin read along each axis, is worked out. Inverting the placement with reaches the same matrix the long way, through cofactors and a division by the determinant.

member.summary: Combines this transformation with another one.
member.returns: The transformation that applies and then this one.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.GetDeterminant
member.summary: Gets the determinant of the matrix.
member.remarks: The determinant is the factor by which the transformation multiplies volume. It is negative for a transformation that reverses handedness, and zero for one that flattens space, which is exactly the case cannot undo. That method judges this value against the size of the transformation rather than against zero, so a transformation it refuses need not have a determinant of exactly zero.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.KeepsLengths
member.summary: Determines whether the transformation keeps every length: a turn, a shift or a mirror, and nothing that stretches, shears or flattens.
member.remarks: Judged on the matrix to the rounding of a matrix built from axes, not against a tolerance: this asks what kind of transformation it is, not whether two shapes are alike.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.KeepsShapes(System.Double@)
member.summary: Determines whether the transformation keeps every shape: a turn, a shift, a mirror or an even scaling, and nothing that stretches one way more than another, shears or flattens. Gives the factor it multiplies areas by.
member.remarks: The three axes have to come out square to each other and of one length, within the global vector tolerance as a share of that length, so that a matrix rounded to six places or to a float is read as the turn or the scaling it stands for. The factor for areas is the mean of the squared lengths of the three axes: 100 for a scaling by 10.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Stretched(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Gets a tolerance a shape that lay flat and had width within another is read within once transformed: its planar threshold stretched as far as the transformation stretches any direction, where it stretches, and its point threshold shrunk as far, where it shrinks.
member.remarks: The stretch is the largest singular value of the matrix without its shift, the square root of the largest eigenvalue of the products of its axes: 10 for a scaling by 10 along X alone, 0.3 for one by 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3. No corner lands further off the plane than that many times as far as it was, and nothing is narrower than its width shrunk that many times or more. Neither threshold is made finer than it was: a polygon built within a coarser tolerance, or a small one standing across a stretch, was kept within the one given and is kept still. The vector and angle thresholds are not lengths and stay as they are.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.ReadCarrying
member.summary: Reads once how the transformation carries a polygon, so that a face or a body hands the reading to every polygon it holds rather than each polygon reading the matrix again: a box's six faces read it once, not twelve times.
member.remarks: The reading is kept, with the global tolerance it was read within, so that a list of polygons transformed one by one pays for one reading; a move or an even scaling does not depend on that tolerance, anything else is read again once it changes. The matrix never changes once the transformation is handed out, and the kept reading is replaced whole, so a thread sees an old reading or a new one, never a mix.

member.summary: Gets the product of the lengths of the three transformed axes, which is the size a determinant of this transformation is measured against.
member.remarks: For a transformation that keeps its axes square this is exactly the determinant, so the test it feeds asks how far the three axes have been flattened towards a common plane rather than how large they are.

member.summary: Tries to get the transformation that undoes this one, without throwing, using the default tolerance.
member.param: The inverse when the method returns true; otherwise the identity.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.TryGetInverse(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3@,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Tries to get the transformation that undoes this one, without throwing, within a tolerance.
member.param: The inverse when the method returns true; otherwise the identity.
The tolerance deciding when the transformation has collapsed.
member.returns: false when the transformation collapses space and cannot be undone.
member.remarks: The determinant is judged against the size of the transformation rather than against zero. A determinant of exactly zero is the only case a bare == catches, and it is not the case that hurts: three axes that are very nearly coplanar give a determinant around 1e-16 while each axis is still of unit length, and dividing the cofactors by that yields a matrix of enormous numbers reported as a valid inverse. Scaling the threshold by the product of the axis lengths is what makes the test mean "collapsed" rather than "small", so a model in millimetres and the same model in metres are judged alike.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPlane3)
member.summary: Transforms a plane.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation is not invertible, or the normal comes out of it of no length to the rounding of its numbers.
member.remarks: A plane normal is not transformed like a direction. Under a non-uniform scaling a direction in the plane and the normal are stretched differently, and applying the same matrix to both would leave them no longer perpendicular. The normal follows the inverse transpose instead, which is the matrix that preserves that right angle. It comes out as long as the inverse makes it, a hundred-thousandth under an even scaling by 100 000, and is made of unit length by its own length, not judged against a tolerance: the plane is carried under any scaling that can be undone, where a scaling of about 1E5 or more threw, the normal read shorter than the vector tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCoordinateSystem3)

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoObb3)
member.summary: Transforms an oriented box.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation collapses the box orientation.
member.remarks: A box stays a box only under a transformation that keeps right angles right. A shear turns it into a parallelepiped, which this type cannot represent, and what comes back then is the box spanned by the transformed axes rather than the true sheared shape.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoAabb3)
member.summary: Transforms an axis-aligned box.
member.remarks: A box aligned with the world axes does not stay aligned once it is rotated, so what comes back is the smallest aligned box holding the transformed corners. That is larger than the true transformed shape whenever the transformation turns it, which is the price of insisting on alignment; transform a instead to keep the shape exactly.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3)
member.summary: Transforms a circle.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation would turn the circle into an ellipse.
member.remarks: A circle survives a transformation only when every direction in its plane is stretched by the same amount: when the two axes of its plane come out so nearly equally long and square to each other that the circle moved lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts each of its points, as a ball is read (). A turn that keeps them alike to the rounding of its numbers moves a circle of any size; a turn whose numbers are rounded to six places on their own leaves them some 1E-6 apart, and moves the circle of radius 100 at the scale it is drawn, 0.000065 off, but not scaled by 1 000, where it would be 0.065 off. Under a non-uniform scaling or a shear it becomes an ellipse, which gives, so the attempt is refused rather than answered with a circle of some averaged radius. The skew that sends X to (1, 0, 0) and Y to (0.6, 0.8, 0) keeps both lengths, and is refused for a circle in the plan: it would be an ellipse of radii 126.5 and 63.2 for a radius of 100. The circle's plane is carried by its normal (), under an even scaling of 1E5 or more as under any other: the circle of radius 10 scaled by a million is the circle of radius 10 000 000, where it threw. An arc on a circle is carried by , through where its ends and its middle land.

member.summary: Determines whether two axes of a plane, square to each other and of one length, come out of the transformation of one length to the rounding of its numbers, as a turn, a skew or an even scaling leaves them, so that an arc in that plane is not stretched into part of an ellipse.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.KeepsRound(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3)
member.summary: Determines whether two axes of a plane, square to each other and of one length, come out of the transformation square and of one length again to the rounding of a matrix built from axes, as a turn, a shift, a mirror or an even scaling leaves them: whether an arc in that plane can be moved whole, by its centre and its radius.
member.remarks: Judged as a share of the squared stretch, as judges it, so alike at any size, and not against a tolerance: this asks what the transformation does to the plane. A stretch square to the plane leaves it round; a matrix rounded to six places or to a float does not.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Carry(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoCircle3,System.Double)
member.summary: The circle moved, its radius stretched as the axes of its plane are.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTransform3.Transform(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSphere3)
member.summary: Transforms a ball.
member.exception: Thrown when the transformation would turn the ball into an ellipsoid, or flatten it.
member.remarks: A ball survives a transformation only when every direction is stretched by the same amount and none is sheared against another, so nearly that the ball moved lands within the global point tolerance of where the transformation puts each of its points, the three axes read in pairs as a circle reads two (): a turn, a shift, a mirror or an even scaling, under which the radius is scaled by the stretch (a ball of radius 50 scaled by 3 has a radius of 150). A turn, a shift or a mirror leaves the radius as it is. Under a non-uniform scaling or a shear it would be an ellipsoid, which this library has no type for, so the attempt is refused rather than answered with a ball of some averaged radius. A transformation that keeps lengths, or shapes round, to the rounding of a matrix built from axes is read by the same rule, its axes differing by a share of up to some 1E-9: the ball of radius 1E8 under X stretched by a share of 4E-10 is refused, where it came through 0.04 off.

Represents a triangle in the plane, defined by three vertices.
A polygon or a face of the plane broken into triangles comes back as these, from and its kin, and a triangle answers the questions every other shape of the plane does. It is laid flat: three points always make a triangle, even one of no area, so nothing is checked at construction.
A triangle asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3
member.summary: Whether a triangle touches another shape.

Represents a triangle in 3D space, defined by three vertices.
The triangle is the unit every other surface in this library is measured through. A polygon answers containment, area and intersection by fanning into triangles, and a solid does the same through its faces, so the hard cases live here once instead of once per shape. Three points are always coplanar, which is why a triangle needs no flatness check while a polygon does.
How far a triangle is from another shape, and how deep inside one it sits.
Where a triangle crosses another shape.
The point of a triangle nearest another shape, the shortest segment joining the two, and which edge of it faces one.
A triangle asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A triangle asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.
A triangle asked about an infinite line: whether they touch, how far apart they are, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.summary: Checks whether the triangle has no area, using the default tolerance.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3.IsDegenerate(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether the triangle has no area, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: A triangle has no area when its height over its longest side is within the point tolerance, so that it lies within the tolerance of that side, a segment; or when its corners lie on one line to rounding, so that it has no normal. The test is a length against a length: a triangle 0.002 by 0.002 is a triangle at the default tolerance, and a sliver 1 000 long and 0.0004 high is not, where twice the area read against the vector tolerance called the first nothing and the second a triangle. The queries of a triangle, CollidesWith, GetIntersections and Locate among them, read no area by this too: the triangle 0.003 by 0.003 is a triangle to them, holding its centroid and crossed by a segment through its middle, and a triangle with none is the segment it has collapsed to, touching what comes within the point tolerance of it and crossed where its sides are.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3.IsDegenerateByArea(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether twice the area is within the vector tolerance: the reading of no area that the library's meshing, booleans and splitting keep, bit for bit, where a triangle with none is left out of a mesh.
member.remarks: It reads a length squared against a length, the trap no longer falls into: a triangle 0.002 by 0.002 has no area by it at the default tolerance, and a sliver 1 000 long and 0.0004 high has. The queries read ; the paths that still read this are pinned to what they answer by it, and moving them is a step of its own.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoTriangle3.TryGetBarycentric(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,System.Double@,System.Double@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Gets the barycentric coordinates of a point with respect to this triangle.
member.param: The point to express; it need not lie on the triangle.
member.returns: false when the triangle has no area by at the global tolerance, its height over its longest side within the point tolerance, in which case all three weights are zero: the triangle 100 long and 0.0005 high gives false at the default tolerance, where twice its area, 0.05, read against the vector tolerance gave true. The containment of a point in a triangle reads it at the tolerance it is asked within instead. A point with a coordinate that is not a finite number gives false too, where it was given weights of NaN.
member.remarks: The point is projected onto the triangle plane first, so a point off the plane gets the coordinates of its projection. The three weights always sum to one, and all three are non-negative exactly when the projection falls inside the triangle.

The segment is never snapped: a triangle a hair off the plane is joined by a segment that short, though the distance, read within the point tolerance, is nought.
