member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3.GetPerpendicularVector
member.summary: Gets an arbitrary unit vector perpendicular to this one.
member.returns: A unit vector perpendicular to this vector.
member.exception: Thrown when the vector has zero length, or a coordinate that is not a finite number.
member.remarks: In 3D a vector has a whole plane of perpendiculars and no way to prefer one, so which of them comes back is unspecified beyond being perpendicular and of unit length. It is stable for a given input. The axis crossed against is the one this vector leans on least, which keeps the cross product well away from zero and the result well conditioned.

member.param: The axis the rotation is measured around, which fixes what counts as the positive direction.
member.exception: Thrown when any of the three vectors has zero length.
member.remarks: An angle between two vectors in 3D has no sign of its own: the rotation that takes one to the other looks counter-clockwise from one side and clockwise from the other. The reference axis is what picks the side, which is why this overload needs one and the 2D case does not.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoXLine2
member.summary: Whether an infinite line touches another shape.
member.remarks: A closed shape is read as filled: a line reaching its material collides with it. The line through (50, 50) along X runs through the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin and collides with it; the line through (-50, 150) along X passes above it and does not.
member.summary: Represents an infinite line in the plane: a point on it and a direction it runs along both ways for ever, the counterpart of with no start, and of the XLINE of AutoCAD.

remarks.para: The line from (-50, 50) along X passes through the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin, entering it at (0, 50) and leaving it at (100, 50); a ray from the same point turned round runs away from the square, but this line does not leave it behind. The same line is also the line from (500, 50) along -X: reads the fields and tells the two apart, reads the line and does not.
It is asked what a segment is asked, as is, and a closed shape is read as filled.

member.summary: How far an infinite line is from another shape.
member.remarks: A closed shape is read as filled, as reads it: a line through a polygon is nought from it. The line through (-50, 150) along X passes 50 above the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin.
member.summary: Where an infinite line crosses another shape.
member.remarks: The crossings are those of the boundary, in the order and with the repeats left out that a segment's are. The line through (-50, 50) along X crosses the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin at (0, 50) and at (100, 50), and a line through the middle of the square gives the same two whatever its origin.
member.summary: The point of an infinite line nearest a point, and the shortest segment joining a line to another shape.
member.remarks: Both ends of a shortest segment sit on a boundary, and it leaves this line. A line runs on both ways for ever, so one through a closed shape crosses its outline, and the segment is the point where it does: the line through (50, 50) along X, in the square 100 by 100 with a corner at the origin, gets the segment of no length at (0, 50) or (100, 50).
member.summary: An infinite line asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.summary: Initializes a line from a direction that is already normalized.
member.remarks: Normalizing a vector that is already of unit length is not the identity in floating point: the computed length comes back a bit either side of one, and dividing by it shifts the last digits. Operations that only move a line around, or turn a ray into one, must not pay that, or a copy would come back unequal to its original and reversing twice would drift. This constructor is how they skip it.

One that misses it by no more than the point tolerance, the line along X through (0, 100.0005) over that square, touches it as says, and is clipped to the rectangle grown by the tolerance: from (-0.001, 100.0005) to (100.001, 100.0005), its ends no more than the tolerance outside the rectangle on either axis. member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoXLine3
member.summary: Whether an infinite line touches another shape in space.
member.remarks: A closed shape is read as filled: a line reaching its material collides with it. The line through (50, 50, 10) along X runs through the box 100 by 100 by 20 with a corner at the origin and collides with it; the line through (-50, 150, 10) along X passes beside it and does not. Two shapes touch where the exact gap between them is no more than the point tolerance, so a line 0.0005 above the top of the box touches it and one 0.002 above does not.
member.summary: Represents an infinite line in space: a point on it and a direction it runs along both ways for ever, the counterpart of with no start, of in the plane, and of the XLINE of AutoCAD.

remarks.para: The line from (-50, 50, 10) along X passes through the box 100 by 100 by 20 with a corner at the origin, entering it at (0, 50, 10) and leaving it at (100, 50, 10); a ray from the same point turned round runs away from the box, but this line does not leave it behind. The same line is also the line from (500, 50, 10) along -X: reads the fields and tells the two apart, reads the line and does not.

It is asked what a segment is asked, as is, and a closed shape is read as filled. Two lines in space are skew unless they happen to cross: they are as far apart as the common perpendicular between them is long, and nought apart where they meet.

member.summary: How far an infinite line is from another shape in space.
member.remarks: A closed shape is read as filled, as reads it: a line through a solid is nought from it. The line through (-50, 150, 10) along X passes 50 beside the box 100 by 100 by 20 with a corner at the origin. The curved shapes (an arc, a circle, an ellipse, an edge and the curved chains) are not measured, as they are not for a ray or a segment: the distance from a curve in space to anything but a point has no closed form, and ToPolyline3(chordTolerance) is the way to ask for it. They are asked whether they touch and where they cross.
member.summary: Where an infinite line crosses another shape in space.
member.remarks: The crossings are those of the surface or the boundary, in the order and with the repeats left out that a segment's are. The line through (-50, 50, 10) along X crosses the box 100 by 100 by 20 with a corner at the origin at (0, 50, 10) and at (100, 50, 10), in that order, and a line through the middle of the box gives the same two whatever its origin. A flat shape is crossed at one point, or nowhere: a line lying in its plane names no place.
member.summary: The point of an infinite line nearest a point, and the shortest segment joining a line to another shape in space.
member.remarks: Both ends of a shortest segment sit on a boundary, and it leaves this line. A line runs on both ways for ever, so one through a closed shape crosses its surface, and the segment is the point where it does: the line through (50, 50, 10) along X, in the box 100 by 100 by 20 with a corner at the origin, gets the segment of no length at (0, 50, 10) or (100, 50, 10). The curved shapes are not measured, as they are not for a ray or a segment (see ), and the boxes go through ToSolid().
member.summary: An infinite line asked about a ball: how far apart they are, whether they touch, where they cross, and where the shortest segment between them runs.
An infinite line asked how far it is from a spline, whether they touch, where they cross and where the shortest segment between them runs.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoXLine3.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoPoint3,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoVector3,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Initializes a line from a direction that is already normalized.
member.remarks: Normalizing a vector that is already of unit length is not the identity in floating point: the computed length comes back a bit either side of one, and dividing by it shifts the last digits. Operations that only move a line around, or turn a ray into one, must not pay that, or a copy would come back unequal to its original and reversing twice would drift. This constructor is how they skip it.

member.summary: Gets the part of this line inside an axis-aligned box, within a tolerance.
member.param: The tolerance: a line that misses the box by no more than the point tolerance is clipped to the box grown by it.
member.returns: The segment where the line is inside the box, running along the direction of the line; null when it misses or the box is empty.

remarks.para: Meant for drawing: the line through (-50, 50, 10) along X, clipped to the box 100 by 100 by 20 with a corner at the origin, is the segment from (0, 50, 10) to (100, 50, 10); the line along Y through (150, 0, 10) misses it and gives null.

A line that crosses the box is clipped to it exactly. One that misses it by no more than the point tolerance, the line along X through (0, 50, 20.0005) over that box, touches it as says, and is clipped to the box grown by the tolerance: from (-0.001, 50, 20.0005) to (100.001, 50, 20.0005), its ends no more than the tolerance outside the box on any axis. One that misses it by more gives null.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Clipper.WalkStarts
member.summary: Where the walk that puts a left bound into the active edge list may start, so that the local minima of one scanline do not each walk the list from its head.
member.remarks:
The walk from the head passes every edge that belongs to the left of the bound and stops at the first that does not, and every edge it passes stands at an X no greater than the bound's. While the minima of one scanline go in, no edge changes its X or leaves the list, and right bounds only move right; an edge that goes in to the left of where an earlier walk stopped belongs left of an edge that walk passed, so it too stands no further right than that walk's bound. A later bound at a greater X than an earlier one therefore passes every edge up to where the earlier walk stopped, and its walk can start there and ends where the walk from the head would have, to the edge. The places a walk stopped are kept by X in as many buckets as the scanline has minima. A zigzag of 100 000 vertices, its minima on one line, was united in 5.9 seconds and is now in 0.11, with the same paths to the point.
Once the walks of a line have passed 16 edges for each of its minima, the edges in the list then are kept too, where they stand in order of X, and a walk may start, or the walk that passed that many go on, at the last of them below the bound's X: every edge before it stands no further right, so the walk from the head passes it. Bounds going in keep every edge before a kept one at an X no greater than the kept one's: a bound goes in after edges below its X, or just after the edge joined to the last of them, which stands no further right than the kept edges after it; and its right bound moves right only past edges at no greater X. Where the list is long beside the minima of a line, each walked from the nearest minimum done before it, in the order they come, past the whole list again for every doubling of those done: a zigzag of 400 000 vertices, its minima at 50 heights and its maxima at 30, spent 6.7 of its 9 seconds so.

member.remarks: A walk that passes many edges keeps the stretch it walked, from the edge it found (or the head) to ae, as one with no such edge inside, and a later walk that comes to the stretch's right end goes on from its left end. The stretch is kept true as edges come to add to output paths, swap places and leave the list; an edge that comes to add to one just inside it becomes its right end, so that the walk from that edge, which follows, starts at the end. The tips of a comb pointing up, offset by -0.5, its horizontals done from the right, each walked past every tooth not yet done to the head of the list, and those of a comb pointing down, offset by 0.5, to the left side of its back: a comb of 20 000 teeth spent 3.8 of its 3.9 seconds so.

member.remarks: A vertex is the top of at most two edges at a time, the two of the path that meet at it, and each edge given a top is noted on the vertex (see ). member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.SetOwner(GeometryHelper.Clipper.OutRec,GeometryHelper.Clipper.OutRec)
member.summary: Makes newOwner the owner of the output path. Owners of newOwner that were emptied are skipped, and when the path itself owns newOwner, newOwner takes the path's own owner first, so that no path comes to own itself.
member.remarks: While every output path of the sweep has no owner or an older one, of a lower index (_ownersOlder), the owners up from newOwner only grow older, so a path newer than newOwner is none of them and is not looked for. Every owner given here, or in ProcessHorzJoins without a polytree, is noted by NoteOwner; every other owner given while the sweep and its joins run is older by how it is chosen: one up the chain of the path, or one given to a path just made, newer than all. Squares of side 10 in a row are joined each into an older one, and the chain up from it ran back along the row: 1 000 000 squares walked 1 750 million owners here and took 9.6 seconds to unite on .NET 10, 4.3 now. Once an owner no older than its path has been given, the path is looked for again whatever newOwner's age: skipping the walk for every older newOwner, case 0 of seed 1 of the clip fuzz, of random paths, never ends, its owners coming round in a ring.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.GetRealOutRecOfEmptied(GeometryHelper.Clipper.OutRec)
member.summary: The first owner of the emptied output path that has points, as GetRealOutRec gives it; on the way, every emptied path walked is given as its owner the next path up the chain that has points or splits, so that the next walk from any of them is short, as the find of a union-find shortens its chains.

remarks.para: Once a path is emptied and given the owner it was joined into, it never has points again (the open path that JoinOutrecPaths empties and fills again has them back before any walk), only this walk changes that owner, and only paths with points gain splits. So a walk up the chain from any path still passes every path with points and every path with splits it passed before, and RecursiveCheckOwners reads the splits of the paths on its way up; it skips only emptied paths without splits, none of them the path SetOwner or IsValidOwner looks for, which has points or was emptied after the last walk. Every answer is the same to the bit; passing over the emptied paths with splits as well, 48 of 20 000 fuzz cases nest their polytrees otherwise.

Each path joined into the next kept the chain of all those joined before it, and every horizontal segment of the answer walked that chain from the path its point was first added to: 50 000 squares of side 10 standing on a strip took 9.8 seconds to unite on .NET 10, and 1 000 000 side by side 18.1, 8.7 of them in these walks; 0.3 and 9.5 now.

member.remarks: Once one walk passes more than 64 points, or the walks between them more than the budget, the ends of each run walked are filed under every point of it, and a segment on a run filed for the same output path takes them from there, as the walk from any of its points finds the same two; a ring lying wholly at the Y and closed is never filed, its ends hanging on where the walk began. Shapes standing side by side along a line make one long run there, and every segment on it walked the whole of it, only to find its left end claimed: 10 000 squares of side 10 in a row walked 600 million points, 3.8 of the 3.9 seconds Clipper2 took to unite them.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.LeftmostOfRuns(System.Int32)
member.summary: For each of the first k horizontal segments, sorted, the least X that its left point, or that of any segment after it, can come to while they are paired; null where they are too few to need it, do not all lie at one Y, or lie on runs too long to walk.
member.remarks: Pairing moves a left point only to a neighbour at the same Y, and only adds copies of points beside them, so a left point stays on the run of points at that Y it lies on, and never goes left of the least X along it. The segments being sorted by their left points, the least of those from each one on rises nearly as they do, and the pairing of a segment can stop where it reaches its right point: the segments after cannot overlap it. A comb of 25 000 teeth spent 1.3 seconds trying every pair of the 50 000 segments along its two edges.

Clipper2's C++ also refuses a ring of two points and a triangle with two corners less than two units apart, but this test of the triangle only runs on rings of two points, where it never holds, so both are left to BuildPath, which drops them. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.CleanCollinearOnward(GeometryHelper.Clipper.OutRec,GeometryHelper.Clipper.OutPt)

member.summary: The lines of the finished path of the output path, made the first time they are asked for and kept by its index, through which points are found against it while the polytree is built; null for a path of fewer than 64 points or with empty bounds, which is looked through point by point.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.GetOwnerToCheck(GeometryHelper.Clipper.OutRec)
member.summary: The first owner up the chain of the emptied output path, which has no splits, that has points or splits, or null; every path walked is given it as its owner on the way, so that the next walk from any of them is short.
member.remarks: RecursiveCheckOwners passes over such paths one by one, and no path emptied without splits gains points or splits while the polytree is built, so its walk from any path goes on as it did. Each hole of 20 000 teeth standing on a strip, one in each, was owned by its tooth's path, joined into the next as the sweep went along: 200 million owners walked, where 20 000 are now.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.CheckSplitOwner(GeometryHelper.Clipper.OutRec,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32})
member.summary: Looks among the paths split off an owner, and those split off them, for one that holds the output path; makes it the owner and returns true when it finds one.
member.remarks: The lists are walked with a stack of their own, in the order the recursion of the C# original walks them, so that a chain of splits thousands deep does not run out of the thread's stack. A path with no points whose splits lead back to a list already being walked is passed over: the original walked that list again from its start, and in some cases came to the same place and recursed until the stack overflowed (case 194 of seed 1 of the LN9 clip fuzz, a polytree of a union of zigzags); where its walk ended, of 3 600 fuzz cases, the owner it chose is the one chosen here.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.SplitWalk
member.summary: Where the walk of one list of splits stands: the split it is at, and how far that split has been looked at, the splits of a path with no points (stage 1 next), those of the path it stands for (stage 2 next) or its bounds.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Clipper.ClipperBase.RingLines
member.summary: Finds points against a finished closed path as PointInOpPolygon finds them against its ring, through the crossings of the path with the line of each point's Y, sorted along X, so that many points on few lines cost a search each rather than a walk round the path.

remarks.para: PointInOpPolygon gives IsOn when the point lies on a vertex or an edge of the ring, else IsInside or IsOutside by the even-odd count of the edges that cross the point's line left of it (and IsOutside when every point of the ring is on that line, which a path with bounds of some height is not). Where the ring runs along the line or touches it at a vertex, it counts a crossing at the last vertex of the run, and the edges counted here, those with one end below the line (smaller Y) and the other on or above it, count it at the first; the two counts differ only for a point on the run between, which is IsOn either way. The finished path is the ring without the points that repeat the one before, so it has the same edges.

The lines are kept in 64 slots by their Y, a line taking the slot of another that falls in it, and one is made the third time in a row its slot is asked for a point on it, while the lines made hold no more than four entries for each point of the path; any other point is left to PointInOpPolygon. So a path asked for a few points on many lines, round a few holes, costs what it did, with no table to look in. Along a line the crossings are kept at X worked out in doubles, off by less than half the margin used, and those within the margin of the point are worked out exactly, by CrossProductSign, as PointInOpPolygon works them out. 20 000 teeth standing on a strip, each with a hole and an island, asked for 40 000 points against a path of 80 000 points, on few lines: 3.2 billion points walked, most of the 32 seconds the polytree took on .NET 10; 0.4 now.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Guard
member.summary: Argument checks that a value which is not a number cannot slip past.
member.remarks: Every comparison with NaN is false, so a check written as "if the radius is below nought, throw" let a NaN radius through: the negative radius was refused and the NaN one taken, and the shape built from it then answered NaN or false to every question without a word. These checks state what the value has to be, so NaN fails them; infinity fails them too, since no size, distance or tolerance is infinite.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.ArcPairs
member.summary: Two arcs of circles in the plane, a piece of a curve and a piece of its partner, met in closed form as the circles meet: where the library's own two circles cross or touch, or, where they are one circle, along the stretch they share.

remarks.para: Two circles nearly about one centre are as near as the digits tell for a long way round, and cut into straight parts they pair every part of the one with hundreds of the other's: the circle splines of radius 100 000 and 100 000.0005 with their centres 0.01 apart ran through two million pairs in 16 seconds and gave no crossing, where the circles cross at (-4 999.995, 99 874.922) and (-4 999.995, -99 874.922). Their two arcs are answered by the rule of with the reach for the point tolerance, so that a spline made of arcs and the circles it is made from say the same: a crossing or a touch where the circles have one, kept where both arcs hold it; and two circles within the reach of each other all the way round, one circle to the rule, lie along each other over the stretch both arcs cover, which gives no place.

For the nearest approach the arcs are measured as they are, not through the reach: where the circles truly cross, the crossings, and otherwise the two points of the first circle on the line through the centres, where two circles come nearest and farthest. The start of the piece is looked at too, where the curve may turn a corner.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.ArcPairs.Exact(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.PieceArc,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.PieceArc,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether two arcs are known well enough to be met in closed form: their centres and radii, as read from the numbers they are made of, within a hundredth of the reach of the true circles for the places, and within a snap for the distance. A flat arc, of radius 1 000 000 and chord 300, has its centre read from its control points to no better than 2E-4, and the rule of the two circles read so would give places the arcs do not have; such a pair is cut as any other, unless the two are one circle to the rule however far the reading may be off, their centres and radii within the reach of each other with the doubt on each counted twice: then they lie along each other, as the arcs do, which no doubt about where they would cross can change.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Bernstein
member.summary:
Polynomials in Bernstein form on [0, 1]: the coefficients of a polynomial of degree n, as an array of n + 1 numbers, are the values its control polygon has, and the polynomial stays inside the hull of them.
Everything a spline needs from a polynomial is done here without leaving that form: the product of two, the derivative, one cut in halves, one evaluated, and every root in [0, 1] found. The roots are found by the variation-diminishing property: a polynomial whose coefficients never change sign has no root, one whose coefficients change sign once has exactly one, and anything else is cut in halves. That is why none is missed, however close two lie, as a search that steps along the interval and looks for a change of sign can.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Bernstein.MostDepth
member.summary: The deepest a root search cuts one interval in halves, and the width at which what is left of it is taken as the root.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Bernstein.MostIntervals
member.summary: The most intervals one search looks at. It is never reached by an honest polynomial; it stops a polynomial that is rounding noise from cutting itself to pieces.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Bernstein.Pascal
member.summary: The binomial coefficients up to the degree of the largest product a spline asks for: the speed of a rational spline of degree p, squared and then differentiated, is 4 p - 3, and it is multiplied by the weights of degree p, so 5 p - 3, which is 122 at the most degree of 25. Rows past 56 hold a rounded sum, as the note on says.

member.summary: Gets the binomial coefficient n over k, which is exact as a double up to n = 56 and good to a unit in the last place beyond.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Bernstein.FindRoots(System.Double[],System.Double,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Double})
member.summary: Finds every root of a polynomial in [0, 1] and adds each to a list, in no particular order and some twice.
member.param: How large a coefficient has to be to count: a polynomial all of whose coefficients are no larger than this is rounding noise round zero, and its middle is given as the one root where it stands, since all of it is as good. The caller knows the size of the numbers the coefficients were worked out from.

remarks.para: Only a root where the polynomial changes sign is looked for, which is the kind that matters here: a distance or a coordinate is smallest or largest where its derivative crosses nought. A root of even multiplicity, where the polynomial touches nought and turns back, is where the derivative of a distance has a flat spot and no extreme, so it is not given. A pair of roots closer together than a double can tell apart is given as one, at the middle of the interval round it, which is as good to rounding as either of them, since all that is asked of a root is the value it gives.
A coefficient of exactly nought at an end of an interval is a root at that end, and is given; the signs are then counted without it, so that the rest of the interval is searched as it was.

member.summary: Finds the one root inside an interval whose coefficients change sign once, by Newton's method held inside the bracket that the sign gives, which bisects whenever a step would leave it.
member.param: The sign of the polynomial just after nought: that of the first coefficient that is not nought.
member.returns: The root, in (0, 1) unless rounding put it on an end.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve
member.summary:
A NURBS curve in two or three dimensions held as flat arrays of numbers: the one engine under and , so that the mathematics is written, and checked, once.
The curve is clamped: its first and last + 1 knots are equal, so it starts at its first control point and ends at its last. It is immutable; every operation gives a new curve and leaves this one as it was, so the arrays are shared freely between a curve and the ones made from it.
A rational curve is worked in homogeneous coordinates, a control point at (w x, w y, w z, w), where the points move in a space one dimension up and are divided by w at the end; with positive weights every step is a mean, and so cannot go wrong by more than rounding. A curve whose weights are all one has no w at all: the weight is neither stored nor divided by, so that a plain B-spline is worked on exactly its own numbers.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.TryGetArc(System.Int32,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.PieceArc@)
member.summary: Says whether a Bézier piece of a curve in the plane is an arc of a circle, to rounding, and gives the circle: a rational quadratic piece whose two outer control points are as far from the middle one, and whose middle weight, against the outer two, is the cosine of half the turn, the half chord over that distance, as every piece of and is made. Worked out once for the whole curve.
member.param: The arc, when the method returns true.
member.remarks: To rounding is to a millionth of a millionth of the size of the numbers: an arc of radius 100 000 has its control points to some 1E-11, and a piece that bows off a circle by more than 1E-12 of its numbers is no arc. The centre is the meeting of the lines square to the piece at its ends, worked out from the middle control point and the middle of the chord, and the rounding of the control points, taken at the size of the radius as the arc was made from its centre, reaches it times four times the square of the radius over the chord (): a quarter turn of radius 100 000 has its centre to 1E-10, an arc of radius 1 000 000 and chord 300 to no better than a fiftieth, 2.3E-4 when it was measured, and one of radius 10 000 000 and chord 1 000 a hundred thousand out to no better than two, 0.6 when it was measured.

member.summary: Makes the curve of a degree that runs through a chain of fit points, by global interpolation (Piegl and Tiller, The NURBS Book, 9.2.1): the parameter of each point is the share of the chain's length before it, the knots are the averages of the parameters of the degree before each, and the control points are what the banded system of the curve passing through every fit point has for its solution.

member.remarks: A tangent gives a direction and nothing else. The curve is over [0, 1] and is asked to leave at a speed, in drawing units for the whole of it, equal to the length of the chain through the fit points, the speed it keeps on average: a curve through three points 100 apart along a line, given the tangent along that line at each end, comes out as that line, run at an even speed.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.ClosestParameter(System.Double[],System.Double@)
member.summary: Gets the parameter of the point of the curve nearest a point, and how far it is.
member.param: The distance from the point to the curve.
member.returns: The parameter. Where two points of the curve are equally near, within rounding, the lower parameter.

remarks.para: The distance is smallest at an end of the curve or where the curve's derivative is square to the line to the point, which is where (C(t) - q) . C'(t) is nought. On each Bézier piece that is a polynomial, found in Bernstein form from the control points measured from q, and its roots are all found, none missed (); the nearest of them and the ends is the answer, to rounding, whatever the shape: a curve that doubles back, a point inside a loop, a point at the centre of an arc.

Pieces are not all solved. A piece lies in the hull of its control points, so it is no nearer than the box of them: the piece whose box is nearest is solved first, and every other is solved only if its box is nearer than the best found. The boxes are kept in a tree (), so the pieces whose boxes are near the point are found without looking at the rest: a query costs time in the logarithm of the number of pieces and the number near the point, 0.5 ms at 100 000 pieces before the tree and about 10 microseconds after. The pieces are solved in the order of their index, as they were before the tree, so the answer is the same to the bit.

member.remarks: The plane is through the first control point of the first curve, the control point furthest from it, and the control point furthest from the line through those two; two curves on one line lie in a plane square to an axis where the line allows it. A plane square to an axis has the other two axes as its directions, in order, so that two curves in the floor keep their numbers to the bit. The curves laid in the plane keep the size of the numbers of space as the size their rounding goes by: a point a million from the origin carries the rounding of a million, whatever its numbers in the plane are.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Flatten(System.Double,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Double})
member.summary: Cuts the curve into straight pieces that stray no further than a chord tolerance from it, and adds the corners to a list as Dim numbers each, the start of the curve first and its end last.
member.param: The largest gap allowed between the curve and the straight pieces; above nought.
The list the coordinates are added to.
member.exception: Thrown when the tolerance would need more than 1 048 576 pieces.

remarks.para: A piece is flat enough when any one of three proofs holds, each of which is a guarantee that every point of the piece is within the tolerance of the chord, from the start of the piece to its end. First, a Bézier piece lies in the hull of its control points, and the distance from a segment is a convex function, so if every control point is within the tolerance of the chord then so is the whole piece. Second, for a piece that is not rational, the curve strays from the chord, at the same parameter, by no more than p (p - 1) / 8 times the largest second difference of its control points (the error of a straight line through the ends, with the second derivative bounded by the second differences). Third, for a rational quadratic, a conic, the farthest the curve stands from the chord's line is exactly w / (1 + w) of the height of its middle control point, where w is its weight with the weights of the ends taken as one; and when that control point lies between the ends along the chord the curve does not run past them, so the distance from the segment is the distance from the line.

A piece that passes none is cut in halves by de Casteljau at the middle of its parameter, rational pieces in homogeneous coordinates, and each half is tried in turn. The corners are the ends of the pieces that pass, so they are points of the curve to rounding, and the promise holds however sharp the bend, whatever the weights, and at a cusp or a loop. Only the first proof is used for a rational piece of a degree above two, which is the safe one and not the tight one: it cuts such a piece finer than it need be.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.SpeedBreaks(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.BezierPieces,System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets the parameters inside a piece, as shares of it, where its speed is least or greatest: the roots of the derivative of the square of the speed.

remarks.para: A rule of integration that samples the speed finds its way over a smooth function and is misled by a corner close to the end of an interval, where neither the rule over the whole nor the rule over the halves has a point beyond the corner to see it: a curve that runs along a line and turns back 5E-4 before the end of a piece has a speed that all but vanishes there, and was measured 5E-7 short. A piece is cut at the places its speed is least, which is where such a corner is, so that each part has a speed that is smooth to its ends.

Most pieces have none, and that is known without finding a root: if the derivative control points of a piece (the numerator of its derivative, for a rational one) all lie within 60 degrees of one direction, the speed cannot fall below half of what that direction carries, and the piece is smooth. Only a piece whose derivative turns back, which is a loop, a cusp or a curve doubling on itself, has its roots found.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.IsMinimum(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether a contact that is not a meeting is a place the curve comes near its partner and not only a point it passes at some distance: the distance D from the curve to the partner is a minimum there, within the reach, or the curve ends or turns a corner there with the distance not falling either way along it.

remarks.para: The slope of D along the curve is the cosine of the angle between the curve's direction and the line to the partner, and its curvature is worked out from the derivatives of the curve and of the partner (). A place is kept where the slope is nought and the curvature is above nought (a minimum, not a maximum, and not a level run, which is at its least nowhere); where the slope is not nought but the curvature is positive and the minimum it leads to is within the reach, which is the same place read to the reach; where the distance falls straight to a meeting within the reach, which is a crossing at an angle found a few snaps short of the last digit; and at a corner or an end, where D must not fall going either way. A piece start on a slope, and a stationary point that is a greatest, as lies between two crossings of a line that passes a hair inside a circle, are not places. Where the partner's nearest point is held at its end, the distance is that to the end only on the side the partner does not go on, and a least there is looked for a little way either side as well ().
A curve that stops, or has a cusp at the contact, or a partner that cannot give its derivatives, is probed a little way either side instead ().

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.FallsEitherWay(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether the distance from the curve to its partner falls, by more than a snap, a hundredth of the size of the curve along it either way from a contact inside the piece the contact is on, or a thousandth of the size, or half that, and so on eleven times to a millionth: a least does not. It is asked of a least that curves up too little to rise a snap a thousandth of the size along. The offset of the cubic y = x³ / 100 from the line y = 0.0001 has fallen 8E-8 a thousandth of the size from its inflection, which a million out is under the snap, and 8E-5 a hundredth of it; and a crossing between two of the looks, as that of the cubic 1 000 across with the line y = 1E-9 a tenth from its inflection, is told by a look in it, the steps being halved and not cut tenfold.

member.summary: Finds the nearest point of a partner to a point and the direction to the point.
member.param: The point; nought in the plane.
The size of the numbers the shapes are given in, which the digits of the point are measured by.
The number of coordinates of the point, 2 or 3.
What was found; its distance is given even when false is returned.
member.returns: false when the partner cannot give its derivatives, or the point is on it.
member.remarks: The direction is the normal of the partner where its nearest point is free to move along it, which is exact, where the difference of two points a few digits apart at a distance of a few snaps is not. In space a curve has no one normal, and the direction is the line to the nearest point with what runs along the partner taken off it. A plane and a ball give their own.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Variation(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Foot,System.Double[][],System.Double@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Gets the slope and the curvature of the distance from a curve to a partner along the curve, by its parameter, at a point of it.
member.param: The nearest point of the partner to the point of the curve.
The point of the curve and its first and second derivative.
The first derivative of the distance.
The second derivative of the distance.
member.remarks: The slope is the cosine of the angle between the curve's direction and the line to the partner, times the speed of the curve, and the curvature is the second variation of half the squared distance, less the square of the slope, over the distance. The second variation is, the partner's nearest point moving to keep as near as it can, with a = u . P'' and b = u . Q'', ((P' x Q')² + g (a |Q'|² - b |P'|²) - g² a b) / (|Q'|² - g b): the first term is |P'|² |Q'|² less (P' . Q')², written as the square of a cross product so that two tangents that run side by side, whose two terms are alike to the last digit, leave no rounding behind. Held at an end of the partner, the point does not move, and it is |P'|² + g a. In space the first term is the squared length of the cross product, which is the same identity. For a surface the nearest point moves in two directions and the curvature is its bend times the speed squared less the slope squared, plus a ().

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Settle(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Partner,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Brings a place of the curve where the distance to a partner is not nought to the least of it, by Newton's method on the distance along the curve, not on its square: where the curve touches a straight partner, tangent to it, the distance is the square of how far from the touch the place is and the squared distance the fourth power, which Newton's method on it takes a halving of the step at a time to reach, where on the distance it takes one step.
member.remarks: It moves only inside the piece it is on, only where the distance has a positive curvature, and only to a place that is no farther from the partner, so it can leave a place where it was but never make it worse.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.RisesBothWays(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether the distance from the curve to its partner has risen a thousandth of the size of the curve either way along it from a contact, by more than the digits can tell, and has fallen nowhere on the way: a least that has no curvature, a distance of the fourth order, has risen by then, and a stretch where the distance is level has not.
member.remarks: A hump between two crossings of a plane, which falls to nought either side of it, is further out than a thousandth of the size of the curve from the middle for a plane a ten-thousandth off the curve, and the distance there is higher than at the middle: the steps taken are a thousandth, a ten-thousandth and so on down to a millionth, and the distance is not to have fallen at any of them by as much as a snap, which a hump between two near touches that are a few snaps deep has done by the second.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.RisesFurther(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double[])
member.summary: Says whether the distance from the curve to its partner, not yet risen a thousandth of the size of the curve along it from a contact, has risen a hundredth or a tenth of it along, inside the piece the contact is on, and fallen at neither: a least of the sixth order, a spline whose inflection a line passes over half a thousandth above its plane, has risen 6E-12 a thousandth of the size along and 6E-6 a hundredth along. The piece bounds it, so that a stretch where the distance is level does not take the rise of the piece beyond it for its own.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.IsLeast(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether a contact is a local least of the curve's distance to its partner, by looking a little way either side along the curve.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.TryGetNearest(System.Collections.Generic.IList{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Partner},GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact@)

The nearest approach, with ties between places as near broken by the lowest knot value of the curve.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.GetMeetings(System.Collections.Generic.IList{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Partner},System.Double)
member.summary: Gets the places where a curve meets its partners or comes within a reach of them without crossing: where it crosses, where it touches, and where it ends near, in the order along the curve.
member.param: How near a place may be, the point tolerance.
member.remarks: A place is a meeting, or a least of the distance between the two within the reach that no other partner is nearer at (). Those no further apart than the reach, one from the next, are one place, the nearer kept, and so are two near touches next to each other along the curve within ten times the reach with no point between them farther from the partners than at either by more than four snaps (); two meetings are only one place when they are within the reach of each other, whatever lies between, a meeting in the plane that is one only to the snap and is no least of the distance is left out beside a meeting to the digits (), and in space a least within the reach of a meeting is left out, so that it does not join two (). A place made of several contacts is a crossing, or a near crossing, if any of them is. Where the curve runs along a partner for a stretch, to rounding, or along another curve within the reach and level for a quarter of the size of the smaller (), it is not crossing it there, and nothing is given along the stretch but a crossing and a meeting far from parallel; where it lies on another curve to the digits between two lobes of the offset, nothing is given in that overlap or within the reach of its ends but the crossing at its end next to the earlier lobe ().

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Loose(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether a meeting is one only to the snap, in the plane: not a crossing the offset found, and further from the partner than the numbers can be evaluated to ().

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Evaluated(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Gets how near nought a distance can be told from nought by evaluating the curves: sixteen units in the last place of the size of the numbers, a sixth of a hundredth of the snap.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.KeepLoose(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact},System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact},GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Gives the meetings that are meetings only to the snap, but for one that lies within ten times the reach of a meeting to the digits on the same partner and is no least of the distance: the curve comes nearer the partner a little way along it, one way or the other, by more than the numbers can be evaluated to.
member.remarks: Along a tangency far from the origin the curve is within the snap of the partner for a long way, and Newton's method settles on points of the slope there that read as meetings: a quadratic sitting on the circle spline of radius 100 a million from the origin is 2.3E-8 from it 0.002 either side of the touch, under the snap of 1E-7 and well over the 3.6E-9 the numbers are evaluated to, and was given those two places besides the touch, where the circle gives one. A meeting to the digits is kept whatever lies beside it, so two crossings a few snaps deep are two places, as the exact curves have them, and a loose meeting with no exact one beside it stays, since it is the only reading of the place there is.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.FallsAlong(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Says whether the distance from the curve to the partner falls below that at a contact, by more than a band, a little way along the curve either side of it: a millionth of the size of the curve, and twice that each time, out to a length.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.DropAlong(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact},GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Takes out the places inside a stretch where the curve lies along another curve to within the reach ( finds them): the places a curve as good as the same as another has are where the rounding of the numbers has the two touch or cross, which is no place. A crossing found there by the offset of the one from the other changing sign by more than a hundredth of the reach each way stays: the curves cross at a shallow angle; and so does, for two curves in space that share no plane, a least of the distance where the two would cross if brought into one plane (), and a meeting far from parallel, which is with another branch of the partner ().

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Steep(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact)
member.summary: Says whether a place is a meeting of the curve and the partner at an angle further from parallel than a degree, the default angle tolerance (): a meeting of two curves that lie along each other within the reach is where the rounding has them touch or cross, all but parallel, while two that cross at a degree are within a reach of 0.001 of each other for 0.11 either side of it, where a stretch along is level for a quarter of the smaller curve. So it is a crossing of another branch of the partner than the one the stretch runs along, as the copy of a loop moved a few ten-thousandths crosses the loop at its own crossing, at the angle of the loop.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.MeetingSine(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,System.Double@)
member.summary: Gets the sine of the angle the curve and the partner meet at, at a meeting, with the speed of the curve there; nought for a contact that is no meeting or a partner that cannot give its direction.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.Elsewhere(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether a place inside a stretch along is a meeting far from parallel () with another branch of the partner than the one the stretch runs along (). The looks of the stretch within twice the reach over the sine of the angle of the place, along the curve, are passed over: so near it the other branch can be nearer than the one the stretch runs along.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.OtherBranchShare(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt,System.Boolean@)
member.summary: Gets, for a meeting inside a stretch along with another branch of a partner curve at an angle (, ), how far along the two curves it lies together: the share of the way along this curve and the share of the way along the partner, added, which is the same whichever of the two is asked first and however the pair is turned; or not a number for any other contact. A meeting far from parallel outside any stretch along counts as one, so that the two crossings a loop's copy makes at the loop's own crossing, one of them just past the end of a stretch, are told apart the same way.
member.param: Whether it lies inside a stretch along.

member.summary: Says whether a crossing of another branch comes before another along the two curves together (), and where the two shares are the same to a billionth, as for the two crossings a copy of a loop moved along the bisector of the loop's tangents makes, the one first being the nearer the point half way between the starts of the two curves: as the two shares, the same whichever curve is asked first and however the pair is turned.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.MinGaps(System.Collections.Generic.IList{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Partner},System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Int32[],System.Double[],System.Int32)
member.summary: Finds, for each of a list of points, the least distance to any of the partners but one, among those within a radius of it.
member.param: The points; nought in the plane.
How far from each point a partner must be to be of interest; no more than nought leaves the point out.
The position of the one partner to leave out for each point, or -1.
The least distance found for each point, or infinity when no partner is within its radius.
The number of coordinates of the points, 2 or 3.
member.remarks: The partners are the edges of a polygon, a chain or a polyline, which may be a million, and the points the few places a curve comes near them: the work is done from the partners' side, each partner looking up the cells of a grid of the points that its box reaches, so that it costs the number of the partners and of the pairs that are near, not their product.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.DropNearerElsewhere(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact},System.Collections.Generic.IList{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Partner},GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Drops the places that another of the partners is nearer to than the one they were found against at their points, so that they are not leasts of the distance to the shape: the places a curve comes near the edges of a polygon are those of the polygon, and an edge's own nearest place that another edge is nearer to is not one.

member.summary: Drops, in space, the leasts of the distance that lie within the reach of a meeting: such a least would be one place with the meeting, the meeting kept, and kept until then it joins two meetings further apart than the reach into one, which two crossings are not. A line a millionth of a radian off the tangent of a spline in space crosses it twice 0.0011 apart, and the slope of the distance between them, falling to each, was a place that made the two one.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve.MergeBasins(System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Contact},System.Collections.Generic.IList{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Partner},GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Joins the near touches that lie in one basin of the distance: two next to each other along the curve, within ten times the reach of each other, with no point between them where the curve is farther from the partners than at either, by more than four snaps. A curve that touches a partner is as near as rounding can tell all along a stretch, and each place the rounding finds in it is the one touch. Two meetings are not joined, whatever lies between them: crossings are places, and are one only when they are within the reach of each other, as the exact curves have it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.PieceIndex
member.summary:
The boxes of the Bézier pieces of a curve gathered in a tree, so that a question about a small part of the plane or of space reaches only the pieces near it, and takes time in proportion to their number and the logarithm of the number of pieces, not to the number of pieces.
The pieces are grouped as the curve runs, the first two, the next two, and so on, each pair under a box that holds both, up to one box over the whole: a curve is a chain, so neighbours lie together and the boxes stay tight. The tree is built with no sorting, so it is the same whenever it is built.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt.OnAnotherBranch(System.Int32,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Says whether a place on the curve, inside a stretch along a partner, is on another branch of the partner than the one the stretch runs along: its point of the partner lies further along the partner from where the two looks either side of it have their nearest points than those two are from each other. A place no look stands either side of is on the branch.
member.remarks: On a closed partner the knot values are read round its seam, a whole period being nothing: the circle spline against the polygon inscribed in it with a corner on the seam at (5, 0) gave that corner as a place, its partner's knot read at the start and the looks either side at the end. The looks are a sixteenth of a stretch along apart, so a loop of the partner shorter than about three of them, which comes back within that of where it left, is not told from the branch the stretch runs along.
member.param: The knot value of the place on the curve.
The partner's knot value at the place.

How far either side of the place, in the curve's knot values, a look may have its nearest point on the other branch rather than the one the stretch runs along, and is passed over: the polyline that comes back square across a line at 50, looked at at 50 itself, has its nearest point there on the square edge, and that look said the edge was the stretch's branch.

member.summary: Gets how far apart two parts of two curves may be, by their boxes, and still be cut again when the curves are searched against each other: the reach, or for the nearest approach the least gap found less a hair, since a pair that could be nearer by no more than that cannot change the answer by more than that, which Newton's method then takes off the pair that was found. member.remarks: The hair is a billionth of the size of the shapes, and never more than a thousandth of the least gap itself: a hair of a hundred-millionth of the size would be 0.01 at a million millimetres, and a least gap of 0.005 would have everything, the pair that crosses included, cut away, and a near miss of 0.0009 read as 0.01. The cutoff is never below the snap, so that a pair that meets is always cut.

member.remarks: The offset of a piece from the line, the part of its offset from the origin that stands square to the line, is taken as two signed polynomials along two directions square to the line (): the curve meets the line where both are nought, and a piece in a plane through the line has one of them nought all along, the other being its signed offset in that plane, as in the plane. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.LinePartner3.PieceCandidates(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.BezierPieces,System.Int32,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Offers the places of one piece where its distance to the line can be least: where it meets the line, and where it stops coming nearer.

remarks.para: The offset of the piece from the line is taken as its two signed parts square to the line (), not as their sum of squares: a crossing is a root of both, and the square of the offset has a double root there, which rounding lumps with every stretch where the curve is within the snap of the line and leaves the distance a V that Newton's method cannot settle on. A piece in a plane through the line is the plane's case: its crossings are the roots of its signed offset, however shallow, and its touches the stationary points of that offset. Otherwise a crossing is a root of either part where the piece is within the snap of the line, and the places it comes nearest are the stationary points of the squared offset, each brought to the least of the distance by Newton's method on it and, where that has no curvature to go by, by a golden section (); those that end in one basin of the distance are one.

member.summary: The surface of a ball: the set of points of space where the distance from a centre is a radius. A Bézier piece put into the form (the squared distance from the centre less the squared radius) gives a polynomial of twice its degree, whose roots are where the piece meets the surface.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner
member.summary: Another curve as a partner: an ellipse made into a spline, or a spline. The pieces of the two are cut in halves while their boxes are near enough to matter and they are not yet straight, then each pair of straight pieces is measured, and the best of those found by Newton's method on the real curves.

remarks.para: A Bézier piece lies in the hull of its control points, so two pieces whose hulls are further apart than the least gap found so far (less a hair, a billionth of the size of the shapes and never more than a thousandth of the gap, and never below the snap), or than the reach asked, cannot come nearer or meet: that is the certified bound, and everything within it is cut again. The hulls are measured by their boxes and by the shadows of their control points on the chord of each piece and its square, so two pieces running side by side are told their distance, which boxes cannot do. The hair is the whole of the doubt about the nearest approach: it is 0.001 at a size of a million, and where the gap is 0.005 it is 0.000005, so a near miss is never read above the point tolerance for a nearer pair left uncut.

A pair whose control points lie within a thousandth of its size of the chord is read as two segments, which is enough to start from when the tangents of the two can never run the same way, since they then meet at most once; where they could meet twice, as two curves that cross at a shallow angle or touch can, they are cut until they are straight to a billionth. When places are wanted, two straight parts that cannot meet and are small beside the reach are measured too, not cut further: a near touch has Newton's method to find it. Newton's method on the two curves, started from the closest points of the segments, brings the pair to rounding, and then on the distance itself along the first curve (), which takes a tangent touch to its place in a step where on the squared distance it would take a halving of the step at a time. A part that lies along the other curve to rounding is not cut: it meets it along its whole length and crosses it nowhere; and when places are wanted, a stretch of the first curve that stays within the reach of the other, level, for a quarter of the size of the smaller curve is found first () and not cut at all.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.FindRuns(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Collections.Generic.List{GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.PiecePair},GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Finds the stretches of the first curve that lie along the second: stretches a quarter of the size of the smaller curve long, along which each curve stays within the reach of the other and the first keeps its distance from the second to within half the reach. Two curves that stay that near and that level for that far are as good as one for the places asked for, and cutting them to find where the rounding of their numbers has them touch or cross would take millions of parts.

remarks.para: A touch is not level: two curves that touch are within half a thousandth of each other for 2 in all if their radii are 1000 and infinite, which is not a quarter of 2000, and the distance there changes by the whole reach before it leaves; and a crossing at any angle goes from nought to the reach and past it. Only a distance that stays about the same for a quarter of the size is a stretch along: two circles 0.0005 apart, a spline and its copy moved by 0.0004, a line and a curve fitted to it by a hundred-millionth.

The first curve is looked at over the pieces that have a piece of the second near enough to matter (the pairs found), at points a sixteenth of a stretch apart along it, so that it costs a few hundred looks at most. Then the second curve is looked at over the stretch the first's ends map to, at points as far apart along it, and where it leaves the reach of the first, as a dart does that goes out of the stretch and back, a gap of two steps either side of where it does is cut out of the run, which is cut in two. A curve that darts away and back between two looks, narrower than a step, is read as staying near; those of a polyline are not missed, since each of its vertices is looked at. Last, the offset of the first curve from the second is followed through each stretch (): where it changes sign by more than a hundredth of the reach each way, the curves cross at a shallow angle inside the stretch, and the crossing is a place, as the exact curves give it. A change of sign by less (a hundredth of the reach is 1E-5) is the rounding of curves that are the same to a hundred-millionth, which is no place.

Past an end of the second curve, within the reach of it, the first is along it as far as the reach goes, as an arc is along an arc of its circle, whatever its distance to that end: a copy moved 0.0007 that overhangs the other's end ended its stretch short of it, and the other's end, 1.5E-5 from the copy, was a place asked from the copy and none asked from the other.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Spread(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve)
member.summary: Gets the size of a curve the stretches along are measured by, the same however the curve is turned: the furthest any control point is from the first. The span along the axes changes as the curve is turned, by as much as the square root of two for a square turned an eighth of a turn, and with it the stretches looked at and where they end, so that a pair answered in the floor gave a place more or fewer in a tilted plane, and in the plane 14 of 60 copies of a spline moved by a few ten-thousandths gave a place more or fewer turned by 0.7 of a radian.

A rational piece lies in the hull of its control points only where its weights are positive, so one with another weight is given whole.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.CrossingsIn(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Gives the crossings inside a stretch along the second curve: the places the offset of the first from the second changes sign, when it goes more than a hundredth of the reach to each side. Lobes of the offset that go no further are noise and are taken with their neighbours, and between two lobes that do, to either side, the curves cross once: the fit through 37 points of a quarter circle crosses an ellipse 1E-9 off that circle 68 times by a few hundred-millionths, which are not crossings; and a cubic that crosses a line at 20, 40 and 60 with lobes of 7E-6 between goes from 1.1E-4 under it to 4.4E-4 over it, and crosses it once. Between two lobes that go further to either side a crossing is given wherever the bisection of a change finds a meeting, so the count of crossings between the stretch's first and last large lobe is odd where they lie to either side and even where not. Where the two lie on each other to the digits between two such lobes, the place is fixed by that overlap (): its end next to the earlier lobe where the lobes lie to either side, and nothing where they lie to one side.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Overlap(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Double[],System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt,System.Double@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Looks for a stretch between the peaks of two lobes of the offset where the first curve lies on the second to the digits: two samples running, and the point half way between them, whose offset is no further from nought than the numbers are evaluated to (). Its ends are bisected to where the offset leaves that, and it is noted (); where the lobes lie to either side, the crossing is offered at the end next to the earlier lobe.
member.remarks:
A polyline over a line from 0 to 10, on it from 10 to 50 and under it after crosses it once, and the bisection of a change of sign or Newton's method put the place wherever the rounding of the overlap had the offset change sign: at 10 as it lay, at 34.95 turned by 0.3 of a radian and 30.18 by 0.7 reversed. It is at 10 however turned. The exit at 50, which a part of the curve cut across the stretch could give as well, is no place. Two corners of a polyline cut from the other curve, sampled on it, are no overlap: the chord between them is off it half way.
The end next to the earlier lobe is the crossing only where the curve comes on the other from that lobe's side and leaves it to the later lobe's: a polyline over the line to 10, a hair under it from 10 to 30, on it to 50 and under it after crosses it at 10 and touches it from under at 30; one that lies on the line from 10 to 30, a hair over it to 40 and under it after crosses it at 40. There the change of side is looked for among the changes before the overlap, or after it, as without one.
member.param: The knot values of the first curve the offset was sampled at.
The offset of the first curve from the second at each.
The knot value of the second curve's nearest point to each.
The sample of the earlier lobe's peak.
The sample of the later lobe's peak.
Whether the two lobes lie to either side.
Where the change of side is to be looked for from, when it is to be looked for.
Where the change of side is to be looked for to.
member.returns: Nought where there is no such stretch; one where there is and nothing more is to be done; two where the change of side is to be looked for between and .

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.CrossingsInSpace(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Gives the crossings inside a stretch along the second curve, for two curves in space: the places where the distance of the first from the second, looked at a sixteenth of a stretch apart, falls to a least with the distance rising to more than a hundredth of the reach either side of it, brought to a least of the two curves by Newton's method and offered as a meeting where it is nought; and for two curves that share no plane, every least of the distance, which is a place where the two would cross if brought into one plane (, ).

remarks.para: Two curves that cross at a shallow angle in a plane are as near as the digits tell for a long way either side of the crossing, and in space the distance has no sign to change; but the distance from one to the other is nought at the crossing and a hundredth of the reach away from it a little further out, so a sample that is nearer than its two neighbours has the crossing between them. Each greatest between two such leasts is tried as well, since two crossings that are nearer each other than the samples leave no least between them (). A change by less than a hundredth of the reach is the rounding of curves that are the same to a hundred-millionth, which is no place.

Two curves that share no plane are looked at four times as close, and closer where the first turns, so that it turns by no more than between two looks; at every join of its pieces, where it may turn a corner; and where each join of the second is nearest it, where the second may. A least of the distance of two curves running side by side within the reach is as wide as the stretch over which one turns away from the other, so these looks have one inside each.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.MayCrossSteeply(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Sub,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Sub,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether two parts, the first inside a stretch along the second curve, may meet at an angle further from parallel than a degree, the default angle tolerance: their hulls meet, and their tangents are not held within that of each other.
member.remarks: A stretch along is not cut, its places being the rounding of two curves that lie on each other, but a curve that comes back across itself has another branch there: a loop and its copy moved a few ten-thousandths lie along each other all the way, and the copy's other branch crosses the loop at the loop's own crossing, at the loop's angle, which was never looked for. Two parts that lie along each other are cut until their tangents are held within the degree, or their hulls part, and put aside then; two that meet at an angle are cut as any other pair, and their meeting is kept where it is on another branch of the second curve than the one the stretch runs along (, ), and not at a corner of a polyline and its copy, which crosses it as its lobes have it. A curve against its own flattening into a spline of degree one pays for the cutting: the arc of radius 100 a million out turning 2 radians against 65 536 chords took 0.12 s and takes 0.65 on .NET 10. Putting a pair aside as soon as its bound is under the reach and its cones overlap takes 0.11 s again, but loses the crossing of the loop above, whose parts are whole pieces, their cones wide, when first paired.
member.param: The part of the first curve.
A bound the distance between the two cannot be less than.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.WouldCross(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Says whether a least of the distance of the first curve from the second is where the two would cross if they were brought into one plane: seen along the gap, the first curve is on one side of the second just before the least and on the other just after.
member.param: The knot value of the least on the first curve.
The knot value of the nearest point of the second curve.

remarks.para: At a least of the distance of two curves in space the gap stands square to both, and the curves seen along it, as if brought into the one plane square to it, cross there or touch there. A polyline spline and its copy moved 0.0005 along its plane and lifted 0.0002 off it come 0.0002 apart at each corner, where seen from above the edge of one goes from one side of the other's to the other: they would cross, and the corner is a place, as the crossing is in the plane. A spline and its copy moved 0.0005 across its plane with a wobble of 0.0001, lifted off it by a few snaps, come nearest where the wobble brings them nearest, but seen from above they stay on one side of each other: no place, as there is none in the plane. Two rings 0.0005 apart in two planes are on neither side of each other, to rounding, and have no place.

The side is that of a point of the first curve from the nearest point of the second there, along the direction square to the gap at the least and to the second curve's direction at that nearest point: the signed offset of the plane, across the curve it is measured from, so that past a corner of the second its next edge is measured from. It is read a thousandth of the reach along the first curve either way from the least, and twice as far each time, until it stands a hundredth of the reach out: it must keep the sign it had once clear of rounding, since one that goes back across sooner is a wiggle of two curves along each other, which the plane reads as no crossing either, and the least is another's if the distance comes nearer on the way by more than the snaps Newton's method stops at: a cubic and its copy moved 0.0001 out of its plane have a valley of the distance so flat, 6E-7 over 90, that a least was settled on its slope and given beside the real one. A least of two curves that cross twice 17 apart, lifted 0.00003 off their plane, rises 0.000004 between the two, where a rise was once asked of each.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Polish(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double@,System.Double@,System.Double)

Where the two curves cross it is Newton's method on the crossing, and where they run parallel it settles on a nearest pair as far as it can.
