member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Straddle(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Sub,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Looks for a crossing inside a part of the first curve by the offset of the curve from the second () at its two ends and at the nearest point found: where it changes sign, the curves cross between, however shallow the angle, and the crossing is bisected to the last digit. Two curves that cross at a millionth of a radian are as near as rounding can tell for a long way either side of the crossing, where the nearest points of two segments are not to be found at all.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Shallow(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Looks for the crossings that a pair of parts hides when the nearest points Newton's method settles on are a greatest of the distance and not a least: two curves that cross twice, a hair apart, run parallel between the crossings, where the nearest points of two segments are the middle, and the distance has nought on either side of it and a hump there that Newton's method on the squared distance sits on, with no slope to go by.
member.remarks: At such a place the distance curves down: it falls to nought either way along the first curve, at the roots of its quadratic model. The offset of the first curve from the second () is tried at those places, then a little nearer and further, and where it has the other sign the crossing lies between and is bisected to the last digit. A crossing is a meeting of the two, so it is offered as one, and the distance is nought.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Hump(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Looks, for two curves in space, for the meetings a pair of parts hides when the nearest points Newton's method settles on are a greatest of the distance and not a least: two curves that run side by side in a plane and cross twice a hair apart, the nearest points of two segments there being the middle, with the distance falling to nought either way along the first curve.
member.remarks: In the plane the offset of one curve from the other changes sign where they cross (); in space it has no sign. The distance has the same hump, though, and its quadratic model reaches nought one way along the curve and the other: from the model's roots, and from a little nearer and further, the pair is brought to a least by Newton's method on the two curves, and what it settles on is offered, a crossing where the distance comes to nought. A least that is not a meeting, as it may be, is a place or not as the distance there makes it.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.SplinePartner.Settle(GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.NurbsCurve,System.Double@,System.Double@,GeometryHelper.Internal.Nurbs.Hunt)
member.summary: Brings a place of the first curve where the distance to the second is not nought to the least of it, by Newton's method on the distance along the first curve, not on its square: two curves that touch, tangent, are at a distance that is the square of how far from the touch they are, and the squared distance is the fourth power, which Newton's method on it takes a halving of the step at a time to reach, where on the distance it takes one step.
member.remarks: It moves only inside the piece of the first curve it is on, only where the distance has a positive curvature, and only to a place that is no farther from the second curve, so it can leave a place where it was but never make it worse.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Planar.OffsetOutline
member.summary:
Builds the raw offset of a loop or a chain: every edge moved sideways, with the corners joined.
The raw offset is not the answer yet. Where the edges pull apart, at the outside of a turn, the gap is closed by the join. Where they overlap, at the inside of a turn, the outline runs back through the original corner and out again. That detour is what makes the result exact: the raw loop is then the sum of the original boundary, a strip swept by every edge and a wedge at every outside corner, so it winds a positive number of times round exactly the points of the offset region and zero or fewer round every other. Resolving it under the positive fill rule turns it into that region, however the strips overlap, split or swallow each other. The solid library resolves it with its own region solver, the plane library with Clipper2; both read the same raw loops, so both draw the same corners.

The plane algebra the internal offset and region code is written in, as shorthands over and .
The engine used to carry its own point-and-vector struct, because the plane and solid halves of the library were separate assemblies and only one of them could see . member.summary:
Segments bucketed on a grid, to tell quickly whether an edge lies along one of them, and which of them come near a point or an edge.
The cells are as wide as the root mean square of the segments' reach (the larger side of each one's box, margin included), so that a long thin chain of short segments is not piled into a few cells, and a few long segments do not fill many: the segments take at most four cells each on average, whatever their lengths. member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Planar.WindingRegion
member.summary:
Resolves directed edges into the region they enclose under a fill rule, and hands back the region's boundary as simple loops.
The edges are laid out as a planar arrangement: every crossing, every endpoint touching another edge and every stretch two edges share becomes a vertex, so what is left are pieces that meet only at their ends. Pieces lying on top of each other are merged, counting how many times the input runs along them each way. The faces of the arrangement are then traced, each is given its winding number by walking across the pieces from the unbounded face, which winds zero times, and the boundary of the region is every piece with a filled face on one side and an empty one on the other.
This is what turns a raw offset, whose loops fold over themselves at every tight spot, into the clean outline it describes; it also reads a polygon whose edges cross under the even-odd rule. Coordinates are expected near the origin: callers move their input there first, so that the snapping distance means the same everywhere.

member.summary: Splits every edge at every point where another edge crosses or touches it. Returns whether anything was split.
Tries the pairs the sweep along X tries, found by a sweep along Y, in the order the sweep along X tries them. Returns whether anything was split.
member.remarks: The sweep along X tries each edge, in the order of its least X, against every earlier one whose X run reaches within the snap distance of its own and whose Y run does so too, the earlier ones in the order they came. A sweep along Y over runs grown by a little more than the snap distance finds every such pair and some more; the pair is then read as the sweep along X reads it, the later edge first, through the same two tests, and the pairs that pass are tried sorted by the places of their two edges in that order. Trying a pair adds the point where the two cross to the points, and which points merge depends on the order they come in, so the order is kept as it was, to the pair. An offset of a comb of 4 000 teeth running along the frame's X, in a plane in space, spent 4.8 of its 4.9 seconds sweeping along X.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Internal.Tessellation
member.summary:
How many straight pieces a round curve is cut into, and nothing else: the shapes themselves place the points, each in its own dimension.
A curve can be cut three ways, and each answers a different question. By chord tolerance: how far the straight pieces may stray from the true curve, which is what drawing and exporting care about. By spacing: how far apart the points may be along the curve, which is what setting out and dividing care about. By count: exactly how many pieces, which is what a caller who has already decided asks for.

member.summary: Hashes a key packed from two numbers as (a << 32) | b, such as the two ends of an edge.
member.remarks: The default hash of a long folds its two halves together with an exclusive or, so the key of an edge between points 1 000 and 1 001 hashes to 1, as does the key of every edge from an even point to the next. member.summary: Initializes cell options, each axis divided its own way.
member.param: How the grid's X axis is divided.
How the grid's Y axis is divided.
How the grid's Z axis is divided.

The gap between two neighbouring cells, along each axis divided, as the joints between blocks: the cells stand a size plus the joint apart. There is no gap at the body's boundary, where the cells are cut to it. Nought for none.

How near a corner of the body a cut has to come to be moved onto it, so that no cell is cut off thinner than this: the slice between goes to the cell beside. Nought, or anything less, takes the point tolerance, which every cut is snapped within, since a cut that close is a cut along the body's own face. However small this is, no cut takes off less than four point tolerances: such a piece is at the scale of the tolerance. With a joint the cuts bound the joints, and are snapped within the point tolerance only, so that no cell is carried into a joint, and none leaves a slice thicker than that past a joint to go with it.
How many threads may cut at once; -1 for every processor.
member.exception: Thrown when the joint or the snap distance is negative or not a finite number, or the threads are neither -1 nor a positive count.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Meshing.GeoCellGrid3
member.summary:
A body cut into the cells of a grid: blocks, bays, lifts or bars, as the divided its axes.
The grid stands in : its axes are the grid's, and its origin the corner where the first cell along each axis starts. Every cell the body holds any of comes as a , a closed body of what the body holds of it, the whole cell beside it as a box; a cell the body holds in several pieces comes once a piece. The cells together hold all of the body, less the joints, and do not overlap. They come layer by layer up the grid's Z axis, row by row along Y within a layer, and along X within a row, the pieces of one cell in turn. The grid is immutable.

member.summary: Gets the cells that share part of a face with a cell: its neighbours along the grid's axes, where no joint stands between and their material meets over some area.
member.param: The cell, by its place in .
member.returns: The neighbours, by their places in , in ascending order; none with joints.
member.exception: Thrown when there is no such cell.
member.remarks: Two pieces of one cell never share a face, and pieces of neighbouring cells only where they meet: across the notch of a U, the piece of one arm meets only the cell beside it in that arm. A neighbour is found where it meets the cell, not by its indexes: a cut moved onto a corner can leave the next cell along an axis empty and the one after meeting this one, and the slabs and bars, each cut to its own corners, can leave a cell meeting one beside the next. Asked below a millionth, two cells meet over more than a strip as wide as the point tolerance, or as what rounding can move a corner, a trillionth of the size of the coordinates, where that is more, along where they overlap: two a place apart across the plane as well share no more than an edge, and at nought a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space, cut into twelve cells, gave 25 pairs of neighbours, those among them; it gives 17. At a millionth and above two cells meet over more than the point tolerance squared, as before.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Meshing.GeoMesh2
member.summary:
A closed shape of the plane broken into faces that share their corners: triangles, the cells of a grid, strips or convex pieces, as says.
Every face is a simple polygon with no hole, running counter-clockwise, given by the indexes of its corners in . The faces lie within the shape's material and cover it without overlapping, holes left open, and meet edge to edge: a corner of one face standing on the side of another is a corner of that one too, so two faces side by side share the same edge, run the two ways round. Such a corner may leave a face with three corners in a row. The mesh is immutable.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Meshing.GeoMesh3
member.summary:
A flat shape of space broken into faces that share their corners: triangles, the cells of a grid, strips or convex pieces, as says.
The mesh is a standing in a plane of space. Every face is a simple polygon with no hole, running counter-clockwise seen from the side points to, given by the indexes of its corners in ; the faces lie within the shape's material, cover it without overlapping, holes left open, and meet edge to edge. The shape's own corners are vertices exactly where the shape has them. is the plane it was laid out in, with its X axis along the grid's first axis, and gives the faces drawn in it, as an elevation of a wall is drawn. The mesh is immutable.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Meshing.Mesh2
member.summary: Breaking the closed shapes of the plane into the faces of a : triangles, the cells of a grid, strips or convex pieces.

remarks.para: Every shape is first read as a face with straight edges: a loop with arcs flattened by the chord tolerance, a circle or an ellipse by the same, a polygon crossing itself as the region reads. Its material is then broken up as says, within the tolerance, and the pieces joined: points the same but for rounding are one vertex, the shape's own corners kept exactly, and a corner of a face standing on the side of the face across from it is made one of that face's corners too, so that the faces meet edge to edge.

A grid and strips run along the X axis unless an angle is given, and along a rectangle's own width; a grid stands against the shape as its alignments say, measured between the shape's furthest corners along each axis, or with a cell starting at its origin. The shapes' own ToMesh members come here.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Meshing.Mesh3.ToCells(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoSolid3,GeometryHelper.Meshing.CellOptions3,GeometryHelper.Meshing.MeshPlacement3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Cuts a body into cells as the options say, its grid standing as the placement says, within a tolerance.
member.param: The body; closed, its openings cut in first.
How each axis of the grid is divided, the joint, and the snap distance.
Which way the grid's axes run, and where a cell starts.
The tolerance the body is cut within: which cells are whole, and the least a cut is snapped by.
member.returns: The grid, every cell the body holds any of a closed body of what it holds, a piece each; none when the openings take all of the body.
member.exception: Thrown when the body, the options or the placement are null.

Thrown when the body is not closed, or closed along its edges but not by its corners, a cell is no larger than the point tolerance along an axis it divides, or the grid would lay more cells through the body than a grid may have.

remarks.para: The cells are cut by planes, along the grid's X axis first, then Y, then Z. A cut that comes within the snap distance of a corner of the part it cuts is moved onto that corner, and one that would take off no more than that from a side is not made: the slice stays with the cell beside, so that no cell is thinner than the snap distance where the body leaves room, and no cut runs along a face of the body a hair off it. Features of the body closer together than that still leave the slice between them.

A cell the body holds in several pieces, as across the notch of a U, gives a cell for each. A body that is not closed holds no volume to cut, and is refused rather than cut into cells that would not hold it either: one reads open, as a cube whose top stands 0.0015 over its sides with a speck of a face at each corner of the top half way up, cut into 8 cells before, and one it reads closed that the ends of its edges, each matched to the first corner seen within the tolerance of it, do not close, as the booleans the cells are cut with read it. Such is a body closed only to the rounding of its coordinates, at a tolerance below that rounding: the union of two turned boxes would be cut into no cell at all at a tolerance of nought. That reading of the corners hangs on the order the faces come in, and a slab 100 by 100 and 0.0012 thick, its side at one end slid up 0.0002, is refused with its faces in one order and cut with them in another, as it was. A body wound inwards, as a mirror leaves one, and an opening wound so, are read the right way out, and the cells are wound outwards. Openings that cannot be cut into the whole body, or leave it open, are cut into each cell they meet; a cell they cannot be cut into either keeps their material, and says so in the log.

Asked at a point tolerance below the rounding of the coordinates, a quadrillionth of the largest of them, nought among them, the body and its openings are cut within what rounding can move a corner off a plane, a trillionth of the size of the coordinates, and each cell whose corners that leaves a rounding apart is welded to close within the tolerance asked. Within the tolerance asked, the two faces beside an edge each cut their own copy of it a rounding apart, and no cut closed: at nought a plate 200 by 100 by 3 turned about in space, cut into cells 60 by 40 along it, came out one cell of 60 000, where twelve hold it, and with a hole 20 by 20 through it one cell of 60 000, the hole left in, each cut not made said so in the log. They are cut so too at and above the rounding while the point tolerance is below both that trillionth and a millionth: a million out, at 2E-9, twice the rounding, the plate with the hole came out in the wrong cells as well. Which bodies are refused is read at the tolerance asked, as before. At a millionth and above, the default tolerance among them, the body is cut as it was, to the bit, but where walls stand apart within the tolerance of one plane.

Where walls of two openings, or of an opening and the body, stand apart within the tolerance of one plane, the openings are cut in, and the cells cut, within a finer tolerance, as cuts them: an L 100 by 80 by 50, a million out, with three openings, the walls of two of them 0.0009 apart across it, cut within a thousandth into 15 cells, held 0.76 too little in six of them, and cut within a thousandth from its material cut exact, 0.06 too much in one.

A body far out, as says, is moved near the origin by whole coordinates, the placement's origin with it, cut into cells there, and the grid moved back: its origin, each cell's box and each cell's material, coordinate by coordinate; where the cells start and end along its axes, and what each holds, are as they were worked out. Where it stood, walls of openings a fraction of the tolerance apart were cut in one plane: an L 100 by 80 by 50 a thousand million out, with an opening up from its floor and one down from its top whose far walls stood 0.0009 apart, cut within a thousandth into 9 cells 50 by 40 by 20, held 0.52 too much, 0.28 in one cell; each holds what it holds at the origin now, to 2.1E-5.

member.summary:
Where a grid, or strips, stand in space: which way the axes run, as says, and, when given, the point a cell starts at.
The same placement serves a flat shape, meshed into a , and a body, cut into a : over a flat shape the axes give the direction of the grid's first axis in the shape's plane, and through a body all three axes of the grid. member.remarks: Without an origin the grid stands against the shape as the alignments of the options say. With one, a cell has its first corner there, as places a grid of the plane: over a flat shape the point is put onto the shape's plane along its normal, so that faces of one building laid from one origin line up across their edges. Along a line of space the cells stand where they would with its axis running the world's way, X before Y before Z, whichever way a face's own runs along it, and so do the joints between them.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.OffsetOptions
member.summary:
How an offset shapes the corners where its edges pull apart: the join, how far a sharp corner may reach, and how finely a round corner is drawn.
The options are immutable, so one instance can be shared between threads and kept as a setting. gives sharp corners, as AutoCAD's OFFSET does with its default gap type.

member.summary: The default : a sharp corner may reach ten times the offset distance from its vertex, which keeps every corner of 11.5 degrees or wider sharp.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.OffsetOptions.AutomaticArcToleranceRatio
member.summary: The share of the offset distance allowed as chord error on a round join when is left automatic: 0.2 %, about 50 segments for a full turn.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.OffsetOptions.Default
member.summary: Sharp corners () with the default miter limit.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.OffsetOptions.#ctor(GeometryHelper.Enums.OffsetJoin,System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Initializes offset options.
member.param: How the gap at a corner is closed.

How far a corner may reach from its vertex, as a multiple of the offset distance; beyond it the corner is cut off square at that distance. At least 1, and keeps every corner sharp. Ignored by the other joins.

The largest gap allowed between a corner and the true arc, in drawing units. Zero (the default) picks of the offset distance. It is met down to 1.15E-9 of the distance, 65 536 chords a full turn: a corner grown by 80 with 1E-4 is drawn in chords of 0.0032 radians, 1 987 a turn. Nor is it met below about a hundredth of the point tolerance the offset is worked to, where corners that close are taken as straight and go. Ignored by the other joins.
member.exception: Thrown when the join is not a defined value, the miter limit is below 1 or not a number, or the arc tolerance is negative, infinite or not a number.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Packing.Algorithms.MaxRectsBin
member.summary: One bin packed by the maximal rectangles method: the space left free is kept as every largest rectangle it holds, which may overlap one another, and each box goes into the free rectangle that puts its top highest, then its left side furthest left. So the bin fills from its upper left corner, row by row as the eye reads, and a box too short for a row slips into the space beneath a taller one.
member.remarks: Coordinates are the bin's own, its lower left corner at nought. A box fits a free rectangle if it is no more than the slack wider or higher, so that sizes that ought to add up exactly still do in floating point: two boxes may then overlap, or the bin's edge be passed, by as much as the slack and no more.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Packing.Algorithms.PolygonContext
member.summary: What the polygons of one packing share: the grid they are worked out on, the gaps they keep, and the no-fit polygons of each pair of them, which are made once and moved to wherever the pair stands.

remarks.para: Two polygons keep a gap apart when each, grown by half of it, leaves the other alone. A polygon grown that way is broken into convex pieces, and the places where one polygon, held by a reference point at the lower left corner of its box, may not stand beside another are the union of the Minkowski sums of the pieces of one with the pieces of the other turned about the point: the no-fit polygon. Each sum is drawn in by a quarter of the tolerance, so that a polygon that fits a notch exactly, or the edge of the sheet, still does.
The sums are made on whole steps of the grid, a tenth of the tolerance or finer, so that the free places, found with Clipper2, are exact for the pieces as they were rounded to it.

member.summary: Judges the packing of polygons as it came out, polygon by polygon, so that one reported placed is one that is: inside the usable area of its sheet, and clear of every other, the gap asked for kept, but those of a kept block it belongs to.

remarks.para: The packing is built to that, and this is the check that it held: it reads the polygons as moved, and knows nothing of the no-fit polygons the packing was made from. Two polygons stand clear when each, grown by half of the gap less half of the tolerance, leaves the other alone: they may overlap, or come nearer than the gap, by up to the tolerance and no more. Only polygons whose boxes, grown by half of the largest gap, meet are compared.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Packing.SheetPacker
member.summary: Packs boxes, or polygons, onto sheets of paper: each group as one block, the blocks from the upper left of the first sheet, or the corner names, and onto a new sheet beside it when the one before is full.

remarks.para: A view cut to a polygon (by VPCLIP in AutoCAD, say) is packed by that polygon: the overloads that take lay it out by its true shape, so that an L- or U-shaped view lets another stand in its notch. What follows is about boxes; the polygons are placed by the same rule, highest top and then furthest left.
The boxes are only moved, never turned or resized. A box that is turned is packed by the upright box round it, and keeps its turn.

The boxes of a group are laid out together first, as says, and the block they make goes onto a sheet whole: the groups keep their boxes together, at from one another, and from other groups. A group too large for one sheet is split, in its order, into blocks that each go onto one. The blocks are placed by the maximal rectangles method, each where its top is highest and then its left side furthest left, so that a sheet fills from its upper left corner as the eye reads it. From another the packing is the mirror image of that one, the same boxes on the same sheets.

The result is judged as it came out: a box reported lies inside the usable area of its sheet and clear of every other box, but the boxes of its own group kept as they stood. The same boxes and options give the same result, and the boxes, the sheet and the options are only read.

member.summary: Packs the polygons onto sheets like the one given, by their own shape: a polygon with a notch lets another stand in it.
member.param: The polygons, in groups of those that belong together: views cut to a polygon, an L or a U among them. A null group is passed over.
The sheet: its size, scale, offsets, where it lies, and where each new one goes.
The gaps, how a group is laid out, the order the groups go in, and the tolerance.
member.returns: Where each polygon goes, in the shape the polygons were given, and the sheets they took: is the polygon moved and the box round it.

remarks.para: The polygons are only moved, never turned or resized, and they are packed by their true shape, not by the box round it. The places a polygon may stand are those where it stays inside the usable area of the sheet and clear of the polygons already there, found from the no-fit polygon of each pair, so that an L-shaped view lets a small one stand in its notch. Each is put where its top is highest and then its left side furthest left, as puts a box. From another the packing is the mirror image of that one, the polygons as they are given taken to the mirror image of the places: the same views, mirrored across the sheet, would pack the same.

is the least gap between two polygons of one group and between two groups, measured between the polygons themselves, not their boxes. A group laid out afresh () is packed together first, in its order from the start corner, as close together as it goes, and goes onto the sheet as one block; a group kept as drawn () moves as one block with its polygons as they stand, overlapping or not. A block is placed by the shape of each of its polygons, so that polygons of another group may stand between them, in a notch, as long as the group spacing is kept. A group too large for one sheet is split, in its order, into blocks that each go onto one.

A polygon larger than the usable area of a sheet is not placed. The result is judged as it came out: a polygon reported lies inside the usable area of its sheet and clear of every other, the gaps kept, but the polygons of a kept group; the tolerance of the options is how far it may pass either. The same polygons and options give the same result, and the polygons, the sheet and the options are only read. A polygon takes time with the number of polygons already on its sheet and the corners of each: 200 polygons of up to a fifth of an A1 take a few seconds.

member.exception: , or is null.
The offsets of the sheet leave it no room; or a polygon is null, not at finite coordinates, encloses no area (its area is no more than the tolerance squared), or crosses itself.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.SolidBooleanOptions
member.summary: How a boolean of two solids is worked out: within which tolerance, how far apart two faces of the two bodies may lie and still be taken as touching, and within which tolerance it is worked out again where the result is not valid.

remarks.para: The tolerance says how near two corners have to be to be one, and a boolean is as exact as it. How near two faces of two parts have to be to touch is another question, one of the model: parts drawn against each other in Tekla Structures come a few thousandths of a millimetre into or off each other. Cut within a thousandth, a part met by a cutter whose face stood 0.0049 inside its own kept a skin of itself 0.0049 thick, 19.6 and 41.7 metres long: 110 square metres of surface on a part of 119, and 0.27 litres of volume. With such faces are taken as touching, and the skin is not left.

Of the 79 864 parts of a Tekla model, each cut one after another by the parts it meets within a thousandth, 3 344 came out with more than 1 % more surface than within a hundredth, 5 466 square metres in all; with a contact of a hundredth, 203 and 220 square metres, the volume of them all within 0.05 cubic metres of 202 236. A contact of two hundredths took away what is there as well.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.SolidBooleanOptions.Contact
member.summary: Gets how far apart a face of the second body may lie from a face of the first, parallel to it, and still be taken as lying against it; nought takes the bodies as they come.

remarks.para: Each face of the second body that lies parallel to a face of the first, either way round, within the angle of the tolerance, with every corner of it within this distance of that face's plane and the boxes of the two meeting, is put onto that plane before the boolean: its corners are moved onto the plane, the corners the second body's other faces share with it moved with them, and those faces built again from their corners (see ). The first body is not moved, and keeps the exactness of the tolerance; the second moves by no more than this distance, and only where it touches the first. Where moving it would leave it open, or leave too little of it to build a body, it is taken as it came. A face lying on such a plane within the tolerance already is not moved: the boolean takes it as lying there.

A face of the second body standing off the first at a slant, nearer than this at one end and further at the other, is not moved, and what lies between the two is cut as it is. A hundredth suits a Tekla model in millimetres: its parts come up to a few thousandths of a millimetre into or off each other.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.SolidBooleanOptions.Fallback
member.summary: Gets the tolerance a boolean whose result is not valid is worked out again within; null keeps the result as it comes.
member.remarks: With a fallback, the result is checked by within : a result that is open, or closed with faces wound the same way along an edge, or one that could not be worked out, is worked out again within the fallback, and that result taken where it is valid. A result closed with two faces lying one on the other the same way round holds the wrong volume: a girder of a Tekla model cut within a hundredth came out of one cut so, 3.4 litres short. Of the 79 864 parts of that model cut one after another within a thousandth, 180 met a cut whose result was not valid or could not be worked out, with a contact of a hundredth 109, and with a fallback of a hundredth as well 19, 136 cuts being taken within it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.SolidClosingOptions
member.summary: How closes an open body: within which tolerance it is judged closed, how far apart the corners across a gap may stand and still be made one, and which holes may be filled.

remarks.para: A body is closed with the least change that does it, and nothing is made up where the change is not certain. Corners standing apart across a gap no wider than are made one, and a corner standing that near an edge of another face left open is put on it: neither moves the surface further than the gap, and no face is folded back onto another. A hole is filled only where it encloses no more than : by one face where it is flat, and by the triangles of least area across it where it is out of flat by no more than , as allows. No hole is filled unless asked: the largest hole is nought by default.

The gap is a question of how the body was made. A boolean cut within a hundredth closes within a hundredth and no closer: read within a thousandth, the default tolerance, it can be open by copies of an edge up to a hundredth apart, which a gap of a hundredth reaches. A face left out is another matter, and no weld closes it: a box 100 by 200 by 300 with its top left out is closed by a face of 20 000 square units, and only where the largest hole is at least that.
The options are immutable, so one instance can be shared between threads and kept as a setting.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.SolidClosingOptions.MaxGap
member.summary: Gets how far apart the corners across a gap may stand and still be made one, and how far a corner may stand off an edge and still be put on it.

remarks.para: The corners of the edges left open are welded within the point tolerance first, then within twice it, four times, and so on while below this, and within this last, the first reach that closes the body taken: a corner moves no further than it has to. The corners of edges the body closes along stay where they are, and two corners of one face are made one only where they are copies of one corner of it, beside each other on its ring across an edge left open, so that a slot cut thinner than this stays a slot. Only where no reach of welds alone closes the body is a corner standing within the reach of an edge left open of another face, between its ends, put on that edge, through the same reaches again: where the crack between them lies in the plane of the corner's face, the corner is moved onto the edge within that plane, and otherwise the edge is bent through the corner where it stands.

A corner is put within the reach of an edge as the edge was, not of the pieces another corner put on it leaves: a crack bowed 0.008 off an edge through five corners closes within a gap of 0.008, and not within one of 0.005. A reach that would leave a ring running out to a corner and straight back, a face lying back to back with another, or a face crossing another, an edge of either reaching through the inside of the other by more than this on both sides where the faces they were built from did not cross, is not taken: a crack 0.004 wide left along a top, a blade 0.002 thick standing in it, is not welded shut through the blade, and is left open, where the blade would pass through the top, the gap not too wide but blocked. What the faces moved sweep of the volume is held to the reach times their area.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.SolidClosingOptions.MaxHoleArea
member.summary: Gets the most a hole may enclose and still be filled; nought fills none, and any.
member.remarks: A flat hole is filled by one face, the loops lying in its plane inside it taken as holes of that face, and its area, holes taken away, is what is held to this: a hole as large as this is filled. The two ends of a hole through the body are held to it each by its cap, or by the walls between them together, and a hole out of flat by the area of the triangles across it. A hole larger is not filled, and the report says . Nor is a hole of any size filled by faces lying back to back with a face of the body, a skin of no thickness, or crossing one, or a face filling a hole before it, an edge of either passing through the inside of the other: a box 30 by 20 by 10 missing its top, a post 4 by 4 standing in it 5 through the plane of the top, is left open, , where a wall of the post passes through the top, and not closed round the post holding 6 208. Caps crossing the body are no way, and the walls between the two ends of a hole through it are taken instead where they cross nothing.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.SolidClosingOptions.MaxOffFlat
member.summary: Gets how far out of flat a hole may stand and still be filled, by the triangles of least area across it; nought fills only the holes flat within the planar tolerance.

remarks.para: How far out of flat a hole stands is how far its corner furthest off the plane through the average of its corners, square to its area, stands off it. A hole further out of flat than this is not filled, and the report says . A hole within it, and further out of flat than the planar tolerance, is filled by triangles on its own corners: of the ways of filling it none of whose triangles lies back to back with a face of the body, the one of least area, and none where its triangles would cross a face of the body, or of a hole filled before it. The ways can close different volumes; which is taken, if any, is 's.

The least area is found in time growing as the cube of the hole's corners, a few hundredths of a second for 256, and a hole out of flat with more is not filled, . Nor is one holding another hole inside it, : triangles on its corners do not go round the hole inside.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.SolidValidation3
member.summary: What found of the faces of a body: whether they bound one, and each thing wrong with them, or worth knowing, and where.

remarks.para: says whether the faces close; this says where they do not, and what else it finds on the way. The edges are matched as it matches them, by overlap along a line within the point tolerance, twin edges by their ends, and within the rounding of the coordinates where the tolerance is below it, so the two agree on whether the body is closed: is its answer, with every stretch it left open in . A speck, a body with no edge longer than the tolerance, is the one exception: no stretch of it is open, and it is closed here and not valid, enclosing nothing, where IsClosed says it does not close. It also reads which way the faces meeting on a stretch run it, which IsClosed does not: a face wound the wrong way round closes the body for it, and is a on each of its edges here.
The faces are read, the openings not: each opening is a body of its own, and is checked by asking it.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoBvh2
member.summary:
A bounding volume hierarchy over the edges of a shape in the plane, the counterpart of in space.
It is built over , so one index serves a straight chain and a curved one alike: an arc is held as an arc and measured as an arc, and nothing is flattened to get it into the tree. Building costs a walk over the edges; after that, asking what is nearest a point, or where a segment crosses, stops looking at whole branches that cannot reach.
It is worth building when the same shape is asked many questions. For a handful of questions the plain methods on the shape are quicker, because they do not build anything.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoBvh3
member.summary:
A bounding volume hierarchy over a triangle mesh: a tree of nested axis-aligned boxes that makes queries against the mesh cost time in the logarithm of its size rather than in its size.
Every operation on a mesh without an index has to look at every triangle, because nothing rules any of them out in advance. A tree of boxes rules them out wholesale: a ray that misses a box misses everything inside it, and a box already farther away than the best answer so far cannot hold anything nearer. One traversal replaces the scan.
Building the tree costs a sort of the triangles, so it pays for itself over repeated queries rather than on the first one. Build it once and keep it for as long as the mesh does not change — which, since every geometry type here is immutable, is for as long as the mesh exists.

member.remarks: Below a handful, walking the triangles directly beats the bookkeeping of another two nodes.

member.remarks:
The index is built over , so it follows the material of every face: a ray fired through the notch of a concave body or through a hole in a plate passes clean through, and the nearest point on the surface is a point that is really on it.
A tree is worth building once and keeping. Nothing about it depends on what is asked of it, so a body that is queried repeatedly — clash detection over a model — should be indexed once rather than through the convenience paths in Collision3 and Distance3, which build a tree per call.

member.summary: Builds one node over a run of triangles and returns its index.
member.remarks: The run is split at the median of the triangle centres along whichever axis those centres are most spread out on. Splitting on the widest spread keeps the two child boxes as separate as the geometry allows, which is what makes a traversal able to discard one of them; splitting at the median keeps the tree balanced, so its depth stays logarithmic even for a mesh that is dense in one place and sparse elsewhere.

member.summary: Finds every point where a ray crosses the mesh, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The results come back in no particular order. A ray passing exactly along an edge shared by two triangles is reported by both of them, so a caller counting crossings should aim the ray away from edges rather than trust the count. Each triangle is crossed by the ray's own crossing of its plane where the triangle holds it, not as reads the ray, as the line without ends along it: a ray starting within the planar tolerance of a triangle's plane and dipping into it, however shallowly, crosses where it reaches the plane, one rising from there touches at its origin, and one level with it to rounding names no place on it. The ray from (5, 5, 0.0004) along (1, 0, -0.01) crosses a mesh whose top lies in z = 0 at (5.04, 5, 0).

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoBvh3.GetIntersections(GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoXLine3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Finds every point where an infinite line crosses the mesh, within a tolerance.
member.remarks: The line runs both ways from its origin, so the answer is the same wherever along it the origin stands, but for a crossing within rounding of the tolerance: it is what the ray gives from before the mesh, and from behind it, together. The results come back in no particular order, and a line through an edge two triangles share is reported by both of them, as a ray's is. Each triangle is crossed as crosses it, so the answer is the plain scan's over every triangle, without looking at the branches whose box, grown by the larger of the point and planar tolerances, the line never enters. The line through (3, 6, 4) along Z crosses a mesh of the box 10 by 10 by 10 from the origin at (3, 6, 0) and (3, 6, 10), the ray from the same point only at the second. Below the rounding of the coordinates, 1E-15 of the largest of the mesh's and of where the line is read from, and only there, a triangle holds a crossing to that rounding, as it holds a ray's (), rather than to the rounding of its own coordinates, and a line whose origin stands further off than the mesh is large is read from a diagonal short of it.

A box is also passed over where the segment stands further than the reach from it across a direction square to an axis and to the segment, and a triangle where it does across the triangle's normal, or across a direction square to the segment or to the normal and to a side: a bar standing up half a thousandth outside a side of that cylinder, through the rim of both caps, lies in the boxes of some 2 500 of the slivers the caps are cut into, and comes within a thousandth of 4 triangles, which are what it is given. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoBvh3.DistanceTo(GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoBvh3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Calculates the shortest distance between this mesh and another, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
Both trees are walked at once. A pair of boxes already farther apart than the closest pair of triangles found so far cannot hold a nearer pair, so the whole cross product beneath them is discarded without being looked at. That is what turns a comparison of every triangle against every other into something usable on a real mesh.
Two meshes that touch or pass through each other are at distance zero. An empty tree is infinitely far from everything, since it has nothing to measure to.

member.returns: false when either mesh is empty, or no pair of triangles comes nearer than the reach.
member.remarks: A reach lets a caller who only cares about what is near stop early: every pair of boxes at least that far apart is passed over from the start, so two meshes farther apart than the reach cost the one test of their outer boxes.

member.param: The segment the answer leaves from.
How short the answer has to be; for any.
member.returns: false when the mesh is empty, or no triangle comes nearer the segment than the reach.
member.remarks: The nearer child is opened first, as for a point, nearer by how far its box is from the box of the segment. A box or a triangle is passed over where it stands no nearer the box of the segment than the nearest found so far, or where the segment itself stands further off, as reads it, than both that and twice the larger of the point and planar tolerances, inside which a crossing may be found and measured as of no length. What is passed over could not have come nearer, so the answer is the one measuring every triangle gives: 50 bars of radius 40 running at a slant 20 to 30 clear of a cylinder of radius 500 and 10 000 sides, in pieces 320 long, measure 13 952 triangles where they measured 169 522.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoBvh3.Walk(GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoBvh3,System.Double,System.Boolean,GeometryHelper.Tolerance,GeometryHelper.Geometry.GeoLine3@)
member.summary: Walks both trees at once, the nearest pair of boxes first, and measures the pairs of triangles under every pair of boxes that could still hold a nearer pair than the best found so far.
member.param: The other tree; neither may be empty.
The bound to start from: box pairs at least this far apart are never opened.
Whether to measure each pair of triangles by its shortest segment, keeping the best in , rather than by distance alone.
The segment of the nearest pair found, when segments were asked for.
member.returns: The distance of the nearest pair found, or when none came nearer.
member.remarks: Of the two pairs of boxes a split gives, the nearer one is opened first. The first pairs of triangles measured are then among the nearest there are, the bound drops to near the answer at once, and every pair of boxes farther apart than it is passed over whole — where walking the children in a fixed order would measure whatever lay first and prune by a bound far from the answer. Under the leaves the box of each triangle is tested before the triangle is measured, since a leaf holds several.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoPreparedSolid3
member.summary: A body made ready to be asked many questions: its openings cut in once, its surface meshed and indexed once, its box kept.

remarks.para: Every question a answers takes its openings into account, and the questions that need the material cut it each time they are asked — a distance cuts every opening, since the nearest material can sit on the rim of one the probe never comes near. A body is a value and keeps no cache of its own, so a plate asked about a hundred bolts is cut a hundred times. Preparing it pays for that once, together with the mesh and the index a large body is searched through.
The answers are the body's own: whatever the prepared body says, the body says too, only slower. It is a snapshot — immutable, safe to share between threads, and holding the body it was made from.

A body far out, as says, is prepared again in its frame the first time it is asked where a point, a ray or a line stands against it, its openings cut, its surface meshed and indexed there, and asked there from then on, the probe moved in and what has a place moved back out. , , and what it weighs another body by stay where the body stands. Where it stood, of 2 080 rays half a hundredth in and out from an L 100 by 80 by 50 with a pocket and a hole, prepared a hundred million out at a hundredth, 48 were given other crossings than at the origin, and of 2 016 a thousand million out, 52; 1 and none are, a ray along the world's Y axis.

member.summary: Locates a point: inside the material, on where it ends, or outside it, within a tolerance.
member.remarks:
A ray is cast through the index and its crossings counted, as Containment3 counts them face by face. A crossing landing near the rim of its triangle may be a seam of the mesh — an edge or a corner the index names once per triangle — or the face beyond an edge the ray leaves past at a shallow angle, and the ray is cast again in another direction; should every direction land so, the body's own test decides.
However small the tolerance, a triangle holds a crossing to the rounding of the body's coordinates, 1E-15 of the largest, on its plane and past its rim, and the rim is read as wide as twice that at least. At a tolerance of nought the prepared cylinder 40 across and 50 tall, its axis leaning in space, reads every one of 1 000 points inside it as inside and one 1.6 outside its side as outside, where the rounding refused the crossing of nearly every face and it read 111 of those points inside and the one outside inside.

member.remarks: A crossing landing on a seam of the mesh arrives once per triangle and is reported once, as the body reports it. member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoPreparedSolid3.IsPartedFrom(GeometryHelper.Spatial.GeoPreparedSolid3,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Checks whether a face of either body parts the two where their boxes overlap: the part of this one there wholly behind the face's plane and the part of the other wholly in front of it, or the other way round, so that they can touch across the plane but share no volume.

remarks.para: What two bodies share lies where their boxes overlap, so boxes meeting only in a face, an edge or a corner settle it at once — every contact square to the axes does — and otherwise only the part of each body inside that overlap need be parted. That part lies within the hull of its own corners, and so does everything on one side of a plane that all those corners are on, so the corners settle it. They are the corners of each face clipped to the box — its own corners inside the box, where its edges leave the box and where the box's edges pass through it — and the corners of the box inside the body. A beam bearing on a column's web between the flanges is parted this way though the flanges reach past the web's plane, since they lie outside the box the two share; so is a beam on a flange, a plate on a cap, two blocks side by side. A bolt in a hole it fills is not, and a pair nothing parts is left for the boolean to decide.

The corners are allowed a thousandth of the point tolerance past the plane, which is rounding and no more: two bodies it lets through overlap by less than that, far below anything the boolean would cut as a region, so where this says the bodies share no volume the boolean finds none.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Takeoff.VolumeTakeoff
member.summary: Takes off the volumes of the parts of a model, each bit of material counted once: by the part ranked first among those holding it.

remarks.para: The parts are ranked by their , the highest first, of two the same by their , the largest first and any id before none, and then by their order in the list. A part keeps all it shares with the parts ranked after it, and loses to them nothing. Where a slab 200 thick sits on a beam 300 wide that runs into a column 400 by 400, and the column is ranked first, the beam second and the slab third, the block the three share, 300 by 400 by 200, is the column's: the slab loses it to the column, and to the beam only what the beam shares with it beyond the column. Taken off by each part it meets, the slab would lose those 24 000 000 twice. So the net volumes add up to the volume of all the parts together, and two exact copies count once: the later comes out nought.

The bodies given are never cut; only what they share is. First every pair whose boxes overlap by more than the point tolerance has its common part worked out, by
of the part ranked later with the part ranked first, which is put onto it as the contact says. Then each part's pieces, in the order of the parts that keep them, have the pieces before them taken out, by , so that each is what that part keeps and no part before it kept already. Both steps run in parallel, and the volumes come out the same, bit for bit, on one thread or on every processor.

A common part the booleans cannot make, one that is not valid, holds more than the smaller of the two, or cannot be worked out at all, is worked out by slicing instead: the part is cut by parallel planes, and the area of what it shares with the keeper and with no keeper ranked before is added up the height, exactly over flat faces and with no tolerance. So is a piece the cut of the pieces before it cannot finish, or that has a keeper before it whose overlap was sliced. A curved wall of 354 faces and a curved girder of 322 of a Tekla model, met within a thousandth with a contact of a hundredth, share a common part of 4 256 faces that is not valid; slicing gives them 2 226 236 967 in 0.04 seconds, where Tekla's own boolean gives 2 226 236 773 cutting the wall and 2 226 236 807 cutting the girder. A pair as near-coincident as these two, with at least a hundred pairs of faces less than a millimetre apart and less than a tenth of a degree off parallel, though neither flush nor parallel, is sliced without the booleans being tried: on these two they run a minute or two before failing, and the take-off of the two takes 0.1 seconds without them. A deduction worked out by slicing is exact, and carries no issue. Only a pair that cannot be sliced either is not taken off: a section of a body crossed an odd number of times, as where a corner sits more than about 1E-9 off its neighbour's edge, a T-junction, even in a body accepts. Its result says so in , and the net volume is then no less than it should be. No failure of the geometry escapes: each comes back as an issue and is logged.

A common part thinner on average than half the point tolerance, its volume no more than the point tolerance times half its area, is taken as touching, and nothing is taken off for it: a beam standing on a slab, flush with it or a hair into it, loses nothing. A volume worked out by slicing has no body to measure, and is judged by the least area a body of its volume can have, a ball's; slicing snaps nothing, so a sheet a hair thick that the contact would have put away is taken off as the faces give it.

The tolerance the booleans work within is the one the options carry. A scope opened with around the call is opened on every worker as well, so that it reaches the few steps underneath that read the global tolerance whichever thread runs them.

member.summary: Takes off the volumes of the parts.
member.param: The parts. A null entry is passed over: its result has no item, every volume nought and one issue, "no item". The same body may be given in two items, and the later loses all of it to the earlier.
How each overlap is worked out, and how many threads to use.
member.returns: The take-off of each part, in the order the parts were given.
member.exception: or is null.

remarks.para: A column 400 by 400 and 3 200 high, ranked first, a beam 300 wide, 600 deep and 6 000 long running through it, second, and a slab 6 000 by 6 000 by 200 on both, third, with the tops of the three flush: the column keeps its 512 000 000; the beam, 1 080 000 000 gross, loses 72 000 000 to the column and keeps 1 008 000 000; the slab, 7 200 000 000 gross, loses 32 000 000 to the column and 336 000 000 to the beam and keeps 6 832 000 000. The three add up to 8 352 000 000, the volume of the three together.

A common part is checked by and by its volume, which can be no more than the smaller part's, within the point tolerance times the area of the two. A valid body can still have lost part of what the two share, since nothing bounds a common part from below; a take-off that matters is worth checking against the parts' net bodies cut by .

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Takeoff.VolumeTakeoff.WorkOut(GeometryHelper.Takeoff.VolumeTakeoff.Pair,GeometryHelper.SolidBooleanOptions)
member.summary: Works out what a pair shares: as a body where the common part is valid and holds no more than the smaller can, otherwise by slicing, which the second phase does. A pair near-coincident, its faces standing beside each other, goes to slicing without the intersection being tried.
member.remarks: Nothing more is tried after the intersection. A girder of 322 faces and a wall of 354 of a Tekla model, met within a thousandth with a contact of a hundredth, shared a body of 4 256 faces that was not valid, in 114 seconds; a cut of the one by the other then took 2 215 seconds and left 80 805 faces, not valid either, where slicing takes under a second. The two are near-coincident, so the intersection is not tried at all.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Takeoff.VolumeTakeoff.NearCoincident(GeometryHelper.Takeoff.VolumeTakeoff.Part,GeometryHelper.Takeoff.VolumeTakeoff.Part,GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Whether a pair is near-coincident: at least pairs of a face of the loser and a face of the keeper beside each other. Two faces are beside each other when their planes are within of parallel, either way round, but further from it than the vector tolerance, so that faces flush or parallel are left to the booleans, which make them well; when every corner of the keeper's face is within of the loser's face's plane, and further from it than the point tolerance; and when their boxes come within of each other.
member.remarks: Only faces whose boxes come within of the other part's box are compared, and only their planes, corners and boxes are read: on the 51 209 pairs of a model of 30 921 parts it took a tenth of a second in all, on 24 processors. The faces of the openings are not read.

member.remarks: An overlap to slice has no body, so the keeper itself stands for it in the later pieces' cuts: within the loser, a piece less the keeper is the piece less what the two share.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Tolerance
member.summary:
Tolerance used for geometric comparisons.
Every comparison in this library that can be affected by floating point error takes a tolerance, and every such method has an overload without one that reads . Neither library compares coordinates with ==.
is one setting shared by both libraries. Changing it for a drawing in the plane changes it for a model in space as well.
Make one with a constructor, or take or . new Tolerance() is not the default tolerance: like default(Tolerance) it runs no constructor and has every threshold at 0, under which only an exact match is equal and a face out of flat by rounding alone is refused.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.DefaultEqualPoint
member.summary: Default tolerance when comparing points: a thousandth of a millimetre in a model in millimetres.
member.remarks: Fine enough that two parts a hundredth apart are apart and a thin overlap holds what it holds: the common parts of 218 pairs of slabs from a Tekla model came out within 450 cubic millimetres of the exact volume at the median, and within 1 084 when the default was a hundredth. Not finer: the faces of a Tekla model stand off flat and off one another by up to a few ten-thousandths of a millimetre, and below a thousandth they are cut as the slivers they then are, many times slower and more often left open.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.DefaultEqualVector
member.summary: Default tolerance when comparing vectors: a hundred-thousandth.
member.remarks: Two directions this far apart turn the far side of a face a hundred millimetres across by the point threshold. The vector threshold is also the length below which a vector has no direction and the area below which a loop is no polygon, so it is set well below the point threshold: at a thousandth, a triangle 0.005 by 0.08 of a millimetre that Tekla Structures gives at the end of each of 1 791 girders of one model was refused for its area of 0.0002, and every one of the girders came out open.

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.DefaultEqualAngleRad
member.summary: Default tolerance when comparing angles for parallelism / perpendicularity, in radians (1 degree in radians).

member.name: F:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.DefaultEqualPlanar
member.summary: Default distance threshold for deciding whether a set of points lies on a common plane: a thousandth of a millimetre in a model in millimetres, the same as .
member.remarks: As wide as the point threshold, a point that counts as one with another counts as on every plane that other is on, and the booleans cut and glue within the planar threshold they are given rather than a narrower one. A modeller's own cuts leave faces further out of flat: a concrete beam Tekla Structures cut a notch into came with the top face beside the notch 0.04 mm out. Such a face is no polygon at this threshold, but the Tekla and IFC conversions keep it as triangles on its own corners (), so the body stays closed and nothing is taken as flat that is not.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.Default
member.summary: Gets the default tolerance: , , and together.
member.remarks: starts as this tolerance, and this stays the defaults whatever is set to or a scope opened with makes it. new Tolerance() is not it: that has every threshold at 0.

member.name: T:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.Held
member.summary: The process-wide setting, held whole so that it is swapped in one step: a tolerance is several numbers, and a struct written while another thread reads it can be read half old and half new.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.Global
member.summary: Tolerance applied for overloads without explicit tolerance. It starts as .

remarks.para: This is one setting for the process, read by the plane and by space alike. Setting it replaces it whole, so a thread reading it while another sets it sees the old tolerance or the new one, never a mix; but an operation already under way may read it more than once, so set it while starting up, before geometry is built.

Where a tolerance has to vary for a while on one thread — one drawing, one model — open a scope with : this property returns the scope's tolerance on that thread until the scope is disposed, and every other thread keeps the process-wide one. Where it has to vary per call, pass it: every affected method takes one, and that overload touches nothing shared.

member.name: M:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.Use(GeometryHelper.Tolerance)
member.summary: Makes a tolerance the one every overload without a tolerance uses on this thread, until the returned scope is disposed.
member.returns: The scope; disposing it puts back whatever this thread used before.

member.summary:
Distance threshold to consider a point as lying on a plane, in drawing units.
This is separate from because coplanarity is checked far from the reference point: a polygon several metres across turns a hundredth of a degree of tilt into a deviation of nearly a millimetre, so the threshold that decides whether two points coincide is the wrong one to decide whether a face is flat.

member.name: P:GeometryHelper.Tolerance.EqualAngleSin
member.summary:
Sine of , computed once here because the angular comparisons in Intersection and Parallel sit inside nested edge loops, where a transcendental call per comparison is a measurable share of the total cost.
The default struct value leaves this at 0, which is exactly Sin(0) for the matching EqualAngleRad of 0, so an uninitialized Tolerance stays self-consistent.
